With about $20,000 of student debt and growing, "out of urgency and out of honestly just being scared that I wasn't going to be able to survive," he applied for jobs and was hired at a web design agency thanks to a skill he had already acquired. **Source:** How To Grow An Audience If You Have 0 Followers (It's Only 2 Habits).md. The fuller version of the story: since he could remember he wanted to do what he loves for a living, but everyone "screams" the opposite — go to school, do what you are told, follow the **preset future** your parents thought possible and you thought possible as a child. He started down that path, went to college and "partied the entire time," while learning creative skills on the side, studying his interests (he went deep into fitness and nutrition, going to the gym with friends since high school) and starting online businesses "as much as I possibly could." In college he learned to code because he heard it was lucrative, got "sucked down that entire rabbit hole" of coding podcasts and community, loved it and built coding projects. As his online businesses kept failing, he decided to "call it quits": he had been in college too long, dropped out despite having been a straight-A student, and took a job as a front-end web developer at a web design agency paying $50–55k a year. **Source:** Learn This Skill If You Want To Thrive In The Next 10 Years.md; The One-Person Business Model (How To Productize Yourself Full Guide).md.

The constant through all of this is what the author calls a **meaningful side project**: "I always had a meaningful side project that I wanted to work on from the ages of like 16 to 25" — coding, a business, learning a skill, digital art "for a long time." It was something to apply his learning to, and it made him happy. **Source:** The One-Person Business Model (How To Productize Yourself Full Guide).md. In a 2023 telling he lists the sequence: "ever since I can remember I've had a project that I was building." First Photoshop art on Instagram, because he saw potential and wanted a large following; then web design and SEO, freelancing in many forms; then the agency job, while still building his own web design business first thing in the morning until freelancing worked; then Twitter, then Instagram, then "I need to actually create a product," and he kept creating: "I had like 10 different lead magnets." **Source:** Solve Your Own Problems And Sell The Solution (Your Niche Is You).md. A 2024 retelling summarizes it: family, teachers and even people he followed online "screamed at me to go down other paths"; he did not finish college after five years, started "every online business imaginable," dropped out because college was wasting his time, and took a $55,000 job as an entry-level web designer — but "the goal of doing what I love for a living stuck in the back of my head," and there was rarely a moment he was not working on a personal project, a habit he still keeps. **Source:** This High-Income Skill Will Make You Irreplaceable (Full Guide).md.

The details of these retellings vary — "front-end web developer, $50–55k" versus "entry-level web designer, $55,000"; "partied the entire time" versus "didn't finish after five years"; $20,000 of student loans in some versions, $2,000 or $8,000 of debt in others (the $2,000 may be a transcription error; this cannot be confirmed). The core is stable: a preset future, a college stint used to delay and experiment, a job taken under financial pressure, and an unbroken habit of building something of his own. That habit is the seed of the **project** as the practical vehicle of change, developed in Chapter 9, and of the "one hour a day" approach to building alongside a job in Chapter 12.

### 2.2 School: The Education of Slaves and True Education

School is the first institution of the default path, the one where the hierarchy of assigned goals is installed. The author's critique of it is among the most developed in the corpus, and it is also the one where his rhetoric is harshest. It helps to know in advance how the critique evolved. In 2022 he called school "a blessing and a curse," necessary for society to function; in 2023 formal education "has its place," but schools "can't and won't" teach you to build your dreams; from 2024 the critique gains causal precision (who pays, whose pace sets the curriculum, what the institution protects) and rhetorical severity — "the education of slaves," the "bottom quintile," the "government-trained expert." Throughout, one concession remains: school gives socialization, literacy and "a base operating system to become a civilized human." The fairest reading, which the author's own concessions support, is that he accepts basic general education and criticizes specialized and professional education presented as the only route to a good life.

#### "If you don't create a purpose, you will be assigned one"

The central thesis comes from the author's book *The Art of Focus*: "if you don't create a purpose you will be assigned one because only slaves were taught to perform one task for the entirety of their life." Slaves were taught career-specific skills — "growing wheat, herding sheep or just riding a horse." "Our current education system reflects the education of slaves. Today we are taught to be useful workers, we are taught to obey the authority, we are conditioned to get good grades out of fear of punishment." By contrast, "a free man on the other hand is expected to have a purpose and do whatever it takes to achieve it." **Source:** The Future Of Work (Avoid Learning These Skills).md. The author's term for this is the **education of slaves**: education for a single task, for obedience, and for grades obtained out of fear.

The idea has a parallel source in Devon Eriksen, a novelist the author interviewed and whose name appears in transcriptions as "Ericson" or "Erickson." The author presents Eriksen's first point — "Only slaves are expected to perform one task for their entire life" — and expands it into a description of the whole trajectory since birth. We are taught to be useful workers; that is what school is designed for. We obey at school and do assignments we do not care about so that we can keep doing things we do not care about, "so that you never actually get around to the things that you do care about." Growing up, "you need to speak this certain way or else you're going to be punished"; you learn specific skills for specific tasks so that you are not punished with a bad life of little money; you learn to get paid for a specific skill by a specific person "so that they can become your master and you become a wage slave." **Source:** The Future-Proof Skill Stack (How Average People Become Millionaires).md. Here "wage slave" is a popular phrase the author redefines: someone who learned a narrow skill so that an employer could become their master. Section 2.3 develops it.

It is important to read "slave" as the author asks it to be read. He insists it is a mental metaphor, not a comparison with physical slavery, and his use of the word shifts over time from almost neutral to normative (see 2.3). In the school context, the contrast is between two kinds of preparation for life: preparation for a single assigned function, and preparation for self-direction.

#### Why school serves someone else

Why would a school system produce useful workers rather than free individuals? The author assembles several explanations, some his own and some from guests, that converge on one idea: a system serves whoever controls it, and the student does not control it.

The cleanest version is Devon Eriksen's, which the author adopts. Eriksen calls it the disease, as opposed to the symptoms "we could go on all day nitpicking." The chain runs: whoever pays for something is the customer; "it is the customer who gets served"; when the government pays for your education — with money taken from other people, through education grants or programs like the Stafford Loan — the government decides, at some level, what you learn. You do not even have veto power, because if you pack your bags and go to another college you get the same thing; the government is paying there too. "You're not writing the checks so you don't decide the curriculum." And whoever decides the curriculum gives you the education that makes you useful to them, not the education that makes you useful to you. **Source:** The Most Important Skill To Learn In The Next 10 Years With Devon Eriksen.md. The principle has a name, **third party is paying**, and it is Eriksen's term rather than the author's.

The author repeats the point in his own words and adds a second layer of pressure: "Since you do not fund this school system you do not control what is taught. You're told to read this and memorize that, and if you don't then your **Industrial Age parents** will scold you and threaten to ground you, and then you can't pursue your own interest or go hang out with your friends or explore." The child receives "double the pain": from the institution and from parents who themselves were shaped by it and punish deviation from the curriculum. **Source:** How To Thrive With Multiple Interests.md.

A third structural constraint is pace. "This education system has to bias the bottom quintile. In other words you are forced to learn at the same pace as the dumbest 20% of the people in the public school system, and this is extremely destructive." **Source:** How To Thrive With Multiple Interests.md. **Bottom quintile** is the author's label for this levelling effect.

A fourth explanation applies a principle the author uses for every institution: systems behave like organisms. "Education is the first step in value creation" — without education or skills you have nothing worth packaging and distributing — but conventional education "won't cut it." The school system "is a system," with an end goal (go to school, get a job), variables, a path and a starting point. It is "intimately tied with government, politics and the economy, the old economy," so you will not find in it an education that threatens it, "because systems survive just like humans do," in the same way that we survive the concept of ourselves; if it starts to break down, its members fight to keep it together. **Source:** The Value Creator (A New Internet Career Path For Intelligent People).md. The parallel with "the concept of ourselves" is a preview of the **law of conceptual survival**, the author's coined principle that ideas and identities defend themselves like bodies (Chapter 3). His practical inference: to make it in the new economy, learn from the people who created it — courses, coaching, content from the brands and creators who invented the new jobs. The school system "aren't creators... they don't have the right to teach you that," whatever their curriculum, because they have not done it. The author's term pair **old economy / new economy** marks this distinction.

The same reasoning yields his bluntest formulation: "Schools can't and won't teach you how to build your dreams." Schools are bound up with government, politics and the economy, and their "conditioning process or education" is set up to keep those running; "anything that gives the individual power is a threat." Self-education therefore becomes a requirement, not an option. And it cannot be skipped, because "you can't reach your goals at your current level of development, or else you'd already achieve them": you need to develop skills, build things, fail and gain experience. **Source:** A Full Guide To Reinvent Your Life (In 6-12 Months).md.

#### The Prussian model and the question of intent

The author grounds the critique historically in the story of Horace Mann. In the early-to-mid 1800s, as America industrialized and needed to educate large numbers of immigrant children, educators such as Mann travelled to Prussia to study its school system. That system "was designed to create obedient soldiers, compliant citizens, civil servants and well-behaved workers," through mandatory attendance, teacher training, a national curriculum and testing, division of students by age, and grade levels. "Students were taught how to work, not how to think." Impressed by its efficiency and standardization, Mann and others brought many of these methods into American schools, especially in Massachusetts, which became a model for other states. **Source:** How To Thrive With Multiple Interests.md; How To Read Books Fast With AI (And Remember What You Read).md. In a 2025 version he calls the Prussian model "not education at all, but a weapon of mass conformity," and concludes that "society wants you simple, predictable, and easy to categorize," because that best serves its interests and the profits of its organizations. **Source:** The Most Important Skill To Learn Right Now.md. One downstream effect he names is that "reading to most people is a performative act" — something done for others rather than for understanding — a theme he develops when he discusses reading (Chapter 16).

**Complementary context:** Horace Mann (1796–1859) was secretary of the Massachusetts Board of Education and a leading advocate of the "common school" movement; his 1843 report praised aspects of Prussian schooling. Historians debate how far the Prussian model was meant to produce obedience versus broad literacy; the author presents his version as his reading of this history, not as a historiographical claim.

This history raises a question the author handles with deliberate care: was this done on purpose? He gives two kinds of answer, and the tension between them is never fully resolved. The strong, rhetorical version appears in some places — schools "were created to keep you narrow-minded and dumb," or, quoting his own book *Purpose and Profit*, "Schools were created to enslave the brightest minds," which he says was "taken quite a bit out of context" but is "largely true." The systemic version appears more often and is the one he explicitly favours when he stops to qualify. From his research, Mann did not want "the whole slave mentality" brought over, "but that's kind of a byproduct of the system itself... a **property of the system**" — the author's term for an unintended effect that emerges from a system's structure. He insists that he does not mean it "as a conspiracy theory." **Source:** How To Thrive With Multiple Interests.md; How To Read Books Fast With AI (And Remember What You Read).md.

The 2025 formulation turns this into a general principle: "If you understand systems, you understand that the system takes the shape of that which most benefits the end goal, which in society's case is keeping you sick and dumb, whether it's intentional or not. It doesn't have to be a conspiracy theory for the system to naturally take shape of the subconscious desires of the humans at the top of the pyramid." **Source:** The Most Important Skill To Learn Right Now.md. The author's name for the principle is **systems take the shape of the end goal**. The principle is important beyond school: it is the same reasoning by which a person's goal shapes their perception (2.1) and by which, in Chapter 6, a goal determines the system that pursues it. The reader should notice, however, that the claim that society's end goal is "keeping you sick and dumb" is an interpretation the author states, not something he demonstrates.

#### What school does to learning and thinking

Beyond who controls it, the author criticizes what school does to the student's relationship with learning. The earliest version (2022) is simple: people are forced to learn things they are not interested in, and as a result they "never go on to learn or pursue their curiosity again." He links this to the brain's reward mechanism, which exists to separate signal from noise; forcing learning against interest works against the very mechanism that makes learning possible. **Source:** Stop Trying To Be Unique... Do This Instead.md. The role of curiosity as a guide is developed in Chapter 14, and the reward system in Chapter 11.

A personal version uses reading. Before his arrest (the episode in 2.7), the last books he chose to read were the *Magic Tree House* and *Alex Rider* series, because they genuinely interested him. In high school you are forced to read books you did not choose; those who liked them probably already had the reading habit, and those who did not "probably just grew to hate reading." "School probably made you hate reading and thus they made you hate learning." The cost is large because "learning is a fundamental human drive": without it activities are less enjoyable, conversations less meaningful, days feel repetitive and lifeless, and you do not see your future changing much. Most people are still "**clones of the school system**... on a life trajectory that they didn't set." **Source:** This Simple Reading Habit Will Change Your Life (I Promise).md. In another formulation: humanity needs education, but not an idealized, regimented form "that antagonizes the wiring of our psyche and makes us hate learning" — and "learning is the one thing that fuels all areas of your life," from the corporation to the individual ("yes, public schools are corporations"). He adds that "reality is decentralizing," and that individuals who realize this can ride one of the most profitable shifts in history. **Source:** Zero To $1 Million As A One-Person Business (Working 2-4 Hours A Day).md.

The critique also concerns thinking. "In schools they don't teach you how to think; you learn how to memorize, you learn how to rewrite things in your own words, and as kids we kind of know deep down that this is silly... so we put in the minimum effort it takes to get good grades." He was an A+ student in high school, but "in college I was not; I failed and dropped out." "That's not how the real world works. You aren't rewarded for thinking someone else's thoughts." He offers his own credentials ironically — a writer "for almost 5 years, not an academic writer, no English degree, just a guy that decided to put his thoughts out on the internet." **Source:** You're Not Boring How To Become An Original Thinker (Fast).md. Original thinking is the subject of Chapters 17 and 18.

And it concerns speed. Most people are wired to believe that success comes from "sticking your nose in textbooks for 12 plus hours at a time to study for an exam where 95% of the knowledge you learn goes out the window." When it comes to getting a job or results in the real world, "I would argue that less than 1% of it applies." The common stories confirm it: a degree followed by a job in an unrelated field, or a job in the field where none of the degree applied because everything had to be learned on the job. "You actually have to learn how to do things by doing them. Shocker." Meanwhile you put off your life and progress for four to eight years, delaying development until you reach the status point that lets you get the job you will then be stuck in. His conclusion is deliberately unhedged: "You're probably completely wasting every second you spend learning... that is not an exaggeration. Schools train you to learn extremely slow." The emphasis matters for reading the claim: the charge is not that schooling teaches the wrong content but that it installs a slow way of learning, one that separates study from use, and that this habit is carried into adult life long after the content is forgotten. **Source:** How To Master Any Skill Fast (Give Yourself 2 Weeks).md. The percentages are the author's argued estimates ("I would argue"), not measurements. The constructive alternative — learning by building — is Chapter 14.

The author once condensed his complaints into a list of the traditional school system's problems. It is worth seeing whole, because each item becomes the negative image of a later principle in the book.

| Problem the author names | What the book later proposes instead |
|---|---|
| Convergent thinking | Original and divergent thinking (Ch. 17–18) |
| Compartmentalized learning | The generalist who learns across fields (Ch. 20) |
| Conformity over authenticity | You are the niche; authenticity as differentiator (Ch. 19, 27) |
| Memorization over process | Build to learn; skill as process (Ch. 14–15) |
| Failure as something to avoid | Errors as feedback and compass (Ch. 15) |
| Authorities as unquestionable | Questioning; creating your own philosophy (Ch. 17) |
| Long work over efficiency and true value | The 4-Hour Workday and leverage (Ch. 12, 34) |
| Intelligence defined as book smarts | Intelligence as steering toward goals (Ch. 6) |
| Decade-old curriculums training you for a replaceable job | Self-education toward self-generated goals (this section) |

He adds that school has benefits, but the deficits outweigh them, and that "a new school system is emerging because it's demanded for us to move forward." **Source:** The One Person Business Model 2.0 (Turn Yourself Into A Business).md. The right-hand column is this book's mapping, not the author's; the left-hand column is his list.

The deepest version of the critique explains how children lose what the author calls their generalist ability. As children we love to adventure, discover, figure things out, make mistakes and learn — touching fire, taking risks. "But then our learning stops being about real mistakes. It starts being about the traits our parents and teachers dislike in us" — traits they find annoying or uncivilized, or that will not lead to the version of success they were conditioned to see as "the only **one true path**." The default path is why so many people feel lost, confused, anxious and overwhelmed: "it was the path that was supposed to be safe and secure, but was the least safe and secure." You were placed in front of "a government-trained expert, trained by government-trained experts who are clearly not doing what you want to do in life," six hours a day, told what to learn and how to act, and prodded toward "the status symbol of a job and degree." The goals that compose your worldview — fancy degrees, high-paying jobs — then determine your mind's potential development and freedom: "Your aim determines what you see." His prescription: "give yourself permission to study and pursue multiple interests. You have the internet. You have AI." **Source:** 12 Rules To Change Your Life In 12 Months.md. The phrase "your aim determines what you see" echoes Jordan Peterson's "what you aim at determines what you see," which the author cites elsewhere; it is the principle of the goal as a lens developed in Chapter 6, here applied to childhood.

Devon Eriksen adds a psychological mechanism that the author adopts. In a government school, success means getting an A on the test: answering every question, at a difficulty "determined by the lowest common denominator," without making mistakes. A child in American public school spends "almost as much waking hours there as with your parents," so this shapes personality. The learned definition of success becomes "avoiding failure" — "except in the real world the real definition of success lies on the other side of a whole lot of failure." An environment that makes children risk-averse, especially high-IQ children, is "psychologically crippling what could be the next generation of hyperproductive people." The author's summary: "the greatest mistake is no mistake at all." **Source:** The Most Important Skill To Learn In The Next 10 Years With Devon Eriksen.md.

Eriksen also supplies the most important qualification in this part of the corpus. "Don't get me wrong, somebody has to do a lot of these tasks that anybody can do... we need certain things done that maintain civilization." The problem is not that such work exists. It is that some people "have the potential to produce amazing things and they've been **raised to be afraid**." Imagine Elon Musk raised timid and nervous — "it's very possible to do that to a child if you're not paying attention or if that makes you feel good or if you are a fearful person yourself." The loss to civilization would be real, and invisible: "we would never have understood what we lost, we would never have seen it." Many people with "wonderful things in them" are selling their time "for minimum wage making sandwiches." **Source:** The Most Important Skill To Learn In The Next 10 Years With Devon Eriksen.md. The qualification matters because it shows that the critique is not a condemnation of ordinary work but of a system that wastes potential by training fear.

#### The lies of career choice and the value of a degree

The school critique culminates in the choice of a degree, the moment when the assigned hierarchy of goals turns into debt. The author argues that "you're set up to fail from the start where you have to be motivated by money." Because the degree comes with student loans that only a lucrative career can repay, the choice is made under financial pressure, not from knowledge of what you want — unless scholarships pay for it, and even then, as in his case, living expenses create debt. **Source:** How Smart Creatives Work Less & Earn More LEVERAGE.md.

He then names three lies of career choice. "For most people they choose the career that will make them the most money, but that's a lie. For others they choose the career that people will respect them for, but that's a lie. For the rest they choose the career that they think they will enjoy the most, but again that's a lie." The degree delivers none of these. "You were sold an illusion by parents and teachers who were sold an illusion": "their degrees or lack thereof had little to no impact on their income, status or enjoyment." A degree "may have opened opportunities," but "ultimately it was their personal choices that led to a higher income, status or level of enjoyment." **Source:** How Smart Creatives Work Less & Earn More LEVERAGE.md.

The consequence he draws is categorical in tone: "There are plenty of rich dropouts and broke graduates." "A degree means absolutely nothing if you have the personal responsibility, work ethic and thirst for personal development and skill acquisition." The people most tempted by college are "the naive 18-year-olds who haven't even had a chance to do those things or prove anything to themselves," and "people are starting to wake up to the fact that the conventional path is not the smartest move for sensible people." **Source:** How Smart Creatives Work Less & Earn More LEVERAGE.md. In another place he states, explicitly as opinion, that "to think that a college degree can teach you something other than getting a job or working for the school is a bit silly in my opinion. If a business professor had a business then why does he have a job?" He qualifies it — some professors are very passionate — and gives Jordan Peterson as an example of a professor who spread his ideas beyond the lecture hall because he had a "business mindset": his lectures went online and he built a personal brand, whereas otherwise "the only other thing he could do is be a professor," and the author is sure Peterson had bigger dreams. He also admits that his own unfinished degree, which he "used and leveraged," got him a $60,000-a-year job. **Source:** Solve Your Own Problems And Sell The Solution (Your Niche Is You).md.

The most balanced version describes a pattern rather than a rule. People spend four to twelve years and tens of thousands of dollars to land a low-level entry job paying barely enough for a decent apartment, then spend another five to ten years self-educating in line with that job to climb the ladder, "while barely using anything in the degree." He calls this an over-exaggerated case, says not every degree fits it, that "everything is context and situation dependent," and that he is not absolutely opposed to college. But for those who want fulfilling work and an open schedule, "a glorified piece of paper called a degree" will not do it: "it will be a stepping stone at best and a financial chain at worst." Later in the same video he offers the contrast: if you stick with forging your own path for two to four years you will be far ahead, and you will be monetizing along the way instead of paying for four to twelve years. **Source:** Become A Digital Renaissance Man (And Join The New Rich).md. The phrase "stepping stone" is important: it is the same term the author will use, with the same ambivalence, for employment.

#### Education is not training

The positive side of the critique begins with a distinction the author takes from Devon Eriksen, who takes it from Cicero. The frame is set by the first post of Eriksen's that the author came across, after Naval Ravikant reposted one of his tweets. Eriksen was responding to a clip of Yuval Noah Harari saying that nobody knows what to teach because nobody knows what will be relevant in twenty years. Eriksen's reply opened with: "that's because this dude doesn't know what education is." The implied argument: the problem of not knowing what will be relevant exists only if education means learning specific content; if education means learning how to learn, uncertainty about the future is not a problem. The author says Eriksen "was saying the things that I knew deep down but did not know how to articulate." **Source:** The Most Important Skill To Learn In The Next 10 Years With Devon Eriksen.md. Note that Harari's position is presented through Eriksen's rebuttal, as a counterexample; the author does not discuss Harari's own argument.

The distinction itself: in Rome, job training was given to slaves. A slave was "essentially a human machine," property who would spend his whole life doing one task, so he was given job training. "Job training is not education, it is preparation to do a specific task." A free man — a Roman citizen with full rights — was expected to do many different things in life, because he acted in his own interest; he existed to benefit his society but also to serve himself, "and hopefully the two would align." Since neither teacher nor student could know what he would need to know, "you taught him how to train himself, you taught him how to learn." Eriksen's application to the present: "what we call education today is mostly actually training, and that is the kind of education that in Rome would have been given to slaves," because those who design it ask "what's going to make this person a useful worker for the moneyed interests that I actually serve." Eriksen notes that "we don't really have an organized version of what Cicero would have considered education" and recommends reading the relevant parts of Cicero's writings. **Source:** The Most Important Skill To Learn In The Next 10 Years With Devon Eriksen.md.

**Complementary context:** The Roman distinction between the *artes liberales*, the "arts worthy of a free person," and servile or mechanical skills is the origin of the later "seven liberal arts" (grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy). The author returns to the liberating arts in Chapter 14.

The author condenses the distinction into his own formula: "**education is not programming**. Slaves were expected to perform one task for the entirety of their lives; free men were expected to do many things throughout their lives because that brings power, flexibility, principles-based decision-making and the ability to change direction with a well-rounded skill set to nearly guarantee success." **Source:** Learn This Skill If You Want To Be Relevant In 10 Years.md. The formula connects directly with Chapter 1: "programming" is the author's word for conditioning, so education in the true sense is the opposite of the process that installs the default path. It also anticipates his defence of the generalist (Chapter 20).

#### True education and self-education

What, then, is education? The author gives three overlapping definitions of **true education**, and they are best read together.

The first, built on Eriksen's third point that the difference between slave and free person is "how to live, how to think and how to learn": "True education is not a clone-producing machine that we call the public school; true education is an orientation for how to live without being dependent on everyone but yourself for your survival." It does not teach only career-specific skills, which is what everyone worries about children learning; it teaches how to become resilient and creative, learn faster, be adaptable, and use technology's new tools "so that you are not used by them." **Source:** The Future-Proof Skill Stack (How Average People Become Millionaires).md.

The second defines it by discovery: "True education is about discovery, not memorization. You have to dive into the unknown, discover, make sense of the world. It's sense-making, it's clarity. It's not being told or forced to learn something that you don't care about that serves a goal that you didn't choose to pursue." And he names its setting: "with entrepreneurship as your vessel you set the scene for true education and sovereignty." **Source:** The Future Of Work (Avoid Learning These Skills).md. **Vessel** is one of the author's recurring words with a sense of its own: the container or vehicle through which something is pursued — here, entrepreneurship as the vehicle for learning and self-rule. Its fuller meaning appears in Chapter 9.

The third draws on Jiddu Krishnamurti, whom the author quotes at length: "Life is really very beautiful, it is not this ugly thing that we have made of it, and you can appreciate its richness, its depth, its extraordinary loveliness only when you revolt against everything — against organized religion, against tradition, against the present rotten society — so that you as a human being find out for yourself what is true. Not to imitate but to discover, that is education, is it not?" The author's takeaway is milder than the quotation: "this leaves us with one task: open our minds, take our own path, and discover our way into a life of meaning." **Source:** Learn This Skill If You Want To Be Relevant In 10 Years.md.

**Complementary context:** Jiddu Krishnamurti (1895–1986) was an Indian philosopher and speaker who rejected organized religion and authority in spiritual matters; he wrote extensively on education, including *Education and the Significance of Life* (1953).

The link between "education equals discovery" and the critique of school is made explicit in 2025. The author grants school its perks — socialization, reading and writing, "a base operating system to become a civilized human" — "but if education equals discovery, it is doing the opposite of just that": everyone learns the same topics, chooses the same classes and looks up the same high-paying skills and jobs "as everyone else to enter a race to the bottom." This is the only path you know because you have not begun self-education, so your mind works only toward getting a job for money and survival. Yet "now you can learn and do anything without permission." **Source:** You're Stuck In The Matrix, Here's How You Escape.md. The author's label for this view is **education equals discovery**.

The practical counterpart of true education is **self-education**, which in 2026 receives its most precise definition. "Schools teach general knowledge or knowledge required to do a job. They do not teach how to navigate your own path. They narrow you into one area of study, which by nature does not prepare you to direct your own work through the path of entrepreneurship or simply doing what you want to do." "Self-education is the process of learning what's necessary to achieve self-generated goals. Again, no hoarding general knowledge to feel like you're learning." **Source:** How To Learn Anything 10x Faster Than Anyone.md. The definition is precise in two ways. It ties learning to a goal, which is why the author's theory of learning (Part VI) depends on his theory of goals (Part IV). And it excludes the accumulation of information for its own sake — what he later calls "tutorial hell" (Chapter 14). The default path, in other words, is not escaped by learning more of the same kind of thing that school taught, but by learning toward a goal one has chosen.

### 2.3 The Job: Modern Slavery and the Eternal Known

If school installs the hierarchy of assigned goals, the job is where it settles. The author's critique of employment is the most polarizing part of his output, and also the one where his position oscillates most visibly. The same video can call the 9-to-5 "the worst outcome" and, minutes later, "a stepping stone." Rather than resolve the oscillation prematurely, this section first lays out the components of the critique — control, the arithmetic of time, the metaphor of slavery, the psychology of a plateau — and then shows how the author himself qualifies it.

#### Conditioned to work for everyone but ourselves

The general thesis appears in an excerpt the author read from a book he was preparing: "We have been conditioned since birth to work for everyone but ourselves. We are given assignments, paths that have already been trodden. We work on these assignments without struggle or conscious thought, leading to a mechanical and replaceable role in society, filled to the brim with people who try to prove their happiness to hide their internal misery." The sequence begins at school — "we're told to read books we don't care about, to complete projects we don't care about, to prepare ourselves for a life we don't care about" — and continues into adult life: "before you know it you are trapped in a **dense cloud of responsibilities**," the time, energy and money that could change your life "are exhausted like clockwork," and "you have no choice but to remain a **productive robot** as society's plan for you intended." **Source:** You Won't Look At Money The Same Again (How To Build Meaningful Wealth).md.

In the same passage he gives a deliberately unflattering definition: "A job is some unpleasant work you do for someone else for the sole purpose of making money. A job is a survival mechanism. A job is one milestone on the path to living up to those who shaped your mind." And he compares it to school: in both cases "good marketing can make up for a bad product." "After centuries of failing to get results, things like schools are still alive and well for the simple reason that very few people go through the trouble of thinking for themselves. Most people do what most people do. Most people aren't okay with the results of most people, but by that point it's much harder to escape." **Source:** You Won't Look At Money The Same Again (How To Build Meaningful Wealth).md. The definition is rhetorical rather than neutral — it describes the job as experienced by someone who does not want it — and should be read alongside the concessions below.

#### The arithmetic of a working life

Much of the author's case rests on a simple accounting of time, which he repeats in several versions. The earliest (2022): working eight hours a day means roughly 70% of your life is not your own, leaving about 30% to live on your own terms — and you are only "possibly" set up for success after 65. This reflection on the **conventional career path** ("go to school, get a job, retire") made him ask why one would do all this "to *possibly* get a job in this market, to *possibly* enjoy life," and was a major reason he decided not to follow it. **Source:** If You Want To Secure Your Future… Follow This New Career Path.md.

The most developed version divides life into thirds. "If you hate your work and it comprises one third of your life and it drains your energy to enjoy the other third, and you are asleep the other third, there doesn't seem to be a higher priority than to create, build, design, write, sell, invest, own, experiment and discover a way to control what you do with your day." **Source:** You Won't Look At Money The Same Again (How To Build Meaningful Wealth).md. In 2026: one-third of life doing unchosen work, one-third mentally exhausted, one-third asleep, "for 40+ years." Elsewhere he says "work consumes about 25 percent of your life if you do the math," and asks whether you would rather spend that share making discoveries in the unknown, with meaning, or in predictable sameness, travelling only briefly because you must go back, with things out of your control. **Source:** Self Improvers Are Creating Their Own Careers (The New Economy).md. The figures differ (70%, a third, 25%) because they count different things — waking hours, total hours, the share drained after work — and the author does not reconcile them. The argument does not depend on the precise number but on the structure: unchosen work consumes not only its own hours but the energy of the hours around it.

The thirds also appear in a personal story, presented as the origin of one of his "traps" to avoid: "do everything in your power to not get a job." Around age fifteen he had an insight he cannot trace to any source: "if I got a job like most people, I would end up like most people." The reasoning: a job takes a third of your time, which you could use to better yourself and create work you enjoy so that you do not hate a third of your life; another third is spent in a low-energy state after work, drained from putting energy into something you hate; and "you become what you focus on," so focusing on something you hate makes you become something you hate. **Source:** I'm 28. Here's How To Get Ahead Of Most 20 Year Olds.md. The phrase "you become what you focus on" links the critique of employment to the theory of attention in Part III: what occupies attention shapes identity.

#### Who controls what pays the bills

A second line of argument concerns control. "You only gain full control over your time and income when you realize that entrepreneurship is the only path to do so." At a job "you are not in charge of the product, the task you are assigned or the customer acquisition process"; "your employer is in charge of everything that pays the bills, therefore they are in charge of your entire life." The chain is causal: every action is tied to money, and money to survival. Whether you can go on vacation depends on time and money; your energy depends on fitness, rest and nutrition; if you cannot afford proper food, have no time to cook, or work so much that stress keeps you from sleeping, "it just gradually ruins your life." Hence "your employer controls your entire life." **Source:** Working Hard Won't Make You Rich (Do This Instead).md. In the same video he immediately qualifies that "there's degrees to this" — not every employer exerts the same control.

A related point concerns earning power. Having learned the skills that pay most, you "realize that you have a hard limit on your earning potential that your employer sets for you." "How much you earn depends on the vessel you choose for that skill, and a job usually isn't the best long-term vessel." The skill is the same; the container — job, freelancing, own business — sets the ceiling. **Source:** How Smart Creatives Work Less & Earn More LEVERAGE.md. Here "vessel" again carries the author's sense of a vehicle or container, in this case for a skill.

Dickie Bush, a guest, describes the same frustration from the inside. On Wall Street he worked fourteen- to fifteen-hour days and learned as much as he could, yet "there was literally no way I could have done one tenth the effort" and earned differently: people who worked far harder or far less "made the same." That never sat well with him. "I sought the ability to have control over my income again where inputs directly led to outputs" — in a sense, getting back to being a tutor. His original goal for Ship 30 for 30 was modest, $10,000 in a year, an extra thousand or so a month, which he calls "a dream," against the assumption that multi-seven-figure founders begin with grand ambitions. **Source:** Dan Koe & Dickie Bush On One-Person Businesses, Creative Workflows, and Lifestyle Design.md. The principle — seek a model where inputs lead directly to outputs — is Bush's, offered as his own experience; the author uses it as corroboration.

The author's own version is based on observation rather than experience. "I could just observe. I could just see that other people had a life that I could potentially want. And if other people had done it, then that means there is a series of steps that I can personally take," especially with technology, the internet and social media, "to achieve close to the same thing; not even the full thing, but I could at least have some control over my money. Therefore I could have some control over my day, my routine, my mind, my emotions, and especially my time." **Source:** What It Takes To Get Rich In Your 20s.md. The reasoning is simple but foundational: an outcome that someone else achieved is evidence that a path exists, and control over money is the lever for control over everything that money conditions.

From these premises he draws a strong conclusion: "If you truly think about what you want in life, starting a business is not optional. A business is the only thing that gives you control over your time." With a job, "you're going to be destined to pursuing the goals that are assigned to you for the rest of your life." He then immediately clarifies: "I'm not saying jobs are bad, I've never said that." A job is "a stepping stone to learn and acquire skills to eventually be able to go and do your own thing and survive along the way." The problem is getting trapped because it is comfortable, then locked in by responsibilities — family, bills, mortgage — with no way out, and then justifying "that that's what they wanted their entire life." What people really want, by nature, is "autonomy, work you enjoy and to have an impact on the world," to fulfil "your human need to be a valuable contribution to humanity." And a business, he insists, "is not some capitalistic pursuit to own a private jet and mansion; a business is how you solve problems, how you build something of your own, how you contribute to humanity through value exchange, how you take back control of your life, how you develop self-confidence in your interest and expertise." **Source:** It’s actually pretty easy to be self-disciplined (if you stop getting distracted).md. **Value exchange** — giving something of value and receiving value in return, "the lifeblood of any society" — is a recurring term of the author's, developed in Chapters 31 and 34.

#### Modern enslavement: the metaphor of the slave

The author's most provocative claim is that most employment is a form of slavery. He builds it in two distinct registers, and it matters to keep them apart.

The first, from 2023 (repeated in 2024), is structural and is named **modern enslavement**. The hierarchical structures of society "present a hierarchy of goals that help frame our attention." In a world of overwhelm, uncertainty and insecurity, the masses flock to whatever most likely heals uncertainty or orders their mind — usually an external, ready-made hierarchy of goals such as the corporate ladder — "because they don't have clarity on anything else." They have not been exposed to another path that makes sense, with clarity about how to reach it, so they believe it impossible. "This is the definition of modern enslavement." The author explicitly rejects a conspiratorial reading: "I don't believe that like someone at the top is just planning being a puppet master." It is human nature, the hierarchical way nature is structured, and the way we focus attention — all normalized and conditioned over time "to the point where we are born as slaves unless we take it on ourselves to free or break those chains," because social conditioning since birth narrows the mind to see the world as everyone else does. Investing our "psychic or mental energy" into these hierarchies of goals becomes automatic, partly to maintain them: "if society collapses then we all collapse." To the objection "someone has to do this job," he replies that this is what creative problem-solving is for; if enough people decide not to take the traditional route and solve problems instead, "the universe will correct itself," perhaps through bad times — which, from a universal perspective, are "part of the process of life, birth and death." **Source:** Society Is A Pyramid Scheme (Take Back Control Of Your Life).md; Get Ahead Of 99% Of People With Deep Work & Monk Mode.md. The video opens with a pull-quote of uncertain origin: "Nobody: I want to be trained into a job I hate, work for 40 years and get angry at a TV until I die. Ninety percent of the population does exactly that. Wake up, it's not too late."

In this first register, "slave" is almost descriptive. "You can opt for doing nothing, you really can, you can be a sheep, you can be an NPC... but you have to understand that you are a human and that you are not going to escape survival. If you opt for doing nothing you are automatically a slave." "You don't have to tie a negative connotation with slave... that's not necessarily a bad thing, in certain cases it can be." And: "don't take what I'm saying as absolutely literal... like a slave from a thousand years ago; we're talking metaphorically here, in terms of the mind, not physicality." **Source:** Get Ahead Of 99% Of People With Deep Work & Monk Mode.md. The logic follows from Chapter 1: since all action serves some goal and survival cannot be escaped, declining to choose one's goals means serving goals set by others. **NPC** (non-player character), the video-game term for a character who follows a script, was introduced in Chapter 1 as the opposite of the "main character."

The second register, from 2023 onward, is financial and more precise. "You are a slave and I'm a slave, and slaves don't know that they're slaves if everyone else is too." "Just because the slavery that everyone knows and hates of the past isn't a thing anymore doesn't mean that slavery doesn't still exist; I'm talking about mental and financial slavery here." He reads a dictionary definition — "slave, noun: a person who is forced to work for and obey another and is considered to be their property" — and singles out its key word: "force." **Source:** How To Escape Wage Slavery (Entrepreneurship Is Modern Survival).md.

He then redefines **force**, a common word that he uses in a specific sense, from the dictionary entry "strength or energy as an attribute of physical action or movement": "there is something that is pushing you to do one thing over another thing, and the stronger that something is that is forcing you in the other direction, the more of a slave you are." The historical analogy he offers is central to the argument: a slave of the past "could, if they wanted, run away, but they would be forced back because of death: they would run out of shelter, they would run out of food, they would run out of water." "They were slaves not only because they were chained and held there by force, but they were also forced because their survival depended on it." So "survival plays a huge role in modern slavery." **Source:** How To Escape Wage Slavery (Entrepreneurship Is Modern Survival).md. The step is subtle: by locating the essence of slavery in dependence for survival rather than in chains, the author can apply the word to anyone whose survival depends on a single employer.

From there he arrives at an operational definition. "Most workers are the literal definition of a slave: if you cannot stop showing up to work for your survival, and have no skills to open other options immediately, and you are the property or employee of a certain company, that's a slave." He puts a figure on it — "95 percent of nine to five workers are slaves, and your feelings do not matter here" — which is his own claim, with no source given. And he anticipates the reaction: "If you do feel threatened by someone talking to you through a screen, then maybe there is some truth to what I'm saying; you would only feel threatened if your survival were at stake; so look inward to see what you're hiding from." **Source:** How To Escape Wage Slavery (Entrepreneurship Is Modern Survival).md.

The 2026 formulation compresses all this into one sentence and adds the identity mechanism. "**Wage slavery** is doing meaningless grind work you didn't choose for someone else just to survive." "If you cannot stop showing up to work without catastrophe and if you have no skills to create alternatives, you meet the definition of a slave, no matter if your feelings tell you otherwise." The problem extends beyond wages: "we are all slaves, usually to ideology and belief systems." And because "slaves don't know they're slaves," a person who has identified with their job will take the argument as an attack: their identity, "your **mental body**," tries to preserve its survival, producing a threat response with no physical threat present — and wanting to argue "only proves my point further." **Source:** How To Become So Valuable AI Can Never Replace You.md. "Mental body" is the author's term for identity as a non-physical body that defends itself, the core concept of Chapter 3; here it explains why the critique of employment provokes such strong reactions.

The same pattern of reasoning appears in a story about his own reaction. On a YouTube community post asking "what is one thing that you find overrated but most people love," the top comment said entrepreneurship: great if you have the skills, but "work is work"; "I'm sick of being told I'm a wage slave for choosing to work a nine to five; most of these entrepreneurs are really just unemployed." He found it "very loaded, very assumptive," though understandable given the people who flex big numbers online. "This irked me at first... my defense systems immediately started going off," producing objections in his mind. He hates getting trapped in social comments, "but our brain loves it," so he turned it into a video. **Source:** Self Improvers Are Creating Their Own Careers (The New Economy).md. The anecdote is instructive because the author applies to himself the same mechanism he attributes to the defensive employee: a threat to one's identity triggers defences.

His replies to the comment are two objections. The first: "people hate what they don't understand." The commenters have not been entrepreneurs and do not understand "the nuances of the brain that you pick up through daily experience." Online you see maybe 1% or less of someone's life, or 5% of their business, and take that as enough to judge without experience. Observing society should serve to correct your own actions, not to reinforce what you were told and justify it as "I chose to do this" when the choice is tied to money. "They think entrepreneurship is overrated because they aren't entrepreneurs." The second reply repeats the financial definition — "your feelings aren't reality: if you got let go and you could not pay the bills then you are by definition a modern slave" — and adds a historical prediction: "slave doesn't have to be good or bad"; we agree past slavery was bad, but "we will look back on the Industrial Age and realize that slavery was the norm, and that is what AI is coming in to fix." Being forced to work for survival removes choice: your choices align with unconscious survival goals. Most people are also unconscious of what happens behind the scenes at their company — exploitation, paying pennies to sweatshops, "a much worse form of slavery" — and becoming conscious of this and continuing anyway is "a terrible thing." He qualifies: not all companies, though mega-corporations and chains like McDonald's serve "the worst food for health." You cannot control any of this at the start; that is the self-actualization journey, and helping create a better world is what makes life meaningful. **Source:** Self Improvers Are Creating Their Own Careers (The New Economy).md. The theme of unwittingly contributing to harm returns in 2.5 as "unconscious destruction."

The author's use of the word changes over time. In 2023 "slave" is "not necessarily a bad thing." By December 2024 it is normative: "if we want to define what a slave is, it's being average." He notes that about 1% of people get upset when he uses the language, which he takes as proof of his point, since they close their minds. He includes himself: "we're all slaves in our own regard; it's not physical, it's mental." He says he is not trying to make anyone feel bad — "you make yourself feel bad by how you perceive it" — and that his intention is awareness; he admits he is exaggerating, since no one is in physical chains, though metaphorically anyone could be in some area. "Most slaves don't know they're slaves because it's just the norm." Awareness of what you do not want — being average and its ramifications — is necessary because "you need to move away from something in order to move towards something." **Source:** How To Make The Greatest Comeback Of Your Life.md. The shift is from a descriptive definition (the consequence of not choosing) to a normative one (the average, to be moved away from). The second sense anticipates the **anti-vision** of Chapter 7: knowing what you are moving away from as fuel for moving toward something.

Finally, the author repeatedly positions himself against both camps of the online debate. "I'm not anti-nine to five, I'm not anti-working a job; I think it's very useful; I think it's an absolutely incredible path to go down if you want to climb up the ranks and get a high-paying job and you love that job." He "worked a nine to five for a good amount of my life." His perspective "always splits people into two camps," but "you don't have to fall within either of those camps; you can agree with both sides." **Source:** How To Escape Wage Slavery (Entrepreneurship Is Modern Survival).md. And later in the same video: "I'm tired of both sides of the argument: one side is like all nine to five workers are slaves, and then the other side is like no no it's okay, you're not a slave, don't worry, you're perfect the way you are. Both are wrong and both are right in some cases, because when people say this online both are trying to maximize the engagement they get; they don't zoom out and think if people are actually slaves." His principle: "a published idea without depth is a disservice to humanity." **Source:** How To Escape Wage Slavery (Entrepreneurship Is Modern Survival).md. The reader may notice that the "95% are slaves" claim and "I'm not anti-nine to five" come from the same video; the author does not reconcile them, though the definitions suggest a reconciliation: the objection is not to employment as such but to dependence on it without alternatives.

#### The 90/9/1 estimate

A more granular version of the "95%" appears in 2024 as the **90/9/1** split, which the author explicitly presents as opinion. "I would argue that 90% of people are in jobs that they hate, and I would argue that statistics back that a select 9% of people are in jobs that they think they enjoy and they're okay with it and they're not trying to get out, but they would be better off if they got out. The last 1% are in the select few jobs where all of the **psychological markers** match perfectly and they thoroughly enjoy their job." The exception is explicit: "if you are in that 1% this doesn't apply to you; if you are absolutely happy and have the autonomy to do what you want in your life, keep the job." No specific statistic is cited. **Source:** Learn This Skill If You Want To Be Relevant In 10 Years.md. A month later he gives a slightly different version: 90% "publicly hate their jobs," 9% lie to themselves that they love their jobs or lack awareness of anything better because they never explored the unknown, and 1% have jobs that let them create the conditions for flow — and not everyone can have those jobs. **Source:** Minimalist Productivity Work Less, Do More.md.

These figures should be read as what they are. Across the corpus the author's percentages for "the masses" — 90%, 95%, "95 plus," 99%, 75–80% conventional, 50% conformist — measure different things (employment, thinking, childhood conditioning, developmental stages) and do not add up to a consistent dataset. In one place he says statistics support him without naming them; elsewhere he calls the figures impressions from observation. They are rhetorical estimates, not data. "Psychological markers" — the author's term for the conditions that must coincide for someone to enjoy a job — connects with the flow conditions of Chapter 10.

#### The psychology of employment: from the edge to the eternal known

The deepest part of the critique is not about money or control but about the psyche, and it is where the author's ambivalence becomes most explicit. In a 2023 video he admits that through questioning and observation he "conditioned myself to believe that getting a 9-to-5 job was the bane of my existence," "honestly the worst outcome." The reason: once people accepted a job offer — leaving college, in or near their late twenties — they seemed "doomed to a life of comfort," "obviously not all of the time but 95% plus of the time." They filled their plates with never-ending responsibilities — mortgage, spouse, kids — before having the financial capacity to devote time and energy to them; "they were quick to become an adult but were never able to reap the rewards of being one"; they "chained themselves to a paycheck" because they never made the choices that lead to more money and time. **Source:** The Future Of Work Is Play (How To Create A Digital Career).md. He frames this as a self-conditioned belief, partly a personal stance; the "95%" is again an impression.

He then shows a graphic he calls **the psychology of employment**, repurposed from an earlier graphic about flow. The reconstruction from the transcript is as follows; the axes are not stated beyond skill and challenge (and, implicitly, meaning), so the details are partly ambiguous.

| Element of the graphic | What it represents |
|---|---|
| Solid line (employment) | At first, skill and challenge rise together; life is fairly meaningful because you are "branching into the unknown," "at your edge where meaning and fulfillment are." The longer you stay without seeking more challenge or skill, the line flattens. |
| Flattened region: "the eternal known" | Life becomes boring; you chase cheap dopamine; an "endless cycle of comfort." |
| Dotted line (entrepreneurship) | "The complete opposite," "the natural progression": skill and challenge keep rising, with highs and lows (revenue, growth) that force you to evolve in an ever-changing marketplace. |
| Circle at the intersection | "A great time to actually switch to entrepreneurship." |

The author's own career illustrates the intersection: he took a job at a web design agency while trying to freelance in web design, in order to learn the skills that would let him do it himself. He adds that entrepreneurship "flows in alignment with nature" because its ups and downs force adaptation, whereas a job with set tasks does not. **Source:** The Future Of Work Is Play (How To Create A Digital Career).md.

**The eternal known** is the author's coined term for this flattened region: the repetitive comfort zone where "you can't make new discoveries." It is the negative image of the edge of challenge and skill where, in his theory of flow (Chapter 10), meaning lives. A related, looser claim describes **the known** neurologically: at any moment one brain hemisphere "controls the known" — "it's either the right or the left, it's one of them" — and that known is all you operate within when you are calm, at home, going about your routine; in that state you rarely become aware of new potentials. The author himself presents the neuroscience loosely, and it should be read as an image rather than a finding; its role in his argument is to set up why a problem-solver mindset is needed. **Source:** Your Future Will Be Determined By 3 Things.md.

Immediately after the graphic, in the same video, the position changes: "I see 9-to-5 jobs as a **stepping stone**; my problem with them is that they breed complacency." A job is not inherently evil; the problem is that "challenge is what makes life fun and interesting," and if you halt your personal evolution by never pursuing more, you lose purpose and fulfillment. Hence, in this video, "entrepreneurship is the only logical option for long-term thinkers." **Source:** The Future Of Work Is Play (How To Create A Digital Career).md.

A 2025 version (repeating the same graphic) locates the problem in time. When the novelty and challenge of school and job advancement stop in the mid-twenties, meaning goes with them. School did not feel purposeless because it offered progression; a new job brings challenge and skills to learn (some of them annoying — "that's life"), and that is where novelty, challenge and fulfilment come from. Once it dies down and you plateau, it disappears and you are stuck in a "repetitive and mundane robotic life." We do not take that as the sign to branch off and self-educate further, which would be the natural path. "When that mundane and robotic life starts to set in, that's the best time to pivot off." He specifies: not "never work a job," but if you want control over lifestyle, novelty, challenge, meaning and fulfilment, "entrepreneurship is the only logical option." **Source:** The creator economy is dying thanks to AI.md. The **plateau**, in his specific sense, is the end of novelty and progression in a job, and the moment to change course.

The fullest psychological explanation comes in 2025, prefaced by a disclaimer: it is easy to lump him into the "all 9-to-5s are bad" camp, which is not his belief, but he understands psychology "to a reasonable extent." As a child "there is a magic to life because everything is new." "Schools simulate this desire to hunt for good dopamine by providing a video-game-like progression to learning" — grade one, grade two, grade three. Your first job is challenging; "you develop skill to cure your anxiety," get promotions and raises. "Then when you reach as far as that career ladder will allow you, the challenge and novelty cease to exist. Your days turn into a blur of repetition. This is incredibly damaging to your psyche." You get stuck in the defined and known "because a monthly paycheck is addictive and you max out your lifestyle to fit what that paycheck allows." Since most people will not get the elite jobs that keep the ladder going, his advice is to take your skills and interests and do your own thing, "so you're in control of the novelty, meaning, fulfillment of your life." **Source:** How To Thrive With Multiple Interests.md. "Good dopamine" — dopamine earned through effort and discovery — is the subject of Chapter 11; the point here is that school and early employment provide it artificially through a ladder, and the supply stops when the ladder does.

The "addictive paycheck" has a counterpart in a concept Dickie Bush describes from his own life: the default track of working the job, slowly increasing income, and "slowly inflate your lifestyle so you're always stuck... you make more but you accumulated more recurring costs... boom, you're 35, you're 40... **golden handcuffs**." Bush is grateful he joined Twitter two and a half years earlier, because exposure to other ideas reshaped his trajectory, and he insists "it's by no means too late to start." The author adds a caution against passive consumption of such conversations: listening "is not going to do much aside from prime you to start... it's up to you to start and then figure out the rest as you go and learn from the people that you resonate most with." **Source:** Dan Koe & Dickie Bush On One-Person Businesses, Creative Workflows, and Lifestyle Design.md.

#### The path of uncertainty

Against the eternal known the author sets **the path of uncertainty**, a passage he reuses almost verbatim in 2023, 2024 and 2025. "When you get stuck in a nine to five or freelance work or agency work or any of the new digital nine to fives, you start to live in the eternal known. You can't make new discoveries in the known; you can't hunt; you get bored, depressed and see life as meaningless, because the only dopamine you get is from superficial sources." "You never take risks, push into the unknown and discover new knowledge, tools and potentials that raise dopamine levels in your brain. You must evolve." Note that the critique extends beyond employment to freelancing and agency work — what the author calls the **new 9-to-5**, models that reproduce the logic of employment online (Chapter 30). Then: "Entrepreneurship is the path of uncertainty, like slashing your way through the jungle: you are required to learn skills that aren't taught in schools; to be okay with failure, rejection and slow progress; to learn from your mistakes, show up again tomorrow and push until you strike gold." **Source:** How To Escape Wage Slavery (Entrepreneurship Is Modern Survival).md.

The 2024 version adds that this is "required in other words to be human," and that as an entrepreneur you "hunt for survival" by gathering knowledge, creating a valuable product and giving it to people who would benefit. It also addresses readers with a bad relationship with money or business: people actually want to buy products that benefit their lives; if a product hurts people, obviously do not sell it, "but that's not all that business is." **Source:** Life Is A Video Game (Here's How You Win).md.

The paradox at the heart of this section is that uncertainty is presented as more secure. Education businesses, he argues, are the future of schooling and a good place to bank one's future: "more secure, though uncertain." Entrepreneurship is uncertain, but "that's what meaningful living is, being constantly exposed to novel experiences; entrepreneurship is the vessel to do that." "Your ancestors were entrepreneurs serving their community." Meanwhile "robotic living in a cubicle," the same day in and out, is "the least safe and least secure path you can take, especially for your psyche and your mental health." **Source:** Zero To $1 Million As A One-Person Business (Working 2-4 Hours A Day).md. Safety, in this argument, is measured psychologically rather than financially — a move developed in 2.6 as "the illusion of certainty."

The 2025 version links the path to the mind's need for challenge. People climb ladders — the corporate ladder among them — because the mind craves challenge, but they get used to it and it becomes boring; so do vacations and retirement. You need the next challenge, which usually involves work; but most people hate their work, so they do not believe good work exists, or that they can create it, pursue their life's work and enjoy and control it. "Entrepreneurship is the only logical option for long-term thinkers. It's the path of uncertainty requiring skills not taught in schools. You must be okay with failure, rejection, and slow progress." "The secret is cultivating a skill set so impactful that you can't help but share it. You solve your own problems, sell the solution, and improve humanity. That's entrepreneurship." And: "Employment isn't our natural state. Your psyche is wired to hunt. But today's threats are psychological and spiritual, not physical. Nobody wants to be a monkey in a cubicle." **Source:** 12 Rules To Change Your Life In 12 Months.md. The hunting psyche is the subject of the next section; "solve your own problems and sell the solution" is the business principle of Chapter 28.

A small textual detail shows how the slogan settled. In September 2023 the author said, referring to his "value creator" videos, that "entrepreneurship is the only long-term option for logical thinkers," without further argument in that transcript. **Source:** How To Reprogram Your Mind & Build Your Intelligence.md (2023-09-24). Three months later, in December 2023, the formula already appears inverted — "entrepreneurship is the only logical option for long-term thinkers" — in the "stepping stone" passage quoted earlier in this section (**Source:** The Future Of Work Is Play (How To Create A Digital Career).md, 2023-12-31), and it is the inverted form that he keeps repeating in 2025. The inversion therefore happens within 2023, not between 2023 and 2025. What it changes is the stress: the first form addresses the reader's reasoning ("if you think logically, you will choose it"), the second the reader's time horizon ("if you think in decades, you will choose it"). The author does not comment on the change, and given how close together the two forms are, it may be no more than a rephrasing that stuck; it should not be read as a considered shift of position.

#### The author's agency job: the ticking clock

The author's own experience of employment supplies the concrete texture of this section. He studied programming because he learned he could do it without a degree, as a backup plan, trusting that he was good at self-education. He got "a very base-level web design job at an agency in Arizona," and spent the first hours of each day on his own projects. He describes "the brutal reality of working a desk job": "most of your work is just procrastination." Most people, with exceptions, can work on their own things, procrastinate until the end, then copy and paste templates — in his case for the e-commerce stores the agency served — and get paid. He knew that if he stayed too long he would get comfortable — "the wife, the mortgage, the kids, the responsibilities," with nothing wrong in any of them — and that this would "pile-drive me into the state of not having any time, money, or energy," and life would "go on autopilot." **Source:** How To Build A Better Personal Brand Than 99% Of People.md. **Autopilot** in this 2025 sense means the state in which the comfort of employment and its accumulated responsibilities leave a life without time, money or energy.

When he got the job he felt that "the clock would start ticking down toward my demise." He had stayed for a fifth year of college, taking out loans to delay employment while frantically trying business models; from observation he believed that once employed it was downhill — responsibilities stack up and "I'd fall into the **conventional life path**." Through experimentation and curiosity he found his way. At the job he procrastinated on his assigned work until the last minute so he could focus on freelance web design, sensing he was close. After a few pivots it worked: typical websites first, clients from referrals, then a more specific system for a more specific target, built from skills he had meshed together — "similar to what he teaches now." Even so, as a full-time freelancer he hated working on projects that were not his own, which is when he turned to social media. **Source:** How Smart Creators Will Grow An Audience From Zero In 2025.md.

The job also cost him something he valued. After a few months in any job, once trained, the challenge plateaus: clock in, do tasks, clock out — and somehow you are exhausted. At the agency, while desperately trying to get out, he stopped wanting to go to the gym, although health and fitness had been a lifelong love. The first time he skipped was after work, exhausted from sitting in a cubicle all day: "the fluorescent lights above me were just sucking the life out of me." You get bored, it is against your nature, and attention drifts to "what else could I be doing?", which for most people means opening the phone and "rotting your brain." Rarely, he adds, does a job require consistent skill improvement to match greater challenge. **Source:** How To Become So Valuable AI Can Never Replace You.md. Another telling gives the schedule that made the gym impossible: an hour's commute, leave at 8, arrive at 9, clock out at 6 (the lunch hour does not count toward the nine-to-five), ten minutes to the gym, an hour of training, an hour's drive home, then bed — because health was a value. It was the only time in his life he skipped the gym. "That sounds horrible." **Source:** I'm 28. Here's How To Get Ahead Of Most 20 Year Olds.md.

#### Reading the oscillation

Across 2022–2026 the author's statements about employment range from "do everything in your power to not get a job" and "95 percent of nine to five workers are slaves" to "jobs are an absolutely incredible stepping stone," "keep the job" if you are the fortunate 1%, "not never work a job," and, in 2026, jobs as "very worthy stepping stones for skill acquisition and experience" alongside the insistence that wage slavery is real. There is no clean chronological turn. The tone oscillates between total rejection and the stepping stone; there is a mild trend from "the only path" (2023–2024) toward admitting paths inside organizations (2025); and the absolute condemnation is presented, by the author himself, as a belief he conditioned into himself.

The reasons he gives point to a reconciliation he never states as such. The object of the critique is not the job as such but three things: permanence (the job as destination rather than stage), complacency (the plateau after which challenge and evolution stop), and dependence (no skills or alternatives if the job disappears). He addresses people who have "that desire for more"; he exempts those who are genuinely happy and autonomous; and his own life — an agency job used to learn skills while building something of his own — is the model of the job as stepping stone. The rejection is his personal rule and his advice to those who want autonomy; the stepping stone is his concession to everyone else. Both versions are his.

### 2.4 The Hunting Psyche in a Cubicle

The previous section explained why the author thinks employment harms the psyche: the plateau, the eternal known, the end of challenge. This section gives the underlying model that explains why a plateau should hurt at all. Its core claim is evolutionary in form: the human psyche was shaped for a way of life that modern work has removed, and entrepreneurship restores it. The reader should keep in mind that the author presents this as a framing — he insists his central image is "a simile, not an insult," and his appeals to science are general — rather than as a demonstrated scientific theory.

#### The monkey in a cubicle

The image appears as early as 2022 and recurs through 2025. Its most complete version is a chain of reasoning. First, "your psyche is wired to hunt." Second, the physical world has changed much faster than our minds can adapt: we have the same neurobiological processes as our ancestors. Third, therefore, if you stay in a 9-to-5 too long you become "like a monkey who lives in the jungle that is trapped in a fluorescent-lit box — is that healthy for the monkey?" The author stresses that this is a simile, not an insult. Fourth, stuck in a 9-to-5 or a "new 9-to-5" — an agency, freelancing — you live in the eternal known, where "you can't make new discoveries"; you get bored, depressed and see life as meaningless because the only dopamine comes from superficial sources. Fifth, you never take risks or push into the unknown to discover the new knowledge, tools and potentials "that raise dopamine levels in the brain." Sixth, as an entrepreneur you "hunt for your survival" by gathering knowledge, creating a valuable product and putting it in front of people who could benefit. **Source:** The Future Of Work Is Play (How To Create A Digital Career).md.

The **monkey in a cubicle** is one of the author's most persistent coined images.
