A 2024 version sharpens it with a thought experiment: "If you were to put a chimpanzee in a fluorescent-lit cubicle for 8 hours a day, do you think it would thrive? Of course not. It lacks the natural environment that contributes to its psychological well-being. You don't need a scientific paper to assume this." "Most people are monkeys in a cubicle: they have the mental wiring that our ancestors did, but they're in a new environment and nobody understands how to act within that environment." **Source:** Learn This Skill If You Want To Be Relevant In 10 Years.md. The phrase "you don't need a scientific paper" is revealing: the author offers the image as intuitive, not as research.

The same 2024 passage adds the mechanism that explains why people do not notice. "The psychological effects that come with boredom and a repetitive string of tasks slowly builds and builds, and because it slowly builds... you don't even notice it, so you're operating at this **Lower State of Consciousness** for so long that you just think it's normal." You no longer believe you could feel better, or that any opportunity is worth pursuing. At such a job "there is no more learning, there is no challenge, there is no growth" — and he qualifies: "of course this is for some jobs." **Source:** Learn This Skill If You Want To Be Relevant In 10 Years.md. The gradualness matters. It is the same structure as the conditioning of Chapter 1 and the "trained to bear the shocks" of 2.1: harm that accumulates slowly is perceived as the norm, which is why awareness (2.7) has to come before change.

The earliest, 2022 version states the positive side: we were not meant to be "metaphorical monkeys in cubicles," deprived of what we are wired to do. "We are wired to be entrepreneurs; entrepreneurs are creators." Social platforms now let anyone connect with the specific community they resonate with, which requires developing communication, writing and persuasive skills. **Source:** How To Make Money As A Creative On The Internet.md. This early statement already contains the link the rest of the book will develop: from the hunting psyche to the creator, and from the creator to writing (Part VIII) and audience (Part IX).

#### What hunting means today

If the psyche is wired to hunt, what does hunting mean when no one needs to chase animals? The author's answer shifts slightly across versions but keeps a common core.

The 2023 version (repeated word for word in a 2024 compilation): "Your psyche isn't wired for modern life... not wired for being under fluorescent lights going and sitting in a cubicle." "A monkey would suffer in a cubicle because its psyche is not wired for that." "We need to hunt, and in this age what I mean by hunting is novel dopamine sources or meaningful dopamine sources" — something new in your life, discoveries, creativity — "being able to find something new, take it, create something with it, and that feels so good," which many people lack. Then the link back to Chapter 1: if "the repetitive NPC automaton lifestyle" — an automaton being "a little robotic doll thing" — feels normal to you, "you are by definition trapped in The Matrix, which is a metaphorical term for you are just enslaved and a slave to routine." **Source:** Change Your Life In 6 Months (My Deep Work Routine).md; Get Ahead Of 99% Of People With Deep Work & Monk Mode.md. Here **hunting** is defined as the search for novel and meaningful sources of dopamine: discovering something, taking it and creating with it. The Matrix, as Chapter 1 explained, is the author's metaphor for the inherited network of beliefs; in this passage it is equated with enslavement to routine.

The 2024 version turns hunting into the skill to learn. "The skill that you need to learn is hunting. You need to learn to hunt for your survival. You can't find enjoyment in life because you don't know how to hunt." The contrast is with assignment: "you're assigned material to read to pass your exams, you're assigned a routine to complete your tasks at a job, you're assigned beliefs and values to survive in your culture." "The problem with assigned goals is that the path to achieve them is known: you are doing something that's been done before, or you're repeating tasks that a visionary assigned to you to build their dream instead of your own." Then the definition: "to hunt is to discover knowledge, skills, ideas and opportunities that help you achieve the goals you set for yourself, and once those goals become known you must have another one ready so you don't get lost." **Source:** Learn This Skill If You Want To Be Relevant In 10 Years.md.

This definition is the bridge between this chapter and the rest of the book. It shows why assigned goals fail psychologically — not because they are imposed, but because their path is already known, and a known path offers nothing to discover. And it explains why the author insists on self-generated goals (Part IV): only a goal whose path is unknown keeps the hunt alive. The final clause — have the next goal ready once the current one becomes known — anticipates the idea that life is a chain of problems (Chapter 8) and the infinite game (Chapter 10).

A practical consequence is the advice not to outsource one's curiosity. "Don't ask me for recommendations, that's against the point, that's not hunting." Lean into "your psyche's nature of wanting to hunt for ideas and knowledge and information in order to reap that good dopamine and make it a sustainable habit. Don't outsource your curiosity to me." He adds, while promoting his own programs, that courses are not necessary if you make time to study and practice, but they help those who know their goals, know the course aligns with them, and find it streamlined while it still emphasizes free and critical thinking. **Source:** Become A Digital Renaissance Man (And Join The New Rich).md. The point is that finding the knowledge is part of the reward; being handed a reading list removes the hunt.

#### Become your own dopamine dealer

The author derives a practical method from the hunting model. He paraphrases an unnamed friend who said to him: "It's wild, I remember asking you why none of your friends take action or follow in your footsteps; I get it now: people are dopamine junkies, even businessmen. The people that don't take action don't know how to replace the dopamine they are getting from their current habits with business, so they either don't start or quit after a week because they couldn't get their hit." The author recognized what had worked for him: "I was constantly chasing the good old dopamine, but in the right direction." **Source:** How To Escape Wage Slavery (Entrepreneurship Is Modern Survival).md. The observation about "dopamine junkies" is the friend's; the coined prescription — **become your own dopamine dealer**, replacing the hits of current habits with those of building and learning — is the author's.

The method has four parts. "Hold a loose idea of what you want in life: money, success, peace, fulfillment. Start building something, anything, that will make that a reality" — he recommends a one-person business "because it is long term." "Learn what you want to learn the most to help build it: skills, courses, websites, logos, whatever, so you get your dopamine hit." And "don't be afraid to change what you're doing if you get bored." **Source:** How To Escape Wage Slavery (Entrepreneurship Is Modern Survival).md. The logic is that motivation does not have to be summoned by willpower if the activity itself produces the reward; the task is to arrange things so that building toward a goal is the source of stimulation.

One detail of this advice changes later. In 2023 he recommends learning "websites, logos" for the dopamine hit; in 2024 he calls focusing on website and logo among the things "you don't need when starting out." He gives no reason for the change. The two can be read as answers to different questions — what keeps a beginner engaged versus what a beginner's business actually needs — but the author does not draw that distinction himself. The relationship between dopamine and goals is treated fully in Chapter 11.

#### Entrepreneurship is modern survival

The hunting model culminates in one of the author's central coined formulas: **entrepreneurship is modern survival**. Its first version (2023) is an argument from ancestry. Our ancestors were, metaphorically, entrepreneurs who served their communities. In the past you belonged to a small, physical niche community, not an unlimited digital one, and you had a specific thing to provide: cook, naturopath who helped people heal, doctor, hunter, fire-maker, caretaker of the children. Things have shifted in tangible terms, but our psyche remains the same; therefore we have to fulfil the same needs through entrepreneurship. Later in the same video: "your psyche is wired to hunt; you are neurobiologically rewarded for hunting for your survival, not for being a monkey in a cubicle"; so hunt for money to ease survival-induced stress and open room for creativity. **Source:** The Future Of One-Person Businesses (Take Advantage Now).md.

A month later he adds the dimension of purpose. "We have the psyche of our ancestors." The external world changed, but ancestors were "metaphorically entrepreneurs": entrepreneurship is a new form of contributing to a community, providing value in exchange for value. In tribes each person had a specific value skill — cooking, cleaning, childcare — that served the community. "If you're just doing the same repetitive task day in day out then life loses its weight; you have to have purpose, and entrepreneurship and modern business is the vessel for purpose." **Source:** Self Improvers Are Creating Their Own Careers (The New Economy).md.

The compact definition: "As an entrepreneur you hunt for your survival by gathering knowledge, creating a valuable product and putting it in front of people that could benefit from it." **Source:** How To Escape Wage Slavery (Entrepreneurship Is Modern Survival).md. The three components — knowledge, product, distribution — map almost exactly onto the structure of the later chapters: learning (Part VI), product (Part XI) and audience (Part IX).

In 2024 the image gains a territory and an instrument: "The internet is one big community." Your ancestors were entrepreneurs within their communities, each fulfilling the role they were best suited for. "Entrepreneurship is modern survival and the internet is your **hunting ground**." You hunt for deep knowledge by pursuing curiosity; "**dopamine is your compass**," but for this to make sense you will need to break free of your "drip-fed dopamine sedation of quick pleasures." **Source:** The Art Of Focus – Official Book Summary By The Author Dan Koe.md. The compass image says that the reward signal can guide the hunt — but only once cheap, effortless sources of stimulation stop drowning it out. Another 2024 formulation uses the jungle metaphor of 2.3: "You have to branch out, you have to dive into the unknown, and entrepreneurship is the only way to do that: to slash through the jungle, to make new discoveries, to hunt for ideas and income, to fulfill the needs of the psyche that is wired the same as your ancestors." **Source:** Working Hard Won't Make You Rich (Do This Instead).md.

The 2026 version adds a warning about the present. "Entrepreneurship is in our nature. It is modern survival. We are wired to create and distribute value to a tribe of like-minded people. Now, that tribe is on the internet and you have to find them or attract them. We are wired to hunt, to explore the unknown, to seek novelty, and never stagnate. And psychologically, this is the most enjoyable way of life" — a claim he grounds in the psychology of flow. "The barrier of entry has collapsed," but it is not easy: you will not have AI "spit out 30 posts and go viral"; "it's all skill-based," though people with multiple interests have an advantage because they love learning. "I don't care how fast AGI is going to speed up things. It still takes time to get any form of result in life. If you were to just get it immediately, then it would become a commodity" — and, like scrolling, it would bring no meaning. **Source:** If you have multiple interests, do not waste the next 2-3 years.md. The final point is a subtle defence of difficulty: meaning depends on effort, so a result obtained without effort would lose the very thing that made it worth pursuing.

#### Even the perfect job is not yours

The last piece of the argument addresses the strongest objection: what about someone who has found a good job? The author's answer appeals to creation and to the intrinsic drivers. Humans have a unique ability to create — "the gift of God within us to create," which "feels amazing" — and creating for someone else, with a purpose assigned by them, is different. He claims there is "so much scientific literature... about how the psyche is wired that all point to entrepreneurship," but names no source. The perfect gig is increasingly hard to find, and "even the perfect gig isn't perfect": there will be something you hate, and because it is not yours you cannot change it, nor can you leverage the **intrinsic drivers** that make life good — curiosity, passion, purpose, autonomy, mastery — "not extrinsic, not something being assigned to you." **Source:** Self Improvers Are Creating Their Own Careers (The New Economy).md.

The list of five intrinsic drivers comes from the psychology of flow; in early versions the author attributes it to Steven Kotler, later he uses it without attribution. **Complementary context:** Steven Kotler, a writer on flow and peak performance, describes curiosity, passion, purpose, autonomy and mastery as intrinsic motivators that can be "stacked" to drive flow; the model also draws on Daniel Pink's work on autonomy, mastery and purpose. The drivers are developed in Chapter 10.

This argument complements, rather than contradicts, the 1% exception of 2.3. There the author conceded that a few people have jobs where all the psychological markers match; here he adds that even then the job is not theirs to reshape. The two together define the author's position: a good job is possible, but ownership — the ability to change the game you are playing — is what employment structurally cannot give.

### 2.5 Pyramids of Domination, Pyramids of Attention and Status Games

School and the job are particular institutions. Behind them the author sees a general shape: the pyramid. This section collects his account of hierarchies — the kind that dominate and the kind that develop — and two extensions of it: society as a pyramid of attention, and status as a game everyone plays. Together they explain why climbing an existing ladder is a poor strategy, and what the alternative looks like.

#### Two kinds of hierarchy

"Everything is structured as a hierarchy," the author says, and hierarchies come in two types. The first are **dominator hierarchies**, "which give the word hierarchy a bad reputation": pyramid-scheme-like structures whose main feature is that "there are more people with less power at the bottom and then there are less people with more power at the top" — and, in a true pyramid scheme, the investors at the bottom are what enable this distribution of power. The second are natural or **actualization hierarchies**, ordered by "increasing wholeness," where the whole at one level becomes a part of the whole at the next: particles, atoms, cells, organisms; letters, words, sentences, paragraphs. **Source:** Society Is A Pyramid Scheme (Take Back Control Of Your Life).md.

The distinction is adapted from Ken Wilber, and the author uses it as the lens for society. Society mimics hierarchical structure, but — "context dependent" — it mostly falls under domination. Its parts — public schools, government, corporate jobs, even some religious institutions (which he considers more a matter of culture, but still parts and wholes) — are "hierarchies within hierarchies," each built as a pyramid. **Source:** Society Is A Pyramid Scheme (Take Back Control Of Your Life).md.

**Complementary context:** Ken Wilber, in *Sex, Ecology, Spirituality* (1995) and *A Brief History of Everything* (1996), distinguishes healthy "actualization" or "growth" hierarchies, in which each level transcends and includes the previous one (a "holarchy"), from pathological "dominator" hierarchies, in which one part tries to dominate the whole; he credits the terminology largely to the cultural historian Riane Eisler. The concepts of holon and "transcend and include" are developed in Chapter 38.

The author uses this pair in two variants. In one, dominator and actualization hierarchies are described in Wilber's terms (pyramid of power versus growing wholeness). In the other, which is more the author's own, a "dominance hierarchy" is someone else's power structure and an "actualization hierarchy" is one's own series of goals-as-problems increasing in creativity, fulfilment and impact. The second sense is the one that matters most in what follows.

#### Climbing the ladder: bad odds

Inside a dominator hierarchy, the standard advice is to climb. In corporate jobs or school "you're taught to climb the ladder through hard work and usually manual labor." But "it's close to impossible to reach the actual top of the pyramid if you go about it this way"; you usually get stuck at one level. "If there's 10 people at the top and a million people at the bottom... those are just bad odds." Not everyone even tries to climb every ladder — most people in a church are not trying to become pastors. Those who want out "have to create their own": start their own business, "create their own actualization hierarchy to escape a dominance hierarchy." And such hierarchies "are created every single day" — "they transcend and include after creative emergence." **Source:** Society Is A Pyramid Scheme (Take Back Control Of Your Life).md; Get Ahead Of 99% Of People With Deep Work & Monk Mode.md. "**Climb the ladder**" is a common phrase the author uses in a specific sense: rising by hard work inside someone else's pyramid, with poor odds.

The 2026 version adds a historical claim and a clarification. "Civilization was quite literally built by tribes enslaving other tribes. That dynamic never disappeared. Instead, it abstracted into employment, law, and culture." "Society has essentially become a pyramid scheme because there are more people at the bottom than at the top"; it is mathematically impossible for everyone to be at the top — one boss, several employees who depend on the boss for survival. You must leave this pyramid behind — but not hierarchies altogether: "you're going to create your own." **Source:** How To Become So Valuable AI Can Never Replace You.md. The clarification matters. The author is not an anti-hierarchy thinker; he argues for changing which hierarchy you are in, from one you climb to one you build. The historical claim about tribes is stated as background, not argued in detail.

The objection "someone has to do this job," and the author's reply that this is what creative problem-solving is for — "if enough people do this then the universe will correct itself," with bad times being, from a universal perspective, part of "the process of life, birth and death" — was presented in 2.3 as part of his account of modern enslavement. **Source:** Society Is A Pyramid Scheme (Take Back Control Of Your Life).md. It is worth noticing here that the reply moves into a second register that coexists with the critical one throughout the corpus: a cosmic acceptance in which "who's to say that Mother Nature is wrong for it being what it is today," and in which, in 2026, "I'm not against capitalism. I think it's going to evolve into something better." The critical register motivates individual change; the cosmic register removes drama and blame. The author does not reconcile them.

#### The collective societal vision and the two-step exit

What keeps people climbing a pyramid whose odds are bad? The author's answer is a vision that no one in particular chose. "The collective societal vision for your future is to get good grades, maybe get a high-paying job, watch TV to ease your mind and maybe retire happily at 65," all driven by "the unconscious seeking of status, survival and approval." Through conditioning it becomes habit. "We go on to mimic others... we become a product of others," chase **status games**, buy fancy cars, invest our attention all day to make the money back, and "never think to consult or create and then consult our own values, vision, wants, needs and potential impact on the world." **Source:** Society Is A Pyramid Scheme (Take Back Control Of Your Life).md; Get Ahead Of 99% Of People With Deep Work & Monk Mode.md. The **collective societal vision** is the author's name for this inherited picture of a good life; it is the social-scale counterpart of the default path.

The exit has two steps, which the author states as a process. "We escape this modern enslavement, one, by becoming aware" — which is what the video itself tries to do — "and then the second thing is by creating your own actualization hierarchy to order your mind and create a better future for yourself and those around you." An actualization hierarchy "will present a series of goals, which are problems, increasing in creativity along the way, and fulfillment and impact," potentially spreading to others. You work your way up: goals imply problems; you solve them over and over; that is where you invest your attention, changing your life and affecting others. **Source:** Society Is A Pyramid Scheme (Take Back Control Of Your Life).md.

This two-step process is the structural outline of the whole book. Step one — awareness — is the subject of 2.7 and closes Part I. Step two — creating one's own hierarchy of goals that orders the mind — is the work of Parts III and IV, where goals are explained as lenses (Chapter 6), as problems (Chapter 8) and as the structure of a game (Chapter 10). The phrase "to order your mind" anticipates the concept of order in consciousness (Chapter 5).

#### The system is rigged: learn the rules

A related principle, from 2022, frames the same situation as a game. In an open-world strategy game like *World of Warcraft*, players follow common patterns: stack gold, choose a profession, level up a character. Life has a "macro game" with similar patterns. "The system is rigged, you can't change it but you can learn it, that is how you rig yourself in the system's favor." The conventional path to success "has already been programmed into the collective psyche before we know it," due to what the author calls the **curse of knowledge**. He uses that phrase in his own sense, different from its usual meaning: the human drive to know and learn more — learning being the foundation of human experience — combined with not questioning what we learn. So before we know it we are pursuing a game others laid out, "usually in favor of maintaining the game itself." And "90% of the time it just doesn't work out that way": the path thought to be secure leaves "90% of people, or however many percent," with too much anxiety, stress and overwhelm, "trapped in this jail or prison of their own doing." **Source:** How I Turned My Life Into A Video Game.md; Get Ahead Of 99% Of People With Deep Work & Monk Mode.md. The percentage is self-hedged.

**Complementary context:** In standard usage, the "curse of knowledge" is a cognitive bias described by economists Camerer, Loewenstein and Weber (1989): once you know something, it is hard to imagine not knowing it, which makes experts poor at explaining things to beginners. The author's usage is unrelated.

The principle has a practical corollary: "You can't break free in an instant because that's just not how things work. First, you learn the rules of the game and then you kind of create your own rules of the game without breaking the other rules." You play the game others want for you, as everyone does, learning from parents, "but then eventually you reflect and you question": what can I actually do, how can I create my own game and get better results than those before me? **Source:** Don't Find A Niche. Become The Niche.md. This is the author's answer to the question of how rebellion should proceed: not by smashing the existing game but by mastering it enough to design a better one. It connects with his later idea that templates and frameworks are training wheels (Chapter 23) and with the stepping-stone view of employment in 2.3.

He also sees signs that the old game is breaking down. "The flaws in the system itself are revealing itself and the programmers can't patch the game fast enough" — "who are the programmers? I have no idea." More people work remotely and do their own thing. School curriculums cannot keep up with the creator economy, which educates people to do their own thing rather than training them into the conventional employment system to which school is tied. In banking, whatever one thinks of Bitcoin or decentralized currency, someone saw a problem and individuals and small teams are building solutions. Freelancers with digital skills are hired by big companies and individuals as contractors rather than employees. These, he says, are the people "actively trying to solve the problem of this faulty system." **Source:** Get Ahead Of 99% Of People With Deep Work & Monk Mode.md. **Patch the game** is his coined image for the system's inability to fix its own flaws at the speed of change; it is labelled opinion and is developed historically in 2.6.

The 2022 formula — "rig yourself in the system's favor" — stands in tension with a 2025 formulation: "society is rigged against you," followed by a list of the ways (your boss, marketing, food, health, social circles, dating, politicians, therapists). The shift is from a strategic, playful attitude to an enumeration of how the system works against the individual. The two are compatible — the system is against you by default, which is why it pays to learn it — and the author's "first learn the rules, then create your own" is the bridge, but he does not make the connection himself.

#### Society as a pyramid of attention

The most original extension of the pyramid image appears in 2023: "Society is a pyramid scheme of attention." The premise is metaphysical in tone: "If something is not given attention it does not exist, and if it does not exist it must be given attention, and should be able to be given attention, in order to not only come to life but to survive." The author connects it to spiritual teachings: "If you stop paying attention to who you are and feeding those thoughts then you'd experience death, ego death; that's what you hear if you're familiar with spiritual teachings and meditation; that's what they're saying: stop giving life to the negative aspects of what you don't want to pay attention to." **Source:** How To Escape Wage Slavery (Entrepreneurship Is Modern Survival).md. The **pyramid scheme of attention** is the author's coined term; the idea of ego death is taken generically from spiritual teachings and adapted.

From this premise he draws two realizations. The first concerns organizations. "How do megacorporations grow and thrive? They start small and they form a power hierarchy over time: fewer people with more power at the top and more people with less power at the bottom." The top tier — the company, its executives and board — "can only do what they do because a plethora of people are giving attention to the tasks, visions and values from the bottom up." This "pyramid of attention" lets those at the top focus on the big picture without doing the technical work. "What do you have to do first in order to work? It's pay attention. Attention is the root of all of it, so the company would collapse if there was no attention to build that company." Yet "often people aren't paying attention to what they're actually paying attention to; they don't see the depth behind their actions." **Source:** How To Escape Wage Slavery (Entrepreneurship Is Modern Survival).md. The idea that attention is the root resource is the thesis of Chapter 6 ("attention is the RAM") and of Chapter 25 (attention as power).

The second realization follows from the shape of the pyramid. "At the bottom of the pyramid it's low-skill grunt work, like a cashier at McDonald's, and by nature it is impossible for every single person that is at the bottom to rise up to higher and higher levels, simply because there's less people" at the top; "there has to be the attention filled from under." "This is why I see many nine to five jobs as a stepping stone to doing what you want, or even job hopping until you get to where you want." **Source:** How To Escape Wage Slavery (Entrepreneurship Is Modern Survival).md. Here the stepping-stone view of employment is derived from structure rather than conceded as an exception: since the base of the pyramid must always be filled, the sensible use of a position there is as a transition.

The first realization also carries a moral charge: "you are contributing to **unconscious destruction**." "The people at the bottom are unconscious of what they're actually contributing to." "McDonald's workers probably don't understand or care that they are poisoning millions of people across the country," because "they probably aren't giving attention to the nutrition knowledge" needed to know what it takes to be healthy. "If they did have that education or health knowledge then they probably wouldn't be working at McDonald's"; they would be working as, or under, a nutrition coach or in other health and fitness jobs, "because they paid attention to the things that gave them that knowledge." Other examples: "military programmers write the code that kills millions of people on the other side of the planet," or "a web designer that creates websites for a person that scams people." He cites the saying "forgive them for they know not what they do." **Source:** How To Escape Wage Slavery (Entrepreneurship Is Modern Survival).md.

**Complementary context:** "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do" is from the Gospel of Luke (23:34), spoken by Jesus at the crucifixion. The author cites it without naming the source.

The examples are deliberately provocative and the claim about poisoning is stated rhetorically, not supported. What the passage contributes to the argument is a concept: one's attention is a contribution, and directing it unconsciously can mean contributing to outcomes one would reject if one saw them. That is why, in the author's system, awareness of where attention goes is a moral as well as a practical matter.

#### The status game

The pyramid image can make status sound like the enemy. The author's treatment of status, from 2024, corrects that impression and adds nuance. "You can reject the status game, but by doing so you choose to be low status" — decreasing your impact, increasing your suffering, and never realizing that you still chase status. Status-seeking is "an immutable principle in human nature" since the dawn of time. "To think that you aren't chasing status as a noble pursuit is still chasing status" — just as the desire to kill the ego is still a desire. That is not bad; it is natural, and once you accept it you begin to be rewarded. People judge you by perceived status; not realizing this means accepting a life of being treated unfairly, with close to zero impact. **Source:** The Value Equation How To Become A High-Status Individual.md. The **status game**, in this sense, is the competition for status inherent in human nature.

Status operates in every circle — your friends, your job or career, your religious organization. People assign it when they first see you, which is out of your control, but you can position yourself to make a high-status perception more likely. On that perception people decide whether to engage with you, offer opportunities, hire, pay or help you. Even the leaders we glorify — the author names Jesus Christ, Eckhart Tolle, Naval Ravikant, Alan Watts, Jordan Peterson, Ken Wilber, any thought leader — "are playing a status game whether they say they are or they aren't"; he doubts it is unintentional given their awareness, since how else would they attract large followings perceived as high status and change the direction of evolution? He rejects the edge case of high-status people who neglect inner work: status is one part of a good life, not the whole, and should not be pursued at all costs. "Money doesn't buy happiness" does not mean you should not try; refusing would close you to the experience of playing the game of life and pushing further toward depth and meaning. **Source:** The Value Equation How To Become A High-Status Individual.md.

Why does it matter to be conscious of this? Because "contributing to humanity is the prerequisite to getting something from humanity," and status-seeking is natural. If it remains unconscious, "you will manipulate and cheat without knowing it; you will be the cause of evil without knowing it," because you will not learn the inner workings of your mind that would let you turn the status you create into something beneficial for others. Even a "consciousness scale" — a hierarchy of levels of consciousness — is a status hierarchy: telling someone to reach the highest level of absolute love is still persuading them it is worth pursuing. He does not say the scale is wrong; it is a tool, an ideology, a construct for moving in a better direction — as is understanding status. **Source:** The Value Equation How To Become A High-Status Individual.md. The parallel with "unconscious destruction" is exact: in both cases the harm comes not from the drive itself but from its operating outside awareness.

**Complementary context:** The "scale of consciousness" most likely refers to David R. Hawkins's "Map of Consciousness" in *Power vs. Force* (1995), which ranks emotional and spiritual states numerically from shame to enlightenment.

Status, however, is not self-sufficient. "To become high status you must become valuable, or else that status is just an illusion and you're deceiving more than you are persuading" people to give you what you want. The author quotes *The Art of Focus*: "the path of the problem solver or value creator is how you escape the world of replaceability. Fall in love with the challenge that problems present, from superficial to metaphysical, and your ideal future will create itself." Value is created by solving problems, creating solutions, forging your own path and creating something unique with the story you carve out. **Source:** The Value Equation How To Become A High-Status Individual.md. "The world of replaceability" ties back to the "replaceable unit of society" of 2.1: the escape from replaceability is not status but value. The **value creator** is a central figure of Chapter 35.

A concrete example shows the author playing the game consciously. "I drive a fairly nice car; that's the one thing that I allow myself to like splurge on": a Mercedes GT63 S, "pretty fast, it sounds good, it's matte black so it's on brand, but it is a status game and I'm aware of that, and I feel like if people are aware that they're playing status games then it helps you not become a slave to those things." The car, the way you dress, nice locations, living somewhere nice give "access to this network and opportunities that are just given to you if you look good." The contrast: if you look "like a homeless guy because you don't care in your hyper-spiritual hippie" way, "but you're struggling to make money and survive and deep down you actually hate your life, nobody's going to come up and talk to you." If you are presentable and "show that you invest in how people perceive you," people approach — "if a billionaire comes up and talks to you and gives you a million dollar opportunity, that's available to you now." He calls it "more of a luck game, but it is a game, and it affects your mindset; it's abundance, being able to spend this money knowing that you have the resources and knowledge and education to make it back." **Source:** A Dangerous (But Effective) Strategy To Get Out Of A Rut.md.

The example closes the loop of this section. The collective societal vision has people chasing status games unconsciously — fancy cars bought with money earned by spending attention all day. The author's car is the same object chosen knowingly. The difference he insists on is not the object but the awareness with which the game is played: "if people are aware that they're playing status games, then it helps you not become a slave to those things." That principle — the same action, transformed by awareness — is exactly what 2.7 sets out to explain.

### 2.6 From the Industrial Paradigm to the Information Age

The institutions described so far — school, the job, the pyramid — did not appear from nowhere. The author places them in history: they are the products of an industrial worldview that made sense in its time and is now obsolete. This section reconstructs that historical frame, the cultural habits that keep people in the old paradigm (the glorification of the grind, the illusion of certainty), and the author's reading of the society that is replacing it. It also contains some of his most speculative claims, which are marked as such.

#### The industrial paradigm

The author's 2026 vocabulary names the source of the default path directly: the **industrial paradigm**, also called "industrial values," "industrial standards" or "industrial mindset." It is the worldview that says "becoming a specialist, getting a job that requires you to perform a mechanical string of tasks for 40 years, and retiring at an age where your money can't be put to great use outside of buying material objects because you were deprived for so long, is still the best route." Because "most people still have a worldview influenced by the industrial paradigm," society "has convinced you that that trait... of loving learning or having multiple interests is a weakness" — and you may believe it, because you spend all day in rabbit holes "and frankly you don't really have much to show for it. All you have is a bit of knowledge." The author "can confidently tell you that that is not the best route." **Source:** If You Have Multiple Interests, Start A One-Person Business.md. The term is new in 2026, but it formalizes a critique the author had been making since 2022 (the school–job–retire route of 2.3). The defence of multiple interests against the specialist ideal is the subject of Chapter 20.

The paradigm's central irony is that it believes itself safe. Most people are still conditioned by industrial values: they think that going to school, getting a job and retiring at some age is safe and secure, "when it's the least safe and secure route." The same holds, he adds, for building leverage and increasing one's ability to generate wealth. The author frames this as both the problem and the opportunity. **Source:** The Writing System That Saved My Brain (Learn Faster & Think Clearly).md.

Industrial standards also produce a specific blindness. Most people were raised to become specialists, study one domain hard, and get a high-paying job so that friends think them successful. So they stayed blind to most of the process: they understood their one skill, "but you didn't try to understand the system that paid you." Not having spent time on other domains, "all you know is how to fill a role in someone else's thing," and the ability to think is crushed. Even if you are smart in your skill and decently paid, you do not feel financially stable, so you get caught in a chaotic **stress loop**, and "stress narrows the mind," making a life of building your own thing seem unfathomable. Stuck in the thirds — sleep, work, exhaustion — you have no capital saved, no time or energy for personal development, and you are too tired, "spiritually, not just physically," to re-educate yourself, because most of your waking life fuels someone else's vision. **Source:** How To Become So Valuable AI Can Never Replace You.md. The stress loop is the author's term for chronic financial stress that narrows the mind; it explains why the people who most need to change course are least able to see the alternative — a version of the perceptual filtering described in 2.1.

The paradigm also supplies a strategy that no one chose. The average person does not solve problems; they "live the same day over and over again because that's what the conditioning process led to." Parents and teachers "injected values and beliefs into their head that put them on the default path heading toward the goal that society wanted for them, which is go to school, get a job, retire at 65... the industrial paradigm." "By the time they turn 20, it had become so conditioned... it's just habitual... unconscious." "Everyone has a strategy, but for most people, it's not one that they created. It's one that they were assigned": be a good student, make a decent amount of money, "be humble, don't stick your nose out. Your dreams aren't worth pursuing because they're risky — which doesn't make sense, because risk is the only way to get reward." **Source:** The Art of Strategic Thinking (How to Become Wildly Successful at Anything You Do).md. The **assigned strategy** is the strategic counterpart of assigned goals (Chapter 1). Strategic thinking, by contrast, moves you to "a more advantageous position where their problems aren't so painful... of a lesser magnitude... more fun and creative problems to solve. You start to see life as a puzzle rather than a death sentence." And the new paradigm of AI and information "requires a completely different strategy whether or not you agree"; the assigned one was "only somewhat beneficial to the old way of life, the American dream." Strategy is developed in Chapter 17.

The author finds an unexpected witness for the prosecution. He opens a 2026 video with Adam Smith, "who had a huge influence on the birth of capitalism": "The man whose whole life is spent in performing a few simple operations generally becomes as stupid and ignorant as it is possible for a human creature to become." He finds it funny, because Smith "contributed to it, if not created it" — the industrial age, capitalism, free markets, employment. He immediately adds: "I'm not against capitalism. I think it's going to evolve into something better, hopefully." **Source:** If you have multiple interests, do not waste the next 2-3 years.md. He labels the idea the video opens with "the death of the expert."

**Complementary context:** The quotation is from Book V of Adam Smith's *The Wealth of Nations* (1776). It appears in a passage where Smith argues that the division of labour, which he praises in Book I with the example of the pin factory, can degrade the intellectual life of workers, and that public education should counteract this. Smith's own position was therefore that specialization is economically productive and humanly costly — close to the tension the author identifies.

#### Mimetic grind culture

One reason the industrial paradigm persists, the author argues, is imitation. "Humans are mimetic creatures": we imitate to survive and to avoid being cast out of our family or of a productivity-obsessed culture; "our mind takes the shape of that which allows us to fit in." The problem is what we imitate. Everyone glorifies the **visible extreme** — the young startup phenom who built a $1M business in three weeks "just from grinding." It feels relatable, and it confirms what we have been told: harder and longer means more likely to succeed. But that is wrong; there is a deeper formula. A social-media **highlight reel** driven by **unconscious competence** is not reality. The phrase is familiar from the psychology of learning, where it names the last stage of skill acquisition, but the author bends it to his own purpose: here unconscious competence is what a highlight reel shows — the visible result of a skill with the process that produced it left out of the frame, whether because the performer no longer notices it or because it does not make good content. (Elsewhere he uses the same phrase for the intuitive command of marketing, sales and writing that successful artists or programmers have without naming it, for brands that are their niche without realizing it, and for people born into success, whom he excludes from the pattern of founders; the common thread is competence whose causes are invisible to the observer.) You can spend 10,000 hours writing ten books that never reach more than fifty readers, while someone who knows how to distribute a mediocre book sells millions because they focused on what produces results. People miss the context: the **invisible extreme** that actually led to the success of most creatives, visionaries and strategists. **Source:** Harsh Truth You Don't Need To Grind 247 To Be Successful.md. The mimetic idea is used here without attribution; the author develops the conscious use of imitation in Chapter 1 (intelligent imitation) and the role of distribution in Chapter 25.

Beneath the cultural pressure the author identifies hidden fears and desires that tie people to the grind. They romanticize the long, hard route. Underlying trauma makes them want to prove themselves to people who will not or do not care. Raised in a frugal family, they delay success because deep down they are afraid to make money, so they work longer hours to feel they are doing something. And they think they do not deserve leverage yet, so they do everything themselves or everything at once. Meanwhile it is no longer socially acceptable to say you found and exploited a shortcut, and stopping overwork brings boredom and the feeling of falling behind. **Source:** Harsh Truth You Don't Need To Grind 247 To Be Successful.md. These are the author's observations about motives, not a clinical typology; their value is diagnostic, as prompts for self-examination. The alternative — working less with more leverage — is the 4-Hour Workday of Chapter 12 and the "leveraged, not hard-working" thesis of Chapter 34.

#### The illusion of certainty

The deepest psychological reason for clinging to the default path is the fear of uncertainty. "It is impossible to know with absolute certainty what the future holds; this is why the masses flock to secure jobs and belief systems. It's an **illusion of certainty** to avoid struggle." In the earlier version he adds: "it's a trap." And because there is no way to know in advance what you will want, you cannot skip making mistakes: "mistakes are your light in the dark on this journey." **Source:** How To Do Whatever The Fck You Want.md; If Your Life Is Spiraling Out Of Control, Here's The Solution To Feeling Lost.md. Note that the author pairs secure jobs with belief systems: both offer the same psychological product — a pre-made order that spares the mind the struggle of creating its own.

From this he draws a warning in the form of a list. "The fastest way to ruin your life": do what others want for you; never question what you are told; "take the route that seems safe on the surface but is the least safe of them all"; avoid "the essence of life, trial and error"; close yourself off to the profound, the deep and the meaningful. "The greatest mistake is not making any mistakes at all." "This is the life of the masses": they bounce around on the surface, live the same day over and over, learn only what they were taught in school, clock in, clock out, and fill the rest of the day "numbing your mind from the thought of what will happen" tomorrow. **Source:** If Your Life Is Spiraling Out Of Control, Here's The Solution To Feeling Lost.md. "The greatest mistake is not making any mistakes at all" repeats, in the author's own words, the conclusion he drew from Devon Eriksen's critique of grades in 2.2. **The masses** is the author's recurring label for people living on the surface, the same day repeated.

A 2025 version explains why the trap is so easy to fall into. "The fastest way to ruin your life is to follow someone else's plan." The mind craves order; without thinking, we seek security, safety and comfort. When he was young his fate was in his parents' and teachers' hands; too young to trust his own thinking, he followed them, because it was the only path he knew — "and that's where things go wrong." "The path of least risk is the greatest risk of all"; "a life of comfort is the most uncomfortable thing in the world." So we loop: seek comfort, become uncomfortable, seek more comfort, become more uncomfortable, until we are deep in a hole that is hard to dig out of. "If it's so comfortable, why do you have to numb the pain with quick pleasure?" **Source:** The Fastest Way To Ruin Your Life (Avoid This While You're Young).md. The **comfort loop** — the cycle in which seeking comfort generates more discomfort — connects to the cheap dopamine of Chapter 11: quick pleasures are the anaesthetic for the discomfort that comfort produces.

The author finds the same idea in Krishnamurti, whom he connects to entropy. Tradition becomes our security, and when the mind is secure "it is in decay." The author's gloss: when you feel stable, "just chilling," you are slowly decaying — like a vacation that becomes normal — and you do not notice until you realize you are in a much worse situation, which is harder to dig out of the longer you wait. "You cannot make discoveries in the known." You cannot live a full, open, non-robotic life by operating according to what parents and teachers planted. You can be happy at times, but deep fulfilment is different; most people have not experienced it, so they do not search for it, and they project their insecurities by claiming fulfilment while working "as a robot would" — "the lines of code are engraved on their brain." **Source:** How To Make The Greatest Comeback Of Your Life.md. The quotation is Krishnamurti's; the connection with entropy is the author's adaptation, which anticipates Chapter 5's claim that there is no such thing as staying the same.

Even those who try to leave often fail at the threshold. The major problem is that it is too easy for modern man to get sucked into "a **mindless trap of mediocrity, degeneracy and roboticism**." When people try to break from the default path into the unknown, they get scared, dip a toe in, realize they are comfortable, and step out: the water is too cold or too hot, there is too much information to explore, too many opportunities causing overwhelm, too many opinions causing anxiety. "To find clarity you have to battle through the chaos"; you cannot shy away at the first sign of struggle. **Source:** Focus Is A Superpower (Take Back Control Of Your Life).md. The image of dipping a toe in water makes concrete the asymmetry of 2.1: years for the default path, a week for one's own.

The author's diagnosis ends in a claim about responsibility. Formal education "has its place," but it has been steadily losing trust in its ability to secure people's future (and, he argues, people never had absolute trust in it). Forging your own path is uncertain: you have to create your own way rather than have one "placed in front of you so that your mind can conform to that and have that clarity" — and only exploring the unknown leads to discoveries and insights. "People inherently know that life enjoyment is a choice, but nobody wants to face that reality, so they **outsource their quality of life** to the over-exaggerated promises of schools and jobs." **Source:** Become A Digital Renaissance Man (And Join The New Rich).md. The phrase names the core move of the default path: handing the responsibility for one's own enjoyment to institutions that promise it in exchange for compliance.

#### A historical lens: technoeconomic bases

To explain how societies come to have the shape they have, the author gives what he calls "a brief history lesson," in a video about the "cheap dopamine epidemic." Societies can be classified by their **technoeconomic base** — "in a nutshell, their basic means of production," the things a society uses to meet its basic needs (the horse-drawn plow versus machine farming). He lists five, as follows.

| Technoeconomic base | What the author says about it |
|---|---|
| Foraging | Hunting and gathering; men hunted, women gathered. |
| Horticultural | Simple planting; women produced most of the food, and the society's deities became female. |
| Agrarian | Animal-drawn plows; women could not continue farming because of increased miscarriages, so roles changed and deities became male; 80% of agrarian societies relied on male slave labour. |
| Industrial | Named, not developed in this passage. |
| Informational | Named, not developed in this passage. |

The pattern he highlights: "whoever produced the most foods, or whoever produced the most in general, whether it was male or female, became the deities of that society." **Source:** The Cheap Dopamine Epidemic Stop Ruining Your Life.md.

He then develops the agrarian shift as a chain. In agrarian societies women could not operate the horse-drawn plow because of too many miscarriages — "it was a Darwinian disadvantage for women to do that thing" — so roles shifted, men produced more of the food, and women took over more "quote-unquote traditional roles of tending to the house and the family." This marks "a massive shift in culture," "the rise of the patriarchy, so to say," notable because women had been the deities "for most of human civilization." And because the plow produced an abundance of food, men did not have to work as much; they had more time for thinking and contemplation, "and this is what led to the invention of writing and mathematics." **Source:** The Cheap Dopamine Epidemic Stop Ruining Your Life.md.

The author does not name a source for this framework in the transcript. Its vocabulary — "technoeconomic base," together with other terms recorded alongside it such as "great chain of being" and "physiosphere/biosphere/noosphere" — suggests integral theory, but this is an inference.

**Complementary context:** Ken Wilber, in *Sex, Ecology, Spirituality* (1995) and *A Brief History of Everything* (1996), uses the classification of societies by "techno-economic base" — foraging, horticultural, agrarian, industrial, informational — drawing on the sociologist Gerhard Lenski, and discusses the plow, women's status and the rise of patriarchy along the lines the author summarizes. The historical claims (for instance, the role of miscarriages, or the 80% figure) are part of Wilber's synthesis, and are debated by historians and anthropologists; the author presents them as background, not as his own research.

The function of the history lesson in the author's argument is clear even where its details are uncertain: societies take the shape of their means of production, and so a change in the means of production — from industrial to informational — implies a change in the shape of society, including its institutions of school and work.

The same video series adds a claim about the mental world. We keep building the physical world, and our minds must adapt, evolve and transcend to have the ideas that create it; every physical thing created demands "ten, a hundred, a thousand ideas and iterations of the ideas in our mind." This makes the information landscape we inhabit drastically different from the old world. At the inception of human consciousness we "transcended and included" the physical and biological world — animal life; each stage of evolution holds everything beneath it, but what lies above it has many times the depth and span (the transcript's numbers are garbled). So the mental world is far larger and more chaotic than the physical and biological, but it gives much more creative ability. **Source:** Focus Is A Superpower (Take Back Control Of Your Life).md. The claim is adapted from Wilber's "transcend and include." Its importance for the book is that it locates the challenge of the information age in the mind: the environment that now needs to be navigated is mostly mental, which is why attention and focus (Part III) become central.

Two other historical-cultural remarks complete the frame. The first, stated as opinion: "In today's world postmodern thinking has largely gone pathological. This has resulted in things like DEI or gender politics and attempting to dismantle all hierarchies, which is stupid and impossible, because by saying all hierarchies are bad, you still form a value ranking. You still form a hierarchy." (The transcript continues, "It's just not a hierarchy that you don't like," which appears to be a slip for "a hierarchy you do like.") **Source:** This mental model will make you think like a strategic genius.md. The remark connects with 2.5: the author does not oppose hierarchy as such, only the dominator kind, and he regards the attempt to abolish all hierarchy as self-refuting. The label **pathological postmodernism** is his; the reader should treat its political examples as the author's opinion.

The second is a framing quotation from Krishnamurti that the author uses to open the history section of a 2026 video, asking the viewer to "think about that as we go through this section": "It is no measure of health to be well-adjusted to a profoundly sick society." **Source:** How To Think Like A Strategic Genius (5-Dimensional Thinking).md. In context the quotation recasts the default path: adjusting well to the industrial paradigm is not, in itself, a sign of health.

#### The age of intelligence: outdated software

If the industrial paradigm was a response to its era, what changes when the era changes? The author's answer from 2026: "Think of where we are right now in the **age of intelligence**. If you are still operating on industrial-age technology as a business, or you think that the right path... is go to school, get a job, retire at 65... you're running on this outdated software and you need to change it." "AI is on our doorstep and no one knows what to do next... That's the biggest problem." Looking back at history lets us "at least tell whether what we're doing is good or not." Running a business on industrial technology "is probably not a smart thing." (The transcript at one point says "if you are integrating AI in some way, transcending and including, then you're probably falling behind," which, given the logic of the passage, is almost certainly a slip for "if you are *not* integrating AI.") For an individual, the risk is keeping the industrial plan "when jobs are at threat of automation" without thinking creatively. He adds a disclaimer: "everything I say obviously isn't going to be correct, but I do think it's heading in the right direction. I'm open to being wrong... I'm not just telling people to sit around and just be bulldozed over." **Source:** How To Think Like A Strategic Genius (5-Dimensional Thinking).md. The image of **outdated software** fits the author's computational vocabulary for conditioning (Chapter 1): the default path is a program written for hardware that no longer exists.

The argument rests on the rate of change. During the industrial age there was "not too much change. That's why it's so deeply ingrained to go to school, get a job, retire at 65, because the societal system was built up according to that paradigm." "Now with AI and disruption... everything is changing every 3 to 6 months, and the rate of change will only increase, and it's going to filter out so many people who get stuck with a rigid strategy." "The future belongs to the true strategist at this higher level of thinking... Masters can adapt on the fly because they have the universal principles that they can apply to all domains. They don't necessarily need to relearn everything. They don't need to upskill or reskill or re-educate, because they can do that extremely fast on their own." And: "Your job is to respond to what's actually happening then and there on the battlefield, not your mental fabrications of worst-case scenarios or your fantasies that are not yet real." **Source:** The Art of Strategic Thinking (How to Become Wildly Successful at Anything You Do).md. The "every 3 to 6 months" is an impression, not a measurement. The conclusion connects to two later ideas: principles over tactics (Chapter 15) and the strategist as a stage of development (Chapter 38). It also recalls Devon Eriksen's reply to Harari in 2.2: if what matters is learning how to learn, an unpredictable future is not a reason for paralysis.

#### The emerging society

The author's positive reading of the transition rests on one principle: society shapes itself around how people earn. "Everyone wants to be a content creator, and this isn't a bad thing, especially if you can predict where the future of work is going." Boomers will tell you to "get a real job" when those jobs will not exist in a few decades; they do not realize that the Industrial Age created those jobs, nor that the information age has created "new and more profitable jobs." "Profitability determines the direction of society and the economy; technology allows for more profitable lines of work." **Source:** How Intelligent Creators Will Make Money In 2024 (The Build Teach Earn Method).md.

He found the same principle in *The Sovereign Individual*, a book whose authors he does not name. As he summarizes it, nations will fragment into millions of city-states and even individual estates with sovereign status, as information technology makes resources available to more people and changes society's political and economic structure. "How people make the most money impacts the evolution of society": society shapes itself around the most profitable jobs and businesses, and a new way of earning makes society adapt to increase wealth. His own mapping: the creator economy is composed of brands (city-states) and creators (the individual estates that maintain their own sovereignty). He says the book predicted what he had been preaching for a year, a conclusion he reached by pursuing his own goals. **Source:** The Value Creator (A New Internet Career Path For Intelligent People).md.

**Complementary context:** *The Sovereign Individual* (1997) is by James Dale Davidson and William Rees-Mogg. It argues that the information revolution will erode the power of nation-states and shift power toward individuals and small jurisdictions. The brands-as-city-states mapping is the author's adaptation.

The new society, in his account, does not arrive all at once. "The first thing is to join the new society, and when I say new society I mean emerging society, because that's what ideas do": they do not just pop up; "they evolve, they come from something, they emerge over time." "The new society is already here, but it's taking time to transition... and the old society is clearly dying and phasing out as it has been." **Source:** If Your Life Is Spiraling Out Of Control, Here's The Solution To Feeling Lost.md. The **new society** — alias "emerging society" — is the author's term for the social order already forming while the old one fades; elsewhere he applies it to social media as "not an app but a new society" (Chapter 25).

The signs of the transition are those already described in 2.5 under the image of the programmers who "can't patch the game fast enough" — remote work, a creator economy that school curricula cannot keep up with, decentralized currency built by individuals and small teams who saw a problem in the monetary system, and agencies hiring skilled freelancers as contractors instead of employees. The image first appears in 2022, in "How I Turned My Life Into A Video Game," where it follows directly from the "system is rigged" principle: the game is rigged, but its flaws are now visible faster than they can be fixed. **Source:** How I Turned My Life Into A Video Game.md.

In 2025 he generalizes the reading of the present as a period of transition. We are in a very noisy time on social media and YouTube; "when there's a lot of conflict, a lot of chaos, that means that a **new ordered structure** is going to emerge," though we do not yet know what. "Thankfully, human nature remains pretty much the same." This period of rapid growth draws a clear line between machines and humans: "Those who lean into their humanity will thrive," while those who identify with mechanical living may not. **Source:** You Have About 36 Months To Make It.md. The idea that order emerges from chaos is the author's adaptation of a principle developed in Chapter 5 (order out of chaos, in the sense of dissipative structures); "mechanical living" — identifying with school, job and repetitive tasks — is the industrial paradigm seen from the side of identity.

The author's most compact argument for the new society is a chain of conditionals from 2023. "If humanity is only as strong as its weakest link, and 99% of people suffer from the same survival problems, and education is what allows the individual to solve their own problems rather than being prescribed temporary relief, and problems are what prevent personal to collective evolution, and if the education system is focused on training people into jobs for its own benefit, then the **new digital society of value creators** is one realistic path out of this mess." **Source:** People Dumber Than You Are Making Millions.md. The argument is worth reading as a structure, because it shows how the chapter's pieces fit together.

| Premise | Where the book develops it |
|---|---|
| Humanity is only as strong as its weakest link | 2.9 (conscious individuals and civilization) |
| Most people share the same survival problems | 2.3–2.4 (employment, survival, the hunting psyche) |
| Education lets individuals solve their own problems rather than receive temporary relief | 2.2 (true education, self-education) |
| Problems block personal and collective evolution | Chapter 8 (purpose as problem) |
| The education system trains people into jobs for its own benefit | 2.2 (the school as a system that survives) |
| Conclusion: a digital society of value creators is a realistic exit | Parts X–XII (the one-person business and the economy of the individual) |

The conclusion is modest in its wording — "one realistic path," not the only one — and the "99%" is again a rhetorical estimate. But the chain makes explicit the author's view that the critique of institutions and the economics of the individual are two halves of one argument.

### 2.7 Awareness: The Healing Sixth Sense

Section 2.5 described the author's two-step exit from modern enslavement: first become aware, then create your own hierarchy of goals. Everything in this chapter so far has served the first step — making visible the institutions that install the default path. This section turns to awareness itself: what the author means by it, how it grows, why he believes it heals, and how it is practised through observation. It ends with the episode the author presents as his own awakening.

It helps to note first how the author frames the purpose of this kind of awareness, since his stance changed. In 2022 he spoke of "breaking free" of the Matrix and of the "red pill"; but already in late 2022, and again in 2024, he distances himself from the phrase — build your own thing, be independent, "break free of the Matrix if you want to frame it that way," and live an enjoyable life on your own terms. **Source:** Get Ahead Of 99% Of People With Deep Work & Monk Mode.md. By 2025 he states outright that the goal is not to "break off from society": the only way out is to understand the system. Awareness, in the mature version, is not escape but comprehension — seeing the program clearly enough that one can stop being run by it.

#### Awareness as a sixth sense

The author's most ambitious definition comes from 2022. Most people are unaware of "the sixth sense, which is awareness. This is the foundation of creativity." Through awareness we perceive things beyond what the five senses make sense of — a feeling, a thought, something intangible that people operating from "the materialist paradigm" do not value. And this awareness is stored in the subconscious, letting you draw on more information when you create. **Source:** How To Make Money As A Creative On The Internet.md. The phrase **sixth sense** here is the author's own metaphor, not a claim about a literal sensory organ; the "materialist paradigm" is his name for the worldview that only values what can be measured by the five senses. The link between awareness and creativity is developed in Chapter 18.

#### Awareness begets awareness

The second feature of awareness is that it grows in sequence. "Awareness begets awareness, thoughts beget thoughts, ideas beget ideas." You cannot become aware of something at a higher level if you were not first aware of something at the level below. The author compares the unknown to the map of a video game: areas you have not explored are not available to you; you are not conscious of them; you do not know what is there and can only guess. You have to reach one location before you can reach the next, and eventually you build a network you can tap into with your awareness — to draw from, to be creative, and to expand your mind toward new perspectives and "new realities in a sense." **Source:** How To Create A Better Life For Yourself.md. **Awareness begets awareness** is the author's coined formula: progress in awareness is sequential, each step unlocking the next.

The same map image gives a measure of how little most people see. If you have not branched into the unknown, "you understand less than .1% of reality." The author doubts anyone reaches 100% — perhaps "the masters, the select few" — and argues that the average person in a repetitive routine, not pursuing their own goals, is "closer to 0.00001%." "It's not all money, girls, Lambos": people chasing those are still solving **survival needs** and "can't even access their **growth needs** yet, of challenge, skill acquisition and understanding." In a game, you cannot progress to new areas of the map until you acquire the skill and ability to survive there; levelling up unlocks quests, dungeons, special abilities, career choices, and the ability to ride or fly to new parts of the world. **Source:** Life Is A Video Game (Here's How You Win).md. The percentages are, explicitly, opinion and rhetorical. The pair survival needs / growth needs is the author's; it resembles Maslow's distinction between deficiency and growth needs, though the author does not cite Maslow here.

A third formula ties awareness to development. Opening the mind does not happen overnight; you will not have "a monk-like perspective" after being closed-minded for a while — "that's why it's called development, because it takes time." First you must understand the signs of closed-mindedness, so that you can become aware of them and improve. "Awareness begets improvement," because you need awareness to improve, "and then improvement begets awareness of the next but better problem to solve." **Source:** Distraction Is The Greatest Trap Of The 21st Century (How To Avoid).md. **Awareness begets improvement** turns the sequence into a loop: awareness enables improvement, improvement reveals the next problem, and the next problem is a better one. This loop is the seed of the author's later view of life as a chain of ever-better problems (Chapter 8).

#### Awareness is curative

The most practical claim the author makes about awareness is that it heals. "When you feel tension or stress or the need to reproduce or react, you have to train yourself to pause. This is what mindfulness is." When you notice a thought, you become aware of it, "and that's really the cure to it: just becoming aware of it over time and letting that correct your actions with time." He states the limit honestly: you may succumb a few times; "it's not going to be perfect the first time around." You may notice you are in an angry phase and see your body react in real time, doing things out of your control — but you have the awareness, and "that will fix itself over time." "Awareness is curative; it's a medicine." **Source:** How To Reprogram Your Mind & Build Your Intelligence.md.

**Awareness is curative** (also "awareness is a cure") is the author's coined principle. In 2023 it means that noticing a thought or reaction is enough to correct it over time; in a 2024 formulation, developed in Chapter 7, it means that you do not need to force yourself to drop bad habits — it is enough to look at them through your vision long enough. The mechanism the author proposes is gradual: awareness does not stop the reaction the first time; it creates a gap in which, over repetitions, a different response becomes possible. This idea is developed as "interrupting autopilot" in Chapter 11.

The author places himself in a tradition here. Among books he recommended in 2022 is *Awareness* by Anthony de Mello, which JK Molina "turned him onto" — "the last spiritual one, kind of." It helps you navigate the world in a "calm, collected and aware way," gaining awareness of almost everything: your thoughts, your actions, other people, how they react and how you can respond. He describes it as a way to develop spiritual well-being and to navigate conversations, becoming aware of certain things so that you can "not only overcome them but kind of dissolve these negative traits and beliefs and mindsets that you have adopted over time through cultural conditioning." **Source:** 7 Books That Will Change Your Life In 2022.md. The phrase "dissolve... through cultural conditioning" connects awareness directly to Chapter 1: awareness is the solvent for the program.

**Complementary context:** Anthony de Mello (1931–1987) was an Indian Jesuit priest and spiritual teacher whose posthumously published *Awareness* (1990) argues that most people are "asleep," running on programming from society, and that simply observing one's reactions without condemnation is what dissolves them. The author's "awareness is curative" is close to de Mello's thesis, though the author presents his formula as his own.

#### Awareness before action

Awareness also has a methodological priority in the author's teaching, which explains the shape of his content and of this book. A section of one video is deliberately not "hyper-actionable," he explains, because you need awareness of a possibility in order to act on it. Steps without a reason, without a "why" that applies to your life and without intrinsic motivation, will not mean anything. Awareness of what is going on and of the opportunities comes first, then actionable steps for clarity — "and even then the actual steps are just a prescription... a temporary fix until you figure out how to do it on your own." His advice is to hold the ideas in mind as you go about life, so you can connect the dots. **Source:** Become A Digital Renaissance Man (And Join The New Rich).md.

In 2026 the same principle is stated more bluntly. Before the practical part of a video, he insists on theory: "you have to change your mind, you have to understand what's going on. You don't understand by me giving you practical steps." If you just want the steps, paste the video into a transcription tool, try to follow it, "and fail." **Source:** How I'd build a one-person business (if I started over in 2026).md. The consistency between 2023 and 2026 is notable. It is the same reasoning that led him to say, about the dog experiment in 2.1, that practical steps toward agency mean little without understanding how the problem applies. It is also why this book places the diagnosis (Part I) and the model of the person (Parts II–IV) before the systems (Parts V–XII).

#### The conscious decision-maker

What does a person look like who acts from awareness? The author's answer is the **conscious decision-maker**, and he defines its core skill in 2024: "There is one extremely important skill, and that is figuring it out for yourself, not doing what people tell you to do, and doing what you want from a conscious mind" — not from a "mediocre mind" that says "I can do whatever I want — you want me to jump off a bridge? Okay." The conscious mind asks questions: what are your desires; what survival mechanism or force pulls you toward them; is it good or bad; do you actually want it; does it align with your values; do you have values at all? What people tell you will not be conducive to what you want. You may have to do it for survival, but in parallel you must pursue a project of your own that leads to autonomy and mastery, full-time and not for someone else. Many of his own aims were deemed impossible by closed minds projecting their opinions. Hence, to pursue mastery and autonomy, you need a skill that monetizes your interests and passions — which is where his argument for writing begins (Chapter 21). **Source:** The One-Person Business Model (How To Productize Yourself Full Guide).md. The **conscious mind vs mediocre mind** contrast is the author's: the first examines desires, values and survival mechanisms; the second obeys. Note that the word "force" recurs here in the sense defined in 2.3: what pushes you, and how strongly.

The same idea appears in a conversation with Dickie Bush about high performers. The author attended a large gathering of entrepreneurs where some of the biggest names were passed out drunk, while other genuine high performers seemed to have enjoyable lives doing similar things. "It breaks your frame": "they're just conscious, they make conscious decisions, and they know themselves to the point where it's like, if I'm not making progress I'm changing something, and it doesn't matter how painful that's going to be, it's done." His own example: quitting *Call of Duty* was not even a struggle once he saw it was not worth it for his lifestyle. Bush's summary: "it's all self-awareness all the way down." The author adds that if you read the real backstories of the figures we praise — Alan Watts, Marcus Aurelius, the philosophers, Alexander the Great — the frame from which they are promoted "is like a highlight reel," which creates false expectations; "everyone's human, and it's really just a matter of making beneficial choices and self-correcting them over time." **Source:** Dan Koe & Dickie Bush On One-Person Businesses, Creative Workflows, and Lifestyle Design.md. "Self-awareness all the way down" is Bush's phrase; the deflation of idols as highlight reels is the author's, and it echoes the visible and invisible extremes of 2.6. The definition of high performance as "making beneficial choices and self-correcting them over time" is a compact statement of the cybernetic model of Chapter 6.

#### Observation of the masses

How is awareness practised? The author's characteristic method is observation, and it starts from a diagnosis. "Sovereign living, or autonomous living, or just being independent in building your own thing, your own way of survival, is difficult; it's uncertain." "The mind craves order, it craves certainty, so if there is a path that is easier or more certain or more secure for someone to take, that's where the masses flock, that's where 99% of people flock." **Source:** Get Ahead Of 99% Of People With Deep Work & Monk Mode.md. **Sovereign living** is his name for building your own way of survival — the hard, uncertain alternative to the default path.

Given that the masses take the certain path, observing them shows where it leads.
