To see where you will end up if you keep doing the same things, observe "the masses" and see where **mindless action** leads — "it's not pretty at all." The key condition is how you observe: sit with your thoughts, think them through, do not close your mind and accept what you see on the surface as reality. "That closed-minded surface-level living is what got you into this situation in the first place; you need to think deeper." **Source:** How To Get Ahead Of 99% Of People (In 6-12 Months).md. The method is the precursor of the anti-vision (Chapter 7), whose raw material is precisely the vivid image of where the current trajectory leads.

The method has an everyday form, which the author returns to again and again: the grocery store. Observe society and discern which daily actions lead to a good or bad life. At the store, see what someone puts in their basket and realize "that's how you end up like this person" — "not in a judgmental way." "You have to be able to make decisions through observation, and then you become less mindless when you put things into your own cart. Do I want to end up like that? No, I want to end up like this." Later in the same video he names the misuse: observing society only "to just reinforce what you've been told to do and then justify it." **Source:** Self Improvers Are Creating Their Own Careers (The New Economy).md.

He traces the habit to childhood. Since he was a child he was "obsessed with finding a better way of living." Everywhere he went he observed people's actions — what they put in their grocery baskets, their daily routines (go to work, go home, watch Netflix, fall asleep, repeat) — to discern whether doing those things would lead to the life they had, and whether he wanted that life. He asked what, how and why: what were they pursuing, how did they get where they are, why did they look the way they did. One example he gives is a person picking up "a 1,000-calorie dessert drink for breakfast with a sandwich that leaked grease from its wrapper." He admits there was some judgment as a teenager — "we all judge people, it's okay" — but says he wants "to shift that from judgment to discernment." The method: with enough observational data, decide "do I want that or do I not want that." **Source:** The Future Of Work Is Play (How To Create A Digital Career).md.

The earliest version (2022) adds the inward turn that makes observation a tool of self-knowledge. He describes himself as having always been a **silent observer** — not judgmental (he admits he was a bit judgmental at first, and that it is hard to escape) but "discerning." The practice has four steps: notice what others do (what they put in the cart, how they look); ask whether you want to look or be that way; notice "the reflection in yourself" — what reaction the observation causes in you; and ask what you can learn from that reaction. **Source:** If You Want To Secure Your Future… Follow This New Career Path.md. The point is not to evaluate others but to use them as a mirror.

#### Judgment versus discernment

The distinction between judging and discerning runs through all these passages, and the author states it as a principle in *The Art of Focus*: "Observation and questioning are how you learn to navigate difficult situations with wisdom and grace." And: "There is a distinction between judgment and discernment: judgment leads to closed-mindedness, but discernment allows you to pull from others' experiences in a way that helps you make wise decisions for your own development." **Source:** The Art Of Focus – Official Book Summary By The Author Dan Koe.md. **Judgment vs discernment** is the author's coined pair: judgment closes the mind around a verdict about the other person; discernment extracts information for one's own choices.

The same distinction governs comparison. At the grocery store he sees a very overweight person in a wheelchair with a cart full of junk food: he can "discern, not judge" that he does not want to end up like that, so he will not take those actions. "That's how you learn": "I don't want to be that guy, I want to be that guy." "Comparison can be a very good thing if perceived correctly," in every area of life. **Source:** Become A Digital Renaissance Man (And Join The New Rich).md. Later in the same video he qualifies the claim. Comparison is good only if you understand that there is a gap between you and the other person. Seeing someone you admire as an "overnight success," because you cannot comprehend the gap, is the danger. Instead, "make a positive assumption": this person did this, this and this to get there, our goals align, so I will follow that path — "in that case it's not comparison but connection." He adds that the assumption can also be a very bad one. **Source:** Become A Digital Renaissance Man (And Join The New Rich).md. **Comparison becomes connection** is the author's formula: comparison helps only when it recognizes the gap and makes a positive assumption about the path across it. The theme returns in Chapter 39 (comparison versus connection as part of happiness).

In 2025 the author adopts the very word he had avoided. His wife, then getting her Pilates certification, learned from her instructor that to fix your own posture over time, in public spaces "you just judge people's posture": noticing what bad posture looks like, you slowly correct your own. "The same holds true for me." Judging sounds bad, "let's call it observation and discernment." As a young man at the grocery store he saw people who did not look or act as he wanted to — what they bought, how they shopped, how they spoke — and corrected his own actions; at school and at church too. "You can see mediocrity all around you, just because that's the natural state of how things are unless people put effort into creating their own vision." "So judge, or observe society more. You don't need to tell them these things. You simply observe and correct your own actions." **Source:** 12 Rules To Change Your Life In 12 Months.md. The change is rhetorical rather than substantive: he uses "judge" where before he said "discern, not judge," but immediately redefines it as discernment and limits it to correcting one's own actions without saying anything to others. The Pilates image is useful because it makes the logic concrete: others' posture is information about one's own.

A broader tension sits behind these passages and the author never fully resolves it. On one side is a relativist empathy: "everyone is right and everyone is wrong, it's all relative"; transfer your awareness into the other person and assume a positive goal behind their actions; move "from judgment to discernment"; raise the collective consciousness. On the other, in parallel, is rhetorical contempt for "the masses": "if a boomer tells you to get a real job, you're on the right track"; the 99% who "blabber about how you should live your life when they wasted their own." The most coherent reading, compatible with what he says, is that empathy serves to understand perspectives, while the sharper dismissal serves to decide whose life advice to take. The discernment method lies between them: it observes without condemning, but it does draw conclusions.

#### The author's awakening: the arrest and *The Power of Now*

The author's account of awareness has an origin story, which he tells often and whose details vary. At eighteen or nineteen, in his first year of college, his roommate had just been left by his girlfriend (in Utah in one telling; for another man in another), and needed to "slow down"; someone told him "just go smoke some weed, you'll be fine" — the first option was "the magical Green Leaf." The author, his roommate and two friends sat in his car in a parking garage across from the dorms, laughing, until a friend saw a bike cop in the rearview mirror. The officer wrote down his license plate and handcuffed them; most of the substance and paraphernalia belonged to the author and his roommate. They were booked, fingerprinted and questioned about who had sold them the drugs, then sent home that night. **Source:** 7 Lessons From 7 Failed Online Businesses (And Making 7 Figures).md; This Simple Reading Habit Will Change Your Life (I Promise).md.

He forgot about it. Months later, in 2016, home for the summer and working as a lifeguard, he found a letter bearing a government seal. It offered two options: go to court and possibly be convicted of a felony for smoking an illicit drug on a school campus — very threatening to a teenager who took school seriously — or enrol in a drug diversion program with regular drug tests, which he could not afford. "My heart immediately sunk into my stomach." "My mind was shattered to pieces." He could not tell his parents, had no money, and could not become a felon; keeping it secret added to the stress. It was "arguably one of the lowest points" in his life. "The worry turned to anger, the anger turned to defeat, then an idea." **Source:** 7 Lessons From 7 Failed Online Businesses (And Making 7 Figures).md; This Simple Reading Habit Will Change Your Life (I Promise).md; Learn New Skills FAST (How I Remember Everything I Learn).md.

The idea came from fitness. He had been following Matt Ogus, one of a few "OG" fitness YouTubers from "the golden era of fitness YouTube," who had got him into the gym and whom he trusted and aspired to be like. Ogus had recommended *The Power of Now* by Eckhart Tolle many times — once during a bodybuilding contest prep, when very low body weight and hormones were wreaking havoc on his emotions and he turned to mindfulness and the book, which he said had really helped. "Spirituality — that's for hippies. But I was desperate." Every morning for about an hour he sat on his patio with a "terrible cup of coffee" — his uncle's favourite gas-station coffee in the blue container, "kind of like Folgers" — and read. **Source:** This Simple Reading Habit Will Change Your Life (I Promise).md; Learn New Skills FAST (How I Remember Everything I Learn).md; 7 Books That Will Change Your Life In 2022.md.

The effect, as he describes it, was immediate relief and a longer opening. "Read through it, and kind of all my worries just washed away." After dissecting the book, his worries vanished — "this isn't bad, I can deal with this when the time comes" — and he regained his drive. He calls the book "a catalyst to it all," one of the first self-help or spirituality books he ever read. **Source:** 7 Lessons From 7 Failed Online Businesses (And Making 7 Figures).md; 7 Books That Will Change Your Life In 2022.md. He read it closely, practised the meditations, and opened his mind to the possibility of a higher power, which he had closed himself off to as a rebellious teenager forced to go to church. The book eased his fear of a felony charge and helped him calm down and be less reactive toward things he disagreed with. "The lessons hit hard," making him imagine how much knowledge he had been missing that could have given him the tools for a better life. **Source:** Learn New Skills FAST (How I Remember Everything I Learn).md; This Simple Reading Habit Will Change Your Life (I Promise).md. The transcripts do not specify which ideas from the book he took, beyond relief from worry, presence and openness to spirituality. He also recommends Tolle's sequel, *A New Earth*.

**Complementary context:** Eckhart Tolle's *The Power of Now* (1997) teaches that suffering arises from identification with the thinking mind and with psychological time — dwelling on past and future — and that presence, the conscious awareness of the present moment, dissolves it. This is directly relevant to the next section on psychological time.

The author draws a learning lesson from the episode as well. He did not remember everything from the book, "but I remembered 10 times more than I did from other books" — those he was told to read or read just because he felt like it. His explanation has two parts. First, intention: "I had the intent; I was in that perfect place in life where the teaching stood out to me," because he had a practical problem to solve and something concrete to try in order to overcome the mental challenge he faced. Second, trust: Ogus was "someone that I aspired to be like and I trusted him," and trust in the recommender plus aspiration fed the genuine curiosity that made him read closely. **Source:** Learn New Skills FAST (How I Remember Everything I Learn).md. This is the origin of his principle that learning sticks when it serves a goal — the meta skill of Chapter 14 — and it shows the episode doing double duty in the corpus: as a spiritual awakening and as a case study in how information becomes knowledge.

The details of the story vary across tellings, as the author's anecdotes often do. The program is "a diversion class with daily color-code texts and drug tests for six months" costing "$5,000–10,000" (2022); "a 12-week program" and "about $5,000" (2022); "about ten thousand dollars" with weekly random tests (2022); "a few thousand bucks" with weekly tests on a random day (2024). The core — the arrest, the letter, the secret kept from his parents, *The Power of Now* — is stable.

The author places the arrest in a series of turbulent episodes from which he learned only after the mistake. "I got arrested for the possession of marijuana in a college parking garage, and they don't take that lightly on campus." Then, "after I'd borrowed two thousand dollars from my dad, maxed out my first credit card and took out loans to fund my fifth year of college while I was trying to make multiple businesses work, but primarily an e-commerce business, at the time, and it failed miserably." And in Costa Rica: after hitting a new monthly high in his business, with a brand-new girlfriend, "riding the money high," he impulsively decided to fly to Costa Rica for two weeks; "we ended up breaking up the first day we got there and flew back the next day." It seemed a stupid decision, but he only realized it after making the mistake and exposing himself to the experience. **Source:** Happiness Is A Skill (How To Get Out Of A Rut).md. The series makes a point that matters for the meaning of awareness: in the author's account, awareness often arrives through exposure and error, not before them. The loan from his father appears as $3,000 in another telling; the variation does not affect the lesson.

### 2.8 Psychological Time

The awakening story of 2.7 turned on a book about presence, and on worries — about a court date, about parents, about the future — that "washed away." This section explains, in the author's terms, what those worries were made of. His concept of psychological time describes how the mind drags the past and the future into the present, and how that habit becomes personality. It is the inner, individual counterpart of the institutional conditioning described earlier: schools and jobs install the default path from outside; psychological time keeps it running from inside.

Most of what the author says on this subject comes from a single 2022 video, in which the author explains conditioning in neurological-spiritual language. In later years he explains the same phenomenon differently — as information repeated until it becomes automatic (2023), as Krishnamurti's "thought is always conditioned and therefore mechanical" (2025), and as self-replicating memes protected by institutions within the industrial paradigm (2026). The underlying idea does not change; the explanatory lens does. The 2022 lens, presented here, is best suited to explaining individual habit.

#### What psychological time is

**Psychological time**, or linear time, is in the author's account "one of the biggest problems humans face," and one that humans are "the only ones that can really face... because of our advanced cognitive abilities." It means that you can visualize a past experience you were made aware of — a time of emotional turmoil, say — and if you do not order your consciousness or focus on that moment correctly or positively, "you are quite literally pulling that experience into the now": you feel the same experience, the same stress. Reminiscing about a bad breakup, you begin to experience the same feelings and emotions you had then. The same applies in the other direction: if you project into a future you can imagine clearly, and it is negative, you pull that experience into the now with its feelings, thoughts and emotions. **Source:** How To Create A Better Life For Yourself.md.

The phrase "order your consciousness" connects this to Part III: the problem is not memory or imagination as such, but memory and imagination without direction — what Chapter 5 calls psychic entropy. And the claim that only humans face this problem is consistent with the author's view, in 2.9, that human cognition is both a superpower and a hazard.

**Complementary context:** The term "psychological time" (as opposed to "clock time") is central to Eckhart Tolle's *The Power of Now*, the book of the author's awakening, and to Jiddu Krishnamurti before him; the author uses the term without attributing it in this passage.

#### The familiar past and the predictable future

The author then explains how psychological time shapes personality, borrowing from Joe Dispenza. As you repeat experiences in psychological time — "the familiar past, possibly negative, and the predictable future," predictable because you have already lived those experiences and project them forward — and allow this "possibly unconscious behavior," "you are quite literally hardwiring neural networks in your brain related to those experiences, so that becomes your personality." He recommends Dispenza's *Becoming Supernatural*, which "does a much better job at explaining the science behind this," and states his own position with unusual candour: he is "not too interested in the science"; it is "not very congruent" with him; he prefers the spiritual aspect, which he can apply easily, while others find the scientific view of the same topics more congruent — "it's just a different lens of viewing it." **Source:** How To Create A Better Life For Yourself.md. The pair **familiar past / predictable future** is Dispenza's, adapted. The author takes the idea and explicitly leaves the science to its source; the reader should therefore not treat the neurological language here as the author's own empirical claim.

**Complementary context:** Joe Dispenza is a chiropractor and popular author whose books (*Breaking the Habit of Being Yourself*, *Becoming Supernatural*) combine neuroscience vocabulary with meditation and spirituality; his scientific claims are widely regarded as speculative, and the author himself elsewhere lists the book as "potentially pseudoscience." The general principle that repeated activation strengthens neural connections ("neurons that fire together wire together") derives from Donald Hebb's work on learning (1949) and is mainstream; Dispenza's further claims are not.

From this the author derives his definition of conditioning in this period: hardwiring neural networks "is what conditioning, programming is." The mind "kind of mimics a harmonic oscillator or a system": hardwiring makes it habitual to tap into an experience. His example is an ordinary morning. You wake up and immediately think "stressful boss at work"; you pull that stressful experience into the now; you have "those chemicals throughout your body"; and this "can quite literally cause you to be sick by **living as your past self**," or by dwelling on the predictable future ("this is going to happen to me"). Then a further step: because you imagine it first, and awareness begets awareness, "what do you know, it happens" — you actualize the vision. **Source:** How To Create A Better Life For Yourself.md.

**Complementary context:** A harmonic oscillator, in physics, is a system that, when displaced from equilibrium, is pulled back toward it by a restoring force and oscillates around it (a spring, a pendulum). The author uses it as an image of a mind that keeps returning to the same states.

This last step deserves attention because it is the hinge between the diagnosis and the method of Part IV. The same mechanism that makes negative imagination self-fulfilling makes a positive vision self-fulfilling. If imagining the stressful boss each morning tends to produce the stressful experience, then imagining a chosen future, repeatedly, tends to produce that. The author's later practices — anti-vision and vision (Chapter 7), bringing the ideal future into the present (Chapter 8) — rely on this symmetry. Here, it is stated as an observation and an interpretation, not as a proven law.

Why would the mind cling to familiar experiences, even painful ones? The author offers an explanation he explicitly marks as speculation: our love of familiarity is a survival mechanism. The brain registers "this past experience happened, it caused a negative experience, it threatened my survival, I need to remember this for later," and builds a system in the body so that the trigger produces a reaction. The result is "living in this **stressful internal environment** because my body and my mind think it's being threatened on a physical survival level." (In the transcript he says "possibly don't take this with a grain of salt, this is speculation" — an evident slip for "take this with a grain of salt.") **Source:** How To Create A Better Life For Yourself.md. The explanation links psychological time to the survival theme that runs through the whole chapter: just as the default path persists because survival depends on it, the familiar past persists because the mind treats it as survival-relevant information.

#### The only solution: awareness and the unknown

The author's remedy has two parts and he presents them as inseparable. "The only way to solve this problem is, one, becoming conscious of those negative thought patterns and experiences, but at the same time it's diving into the unknown." Awareness alone is not enough, because the pull of the familiar is strong: humans love familiarity, habits, automating thought processes and taking shortcuts. So you must "think new thoughts," "have new ideas," and "gain awareness that we didn't have before by doing the hard thing and kind of leaning into the discomfort of life that will threaten our survival." **Source:** How To Create A Better Life For Yourself.md.

The two-part solution maps exactly onto the two-step exit of 2.5. Becoming conscious of patterns is step one, awareness. Diving into the unknown is the beginning of step two: building a hierarchy of goals whose path is not yet known, which is where, in 2.4, the hunt takes place. It also explains why the author treats the unknown as both frightening and necessary: the discomfort that "threatens our survival" is precisely the signal that one is leaving the familiar past behind.

#### Mental health as making sense

A related video from 2022 extends the idea to mental health, with a caveat the author states first: "I'm not a doctor here." He acknowledges how defensive people can be about their mental health and "how they kind of hide behind that," and adds: "I'm not saying that you're wrong, I'm just saying why not exhaust every single solution available to you" — offering a solution "that has worked for me and many others." **Source:** How To Stop Feeling Lost, Anxious, Or Uncertain About The Future.md. The caveat is important for reading what follows: it is a personal and philosophical perspective on mental distress, not a clinical theory, and it is offered as one option among others.

His definition: "In this sense mental health is about making sense, understanding and clarity." If you let a compulsive negative thought hijack a situation — you are talking to someone and suddenly think "I have to get this done" — you feel the stress associated with "that alternate situation that you are projecting into," and "you can't make sense of the current one because your mind is influenced by something that is not even relevant at that point." **Source:** How To Stop Feeling Lost, Anxious, Or Uncertain About The Future.md. **Making sense**, in this sense, is the author's term for mental health as clarity about the present situation. The connection to psychological time is direct: the to-do thought is a small piece of the predictable future pulled into the now, displacing the conversation actually happening.

He frames the idea with a quotation from Anthony de Mello and extends it: "Remove the obstruction from your mind and you have peace; remove the obstruction from your heart and you have love." The author adds: "I would go as far to say remove the obstruction from your business and you have money; remove the obstruction from any given system and you have result." **Source:** How To Stop Feeling Lost, Anxious, Or Uncertain About The Future.md. The first two clauses are de Mello's; the extension to business and to any system is the author's. The principle — that the desired state is the default once an obstruction is removed — is characteristic of his thinking: clarity, like peace, is not built but uncovered.

The video's central example makes the idea concrete. "Does a bodybuilder care if he brings chicken and rice as his own meal to dinner?" Yes, "but only if he **projects outside of his reality**, which means he loses control of his attention." If he remembers what matters to him and what his goals are, and perceives the situation — including "the little jabs of insecurity that other people are throwing at him" — accurately, he will not care, "because he is focused." If he were operating robotically, a comment like "oh, you're bringing chicken and rice to dinner" would provoke a defensive or flustered reaction, rather than a joke, or an explanation of his perspective and goals — "and if other people don't accept that, then what can you do?" The lesson: "we have to exchange robotic living for intentional living." And an extension: if he adopts the others' goal — just having a very pleasurable meal — which lies outside his reality, and sacrifices his values to pursue it, he will feel bad and create problems he could have avoided by asking "what am I stretching towards?" **Source:** How To Stop Feeling Lost, Anxious, Or Uncertain About The Future.md.

The example is a miniature of the whole chapter. The dinner table is a small society with a default (eat what everyone eats); the bodybuilder has a self-chosen goal; the jabs of insecurity are the social pressure that keeps people on the default; and the difference between being hurt and being unbothered is whether attention is anchored in one's own goals or projected into others'. **Robotic living vs intentional living** is the author's pair for reacting automatically versus living with one's goals in mind. And the closing question — "what am I stretching towards?" — anticipates the author's definition of intention in Chapter 7, which he derives from the Latin *intentio*, "stretching toward."

### 2.9 Why Waking Up Matters

The chapter has so far treated awareness as a personal matter: how an individual sees the default path and begins to leave it. This final section widens the frame. The author gives three kinds of reasons why awakening matters beyond the individual: a metaphysical one (perception itself is a survival interface, which limits what "waking up" can mean), a social one (conscious individuals hold society up), and a civilizational one (the metacrisis, borrowed from Daniel Schmachtenberger). The section is the most speculative in the chapter, and most of its frameworks are taken from others; the author's own contribution lies in how he applies them.

#### Perception as a user interface: you can't escape the Matrix

In a 2023 video titled "Life Is A Video Game (You Can't Escape The Matrix)," the author offers what he calls a metaphysical perspective: we live in "a survival-based simulation." He draws on Donald Hoffman, a cognitive psychologist, and his book *The Case Against Reality*, quoting: "If you play a video game on your computer such as Doom or Uncharted, you see compelling 3D worlds and 3D objects, yet the information is entirely 2D, limited by the number of pixels on the screen. The same is true when you look away from your computer to the world around you; it too has pixels and all information is 2D." In the book and in podcasts the author has heard, Hoffman argues that human perception is a user interface for survival that hides the true nature of reality, because "if we saw the truth we wouldn't survive": in simulations, "natural selection does not favor those that see the truth, or the ones that see reality as it is"; organisms that saw the truth went extinct. Hoffman's examples include an ant trying to mate with a glass bottle because its perceptions were distorted, and frogs that see a completely different range of colours. Hoffman also argues that space-time is a visualization tool — space and time are "compression algorithms," "the operating system of the user interface." **Source:** Life Is A Video Game (You Can't Escape The Matrix).md.

**Complementary context:** Donald Hoffman is a cognitive scientist at the University of California, Irvine. His "interface theory of perception," set out in *The Case Against Reality* (2019), argues on the basis of evolutionary game simulations that perception is tuned to fitness rather than truth. The jewel beetle that tries to mate with discarded beer bottles is one of his standard examples (the author's "ant" may be a slip). The theory is debated in philosophy and cognitive science.

The author then extends Hoffman's metaphors. Subjective reality is like a desktop screen programmed to help us see what we need to see and do what we need to do. Every material object is like an icon you can move around, play with, delete or lose. The screen is attractive, has properties and qualities, "and we should take them seriously but not literally," as Hoffman says. You click around and perform tasks for desired outcomes, which Hoffman calls **fitness payoffs**; these are "like points in a video game": through trial and error we learn to win and evolve, and by winning, your offspring goes to the next level. "Everyone thinks they're seeing the truth, but... it's like we're all playing a game of Grand Theft Auto": consoles are packaged nicely; we do not see the wires and diodes; and even if we did, it would not serve survival — we could do nothing with the jumble of electronics and could not comprehend the code running the game. **Source:** Life Is A Video Game (You Can't Escape The Matrix).md. The game metaphor connects Hoffman to the author's own central metaphor of life as a video game (Chapter 10); "fitness payoffs" become, in effect, the points of the survival game.

The author's own contribution is a limit. If you removed the user interface — with a tool such as psychedelics — you would eventually go insane. "I'm not saying that insane is bad necessarily; maybe that's the truest thing there is, maybe that's ultimate reality, maybe that's ego death." But for operating in the real world, "this survival game," it would not serve you; you would probably die sooner because you would lack the survival instinct. "There is a reason why people aren't on psychedelics 24 hours, seven days a week: we aren't at that phase of evolution yet." That does not mean, he adds, that you cannot have awareness of this, or grounding in it, to make better decisions and live a meaningful life. **Source:** Life Is A Video Game (You Can't Escape The Matrix).md.

This passage matters for the chapter because it qualifies what "waking up" can mean. The author's use of "the Matrix" evolves. In 2022 it is "what you think you know," and the red pill and a "glitch" in robotic cycles can break you out. By September 2023, with Hoffman, perception and language form a closed system, a survival interface that would drive you mad if removed: you cannot escape the Matrix in that sense. By 2025 the Matrix is a structure of "circular validation" among institutions, and "we're not talking about some kind of red pill... break off from society — no": the only way out is to understand it. The shift is from a problem of individual habits that can be broken to a structural and epistemological condition that can be understood but not exited. Both versions can apply at once: "breaking" applies to conditioned expectations (the psychological level), and is a practice within the larger frame; "not escaping" applies to perception itself (the metaphysical level) and to society (one should not isolate oneself from it). The awareness of 2.7, then, is not a departure from the interface but a way of using it more consciously.

#### Conscious individuals hold up society

The second reason is social and is stated with more urgency. The fate of humanity is not guaranteed: every life form is fighting to survive in "this little competition," and humans may or may not stay on top. If we do not make intelligent, conscious choices we may eradicate ourselves — a worst case, but possible. Species go extinct all the time because they do not make conscious decisions or decide their fate; they live by instinct. Humans are different, but a majority of them also live by instinct, in a "narrow-minded, mechanical state of stress — robotic, unconscious, mindless," the same as animals. If "95 plus percent of society" operates robotically, doing what they are told, following the path laid out by society, "being a slave to their programming and conditioning," those masses are "leading us off of the cliff." Hence: "society, by my standards, is held up by the **conscious individuals**; it's like they have the world on top of them, carrying it towards something better" — by building businesses that contribute to humanity, writing, creating, and putting things out that affect others and wake them up. **Source:** Most People Won’t Change (How To Recreate Yourself).md. The percentage is again an estimate; at the end of the same video he says "90 to 95%." The image of individuals bearing the world is the figure of Atlas.

From this follows a duty that the author states in terms of persuasion. "Wake up, learn to persuade." If you do not, "you are actively choosing to let unethical people win this **spiritual war**." You are not conscious by opting out of the game of life; you are arguably less conscious than the "sleazy businessman" who at least provides a fraction of value with a product that genuinely improves some people's lives — others not so much, "and that's okay." **Source:** The 7 Best Internet Business Models (From Zero Experience To Advanced).md. The argument is aimed at a specific reader: the person who, having seen through the default path, concludes that the right response is withdrawal. For the author, withdrawal is a failure of consciousness, not its expression, because it leaves the field of persuasion to those with fewer scruples. The ethics of persuasion is developed in Chapter 32.

The third piece explains why individual creation can change society at all. The more attention a creative person attracts to a theory that leads society in a new direction, and the more supporters it gains, the more it tends to create culture and society. "The more attention that is invested into a creative idea, the more likely it is to come true than not. Things just don't happen. Humans build what they want to see in the world." His example is post-labour economics, a theory that could become real if enough attention is invested in it. **Source:** The Future Of Work (& The New High-Income Skill Stack).md. The principle closes a loop with 2.5: if society is a pyramid of attention in which what receives attention exists, then directing attention toward a better idea is a way of building it. It is the social version of the self-fulfilling vision of 2.8.

#### The metacrisis

The widest frame comes from Daniel Schmachtenberger, whom the author calls "one of the greatest thinkers of our time": someone who rarely posts on social media (and has not in years), appears occasionally on podcasts, and is calm, nuanced and non-polarizing, and who has dedicated his life to what he calls "the metacrisis" — a subject, the author notes, much deeper than his own video's focus on posting content and writing essays. The framing quotation: "As technology is empowering our choices and we are getting something like the power of gods, you have to have something like the love and the wisdom of gods to wield that, or you self-destruct." **Source:** I'm begging you to start writing essays (even if you hate writing).md.

**Complementary context:** Daniel Schmachtenberger is a social philosopher associated with the Consilience Project and the "Game B" discussions. His central thesis is that humanity's many crises — ecological, technological, geopolitical, informational — share underlying causes, which he calls generator functions, and that addressing them requires improvements in collective sense-making.

The **metacrisis**, as the author presents it, is not one crisis but a convergence of three, driven by three **generator functions** — "a deep structural pattern that creates surface-level problems," that is, root causes. Treating symptoms without addressing root causes is, in the author's own gloss, "like mopping water while the faucet runs." The author explains the three in 2025 and again, almost verbatim, in 2026.

| Generator function | What it is | Examples the author gives |
|---|---|---|
| Rivalrous dynamics | Win-lose games in which one party's gain requires another's loss | Arms races, corporate competition, social media content, academic publishing (hoarding data to publish first) |
| Substrate consumption | Systems consuming their own foundation — what they need to exist — faster than it regenerates; "when systems consume their foundation faster than they can regenerate, that's bad" | Soil for plants (depleting topsoil that took millennia to form), attention for media (the attention economy consuming human cognitive capacity faster than it recovers), trust for markets |
| Exponential technology | Tools and systems that improve themselves at accelerating rates, "outpacing human wisdom" — "that's the key point" | AI doubling in capacity, automated weapons, social media algorithms evolving faster than their psychological impact can be studied |

**Source:** The Death Of Social Media (& The Future Of Content Creation).md; I'm begging you to start writing essays (even if you hate writing).md.

When the three forces converge, they can produce outcomes that Schmachtenberger calls **attractors** — basins into which many complex societies already fall. Two are to be avoided: civilizational or catastrophic collapse (nuclear war, unaligned AI, ecological destruction, engineered pandemics) and dystopian control (total surveillance, digital authoritarianism, the elimination of agency and of the ability to make one's own choices). The third attractor, the good outcome, is "a world where sense making, shared understanding, and aligned incentives exist." **Source:** I'm begging you to start writing essays (even if you hate writing).md. In the 2025 version the author does not detail the third attractor; he recommends studying it himself — "binge-watch 10 hours of his lectures" — and pivots to the question of what social media can do about it and how that aligns with getting civilization back on track. **Source:** The Death Of Social Media (& The Future Of Content Creation).md.

The author's use of the framework is specific. One generator function — substrate consumption, with attention as the substrate of media — describes precisely the information environment that Chapter 1 identified as an amplifier of unconsciousness. And it gives him a reason for one of his practical recommendations. He quotes Schmachtenberger: "The written word as the primary type of media was probably required for democracy to work," because people had to think well enough; reading meant a longer attention span for "non-dopaminergic stuff" and enough working memory to hold multiple perspectives. **Source:** The Death Of Social Media (& The Future Of Content Creation).md. The author uses this to introduce his "level three creators," who produce long, thoughtful content, and to argue that writing essays is part of the response — a theme developed in Chapters 21 and 24.

The author's view of the internet across these years is not linear, and it frames how this section should be read. In 2022 the internet was "a giant mind" documenting collective consciousness, but also a "socialization chamber" that made conditioning "10 times easier." In 2023–2024 he emphasized the user's responsibility and the potential of social media — "not an app, it's a new society," "devil or vessel," the engine of most of his own success. From 2025 he shifted toward a diagnosis of systemic contamination, using Schmachtenberger's frame: the attention economy consumes cognitive capacity faster than it recovers, and social media and AI amplify unconsciousness. He gives no explicit reason for the 2025–2026 turn. Throughout, one idea remains: that creating good content, especially long-form writing, is part of the solution.

#### From the institutions to the self

The chapter has moved from institutions to awareness and from awareness to civilization, and the argument can now be stated as a single chain. The default path is a hierarchy of goals assigned by school, the job and the culture of the industrial paradigm; once installed, it steers perception and behaviour toward its own fulfilment. Its costs are psychological as much as economic — the plateau, the eternal known, the hunting psyche trapped in routine — and they are hidden by gradualness and by the illusion of certainty. The exit begins with awareness, practised as discerning observation, which the author found through his own crisis and *The Power of Now*, and which extends to the inner habit of psychological time. And it matters beyond the individual, because conscious individuals, in his view, carry society and shape culture by what they choose to build and to give attention to.

One question remains open, and it is the question of Part II. Every step of this chapter has assumed someone who becomes aware, discerns, chooses and builds. Yet the same chapter has shown that this someone was itself produced by the conditioning it now observes — that identification with a job can make criticism of employment feel like a threat to survival, and that a "mental body" defends itself. Before the author's method for creating direction can be understood, it is necessary to understand what that self is, why it defends itself, and how it changes.

### Exercises

1. **Diagnosis of your own default path.** Write down, as specifically as you can, the default path that was handed to you: the goals, the timeline, the definition of success, and who conveyed them (parents, teachers, peers, culture). Then apply the author's cybernetic explanation from 2.1: identify one "error correction" you have made in the last few years that kept you on that path, and one opportunity you suspect you could not perceive because your current goal did not demand it. How confident are you in the second answer, and why is it inherently hard to be confident?

2. **Testing the slavery metaphor.** The author defines wage slavery operationally: "if you cannot stop showing up to work without catastrophe and if you have no skills to create alternatives, you meet the definition of a slave." Apply the definition to three cases — a salaried employee with six months of savings and a portable skill; a freelancer with one client who provides 90% of income; a business owner whose company cannot survive a month without them. Does the definition sort them in a way you find illuminating or misleading? What does the author's emphasis on "force" and survival capture that the ordinary meaning of "slave" does not, and what does the metaphor risk obscuring?

3. **Reconciling the author's two voices on employment.** Section 2.3 shows the author calling employment both "the worst outcome" and "a very worthy stepping stone." Construct the strongest argument that these are compatible, using the concepts of the plateau, complacency and dependence. Then identify at least one statement in the corpus that your reconciliation cannot accommodate. What does that residue suggest about the difference between rhetoric aimed at motivating change and analysis aimed at describing reality?

4. **The psychology of employment graph applied.** Sketch the author's "psychology of employment" graph (challenge and skill over time, with the employment line flattening into "the eternal known") for your own working life or studies so far. Where are the plateaus? Where was the "intersection" at which, by the author's logic, a change would have been well timed? If you have never experienced a plateau, explain what has kept the challenge rising, and whether that contradicts or confirms the author's model.

5. **Observation without judgment.** For one week, practise the author's "silent observer" method in one setting (a store, a commute, a workplace): notice what people do, ask whether you want to end up as their actions suggest, and — the step most often skipped — record what reaction the observation provoked in you and what it reveals. Afterwards, evaluate the method critically: where did discernment slide into judgment? Does the author's 2025 move from "discern, not judge" to "just judge people's posture" clarify or blur the distinction?

6. **Conspiracy, property of the system, or neither.** The author oscillates between "schools were created to enslave the brightest minds" and the claim that obedience is "a property of the system" that "takes the shape of that which most benefits the end goal... whether it's intentional or not." Choose one institution you know well (a school, a company, a profession). Identify a feature of it that serves those at the top, and argue for which explanation fits better — design, emergent property, or something the author does not consider (for example, a feature that serves its members or users). What evidence would distinguish the explanations?

7. **Psychological time in practice.** Identify one recurring thought that pulls a "familiar past" or a "predictable future" into your present (the author's example is waking up and immediately thinking of a stressful boss). Using the bodybuilder-at-dinner example, describe what it would look like to stay anchored in your own goals in that situation instead of "projecting outside of your reality." Then assess the author's claim that negative imagination is self-fulfilling by the same mechanism as a positive vision: what in your own experience supports it, and what would count as evidence against it?

8. **When would the author's prescription stop applying?** The author argues that "entrepreneurship is modern survival" and "the only logical option for long-term thinkers." Identify at least two conditions under which this principle would fail or become harmful — for a particular person, a particular economy, or a society in which most people followed the advice. Use the author's own concessions (the 1% who should keep their job, Devon Eriksen's "somebody has to do a lot of these tasks," the pyramid whose base "has to be filled") as material, and decide whether they are exceptions to his thesis or evidence that it needs reformulating.

# Part II — Identity: Who You Think You Are and How It Changes

## Chapter 3 — What Identity Is and Why It Defends Itself

Part I described a mind programmed from the outside: a Matrix of inherited beliefs, a childhood of conditioning, goals assigned before anyone asked whether you wanted them, and a default path that most people walk on autopilot. That diagnosis leaves an obvious question open. If the program was installed, *where* is it installed, and why is it so hard to uninstall even after you have seen it? This chapter answers by building the model of the person on which the rest of the system rests. In Dan Koe's account, the program lives in your identity: a web of ideas, beliefs, values, standards and, above all, goals, which works as the lens through which you perceive everything and which your mind defends with the same machinery it uses to keep your body alive. Once that model is in place, several things that look like separate problems (lack of discipline, closed-mindedness, the inability to "be yourself", the excuses that appear whenever an opportunity shows up) turn out to be one phenomenon seen from different angles. The next chapter will use this model to explain how identity changes; this one explains what it is and why it resists.

### 3.1 Identity as a Mental Body

#### One phenomenon, many names

The first thing to understand about Koe's vocabulary is that he deliberately collapses a family of words into a single concept. *Identity*, *ego*, *self*, *self-image*, *concept of self*, *character*, *personality*, *sense of self* and, in his own coinage, *mental body* are treated as synonyms. He says so explicitly and more than once: identity, sense of who you are, self-image and concept of self are "synonymous" (**Source:** `Most People Are NPCs (Don't Waste Your Life On Autopilot).md`, 2023-05-08); "ego, identity, self" are the same thing "for now" (**Source:** `How To Take Back Control Of Your Life With Strategic Thinking.md`, 2025-03-16). His justification is that different traditions are pointing at the same object with different labels: in spiritual teachings it is called the ego or the self, in psychology the ego or identity, in self-help personality and identity. What all of them name is "the idea of who we are" (**Source:** `How To Reprogram Your Mind & Build Your Intelligence.md`, 2023-09-24).

This is a choice with consequences. A psychologist would distinguish the ego as a psychic agency from the self-concept as a set of beliefs about oneself, and a contemplative teacher would distinguish the ego as a false sense of separateness from the deeper self. Koe sets those distinctions aside on purpose, because his argument does not depend on them. What he needs is a single object that (a) is made of information, (b) shapes what you see and do, and (c) behaves, when threatened, like something alive. Whenever this book uses "identity" without qualification, it means that object.

The term he coins for it is the **mental body**: "our self image or our concept of self or the idea of who we are, our identity" (**Source:** `How To Reprogram Your Mind & Build Your Intelligence.md`, 2023-09-24). He calls it a *body* to set up an analogy with the physical body, which can be trained. The analogy carries two implications that the rest of the chapter develops. First, a body can be developed, so the mental body can be built up the way a bodybuilder builds muscle (what the corpus elsewhere calls "mental bodybuilding"). Second, a body is something an organism defends, so the mental body will be defended too. Over the years he also uses *psychic body* (2023), *mental form of self* (2023) and *psychological body* (2026) for the same thing; these are renamings, not new concepts. Section 3.4 returns to them.

| Term in the corpus | How Koe uses it |
|---|---|
| identity, self, ego, self-image, concept of self, personality | Interchangeable names for "the idea of who we are" |
| character | The same, framed through the video-game metaphor ("that little character you've been playing in the game of life") |
| mental body / psychic body / psychological body | The same, framed as a second body that can be trained and that the mind tries to keep alive |
| puppet master | The same, framed by its function: what sits at the root of the mind and decides which information gets in |
| storytelling engine / interpretive filter / mental filter | The same, framed by its function of interpretation |

#### What identity is made of

Across five years the definition stays stable in substance while gaining precision. In 2023 Koe defines character as "your concept of self, who you think you are, an amalgamation of ideas, beliefs, experiences and information you've processed that compose the operating system from which you interact with reality" (**Source:** `Most People Won’t Change (How To Recreate Yourself).md`, 2023-05-19). Later that year the list becomes "a web of concepts, beliefs, ideas, experiences and perceptions that allow you to navigate the world" (**Source:** `Turn Your Knowledge Into A Business (How To Productize Your Mind).md`, 2023-11-26). In the same passage he states why the definition matters at all, and the statement sets a hierarchy that the rest of this chapter follows: "Your identity shapes your perspective and your perspective is the most important thing you can understand and expand. Your perspective is your reality." Identity is studied, in other words, not for its own sake but because it is the thing that fixes the perspective, and the perspective is what you actually live inside (Section 3.3 develops this). Shortly afterwards the definition becomes "a system of ideas, beliefs, values and standards that shape your perspective" (**Source:** `You Won’t Be The Same Person In 6 Months (Master Anything, Fast).md`, 2023-12-17). In 2025 the most complete formulation appears: identity is "a web of ideas and goals and beliefs and values that act as this mental filter… It's your interpretive filter for the world, it's your storytelling engine, it's how you make sense of the world" (**Source:** `How To Take Back Control Of Your Life With Strategic Thinking.md`, 2025-03-16).

Three images recur in these definitions, and each adds something.

The **operating system** image says that identity is not one belief among others but the platform on which all other mental activity runs. You do not consult your identity before acting; you act *from* it, the way a program runs on an operating system without asking it permission.

The **web** or **system** image says that identity is relational. No single belief is your identity; the identity is the pattern of connections among ideas, goals, values and standards. This matters later, because it explains why changing one belief can feel like a threat to everything: pulling on one node moves the whole web.

The **filter** image (interpretive filter, mental filter, storytelling engine) says what identity *does*. It decides how raw experience becomes meaning. In the 2023 version this function gets its most vivid name: "At the root of your mind is your identity like a puppet master." Identity "is what accepts or rejects information, allowing your mind to form systems. It limits the information it can perceive; if it receives information that doesn't match its beliefs, values or standards, it rejects it" (**Source:** `You Won’t Be The Same Person In 6 Months (Master Anything, Fast).md`, 2023-12-17). The puppet master is not a villain in this image. It is simply the part of the mind that pulls the strings of perception before you are aware that anything was decided. Section 3.3 develops this filtering function in detail.

The same definitions also say where the content of the web comes from. For most people, character "was created for them": every person since childhood "has been a product of the environment they were in" (**Source:** `Most People Won’t Change (How To Recreate Yourself).md`, 2023-05-19). Early in development, identity "wasn't created by you"; it was produced by environment, parents, society, the culture you grew up in, religion, television and the news (**Source:** `How To Take Back Control Of Your Life With Strategic Thinking.md`, 2025-03-16). And "the information you learn and use since birth shapes the self" (**Source:** `Turn Your Knowledge Into A Business (How To Productize Your Mind).md`, 2023-11-26). This is the point at which the model of identity connects to Part I: the conditioning described there is the process by which the web was filled.

The same 2025 passage adds the qualification that keeps the model from being fatalistic. Identity is not "set in stone… assigned at birth along with your name"; it is "a living, breathing and evolving entity." That qualification is what makes the next chapter possible.

#### The body changes; the idea stays

Koe offers a short argument for why identity is an idea rather than a fixed fact about you. "Our body changes every seven years, all of the cells are different, they change, they die and they reproduce, and our body is completely different than who we were seven years ago, but our concept of self is kind of the same." From that contrast he draws the conclusion that "who we are is not the idea in our head, and that that can also change"; and yet people tend to stay static and comfortable and "allow their identity to rule their life" (**Source:** `How To Reprogram Your Mind & Build Your Intelligence.md`, 2023-09-24).

The seven-year figure is presented in the video as a fact, without a source.

**Complementary context:** the "every cell is replaced every seven years" claim is a popular simplification. Cell turnover rates vary enormously by tissue (some cells are replaced in days, others, such as many neurons, last a lifetime), so the figure should not be taken literally.

The argument does not actually depend on the number. Its logic is this: the physical substrate changes continuously, while the self-concept stays remarkably constant; so the constancy of the self-concept cannot come from the body. It must come from the idea maintaining itself. That points directly to the question this chapter is built around: *why* does the idea maintain itself so well? The short answer, developed in section 3.4, is that the mind defends it.

#### Identity as a story

A second strand of the definition treats identity as narrative. In 2022 Koe describes the need to understand "the story we're being told at any time." The question "Who am I, why am I me?" is answered by two halves of a story. The first half is the psychological past: memories that explain who I am today. The second is forward-looking: "I may or may not have a hierarchy of goals or a later part of the story that is coming that will form who I am in the future" (**Source:** `Stop Trying To Be Unique... Do This Instead.md`, 2022-05-28). Notice what this does to the definition. The past half is fixed in memory; the future half is written by goals. Section 3.2 will show that this is not a loose metaphor: in Koe's model, goals literally compose the identity, so whoever writes your goals writes the rest of your story.

In 2023 he widens the frame. Rather than "God", he prefers to speak of "life" or "story", because story is symbolic of the patterns of the universe: "uni-verse, one song", a harmony of happening visible in architecture, music, scripture, systems, economics and an individual life. The mind interprets the world through concepts, stories, metaphors and symbols, and nothing makes sense in isolation: a cup would not make sense without a hand, gravity without force or mass, your life without the current state of society and culture. Everything you know is "a layer of stories" built out of billions of on/off bits assembled for your current level of understanding. Stories give meaning, and "your identity is the story that you tell yourself." You live it on autopilot unless you make it conscious. He closes the passage with a question meant to be applied personally: what word, sentence, paragraph, section and chapter is unfolding in the book of your life? (**Source:** `Get Mad At Where You Are In Life (A Deep Explanation).md`, 2023-06-11).

The practical consequence of the story framing is that a story can be rewritten. The corpus contains a clear illustration from a guest rather than from Koe himself. Sahil Bloom, asked about his book *The 5 Types of Wealth*, explains that he "was very much not supposed to write this book": "The story that I told myself for the vast majority of my life was that I was not the type of person that could do these things. I was not smart enough." The book, he says, "is me formally rewriting that story that I used to tell myself… proving to the world and to myself that I am capable", and he offers it as "a tool for you to rewrite the story that you tell about yourself… to start rejecting the defaults and to start living by design" (**Source:** `The Time Billionaire (A Concept That Will Change Your Life) With Sahil Bloom.md`, 2025-01-30). This is Bloom's experience, not Koe's theory, but it fits the model exactly: the limiting element was a sentence in the story ("I am not the type of person who…"), and the change happened by acting against that sentence until it no longer held.

#### Who you really are and who you think you are

If identity is an idea built mostly by others, then there must be a difference between the idea and whatever it is an idea *of*. Koe addresses this in a 2022 video with a framework he drew on screen, the **concentric rings of identity**.

He begins with a quotation from Alan Watts: in a world with no eyes the sun would not be light, with no soft skins rocks would not be hard, with no muscles they would not be heavy; "existence is relationship and you are smack in the middle of it." Koe extends the thought: in a world with no others, the self would not exist. Your identity can only exist when you draw a distinction between yourself and everything around you, and that is precisely what the ego does: it creates boundaries, "partitions in a hard drive". Later in the same video he adds, again leaning on Watts, that we should not lose sight of the similarities between things; understanding something as a whole requires holding differences and similarities in mind at once (**Source:** `Why You Can't Be Yourself (The Power Of Being Alone).md`, 2022-11-13). The Watts line is a third-party idea; what Koe does with it is his own: he turns "existence is relationship" into an account of the ego as a boundary-making function.

**Complementary context:** Alan Watts (1915–1973) was a British writer who popularized Zen Buddhism and Taoism for Western audiences. His recurring theme was that the separate ego is a social convention rather than an independent thing.

On that basis Koe draws a set of nested layers. The transcript does not let us see the graphic, but he describes it verbally and the order is clear:

| Ring (from the center outward) | What it is |
|---|---|
| Who you really are | "This little thing in the middle" |
| Who you think you are | A web of your own thoughts and beliefs about yourself |
| Who your friends think you are | Something you "probably give too much conscious thought"; the ring of comparison, where the boundary between you and others is drawn |
| Who society wants you to be | Expectations of the wider social system |
| Who culture says you are | The outermost layer of inherited definition |

Each ring outward is a further distortion from the center. Koe says this layering is what spiritual teachers, mystics and especially Buddhism are trying to point at. Two things about the framework are worth noticing. First, the center is defined only negatively: Koe does not say what "who you really are" contains, only that everything around it is borrowed. Second, the ring "who you think you are", which is what the rest of this chapter calls identity, is already one layer removed from the center. Identity, in other words, is not your essence. It is your model of yourself, and it was largely assembled from the outer rings.

The framework is attached to a practical exercise. Koe asks viewers not to follow him blindly ("if what he says isn't true to you, it isn't true to you") and to spend a week trying "to catch yourself being someone else." Notice the new words you pick up ("oh, that's a new word I said"), question them, follow them to their source, and decide whether you really want them in your vocabulary. Notice your decisions too, and whether they are influenced by others online or offline. His example turns the exercise on himself: if you follow a marketer and start to believe that "the one-person business model this guy Dan Koe promotes" sounds amazing because of how it changed his life (the one-person business is his name for a business built on yourself, without a team, that turns your own interests and development into products; Chapter 28 develops it), ask whether you are starting one because he said so, or because it resonates with intrinsic goals you created and is a worthy path toward them (**Source:** `Why You Can't Be Yourself (The Power Of Being Alone).md`, 2022-11-13). The exercise is a direct application of the rings: it asks you to locate, in real time, which ring a given word or decision came from.

#### The anatomy of identity: how the web is formed

If identity is made of information that came from outside, how does that information become "me"? Koe's answer evolved through three versions, each a fuller statement of the same loop.

The earliest is a two-term loop: "Character creates action and action reinforces character" (**Source:** `Get Mad At Where You Are In Life (A Deep Explanation).md`, 2023-06-11). His example is a bodybuilder who became one through passion and self-study. Because the goal composes the identity, nutrition, training and lifestyle fall into alignment with it, and anything done outside that alignment produces suffering, "which is not bad but it is a useful compass towards better." Suffering, in this framing, is information: it tells you where your actions and your identity diverge. To change who you are, he says, challenge your beliefs, adopt new self-generated (not assigned) goals, and self-reflect over time ("I mean a lifetime"); the result is a life of "less involuntary pain."

In 2024 the loop is restated in terms of habits, as a chain of steps (**Source:** `The Power Of Walking – How One Habit Can Change Your Brain, Health, & Life.md`, 2024-06-16):

1. You can only have so many habits.
2. Most of your current habits were not chosen by you.
3. If identity determines habits, your current habits reflect your identity.
4. Habits reinforce identity through conditioning, because "you become what you repeatedly do."
5. So most people's identity is not chosen: "it's something that's subservient to the system that created it."
6. To recreate who you are, change the very few habits that occupy your day, creating a new conditioning cycle that eventually becomes a new identity of your choice.
7. If habits and identity bounce back and forth to create the quality of your experience without your control, you feel depressed, anxious or overwhelmed, precisely because you are not in control of it.

The phrase "you become what you repeatedly do" is used without attribution and treated as a principle in its own right. **Complementary context:** the line is commonly (and inaccurately) attributed to Aristotle; it is Will Durant's paraphrase of Aristotle's ideas on habit.

The fullest version arrives in December 2025, under the name **anatomy of identity**. Koe introduces it with a quotation from Maxwell Maltz: it does not matter how you got an idea or where it came from (yourself, teachers, parents, friends, advertisements); if you have accepted it and are firmly convinced it is true, "it has the same power over you as the hypnotist's words have over a hypnotized subject" (**Source:** `How to fix your entire life in 1 day.md`, 2025-12-28). Then he lays out the steps by which an accepted idea becomes a self. He is explicit that this is a condensed reconstruction, "reverse-engineered so we can change it", not a description of what happens every time:

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| 1 | You want to achieve a goal. |
| 2 | You perceive reality through that goal's lens, noticing only the information and ideas that help achieve it. |
| 3 | "This is the learning process." |
| 4 | You act toward the goal and receive feedback that you are progressing. |
| 5 | You repeat until the behavior is automatic and unconscious: "this is conditioning." |
| 6 | The behavior becomes part of who you think you are: "I am the type of person who…" |
| 7 | You defend that identity to maintain psychological consistency. |
| 8 | Your identity shapes new goals, and the cycle restarts. |

The counting in the transcript is loose (he says "fourth" after only two explicit steps), so the exact numbering of steps 3 and 4 is a reconstruction; the sequence itself is clear. If the identity that comes out of the cycle is disadvantageous, he says, "this gets very bad very quick", and the place to intervene is between step six and step seven: after the behavior has become "who I am" but before the defense kicks in (**Source:** `How to fix your entire life in 1 day.md`, 2025-12-28).

The three versions are refinements of one framework, not changes of position. The 2023 loop names the mutual reinforcement; the 2024 chain explains why most identities are unchosen; the 2025 anatomy shows the full path from goal to defended self and adds the two elements that the rest of this chapter depends on. The first is that the cycle *starts with a goal* (section 3.2). The second is that the cycle *ends with defense* (section 3.4). Between them sits perception (section 3.3).

#### You are the manifestation of your past choices

The anatomy of identity has a temporal corollary that Koe states repeatedly and treats as one of his central realizations: "You at this moment in your life are a manifestation of your past choices, all of them have compounded into who you are today, and your future self is going to be a manifestation of the choices you make from this moment on." He adds that making better decisions "is much easier when you have a purpose and process to frame your attention and decide in alignment with" (**Source:** `Society Is A Pyramid Scheme (Take Back Control Of Your Life).md`, 2023-01-15). The passage reappears almost word for word in a 2024 compilation, introduced as "such, such, such a big realization" (**Source:** `Get Ahead Of 99% Of People With Deep Work & Monk Mode.md`, 2024-03-21).

In 2024 the same idea takes a more confrontational form. "You feel terrible because your future self is watching your every move and they don't like what they see." You are not where you want to be because you did not make the choices that lead to a purposeful career, fulfilling relationships, or a healthy and aesthetic body; so, if you want to control who you become, "your choices are the most important thing in this world" (**Source:** `Disappear And Come Back Unrecognizable (12 Rules To Change Your Life).md`, 2024-04-14).

The book version, read aloud in his summary of *The Art of Focus*, makes the claim cover every domain: "You at this very moment in time are a manifestation of your past mental, physical, financial and spiritual choices. Who you want to become is a manifestation of the choices you make at this moment and the next until it all comes to an end." From there he builds a short argument about failure (**Source:** `The Art Of Focus – Official Book Summary By The Author Dan Koe.md`, 2024-01-18):

1. To decide better you cannot go through life "as a mindless robot"; you need to pause, gain perspective, perceive from non-reaction, and make the choice that actualizes your ideal future.
2. If the good life is created by a series of high-quality decisions,
3. and high-quality decisions only come from improving after low-quality ones,
4. then "it is in your best interest to fail hard and often with a smile on your face."
5. Given the same amount of time, a person who makes 100 decisions regardless of how they feel makes exponentially more progress than one who makes a single decision because "they are a slave to their thoughts."

In 2025 he condenses the same attitude into what he calls "the brutal truth": "you haven't failed enough, you gave up too soon, and you didn't learn how to view failure as the only path to success" (**Source:** `How To Take Back Control Of Your Life With Strategic Thinking.md`, 2025-03-16). This is an opinion addressed to his audience, not a law, but it follows from the model. If identity is a compounding of choices, the number of choices you make (and correct) is the variable that determines how fast the identity can change, and fear of failure reduces that number.

The connection to the anatomy of identity is direct. Choices are the "act" step of the cycle; repeated, they condition; conditioned, they become "the type of person I am." Saying "you are the manifestation of your past choices" is the same claim as "most identities are subservient to the system that created them", stated from the inside. The difference is one of emphasis: the first sentence assigns responsibility, the second explains why that responsibility was mostly exercised by someone else.

### 3.2 Goals Compose Identity

The anatomy of identity begins with "you want to achieve a goal." That is not an incidental starting point. In Koe's model, goals are what identity is mostly made of, and the idea from Part I that you are always pursuing some goal, chosen or assigned, becomes here a claim about the structure of the self.

#### All behavior is goal-oriented

Koe calls this "the first step to understanding the mind": "all behavior is goal-oriented" (**Source:** `How to fix your entire life in 1 day.md`, 2025-12-28). At the surface level the claim is trivial. You step forward to reach a location; you scratch your nose to remove an itch. Even moving your hand while talking "has the goal of getting something across" (**Source:** `Get Mad At Where You Are In Life (A Deep Explanation).md`, 2023-06-11). The claim stops being trivial at the next level down. Surface actions are sub-goals of greater goals that you are usually not aware of. Sitting on the couch or doomscrolling serves a bigger goal that was injected at birth during conditioning, or by society, or that is simply your own goal of protection, safety, pleasure or feeling good; it is unconscious, and "you do it like you breathe." At a more complex level, people often pursue goals that harm them and then justify those goals "in socially acceptable ways or ways that don't make us feel like a loser" (**Source:** `How to fix your entire life in 1 day.md`, 2025-12-28).

The principle comes right after a quotation from Alfred Adler that the source does not reproduce, and Koe presents it as his own without explicit attribution. In the same video he opens the following point with a second Adler line that he does quote: "Trust only movement. Life happens at the level of events, not of words." His use of it is methodological. If behavior always serves a goal, then behavior *reveals* goals, and what someone says they want is weaker evidence than what they do. To change who you are you must understand how the mind works so you can reprogram it, and the first datum is your own behavior.

In 2025 he restates the principle as the second step of a method for changing your mind: "You act the way you do right now because you already have a goal. That's how the mind works. Your mind is a goal striving machine that perceives the world in a way that allows it to collect useful information to achieve that goal. The thing is you're unconscious of the goal you're pursuing and it's ruining your life." All humans have goals at all times; even taking a step is aligned with one (**Source:** `How To Gamify Your Life (And Reinvent Yourself... Fast).md`, 2025-05-08). The phrase "goal striving machine" is Koe's adaptation of Maxwell Maltz's "goal striving mechanism", discussed below; the claim that the goal is unconscious and "ruining your life" is his own.

#### Identity has goals baked into it

If every action serves a goal, and identity is what you act from, then identity must contain goals. Koe says it directly in 2023: identity "has goals baked into it", because identity is required to navigate the world and it determines what you do. His examples come from ideology. People heavily tied to a religious, nutritional, business or political ideology almost always act in alignment with goals assigned by that "intellectual construct." The political ideologue adopted the parents' beliefs without question and acts toward the party's goals. In election season people "become new people": they agree with an idea when it is framed non-politically but get "up in arms" when the same idea is framed politically, because now their identity is at stake and they feel they will die, "because that's what death is, it's conceptual." Religion works the same way. When Koe wrote a newsletter about God that was not framed through any religious lens, people emailed him "you didn't provide proof", which he reads as regurgitated, "unconscious… mindless… robot" responses. By contrast, people who seek truth, awareness and understanding make decisions more conducive to their ideal future (**Source:** `Get Mad At Where You Are In Life (A Deep Explanation).md`, 2023-06-11). The phrase "death is conceptual" anticipates section 3.4; here the point is only that the ideologue's actions are explained by goals that came packaged with the identity.

The general statement comes in 2024: "You've been assigned goals since the day you were born. These goals went on to frame how you view the world because your goals compose your identity. You learn skills to achieve those goals. You registered opportunities in alignment with those goals. Everything you experience in life is through the lens of the conscious or unconscious goals guiding the systems being formed in your head." The same passage states the alternative in Koe's characteristic terms: to build a life of meaning, money and impact "we must pursue our ideal future, create a story worth telling, and pass that path to those who are ready to receive it" (**Source:** `Disappear And Come Back Unrecognizable (12 Rules To Change Your Life).md`, 2024-04-14). The phrase "a story worth telling" links back to identity-as-story: the goals you pursue write the second half of the story.

#### A web of conscious and unconscious goals

The most precise formulation of the idea appears in late 2023, and it introduces a vocabulary of systems that Part III will develop. "The information we are exposed to as children and throughout our lives programs our minds to run on certain systems. A system in brief is the process of reaching a goal." He immediately limits the definition ("obviously this can get extremely complex, so let's just keep it to that"). Then: "Our identity is a web of conscious and unconscious goals that determine the skills we acquire, the interests we learn and the choices we make in alignment with those goals." The systems in the mind are "the information roads that our mind operates on", all running toward goals related to survival and other things, and daily decisions are made on the basis of the information collected and the systems formed over time (**Source:** `The Daily Routine That Changed My Life (4 Habits Most People Ignore).md`, 2023-11-19).

**Information roads** is Koe's term for these mental systems: the routes along which information habitually travels toward a goal. The image is useful because roads are built by traffic: a route traveled often becomes easier to travel, and a route never traveled does not exist for practical purposes.

A month later he uses the same model to correct a common misunderstanding. "The general misunderstanding here is that you either have a goal or you don't." You always have goals; your mind is "a web of conscious and unconscious goals with accompanying systems to achieve them" (**Source:** `You Won’t Be The Same Person In 6 Months (Master Anything, Fast).md`, 2023-12-17).
