"When you have a meaningful project to build, not one assigned to you by parents, teachers or society at large, you see life in a completely different way." Writing a book differs from writing a social post: "my mind expands to match the frame of that book. I notice more in my everyday experience, the information I consume and the conversations I have, because I have an **anchor for those ideas**." "My mind can zip through complex reasoning and make sense of ideas I couldn't before," articulating "novel lines of thought that AI can't, because I would have to train it on that same frame." "Most people don't optimize for pattern recognition, and by doing so they rarely become curious or obsessed; they haven't invested energy into a project that encourages their mind to take a new shape" (**Source:** same file).

Connect is less an activity than an effect: the expanded perception that a large, self-chosen project produces, in which everyday inputs start to fit somewhere. It is the goal as lens of Chapter 6 at the scale of a book. Koe's remark about AI is a claim about originality: an AI could produce lines of thought within a frame it was trained on, but the frame his mind has built through months of work on a project is his, and that is where its novel connections come from (Chapter 18 develops originality). The insistence that the project not be "assigned" repeats the polarity argument: only a chosen project expands the mind to its frame, because only a chosen project is something the mind keeps working on when unattended.

#### How the framework evolved

The corpus records the evolution of this framework as a renaming and refinement, with experimentation as the only reason given:

| Version | Date | Parts | Time assignment | What it adds |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Three habit morning routine | 2022-06 | Sun walk, creative habit, focused work; curious consumption | Morning and afternoon | Purpose as the reason consumption converges |
| Creativity block | 2022-11 | Productivity and creativity, "two sides of the same coin" | Creativity blocks outside productive blocks | The warning against "creating on an empty tank" |
| Fill, Empty, Use (tweet and holistic routine) | 2023-03 to 2023-06 | Fill, empty, use | Afternoon, evening, morning | Nine detailed activities; experimentation as a daily need |
| Book version | 2024-01 | Fill, empty, use | None | Creative firepower and creative emergence |
| Read, write, build | 2024-01 to 2024-07 | Read, write, build | None; conditional on the bottleneck | Diagnostic form; overwhelm as a sign of learning |
| Macro states of consciousness | 2024-06 | Productivity and creativity blocks | Alternating within the morning | The walk between blocks; the gym as cutoff |
| Balance version | 2024-08 | Fill, empty, use | Afternoon, evening, morning, or all three in the morning | Anxiety and boredom as the two imbalances |
| Four modules | 2024-12 | Clear, consume, create, connect | None: "you don't have to do them in order" | Connect; the project as a magnet; titrating |
| Keystone habits | 2025-03 | Build, learn, walk | Daily blocks | Applied to learning with AI |

Across the versions, the constant is the cycle: take in, process, produce, with something in the cycle that empties or connects. What changes is the rigidity of the schedule, which loosens from fixed slots to modules done in any order. This is the same movement as the routine itself in section 13.2, from a fixed day to "a guess" that keeps changing, and the same as the view of systems: principles last, schedules are experiments.

### 13.4 Maintaining Order: Hard Reset, Weekly Plan and Reflection

#### Entropy applies to the organization of your life

The routines of section 13.2 and the cycle of section 13.3 describe a life when it works. This last section is about what happens when it stops working, and why it inevitably does. Koe's answer is the law of Chapter 5. In a January 2023 video he again calls entropy the "supreme law of the universe," present in almost every situation, and the reason "you're in a state of chaos." "The organization of your life, and therefore your mind, tends towards disorder" if you do not perform what he calls **mental housekeeping**: writing down everything on your mind, restructuring and reorganizing it, "literally taking your mind, putting it on paper and ordering it in a way that makes sense," so that it gives you clarity to execute. Not doing this is dangerous, he says, because you can pick up bad habits along the way, and bad habits are hard to break (he defers that topic to another video or "a book on habit formation"). But eliminating them becomes much easier with clarity: "prioritizing clarity in your life" (**Source:** `How To Hard Reset Your Life (In 30 Minutes).md`, 2023-01-05; the same passage is reissued in `Get Ahead Of 99% Of People With Deep Work & Monk Mode.md`, 2024-03-21).

The phrase "the organization of your life, and therefore your mind" carries an assumption worth making explicit: the structure of one's days and the structure of one's mind are the same structure seen from two sides. A cluttered schedule is a cluttered mind, and ordering one orders the other. Mental housekeeping is therefore not a productivity trick but an application of Chapter 5's thesis that clarity is order in consciousness. The link to habits completes section 13.2: bad habits are what accumulate in the gaps of a disordered life, and they are easier to replace once the disorder is visible on paper.

#### The invisible building

In November 2023 Koe gives the same idea its most memorable image. "When we don't have clarity on how to achieve a goal, our mind becomes disordered: we become overwhelmed, anxious and narrow-minded, because the challenge of the goal does not match the skill that we have. Our mind starts to decline into chaos. This is known as entropy." "Entropy is universal; it doesn't only apply to things like buildings that fall apart with time and less maintenance. **The structure of your mind or identity is an invisible building.**" The remedy has three parts: "You reverse entropy by making a goal conscious, creating a path to achieve it, and focusing your attention on priority actions that bring results as feedback." The priority actions "revolve around daily self-education and practice," so that you are exposed to information that creates a new identity, which lets you "perceive certain situations as advantageous towards your conscious goals" and "see problems in situations as opportunities." The lesson he draws is blunt: "you need a plan; there isn't any other way, because if you don't have one, society does, and they've been planning your life for decades." "Nobody wants to wake up 40 years later wondering where the time went" (**Source:** `The Daily Routine That Changed My Life (4 Habits Most People Ignore).md`, 2023-11-19).

The passage condenses most of the book into a maintenance problem. The invisible building is the identity of Part II; its decay is the entropy of Part III; the goal, path and priority actions are the direction of Part IV; the daily self-education and practice are the routines of this chapter; and the feedback is the cybernetic loop of Chapter 6. The diagnosis of overwhelm and anxiety as a mismatch between challenge and skill is Csikszentmihalyi's flow channel (Chapter 10). And the closing threat, that society has a plan if you don't, is the "assigned goals" thesis of Chapter 1. The image of the building explains why maintenance is never finished: buildings do not decay because they were badly built but because time passes. An identity that was ordered once will drift unless the order is renewed.

The corpus records a tension with this "you need a plan." In December 2023 and again in 2024 Koe says that "success is not planned, it is automatic," because a mind programmed with the right goals stores the information that leads to them. He does not reconcile the two formulations. They are compatible if read in sequence: the plan makes goals conscious and reprograms the identity; once the identity is programmed, success happens "automatically" in the sense that perception and action follow the goal without deliberate effort. The plan is the maintenance; the automaticity is what maintenance makes possible.

#### A project keeps you sane

In January 2024 Koe makes the remedy more concrete and more personal. Working on a personal project, he says, "is really the only thing that keeps me sane." When he gets overwhelmed or anxious, has negative emotions or thinks about meaningless things, it is usually due to "the concept of **psychic entropy**, or the mind tending toward disorder." He falls into a rut or a "season of overwhelm or anxiety" only because he lost focus, letting it split among other things. "In order to reverse entropy you need to order your mind; you need to focus on something that brings structure to your mind, and in most cases that is a project." And a project is not only computer work: your relationship, your life, your health, your business and its skill set can all be projects. At the time, his own were Cortex (his software), an education platform and community for creators, the promotion of his book, the planning of another book, and gaining a few pounds before cutting for summer (**Source:** `This High-Income Skill Will Make You Irreplaceable (Full Guide).md`, 2024-01-28).

The passage reverses the usual relation between rest and order. The common assumption is that overwhelm calls for a break. Koe's diagnosis is that overwhelm, for him, is usually split focus, and the remedy is not less structure but more: a single project that gives attention somewhere to go. This is why the polarity argument of section 13.1 said that "work brings order to the mind," and why endless free time is miserable. A project is the structure that rest needs in order to be rest rather than drift. The inclusion of a body goal (gaining weight before a cut) in his list of projects shows how broadly he uses the word: anything with a goal, a path and feedback is a project.

Psychic entropy is Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi's term; as Chapter 5 noted, Koe first attributed it to him and later used it as his own vocabulary, as in this passage, where no author is named.

#### Order is balanced with chaos

Maintenance is necessary because order does not last, and Koe insists that this is normal rather than a failure. In May 2024: "Order is balanced with chaos. Your mind isn't always going to be ordered, it's often going to be chaotic, and you need to be able to zoom out, create order, remind yourself of your goals and fill in the gaps that created the chaos in the first place." He names three constants: a constant reminder of your vision; constant self-education; and constant building toward your vision, so that you practice the skills to achieve it and identify new paths or gaps in your knowledge to fill. And then the diagnosis of self-discipline that justifies them: "**The reason people struggle with self-discipline is because they get distracted from what matters**: they forget who they want to become, they forget what they are capable of, they forget the impact they want to have" (**Source:** `It's actually pretty easy to be self-disciplined (if you stop getting distracted).md`, 2024-05-12).

The redefinition of self-discipline as memory is the important move. A lapse in discipline is usually explained as weakness of will; Koe explains it as forgetting. If that is right, the remedy is not more willpower but better reminders: practices that bring the vision back into attention regularly. The three constants map onto the earlier sections. The reminder of the vision is the anti-vision and vision of Chapter 7, revisited; self-education is the "fill" of section 13.3; building is the "use." The phrase "zoom out" is the zoom of Chapter 6, here used as the first step of restoring order.

A year later he adds a line that connects order to novelty: "Your life loses the spark of novelty and pattern recognition when you have a vague or unconscious story you are living out. So **when you create the order your mind craves, chaos is much easier to keep at bay**" (**Source:** `How To Gamify Your Life (And Reinvent Yourself... Fast).md`, 2025-05-08). The claim is counterintuitive: one might expect order to reduce novelty. Koe's view is that a clear story (a goal, a project, a game) is what makes things noticeable at all, because pattern recognition needs something to recognize patterns *for*. A vague story makes everything equally irrelevant, which is experienced as dullness, and dullness invites the chaos of cheap stimulation.

#### The hard reset: when to use it

The most fully specified maintenance practice in the corpus is what Koe calls a **hard reset**, "a process that I run through when my life gets a bit too messy." It first appears in January 2023 as a thirty-minute exercise, and it is reissued with small additions in 2024. He gives the conditions for using it precisely: when you start thinking back to when life was better; when things get bogged down and you don't feel like you're living the same life; when you're not making the progress you used to and you wonder what you're doing differently and why you feel this way; when "your routines start to fall apart and little tasks work their way in unconsciously," and you feel you have no time, or can't do the work you used to do well. The tools are minimal: paper or a notebook ("I recommend buying a journal," and always having one on hand), or his free printable planner (**Source:** `How To Hard Reset Your Life (In 30 Minutes).md`, 2023-01-05; `Get Ahead Of 99% Of People With Deep Work & Monk Mode.md`, 2024-03-21).

The symptoms describe entropy at the scale of a life rather than a task. Nothing has gone catastrophically wrong; routines have simply eroded, and small tasks have crept in without being chosen. The nostalgic thought ("when life was better") is treated as a signal, not as an evaluation: it means the current structure has drifted from the one that worked. The name "hard reset" is also used in the corpus for the gym as the transition between work and rest (section 13.3); the two practices share a name but not a function.

#### Step one: put your mind on paper

The first step is observation. Pull out a piece of paper or a notebook and note two things: exactly what you are doing on a daily basis, "every single thing," as you go about the day (what you are doing, what you are thinking about, what you feel you have to do); and exactly how you feel during those times. Be very specific, because "you're putting your mind on paper, your mind is very complex, and **if you don't have accurate data on your paper, you're not going to be able to move on to the next step**" effectively (**Source:** `How To Hard Reset Your Life (In 30 Minutes).md`, 2023-01-05; `Get Ahead Of 99% Of People With Deep Work & Monk Mode.md`, 2024-03-21).

The January 2024 version of the reset compresses this step into a ten-minute exercise. Use it, Koe says, when you constantly think back to a time when life was better, when routines fall apart, tasks fill your day and you feel nothing gets done. Write exactly what you do daily and how you feel in the morning, the afternoon and the night; take ten minutes; get specific. The purpose: "identifying **unconscious parasites**, time and energy suckers." He does all of this in his planner, which has daily, monthly and quarterly pages; the quarterly page is for mapping out your vision and "creat[ing] the game of your life" (**Source:** `How To Reset Your Life In 7 Days.md`, 2024-01-07).

The two versions differ in method. In 2023 you record the day as it happens, which produces real data but takes a day; in 2024 you reconstruct it in ten minutes, broken down by morning, afternoon and night, which is faster and organizes the data by energy level, the variable that Chapter 12 used to order tasks. The "unconscious parasites" are what the exercise is designed to expose: activities that consume time and energy without ever having been chosen, the "little tasks" that "work their way in unconsciously" from the list of symptoms. Recording how you *feel* is as important as recording what you *do*, because the parasites often reveal themselves as states (drained, scattered, anxious) before they are identified as activities.

#### Three reasons you aren't getting results

Before reorganizing, Koe offers a diagnosis of why results stop. There are three causes, he says, and the same three appear in all versions. First, feeling too pressed for time, which "is usually the cause of stress": you are in a "very **narrow state**" and feel that you have no time, "but in reality you're just sitting there thinking you don't have any time when you could actually be doing the thing that you're putting off." Second, not having the energy: living in that stressed state "takes a lot of mental energy," narrowing your focus on random thoughts or other things, precious mental energy that you were not structuring in a way conducive to results. Third, "maybe you've just stopped doing the things that get results." His business example: "hey, I'm not reaching out to get clients, why am I not getting clients? And it's like, you kind of are answering your own question there" (**Source:** `How To Hard Reset Your Life (In 30 Minutes).md`, 2023-01-05; `Get Ahead Of 99% Of People With Deep Work & Monk Mode.md`, 2024-03-21; restated in `How To Reset Your Life In 7 Days.md`, 2024-01-07).

The three causes form a sequence rather than a list. The feeling of having no time produces stress (narrow, unconscious focus in the terms of the Focus Matrix); stress consumes the mental energy that the work would have needed; and without energy, the actions that produced results quietly stop. The first cause is also a perception, not a fact: the time spent thinking that there is no time is time that could have been used. The client example is deliberately banal, because the third cause is usually invisible to the person inside it: they experience a lack of results without noticing that they stopped the activity that produced them. The log of step one exists to make that visible.

#### Step two: prioritize, remove, restructure

The second step is reorganization. Look over what you wrote and ask what you can change. Create your own structure: circle or write down the things that get you results, and **prioritize** them; **remove** the things that "snuck in there... and don't deserve to be there," which could be draining mental, monetary or even physical energy; and **restructure** specific tasks and obligations. The aim, in a phrase he repeats in every version: "**get the chaotic structure of your mind onto paper and reorganize it**" (**Source:** `How To Hard Reset Your Life (In 30 Minutes).md`, 2023-01-05; `Get Ahead Of 99% Of People With Deep Work & Monk Mode.md`, 2024-03-21). In the 2024 version, the step draws on both the brain dump and the vision: look over your notes and your vision, prioritize what gets results, remove what "snuck their way into your day and don't deserve to be there," and restructure tasks and obligations "to free up more time" (**Source:** `How To Reset Your Life In 7 Days.md`, 2024-01-07).

The three verbs correspond to three operations on the log. Prioritizing selects (it is the priority ladder of Chapter 12 applied to the whole day). Removing subtracts the parasites. Restructuring moves what remains, because some obligations cannot be removed but can be placed where they do less damage, as Koe placed email at the end of his mornings. The addition of the vision in 2024 matters: without it, "what gets results" is measured against whatever goal was already operating, which might be the assigned one. With it, prioritization is measured against the goal you chose.

#### Step three: the week-long plan

The third step turns the reorganized structure into a plan. Take ten minutes and, on a new page, write every single thing you will do over the next week: your morning routine; the tasks you will complete during your focused work routine; other specific tasks and obligations, like meetings, and how they lay out in your day; what you will do in between; and your nightly routine. "**Just doing this alone reduces the friction that allows you to make better decisions**" (**Source:** `How To Hard Reset Your Life (In 30 Minutes).md`, 2023-01-05; reissued, together with the mental housekeeping passage, in `Get Ahead Of 99% Of People With Deep Work & Monk Mode.md`, 2024-03-21).

Why should writing a plan reduce friction? The answer is in the default mode of a disordered mind. Each unplanned moment of the week requires a decision, and each decision, made in a narrow or tired state, tends toward the easiest option. A written plan converts those decisions into a single decision made in advance, when the mind is clear. The plan does not make the week rigid; it makes the default the chosen option rather than the available one.

Koe immediately warns that this is not a quick fix. Some people will write the plan and it will work well; others will have to experiment. While executing, "you're going to hit a problem, and then you're going to have to deal with that mentally, and you're going to have to go back to what you wrote down and change it for the next day" to something you think will work better: trial and error. Over the week, "you just get into this flow by solving the problems that come up along the way, and then you have a system that over the next month you can just do every single day," which becomes easier and eventually a habit. Preferably, he adds, the habit is doing the things that move you toward your purpose, your vision or "the highest version of yourself" (**Source:** `How To Hard Reset Your Life (In 30 Minutes).md`, 2023-01-05; `Get Ahead Of 99% Of People With Deep Work & Monk Mode.md`, 2024-03-21).

The progression is the one section 13.2 described for routines: plan, problem, revision, system, habit. Its mention of "flow" is not loose. Solving the problems that arise in executing a plan is a challenge matched to one's skill, with clear goals and immediate feedback, which is the structure Chapter 10 identified as the condition of flow. Maintenance done this way is not a chore but a game.

#### The loop, and the lifestyle design process

The January 2024 version of the reset makes the loop explicit and calls it "one of the most important things I've ever done." You are in a chaotic spot because of entropy: routines and habits tend toward disorder unless you put energy into maintaining them. Write every single thing you will do next week (which reduces the friction of making better decisions): morning routine, focused work routine, other tasks and meetings, nightly routine. You will experiment; if your routine does not flow, there is a problem, and you go back and change what you wrote: "**this is why we write it down, so you can go back and change it.**" Repeat week after week until it gets better: that is how you refine a system, make it second nature and "become a new person." The loop: map your week, stick to the plan, identify problems, experiment with solutions, and repeat until you reach your ideal future. It gets more efficient with time; making this mental housekeeping regular is what makes new skills second nature. He did it himself, he says, the same day, in the weekly section of his planner (**Source:** `How To Reset Your Life In 7 Days.md`, 2024-01-07).

The book summary of the same month gives the whole procedure under the name of **lifestyle design**, with an extra audit step and an explicit goal (**Source:** `The Art Of Focus – Official Book Summary By The Author Dan Koe.md`, 2024-01-18):

1. Pull out a notebook.
2. Write down exactly what you are doing, and why, at every minute of the day.
3. Write how you feel in the morning, the afternoon and the night.
4. Prioritize, remove and restructure your day so that you feel better and have more time; "this requires honesty with yourself."
5. Create a week-long system "**to reverse entropy in your daily routine**": plan your morning routine, focused work routine, other tasks and meetings, and nightly routine.
6. Over the next week, return to the notebook and iterate on what does not work, to ensure maximum mental output, creativity and life enjoyment.

The "why" in step 2 and the "honesty" in step 4 are the additions that matter. Recording *why* you do each thing exposes activities that have no reason, or whose reason is someone else's goal. Honesty is needed because the parasites are often things one enjoys or identifies with, and removing them meets the same resistance as any identity change.

The versions of the reset can be compared:

| | Hard reset (2023-01; reissued 2024-03) | Seven-day reset (2024-01) | Lifestyle design process (2024-01, book summary) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trigger | Life "a bit too messy"; routines fall apart; little tasks creep in | Same symptoms | Presented as the general method of lifestyle design |
| Observation | Log what you do and feel, as the day goes | Ten-minute reconstruction by morning, afternoon, night; "unconscious parasites" | Every minute: what and why; feelings by time of day |
| Diagnosis | Three causes: no time, no energy, stopped doing what works | Same three causes | — |
| Reorganization | Prioritize, remove, restructure | Same, informed by the vision | Same, "with honesty" |
| Plan | Ten-minute week-long plan | Week-long plan with an explicit loop | Week-long system "to reverse entropy" |
| Iteration | Not a quick fix: trial and error until system, then habit | Map, stick, identify, experiment, repeat | Iterate over the next week |

The procedure is stable; the 2024 versions add the vision as input, the explicit loop, and the "why."

#### Reset from scratch

In October 2024 Koe proposes a more radical variant. Tomorrow when you wake up, start completely new: everything you have done before does not matter; be intentional about doing different things from the second you wake up, because your habits, choices and decisions got you where you are. He clarifies that not everything you currently do is bad; this is a way to reset completely: "you need to **drop everything and see what sticks**... do nothing, and that alone will shine light on what your priorities are." Then fill your time with learning, building and experiencing as much as possible (**Source:** `The Fastest Way To Change Your Life (Starting Right Now).md`, 2024-10-10).

The method inverts the hard reset. The hard reset starts from the current day and subtracts what does not belong; the reset from scratch starts from an empty day and lets what is essential return on its own. What comes back first, unbidden, is either a real priority or a strong habit, and the exercise makes it possible to tell them apart. It is the experiment of the dopamine detox (Chapter 11) applied to the whole routine: remove everything, and the things you miss reveal what matters.

#### Nightly reflection: closing the loops

The daily counterpart of the weekly plan is reflection at night, and in October 2025 Koe calls it "arguably the most important one that nobody does," the seventh and last step of his thirty-day dopamine detox protocol (Chapter 11 presents the protocol as a whole). Your brain constantly tries to process experiences; without dedicated time, "it hijacks your attention at the worst possible moments." "This is the **Zeigarnik effect**. Your brain holds on to incomplete tasks and unprocessed experiences, creating tension that drains your cognitive resources." Reflection does several things at once. It closes open loops. It is "an act of metacognition, or thinking about your thinking, the highest form of human intelligence." It builds a feedback loop: after thirty days you have "30 data points about what actually moves your life forward." "**It transforms mistakes into data, rather than regrets.**" And it reduces decision fatigue for tomorrow. How to do it: set a non-negotiable alarm for 9:30 p.m., or thirty minutes before bed; use the **3-2-1 framework**, "three wins, two lessons, one intention for the morning"; use a physical notebook, to avoid digital rabbit holes before bed; and start with two minutes if ten feel like too much (**Source:** `A Full Dopamine Detox Protocol To Reset Your Life In 30 Days.md`, 2025-10-26).

Reflection here is the evening "empty" of section 13.3, given a mechanism and a format. The mechanism is the open loop: unprocessed experience occupies attention, the "RAM" of Chapter 6, until it is closed, and writing closes it. The format is minimal: three wins (evidence of progress, which feeds motivation), two lessons (mistakes converted into data, which feeds correction), one intention (a goal for the morning, which gives the default mode network something to work on overnight, as in Bush's practice of sleeping on one idea). The thirty data points are the cybernetic loop of Chapter 6 accumulated: a month of reflections is a record of what actually moved life forward, against which the vision can be checked. The physical notebook is a small application of Chapter 11's environment design: the phone at night is the gateway to the cheap dopamine the protocol is meant to remove.

**Complementary context:** the Zeigarnik effect is named after the psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik, whose experiments in the 1920s suggested that interrupted tasks are remembered better than completed ones. Koe uses it in two opposite directions: elsewhere, to stop a work block before finishing so that the mind keeps working on it (Chapter 12); here, to explain why unprocessed experiences drain attention and must be closed at night. The research on the effect is mixed; Koe uses it as an explanatory frame.

#### The weekly review

At the scale of the week, Koe's practice is a review. In October 2024 he describes it: at the start of each week he does a **weekly review** to refine his system, asking four questions. What went well last week? What didn't go well? What am I grateful for? What are my focus projects? (A template was available in Cortex.) He gives three reasons. It is a weekly way to shine light on what to add to your vision or anti-vision. It clarifies and evolves the goals you pursue, so that "the journey can take shape with the shape of the destination." And it shows the minor changes that improve progress over time. "If you were to just focus on this weekly review the entire time and iterating on your vision, then you're going to make it pretty far" (**Source:** `It's actually pretty easy to focus 12 hours a day (if you do this).md`, 2024-10-13).

The four questions cover the past (what went well and badly), the emotional register (gratitude) and the future (focus projects). The reasons connect the review to Chapter 7: the anti-vision and vision are not written once but extended every week with what the week revealed. The phrase "the journey can take shape with the shape of the destination" restates Chapter 6's principle that the destination determines the journey, with a dynamic twist: the destination itself is refined weekly, and the journey follows.

In December 2024 Koe shows the tool he was using at the time, a weekly creative planner template in Cortex, in a walkthrough partly shown on screen (details beyond what he narrates cannot be reconstructed from the transcript). You duplicate the template into your workspace and duplicate it again each week. Each day is an "element" (a sub-note in the software). Inside each day are four parts: a **brain dump** ("clear your mind, turn thoughts, reflection and experience into five to 10 ideas," at any time of day, since it is modular); **learning**, where you link the sources you are consuming (his example is a book by David Deutsch he was reading, stored as a PDF in the software's library) or create documents such as "notes on creativity"; **projects**, what you are working on (his example: a newsletter on AI with its outline, and a book, newsletter and social posts for the week, also favorited for quick access); and **tasks**, the structure of priority tasks, walks and meals. Weeks are organized into monthly folders ("planning December 2024"). Ideas captured on the phone can be sent to a specific document (for example, the page for the second week of December), and for his book he saves ideas to each chapter every day as they come to him while consuming: "If you write newsletters or social posts and you're not capturing ideas to where you're going to write those things, you're missing out" (**Source:** `A Daily Routine To Work Less, Earn More & Enjoy Life.md`, 2024-12-29).

The template is the four modules of section 13.3 given a container: the brain dump is "clear," learning is "consume," projects are "create," and capturing ideas into the documents where they will be used is the practical form of "connect." It is also, unavoidably, a demonstration of his product, which should be noted: the structure he recommends coincides with the features of the software he was selling.

In August 2026 his advice about tools reverses. The way to practice adaptability, he says, is "review, reflection, and prediction. You need to schedule this weekly. You need to review your week, see if you're on track, reflect on your progress, and predict where you're heading." But no fancy template: "just keep a piece of paper by your computer. I have this little tiny notebook where I just jot things down, because I understand that if I try to keep up with a note-taking system, I don't keep up with it. That's not how your mind works. **It kind of has to be messy.** You have to embrace just putting an idea down and letting it get lost. And if it's important, you will remember it." Apple Notes, a notebook, anything: "just get in the habit of writing things down" (**Source:** `The Art of Strategic Thinking (How to Become Wildly Successful at Anything You Do).md`, 2026-08-19).

| | 2024 | 2026 |
|---|---|---|
| Practice | Weekly review: went well, didn't, grateful, focus projects | Weekly review, reflection and prediction |
| Tool | Cortex template; weekly creative planner with daily elements, monthly folders, ideas captured to specific documents | A tiny notebook by the computer, Apple Notes, anything |
| View of structure | Capture everything to where it will be used | "It kind of has to be messy"; let ideas get lost; the important ones return |
| Reason given | Ideas not captured to projects are lost | "If I try to keep up with a note-taking system, I don't keep up with it. That's not how your mind works." |

The content of the review is stable; the tool and the philosophy of capture change. The corpus classifies this as a correction of personal practice, from a structured system tied to his product to minimum friction, and Koe's reason is a claim about how the mind works. There is also a third position, recorded elsewhere: in a 2026 creativity protocol he tells people not to write ideas down at all for its duration ("if it's important it will come back"), while admitting that this is "antithetical to everything that I preach" and limiting it to the protocol. The three positions can be read as a progression in where trust is placed: first in the system that stores ideas, then in a light habit of writing things down, and in the protocol, for a limited time, in memory itself. What survives every version is the review: the weekly act of looking back, checking the direction and correcting it. That is the same conclusion section 13.2 reached about systems. Principles last; tools are experiments.

#### Maintenance as the last practice of self-government

The four sections of this chapter form a single cycle, and the cycle closes the part of the book on self-government. Focused work narrows the mind and spends its energy (Chapter 12). Rest opens it, lets the default mode network connect what the work gathered, and recovers the energy, provided the rest is real and the work was worth recovering from (13.1). A routine holds the two in rhythm, as the rules of a game you chose, built from a few high-leverage habits and revised by experiment (13.2). Within the routine, the mind is filled, emptied and used, so that it neither overflows into anxiety nor runs dry into boredom (13.3). And because every order decays, the whole arrangement is maintained by regular acts of putting the mind on paper: a nightly reflection, a weekly review, a week-long plan, and, when life drifts too far, a hard reset (13.4).

The common assumption beneath all four is the one Chapter 5 established: disorder is the default, and order is something done, not something had. What this chapter adds is that the doing includes not doing. Rest, leisure and reflection are not breaks from the maintenance of order but part of it, because they are where the mind does the work of connecting, processing and closing that focused attention cannot do. Part VI turns from governing attention to using it: how the mind learns, and how it thinks.

### Exercises

1. **Audit your rest.** List everything you did in the last seven days that you would call "rest." Sort each item using Koe's double criterion from section 13.1: did attention leave work, and did it go somewhere that regenerated mental energy or fed the mind? Which items were "deep recovery" and which were "numbing"? Then apply his 2025 correction to yourself: is your problem too little rest, or work that gives you nothing to recover from? Defend your answer with specific evidence from the week.

2. **Reconstruct the argument, then test it.** In your own words, rebuild the chain that leads from "work contracts the mind, rest expands the mind" to "the most effective and result-generating work you do is when you don't work at all." Identify which links are borrowed findings, which are Koe's interpretations, and which are rhetorical. Then describe one kind of work for which the conclusion would clearly fail, and explain which link breaks.

3. **Compare two routines.** Choose two of the routines in section 13.2 (one of Koe's versions and one guest's, or two of Koe's versions). For each element that differs, state what problem the difference solves for that person at that stage. Then, following Dickie Bush's warning, describe what the routine of the person you are studying probably looked like at your own current stage, and what in it you could test next week.

4. **Design a replacement, not a removal.** Pick one habit you would like to end. Using the four domains (mind, body, business, connection) and the criteria "high leverage, high impact, highly enjoyable," design the habit that will occupy its slot. Explain why you expect the replacement to survive past the third week, and what you will treat as a "problem to solve" if it does not, in the sense of Koe's disliked gym exercise.

5. **Diagnose your ratio.** For one week, keep a rough record of how much time you spend consuming, clearing (writing, reflecting) and creating. Using the anxiety–boredom diagnosis of the Fill, Empty, Use framework, interpret what you find. Then decide which version of the framework fits your life better (the time-assigned tweet, all three in the morning, or the four modules in any order) and justify the choice by your circumstances, not by preference.

6. **Run a hard reset on paper.** Carry out steps one and two of the hard reset: log what you do and how you feel in the morning, afternoon and night, then circle what gets results and mark the "unconscious parasites." Which of Koe's three causes (no time, no energy, stopped doing what works) best explains your current situation? Is any item on your list something you identify with, so that removing it would feel like a small loss of self? What does that tell you about the "honesty" step?

7. **Question a claim.** Koe says that people who believe the four-hour workday is impossible "don't have the awareness or experience that allows you to believe that it's possible." Evaluate this argument. What does it get right about the relation between belief and experiment? In what way could the same form of argument be used to dismiss any objection, and how would you tell a legitimate objection from a lack of experience?

8. **Choose your review tool.** Koe moved from a structured weekly template to a "messy" notebook, and in one protocol to writing nothing down at all. Considering your own record with note-taking systems, decide which approach you will use for a weekly review of what went well, what didn't, what you are grateful for and your focus projects. Explain what would have to happen for you to conclude, after a month, that your choice was wrong.

# Part VI — Learning and Thinking

## Chapter 14 — Learning How to Learn: Build to Learn

Part VI begins where the self-government of Part V leaves off. Chapters 11 to 13 described how Dan Koe protects attention, organizes a few hours of focused work and restores order through rest. None of that says what the protected hours should be filled with when the person does not yet know how to do the thing they want to do. That is the question of this chapter: how a person acquires the knowledge and skill that a self-chosen goal demands.

The chapter depends on four earlier pieces of the book. Chapter 2 supplied the critique and the first definitions: Devon Eriksen's distinction between education and job training, the author's formula "education is not programming," and his 2026 definition of **self-education** as "the process of learning what's necessary to achieve self-generated goals," with "no hoarding general knowledge to feel like you're learning." Chapter 6 supplied the mechanism: a goal acts as a lens, and in its 2026 cybernetic version, "a goal creates the error signal, the error signal creates the filter, the filter creates relevance, and relevance creates retention"; from this Koe concluded that "learning is an output process." Chapter 9 supplied the basic vehicle of practice: the project, as anchor, outline and lens, which in 2024 he named the Clarity Catalyst. Chapter 11 supplied a warning that becomes central here: the difference between cheap dopamine, received without effort, and dopamine earned through struggle.

With those pieces in place, Koe's theory of learning can be stated in five steps, which are the five sections of the chapter. Section 14.1 presents learning how to learn as "the meta skill," the case for daily self-education, Devon Eriksen's seven "liberating arts" and the three "vessels" Koe proposes for practicing them, and the author's own education as the story from which the theory was drawn. Section 14.2 treats curiosity as the guide that tells a person what to learn, together with the attitude Koe calls moving "from cope to curiosity" and the three conditions he identified for retaining what he reads. Section 14.3 diagnoses the main failure: information consumed without application, which feels like progress and is not ("tutorial hell"), including the author's account of how he fell into it for years. Section 14.4 presents the remedy, the central idea of the chapter: "don't learn to build, build to learn," with the reasons Koe gives for why building works, the sequences he has proposed over five years, the guitar method and the Build Teach Earn method. Section 14.5 adds the last link: teaching is the strongest form of learning, and teaching in public turns learning into feedback, an audience and, eventually, a business.

One feature of the corpus should be kept in mind throughout. Between 2022 and 2026 Koe described the same learning method under many names ("become a builder," "start then learn," "rapid building," "start, build, learn," "build then learn," the Clarity Catalyst, "project-based learning," "start with the purpose") and with a varying number of steps. The core does not change: have a project, start with what you know, learn what the project's problems demand at the moment they appear, and teach what you learn. What changes is emphasis (how much to study before starting), vocabulary and the theoretical frame used to justify it (from novelty and dopamine in 2022 to cybernetics in 2026). The chapter presents the versions where they differ, rather than collapsing them into one.

### 14.1 The Meta Skill and Self-Education

#### "The skill of all skills"

Koe's most compact statement of why learning matters comes from a 2025 video: "The mark of a free person is that they learn how to learn; that is the meta skill, that is the skill of all skills." His reasoning has three links. First, to pick up any skill that changes your life, you need to know how to learn it effectively; every other skill passes through this one. Second, the choice of what to learn is never neutral: "If you don't choose what to learn you will be told what to learn, and if your mind is the operating system for reality the options available for your future will be drastically limited and you won't even realize it." Third, the world is changing fast (he names technology and AI), which makes learning "the single most important skill, because it allows you to learn the skills that can't be taught in schools." Schools are a large and possibly outdated system; changing a curriculum takes far longer than it takes an individual to learn a topic and make a YouTube video from which you can learn it even faster. If you keep up and adapt, "adding the latest skills to your tool belt," you "can do some incredible things" (**Source:** `How To Learn Anything 10x Faster Than Anyone With AI.md`, 2025-03-09).

Two of the phrases deserve comment. **Meta skill** is Koe's label for learning how to learn: the skill whose object is the acquisition of other skills. **Operating system for reality** is one of his recurring images for the mind, which he uses in several senses across 2024 and 2025 (most people run "Windows 98"; the mind is made of goals mostly programmed by others). Here it carries a specific consequence: since the mind determines which options you can see, a mind filled with what others chose for you limits your future invisibly. The sentence is the learning version of the book's central thesis from Chapter 1, that you always pursue goals, assigned or self-generated. Applied to knowledge, it reads: you always learn something; if you do not choose it, it is chosen for you.

The phrase "the mark of a free person" echoes the conversation with the novelist Devon Eriksen that Chapter 2 reported, and the definition of education is his, not Koe's. "Education is not about how to do a task, it's about how to learn a task." Education is "learning how to teach yourself": whenever you take on a hard task, you have to learn how to do it. The consequence Eriksen draws is the one that matters here: "if you don't learn how to learn, then you can only do things that somebody already understands how to do." He adds that there is no "systematic education in this society in the modern West about how to learn and educate yourself" (**Source:** `The Most Important Skill To Learn In The Next 10 Years With Devon Eriksen.md`, 2024-12-08). The point connects learning to originality: someone who can only follow instructions can only reproduce what already exists, a theme that returns in Chapter 18.

Koe attaches quantitative promises to the meta skill, and they should be read as he qualifies them. In 2024: "When you learn how to learn you can accomplish 6 years of results in 6 months." He immediately adds, "this really varies," and explains the comparison he has in mind: most people stop learning after college, and it takes them six years to learn something very basic and do something new; following his process and continuously reinventing yourself "over and over again" compresses that (**Source:** `The Fastest Way To Acquire High-Value Skills (And Finally Change Your Life).md`, 2024-02-11). He repeats the "6 years in 6 months" line later in 2024 (**Source:** `Life Is A Video Game (Here's How You Win).md`, 2024-07-21). In 2025 the promise takes another form: "If learning allows you to be useful and get what you want out of life, imagine what you could do if you actually spent time learning how to learn." If you knew how to learn fast, "you could achieve 10 goals in the same amount of time that it would take the average person to achieve one," and the average person probably would not achieve it until graduating or until they had "learned enough." In the same video he deliberately skips the science and psychology of learning to focus only on what to do, which he calls "pretty freaking simple. But sometimes the simplest things are the most complex things in the world" to get yourself to do (**Source:** `How To Master Any Skill Fast (Give Yourself 2 Weeks).md`, 2025-08-10).

These figures are rhetorical comparisons, not measurements, and the corpus itself shows that they move. Koe's estimates of how long learning takes vary across the years: "give yourself 20 years, not two weeks" (2023), top 10 percent in six to twelve months (early 2024), "6 years of results in 6 months" (2024), "you can learn anything in two weeks" (2025) and again "2 to 5 years" to master brand, content, marketing and sales even with AI (2026). In 2025 he clarifies that "two weeks" means substantial progress toward a goal, not mastery, which "obviously takes like 10 years." The numbers apply to different scales (a technique, a skill, a business, mastery) and are best read as claims about relative speed: the person who has learned how to learn moves several times faster than the person who has not.

A 2026 video adds an argument about why speed of learning matters at all. If the gap between where you are and where you want to be is a gap of knowledge, then "the future belongs to those who can learn the fastest." Most people stop learning after graduation and run on what Koe calls "preset knowledge." Writing is his antidote, because "80% of writing is research and learning"; it is at once teaching and understanding. He says he learned more in six months of writing when he started out than in all of college or high school. His example is history: he never applied himself to it in school, but since writing about history in some of his newsletters he understands it far better than he did from lectures (**Source:** `The Writing System That Saved My Brain (Learn Faster & Think Clearly).md`, 2026-07-27). The claim about writing anticipates section 14.5 (writing as a form of teaching) and Part VIII.

#### The earliest version: "figuring it out for yourself"

The meta skill has a precursor in 2022, under a plainer name. In a video whose title announces writing as "the skill" to learn, Koe first names a different one: "there is one extremely important skill, and that is figuring it out for yourself." He defines it by two contrasts. It is not doing what people tell you to do; and it is doing what you want "from a conscious mind," not from a "mediocre mind." He guards against the naive reading. "I can do whatever I want" is not what he means; the caricature of the mediocre mind is the person who replies, "you want me to jump off a bridge, okay, I'll go do that." The conscious version examines itself: what are your desires; what survival mechanism, or whatever else, is pulling you toward those things; is it good or bad; do you actually want to do it; does it align with your values; "do you actually have values." What other people tell you to do will not be conducive to what you want. Then comes a realistic nuance: much of the time you may have to do what others tell you, for survival, but at the same time you need to be pursuing a project of your own that leads to autonomy and to mastery of what you want to master, full time, "not for someone else" (**Source:** `Learn This Skill If You Want To Thrive In The Next 10 Years.md`, 2022-08-28).

**Figuring it out for yourself** and the pair **conscious mind / mediocre mind** are Koe's terms. There is a small tension inside the video: the title calls writing "the skill," while the first skill named is figuring it out for yourself, with writing then presented as the skill that monetizes it. The tension resolves if the two are read as layers: figuring things out is the meta skill, writing the skill through which it becomes income. The move from "figuring it out for yourself" (2022) to "learn how to learn" as the meta skill (2024–2026) is a renaming and formalization, not a change of position. The 2022 version keeps something the later one leaves implicit: the meta skill presupposes self-examination. You cannot choose what to learn if you have not examined what you want and why.

#### Daily self-education as a necessity

From the meta skill Koe derives a habit. In 2023 he presents it as the second step of a daily routine and calls it "an absolute necessity." His argument starts from a judgment about school: "Schools are necessary in many cases, but they teach you a fraction of what actually exists in reality; they train you into a compartment of reality, like chemistry, physiology or literature," without regard "for the holistic interconnectedness that breeds true intelligence." **Compartment of reality** is his term for this: an isolated slice of the world, taught without its connections. The consequence is about identity: "Without self-education you go through life with the same narrow identity and perspective as everyone else; you're not a unique individual if you never self-educate." He then lists what education does. It "expands your mind, introduces you to novel perspectives, increases dopamine in the brain as a consistent source of energy, gives you the knowledge to act with clarity," and "over time education conditions your mind to run on new systems." His example of the last point: immerse yourself only in information about building a profitable business and you would build one. Most people skip this step; their morning has no section "dedicated to reading or consuming or researching or pushing into the mental unknown" (**Source:** `The Daily Routine That Changed My Life (4 Habits Most People Ignore).md`, 2023-11-19).

The dopamine claim should be read in the terms Chapter 11 established: Koe uses dopamine as a name for the anticipation that accompanies novelty relevant to a goal, and the claim here is that learning toward something is a renewable source of that drive. He presents it as part of his model, not as a measured effect of studying.

Earlier in 2023 he states the same necessity in starker terms. "You own one thing: your mind; everything else can be taken away." School, he grants, got one thing right: consistent daily education and the hope of a better future. But it does not prioritize curiosity, so most students hate learning by graduation. "Learning is the foundation of the human experience, and once you stop you die." The prescription is modest in size and absolute in frequency: learn something every day, whether ten minutes or three hours. His reason is that learning is the only way to discover a potential that was not assigned to you. You cannot act on opportunities that do not exist for you, and you cannot even register them without having reached a level of skill by doing your own thing. His example: until you have started a business, you cannot look at someone online and think, "he has this business, I have this offer, he can pay me this much, I'll reach out in a way I know, then systemize it." When you stop learning, life stops progressing, "feel-good chemicals" stop flowing, and life becomes "mediocre, repetitive, mechanical, robotic" (**Source:** `The Cure To A Mediocre Life (Become Multidimensionally Jacked).md`, 2023-08-30).

In 2024 he gives the mechanism behind that example a name. While you learn and build, "you're increasing your awareness surface area": "when you have more skills, you have more education, you have exposure to different opportunities, you can identify more profitable problems and opportunities that you can solve and go into" (**Source:** `If Your Life Is Spiraling Out Of Control, Here's The Solution To Feeling Lost.md`, 2024-03-10). **Awareness surface area** is a coined term: the extent of reality in which a person can recognize problems and opportunities, which grows with skill, education and exposure. It explains why the person who has started something sees opportunities that the person who is still waiting cannot see, and it connects to the reticular-activation argument of Chapter 6: what you know and pursue determines what registers.

Two further passages from 2023 tie self-education to creativity and to the unusual life. The first places it at the foundation of a creative career. The first step is self-education (not formal education, "though that can be useful"). Creativity is "using your diverse knowledge and interest to help you achieve a goal." If you have never learned anything outside what you were told to learn, you are not "an actual creative"; if you only know what schools teach, you can only create what may already exist, because "you can't create something rare or unknown without going down a rare or unknown path." This is less about becoming an expert than about "a constant influx of information" to fuel your goals and what you build. Without unique interests, knowledge and skills you lack **creative firepower**, Koe's term for the reserve of unusual inputs that creation draws on (**Source:** `The Future Of Work Is Play (How To Create A Digital Career).md`, 2023-12-31). The second passage draws the conclusion about who can take that path: "The only people who have the choice to take a rare path that breeds rare results are the self-educators." It repeats the list of what education does and adds one more: it exposes you to potentials you were not aware of. A consistent flow of education increases the chance of encountering meaningful events, which "occur at the edge of the known, when your nervous system signals that you should pay attention": with one foot in the unknown you can "just barely metabolize new aspects of reality" and use them (**Source:** `You Won’t Be The Same Person In 6 Months (Master Anything, Fast).md`, 2023-12-17). The **edge of the known** is the same border that Chapter 10 described as the place of flow, where challenge slightly exceeds skill; here it is described from the side of information rather than effort.

A 2023 video turns the necessity into a protocol for the digital age. "Lifelong self-education will be a requirement to continue adapting to the digital landscape." "Education shapes the future because it shapes human behavior"; it "expands your perspective and allows you to spot opportunities in unknown territory." "The new education system is being built online before your eyes." The steps: set a goal; find creators you resonate with; drown yourself in their information; watch new opportunities register in your awareness; and act on them "like your life depends on it" (**Source:** `The Value Creator (A New Internet Career Path For Intelligent People).md`, 2023-07-19). The order matters. The goal comes first, so that the "drowning" is filtered; the creators come second, chosen by resonance; and the last step is action. Without the last step the protocol degenerates into the consumption that section 14.3 criticizes.

#### Why daily learning fails

Self-education has a habitual form, and in 2024 Koe makes it the seventh of twelve rules. "You aren't where you want to be because you aren't as smart as you think you are." Every project requires a skill set and a mindset, so you need education to achieve goals and complete projects. "Daily self-education must become a cornerstone habit in your life. If you stop learning you stop evolving, opportunities stop presenting themselves and you get trapped in your current stage of development. Education is the fuel for experimentation, and without experimentation you are doing what other people tell you to do" (**Source:** `Disappear And Come Back Unrecognizable (12 Rules To Change Your Life).md`, 2024-04-14). A **cornerstone habit**, in his usage, is a habit that supports the rest of a lifestyle; here it is the habit that keeps a person developing. The last sentence of the rule links learning to the experimentation of Chapter 15: education feeds experiments, and without experiments you fall back on instructions.

In 2025 he explains why the habit so often fails to produce change. "Daily learning and self-education is so freaking important because all of these things overlap and intertwine. Just treat daily self-education toward your goals as a habit and your life will change." The phrase "toward your goals" carries the weight. Recounting how he transformed his health, he says he did not pick a random diet or random exercises, "because that's extremely chaotic. The mind craves order"; he refers to the psychology of the hierarchy of goals and to "turning your life into a video game" (Chapters 8 and 10). He was not forcing anything random: "I had clarity and novelty and dopamine that was leading to me doing something." Most people, he says, have two problems. First, they are not hyper-aware of a painful problem, "so their mind doesn't release dopamine at the sight of a potential solution." Second, "they learn without experimentation. So they never make the progress necessary to act as a feedback loop that keeps them motivated" (**Source:** `How To Become So Self-Disciplined It Feels Illegal.md`, 2025-08-24).

The two failures are the two halves of the cybernetic loop of Chapter 6. Without a felt problem there is no error signal, and information about solutions does not register as relevant. Without experimentation there is no output, and therefore no feedback telling you whether you are progressing. The 2023 passages emphasize the necessity of self-education and its effect of expanding the mind, while the 2025 passage adds this diagnosis of why it fails. There is no change of position; the later version explains the conditions under which the earlier one works.

The durations Koe attaches to the habit vary across videos: a "general education habit" of ten to thirty minutes a day (2023), thirty to sixty minutes of self-education plus thirty to sixty of building (late 2023), "a daily 30 to 60 minute habit, this isn't optional" (2024), a book for thirty minutes a day (2025). The variation reflects different purposes (general education, acquiring a skill, reading) more than a change of view.

#### Becoming your own expert

A group of early passages, mostly from 2022, makes a broad claim about what self-education can reach. "Anything you want, any skill, you can learn online." If you have a problem in your life, there is something you can learn and "become directly conscious of until you can test a system for getting that desired outcome." By self-educating "you are literally creating a better life." He extends this to the inner life: self-development includes not only tangible aspects but mindset and intellectual development, which "has to be a top priority"; you must consistently learn to break through stages of development and to build creative solutions for those behind you (**Source:** `How To Make Money As A Creative On The Internet.md`, 2022-06-25). The criterion embedded in the claim is practical: learning ends not when you know about a problem but when you can test a system that produces the outcome. Chapter 15 develops this as self-experimentation.

He illustrates it with his own example. Everything he knows about the gym he learned from fitness YouTubers. There are "infinite perspectives" to study, so "I can become my own personal trainer, I can become my own relationship therapist, I can become my own psychologist," "anything that I want to become," because ample education exists without paying more than $40,000. He specifies the scope: he gives advice to others on business, spirituality and personal development, but in areas like gym and health he simply uses his desire for self-education to become his own expert (**Source:** `The Rise Of The Value Creator (A Career Path For Polymaths & Self-Improvers).md`, 2022-10-31). The claim is a statement of his practice and his opinion; he does not argue that self-taught therapy equals professional care, and the reader should not read that into it.

The same optimism appears in career terms. "We're all lucky," he says in 2022: to learn graphic design you can watch an hour-long YouTube video that teaches what you need, make a few projects and apply for a design job. If you are smart enough, and if the employer does not write off talent without a degree ("a lot of them are opening up that option"), you could get a job for watching a few hours of YouTube, or freelance and do what you want (**Source:** `If You Want To Secure Your Future… Follow This New Career Path.md`, 2022-05-21). The conditions are his: a few projects (not only the video), an employer willing to hire without a degree. In the same video he floats an idea about the other side of the market: in school you get an hour of after-school one-on-one mentoring, so "why isn't online mentoring a bigger thing?" If you know design well and some of your followers want to learn it to increase their own value, they can hire you for a Zoom call in which you walk them through the fundamentals; you earn an income and freelance work may come to you (same source). **Online mentoring** is presented as something he was "toying with," an opinion rather than a method; it foreshadows the education businesses of Part X.

A 2023 video gives the most concrete early recipe, framed as the second step of recreating yourself. "It's silly to think you can achieve self-generated goals without self-education." "Immerse your conscious mind in the information that will program a new identity and give you the knowledge to attack your goals." Concretely: follow social media accounts that give specific information related to your goals; then "purchase one to three books on the topic and devour them." He answers those who object to social media: they do not understand how integrated and powerful it is; people see it as bad (news, toxicity) but you can curate your experience; it is woven into society, "necessary," part of our lives "whether you like it or not" (**Source:** `Most People Won’t Change (How To Recreate Yourself).md`, 2023-05-19).

This recipe is the starting point of one of the unresolved oscillations of the corpus, and it has to be read alongside what comes later. In December 2023 Koe says "reading books is not learning, watching tutorials is not learning" (section 14.4). In September 2025 he says books and YouTube used for learning are "entertainment" and that reading to learn "is just creating more chaos" (section 14.3). Between those, in 2024, he still recommends buying three books and "burning through them," and says reading is how you absorb years of others' experience. On the question "is reading books learning?" the corpus contains an unresolved contradiction. The most defensible reading, which the corpus supports without stating it in one place, distinguishes two purposes: reading to learn *how to do* something, which in his later view only works when a project gives it a use, and reading to see the world differently, which he continues to value (Chapter 16). The 2023 recipe is closer to the first purpose, but it sits inside a process whose next step is building, which is why it is less opposed to the later view than it first appears.

#### Study human nature first: the seven liberating arts

If the future is unknowable, what should one learn? Koe's 2024 answer begins with a principle: "Study human nature, then study whatever you want." It is impossible to know the future; all we know is that there will be a way of life that leads to the most satisfaction. You cannot depend on school, government, parents or anyone else to secure your future; every successful person "by any measure" has taken it into their own hands. An ideal future lifestyle will have unique aspects, but also "immutable principles of human nature that have persisted and will persist," and those you must learn. To find them, look at what schools do not teach: if schools train "modern slaves" for one task, what do "sovereign individuals" teach themselves? (**Source:** `The Future-Proof Skill Stack (How Average People Become Millionaires).md`, 2024-03-24). The argument is a bet on invariants: since content changes, learn what does not.

His answer to the question comes from Devon Eriksen, whose list he reads aloud in several videos in 2024. The attributions must be kept clear: the list and its definitions are Eriksen's; the remarks about agency, the method of learning the arts and the mapping onto vessels are Koe's. Eriksen calls his list the **Seven Liberal Arts of the modern world**, and prefers the name **liberating arts**, so as not to be confused with "the ideological monstrosity that is taught in liberal art school"; in Koe's paraphrase, "the liberal arts are liberating arts; what's taught in Liberal Arts School are not liberating" (**Source:** `The Future-Proof Skill Stack (How Average People Become Millionaires).md`, 2024-03-24; `The Future Of Work (Avoid Learning These Skills).md`, 2024-07-28). Each art is defined by what it lets you do:

| Liberating art (Eriksen) | What it lets you do (Eriksen's definition) | Koe's vessel for practicing it |
|---|---|---|
| Logic | Derive truth from known facts | Writing and thinking |
| Statistics | Understand the implications of data | Entrepreneurship |
| Rhetoric | Persuade, and spot persuasion tactics | Marketing and sales |
| Research | Gather information on an unknown subject | Writing and thinking |
| Practical psychology | Discern and understand the true motives of others | Marketing and sales |
| Investment | Manage and grow existing assets | Entrepreneurship |
| Agency | Decide what course to pursue and proactively take action to pursue it | Entrepreneurship |

(**Source:** `The Most Important Skill To Learn In The Next 10 Years With Devon Eriksen.md`, 2024-12-08; vessels from `The Future Of Work (Avoid Learning These Skills).md`, 2024-07-28.)

The list is presented as the answer to the question "what should we learn if we don't know what will be relevant?": these are meta-skills of self-education rather than task training. The March 2024 version ends with the strongest conclusion: with these arts, technical or career-specific skills "won't matter," because you can adapt to and change them at any time. Whose conclusion this is remains uncertain. The sentence follows directly on the quoted list, in a passage where Koe is reading Eriksen, and nothing in the transcript marks it off as his own commentary; it may be Eriksen's claim, read aloud, or Koe's gloss on it. What is clearly Koe's comes later. In the December 2024 version he adds a remark of his own: agency, "the last art," "could be the glue between it all," and asks why the liberating arts are not taught. The transcripts give only the list and one-line definitions; no order of learning and no relationship among the components is stated beyond that remark about agency. The name of the author of the list appears as "Devon Ericson" in March 2024 and "Devon Eriksen" later; this is a transcription variant of the same person, and the content of the list is stable across the versions, with a small addition in each.

**Complementary context:** The classical seven liberal arts were grammar, logic and rhetoric (the trivium) and arithmetic, geometry, music and astronomy (the quadrivium), the curriculum considered fitting for a free person, as Chapter 2 noted. Eriksen's list keeps the classical idea (the education of a free person) and two of its arts (logic, rhetoric), and replaces the rest with capacities oriented to acting in a modern economy.

How does one learn such arts? Koe's answer in July 2024 is the most interesting part of his treatment, because it applies the theory of this chapter to them. "You must hold them in your mind as you dive into the unknown, or as you take a new path, because you don't just learn something by reading it. You hold it in your mind and you let new experiences and the chaos of the unknown bring that clarity to your mind and allow you to practice those skills in real time." Prepared in this way, "they slowly just become a part of who you are and your identity," and whatever technical skills are or are not relevant in twenty years, "you'll be able to learn them fast and get results with them fast, because you have the underlying traits that make those skills successful" (**Source:** `The Future Of Work (Avoid Learning These Skills).md`, 2024-07-28). The method is build-to-learn applied to abstract capacities: the arts are not studied as subjects but carried as lenses into real situations, where the situations do the teaching. The goal is identity change (Chapter 4), not information.

Because abstract arts need concrete situations, Koe proposes three practical skills as **vessels** through which they are practiced. "Think of these next skills as vessels for learning the softer skills that we just talked about." The first is marketing and sales, "because if you don't know how to attract and persuade you will never get what you want, and your only option will be for an employer or the government to give it to you"; it exercises rhetoric and practical psychology. The second is writing and thinking, "the ability to communicate the value in your unique mind, the foundation of getting in front of other people"; it exercises logic and research. The third is entrepreneurship, "the process of taking my future into my own hands, hunting for my survival in building products that I want to see in the world that others care about"; it exercises statistics, agency and investment. He calls them "futureproof skills" and "evergreen." He also describes how they interact: "with writing and thinking you attract like-minded people, with marketing and sales you persuade them," and through marketing and sales "you understand the minds of your customer so that you can solve your own problems and create a solution for them" (same source). The mapping in the table above is his, not Eriksen's. **Vessel** keeps the sense Chapter 2 and Chapter 9 gave it: the vehicle through which something is pursued. Here the vessels are the vehicles through which deeper capacities are trained. The three vessels also correspond to the structure of the rest of this book: writing (Part VIII), audience and persuasion (Parts IX and XI), and the one-person business (Part X).

#### Knowledge not found in schools

Koe sums up one strand of his thinking in a tweet he quotes in two videos in 2023: "Knowledge not found in schools is the source of money not found in employment." In the first, he states it after telling the story of learning web development faster than his college course (below) and adds that "we are in the middle of a massive shift"; shifts are slow ("we don't go through an Industrial Revolution in five seconds"), and this shift is not only about money (**Source:** `Become A Digital Renaissance Man (And Join The New Rich).md`, 2023-02-19). In the second, the tweet sums up the video and he adds an image: with the internet, information has spread beyond measure, like "a wildfire," leading to a more advanced, global and accessible society online (**Source:** `The One Person Business Model 2.0 (Turn Yourself Into A Business).md`, 2023-06-25). The tweet joins two of the book's threads: the critique of school (Chapter 2) and the economy of the individual (Part XII). Its logic is symmetrical: if the employed path is defined by the knowledge schools give, the knowledge they do not give is what opens the other path.

Why must that knowledge be turned into income at all? In 2022 Koe builds the argument as a chain. You want to do what you love full time; that requires mastery and autonomy; to have those you must be able to earn from them; so "you need to learn a skill that will allow you to monetize those things, to monetize your interests and your passions." He then presents writing as that skill, one that lets you thrive "no matter whether there's a recession" (**Source:** `Learn This Skill If You Want To Thrive In The Next 10 Years.md`, 2022-08-28). In another 2022 video he states the position more modestly. He is a fan of doing what you want with your life, which usually implies pursuing and developing the skills that let you make an income doing it. "That doesn't have to be via entrepreneurship, but that's what I've done for the past three to four years" and what he teaches; you can also get a job with these skills. He speaks, he says, "from the lens of entrepreneurship and the creator economy" (**Source:** `Stop Trying To Be Unique... Do This Instead.md`, 2022-05-28).

That modesty does not last. From 2024 Koe calls entrepreneurship "the only path" to total control of one's work, and across the corpus his stance on employment oscillates, without resolution, between "the worst outcome," "slavery," "a stepping stone" and, by 2025, admitted routes inside organizations (Chapter 2 traces it in full). For this chapter the relevant point is what the oscillation does not touch: in every version, doing what you want requires learning skills that produce income.

And learning them is hard. In 2025 he says so bluntly: "None of this is anywhere close to being easy. That's the entire [damn] point. You're going to have to learn more skills": how to attract people, write, persuade, market, sell. "You're the CEO. You need to learn every single skill that requires you to operate a business along with your multiple interests." You need to become a generalist, have taste, "package up and deliver signal to attract people," and merge art and business (**Source:** `How To Thrive With Multiple Interests.md`, 2025-02-23). **CEO** here is used in his own sense: the person who operates their own business and therefore has to learn every skill it requires. The passage is a bridge to Chapter 20 (the generalist) and Chapter 18 (taste); for this chapter its importance is that it sets the scale of the learning task. The meta skill is not a luxury for curious people; it is the condition of running a one-person business.

#### The author's education: learning from the people he wanted to become

Koe's theory of learning is drawn from his own history, and he tells that history often. The story has two strands: learning online from people he admired, and learning to code faster than college could teach him. Both are told with variations, and the variations are noted where they matter.

The first strand begins in childhood. As a child he "didn't trust the education system or my parents or even my religious teachers to equip me with the knowledge necessary to secure my future." Instead he consumed content from YouTubers, bloggers and people on social media whose information aligned with his interests or sparked new ones, to pursue what schools were not teaching, usually around increasing his quality of life. He names three areas: fitness (for him, bodybuilding; for you, he says, it could be running or cycling); business (he started with freelancing); and philosophy and meaning, "the need for Spirit, something beyond yourself," because he questioned the religion he grew up in. He bought affordable courses to learn skills he probably could not have learned better through a degree (**Source:** `Solve Your Own Problems And Sell The Solution (Your Niche Is You).md`, 2023-04-30). Chapter 2 described that upbringing; here it matters as the origin of a habit: when the institutions around him did not supply what he wanted to know, he went to the internet for it.

He describes the internet of his youth as a refuge.
