By 2025 he describes the plan as an "evolving blueprint" and "a guess that starts out dumb and becomes educated," and says that without action and iteration, plans and strategies are "a list of things that aren't going to happen." The change, which Chapter 8 discusses, is one of emphasis: the plan loses weight as a script and gains weight as a frame of perception subordinate to action. The two can apply to different moments: detailed planning appears at the start of a reinvention, when order must be imposed on a disordered life (the entropy of Chapter 5), while the provisional plan describes ongoing experimentation.

The same 2022 video, reissued in 2024, contains a warning about time that is essential to the mad scientist's temperament. When starting something new, everyone asks when they will see results, like a tennis player asking when they will be able to compete. Stop asking, "because you're going to get an answer that you don't want to hear and it's going to throw you off track." It takes years: "it takes an entire lifetime of trial and error to create a project." Since "**the essence of science is trial and error**," being the mad scientist of the project of your life means it will take a lifetime to perfect; "get comfortable with that thought" (**Source:** `How To Get Ahead Of 99% Of People (In 6-12 Months).md`, 2022-12-25; reissued in `Get Ahead Of 99% Of People With Deep Work & Monk Mode.md`, 2024-03-21). The video's title promises getting ahead "in 6-12 months," and the passage insists on years and a lifetime; the tension is in the source. The two are compatible if "getting ahead" means relative progress over most people and "perfecting the project" means the open-ended work; but Koe does not say so in the video.

The temperament has an emotional cost, which a June 2022 video names. "Patience, surrender, faith" are necessary during experimentation, because many people aren't comfortable with uncertainty ("why can't I get this result right now?", instant gratification). "You need to surrender, have faith, trust the process," and allow it the time it needs "to manifest, or in order for you to just test enough things and gain enough awareness and clarity to make it work." Two options present themselves. Limiting beliefs and uncomfortable emotions arise during testing in the unknown; if you can't navigate them and approach them mindfully, the only other option is "I'm gonna go back to this certain lifestyle," getting a job you may not like but that is secure and predictable. His answer: no, you don't need that predictability (**Source:** `How To Create A Better Life For Yourself.md`, 2022-06-12).

The passage makes explicit why most people abandon experimentation: not because the experiments fail, but because the uncertainty during them is uncomfortable, and a predictable job is the most available relief. "Surrender" and "faith" are unusual words in a description of the scientific method; Koe uses them for the emotional stance of tolerating unresolved outcomes, not in a religious sense.

His answer to "how long will it take?" appears in a 2022 video and its 2024 reissue. Someone asked how long it would take to grow an audience around their interests and make an income. If you see yourself doing this for the rest of your life, "why does it matter how long it takes?" If you would come back to it anyway, start now. "You have to have a certain amount of failures to see success"; the sooner you get them out of the way, the sooner you see success and can do it for the rest of your life. If you don't, you won't be doing what you want for the rest of your life (**Source:** `If You Are High Value, Start A One-Person Business.md`, 2022-10-02; reissued in `The One-Person Business Model (How To Productize Yourself Full Guide).md`, 2024-02-06). And in January 2023 he gives the time horizon a number: "**one percent of 50 years is six months**," "such a tiny amount of time," yet people can't even make it that far because they want quick results and "don't see the gap" (**Source:** `How To Do Whatever The Fck You Want.md`, 2023-01-12).

The two arguments work together. The first dissolves the question of duration by changing the horizon: if the activity is a lifelong one, the time to the first results is irrelevant; what matters is getting through the necessary failures, and starting earlier makes them happen earlier. The second puts the impatience in proportion: six months, which feels long, is a negligible fraction of a working life. Section 15.6 shows the same figure reappearing in Koe's account of the path of mastery.

#### There is no right way, only your way

Why experiment rather than follow the best available method? Koe's answer is a rule from a 2024 list of twelve rules for changing one's life. Rule 12, experimentation: "If you only do the same thing as everyone else, you are bound to the results of everyone else." Research processes others teach that they have had success with; try multiple techniques to see which get the best results; create your own process that you can stay consistent with. In fitness, try different training and nutrition programs; in relationships, try therapy or self-help books; in business, try cold outreach or organic content. "Avoid becoming dogmatic about the single right way, because **there is no right way, there is only your way**, because people can't teach you what to do, how to write, how to start a business; they can only teach you how they did it" (**Source:** `Disappear And Come Back Unrecognizable (12 Rules To Change Your Life).md`, 2024-04-14).

The rule has two justifications. The first is competitive: copying everyone yields everyone's results, so a distinctive outcome requires a distinctive process. The second is epistemic: no one can transmit "what to do," only "how they did it," because their method was fitted to their situation. A third justification, implicit in the phrase "that you can stay consistent with," is practical: a process tailored to your preferences is more likely to be sustained.

Koe's own experiments are the examples he uses most often. In a 2022 video he describes his fitness history: he started with StrongLifts 5x5, then studied Greg O'Gallagher's approach of training two or three days a week, tried Wendler's 5/3/1 (a powerlifting program) and super high-volume bodybuilding splits. With all that data, he understands that "**there are billions of different ways to go about getting one specific result**," and if he finds a way he enjoys and creates his own program, he could package and sell it (personal brands are dynamic, he adds: no fixed niche is needed as long as you make your interests interesting). In diet, he tried If It Fits Your Macros, ancestral eating, veganism and keto, taking something new from each: from Greg Doucette's low-calorie-density approach he eats the "anabolic French toast"; from ancestral eating he incorporates nutrient-dense foods like liver, ground beef and eggs. This big-picture understanding, he says, lets him create ten times more valuable information than people trapped in one ideology (**Source:** `You Have A $100,000 Product In Your Head (One Person Business Series).md`, 2022-12-04). He calls the result **holistic understanding**.

In 2023 he repeats the account as step three of a system and adds business. Your daily education habit surfaces techniques to test (in business: writing advice, lead generation advice, the "best business models"), easily accessible information everyone tries, which means lots of competition. The method is simple: when you learn something and "the dopamine increases," note it and actually try it for results. Do this with multiple techniques and you create your own. In the gym he experimented with high-intensity training (Mike Mentzer), high-volume training, CrossFit and running; pulled the principles; and does what he enjoys, knowing he is progressing whether or not it is optimal, which is sustainable and gives the best results. In business, he tried and failed at seven business models, "I let **truth blur in the middle**," connected the dots, and created something unique from his "**amalgamation of skills and interests**" (**Source:** `Asking For Advice Is Keeping You Unsuccessful (Here's Why).md`, 2023-08-23).

**Complementary context:** StrongLifts 5x5 is a beginner strength program built on five sets of five repetitions of compound lifts; Jim Wendler's 5/3/1 is a periodized powerlifting program; Mike Mentzer popularized "Heavy Duty" high-intensity training, with very few sets taken to failure; Greg O'Gallagher (Kinobody) combines intermittent fasting with low-frequency strength training; Greg Doucette is a coach known for low-calorie-density recipes; "If It Fits Your Macros" (IIFYM) is flexible dieting by macronutrient targets. The variety matters to Koe's argument: these programs contradict each other on volume, frequency and intensity, so trying several forces the extraction of what they share.

"Let truth blur in the middle" is Koe's phrase for that extraction. Each method contains a partial truth exaggerated into a system; trying several lets the exaggerations cancel and the common core (the "middle") emerge. It is the experiential version of the "both sides of the coin" research in section 15.3.

#### Intelligent imitation: research, test, experiment, discover, document

In 2023 Koe gives the mad scientist a five-step procedure as part of what he calls intelligent imitation, the way out of living as a non-player character (an NPC, the person on autopilot of Chapter 1). "The good life is a series of experiments; you can't copy it from someone else; you have to try, fail and collect the pieces that make your individual life great." The NPC takes what was put in front of them; the main character leans into trial and error, which reflects nature's tendency toward evolution and growth. Keep the scientific method in mind while immersing yourself in your mentors' information (**Source:** `Most People Are NPCs (Don't Waste Your Life On Autopilot).md`, 2023-05-08):

| Step | Instruction | Koe's gloss |
|---|---|---|
| Research | Don't mindlessly consume content; gather it and apply it to your goals | Consumption filtered by the goal |
| Test | Don't take advice as law; test whether it works for your situation | "This is called critical thinking" |
| Experiment | Don't be dogmatic about one method; try different diets, business models, religious ideologies | "Until the truth of each blurs in the middle" |
| Discover | Note the patterns that get results aligned with your goals | Pattern recognition (15.2) |
| Document | Write down what gets you results | "This is the valuable information you can sell, leverage, use and help others with" |

The inclusion of "religious ideologies" among the things to experiment with shows how far Koe extends the method: not only techniques but worldviews are treated as hypotheses. The fifth step anticipates the self-experimentation process that follows, whose last step is to pass the results on.

#### The self-experimentation process

Between March and July 2024 Koe states a five-step process several times with almost identical wording, and once with a sixth step added. The premise comes first: "What makes these skills beautiful is that **nobody can teach you how to market, sell, think or write; they can only show you how they did it**." So you must self-experiment, "the only way to learn them" (**Source:** `The Future-Proof Skill Stack (How Average People Become Millionaires).md`, 2024-03-24). In July he spells out the consequence: "I can only show you how I write or how I market or how I sell, and that's completely different from other people, and that's a great thing, because you can study multiple perspectives, practice them all and create your own way." To learn any skill "you have to embrace a **self-experimentation mindset**; you can't just watch tutorials all day; that's not how learning works" (**Source:** `The Future Of Work (Avoid Learning These Skills).md`, 2024-07-28).

The five steps, in the March and May versions (the May version repeats the March wording and adds only that the last step is "rather important"):

1. **Research processes that others have found success with.** "Thankfully you can do this with a simple search."
2. **Experiment with various techniques.** Implement the processes you learn and attempt to get results.
3. **Identify patterns and principles.** Note the similarities between each and double down on them.
4. **Create your own process.** Tailor what you learn to your unique lifestyle and situation.
5. **Contribute to true education by passing it down.** Give people "education that can't be taught in schools, with a fundamental grounding and critical thinking."

(**Source:** `The Future-Proof Skill Stack (How Average People Become Millionaires).md`, 2024-03-24; `How Smart Creatives Work Less & Earn More LEVERAGE.md`, 2024-05-26.)

In mid-July 2024 the same five steps appear as the answer to "how do you create a system?" "Self-experimentation: nobody can teach you how to do something; they can only teach you how they do something." Research processes "on social media, in courses or with a simple Google search"; experiment; "discover patterns and principles"; create your own process; contribute to true education. Here Koe points to his course *Mental Monetization* for turning such systems into digital products, software or physical products (**Source:** `Learn This Skill If You Want To Be Relevant In 10 Years.md`, 2024-07-13). Two weeks later the process has six steps, because a daily habit becomes an explicit step: (1) research processes others have found success with ("read books, use Google... binge-watch YouTube tutorials"); (2) "**self-education must become a daily 30 to 60 minute habit; this isn't optional**"; (3) experiment with various techniques; (4) identify patterns and principles; (5) create your own process; (6) contribute to true education by passing it down (**Source:** `The Future Of Work (Avoid Learning These Skills).md`, 2024-07-28).

The process formalizes the arguments of the preceding sections. Step 1 is learning from those with results (15.1); step 2 of the five-step version is technique stacking (15.2); step 3 is principles over tactics (15.3), with the important addition "double down," which turns pattern recognition into action; step 4 is "no right way, only your way"; step 5 is the teaching of Chapter 14. The phrase **true education** has a specific sense in Koe's vocabulary: education as discovery rather than memorization, oriented toward self-reliance and opposed to schooling that forces people to learn what they don't care about for goals they didn't choose. Contributing to it means passing on what one has discovered, with its grounding and with the critical thinking that produced it, rather than passing on a recipe.

The variation in the number of steps and in the duration of the daily habit (thirty to sixty minutes here; ten to thirty minutes for a "general education habit" in 2023; thirty minutes in a 2024 reset protocol) is not explained. A reasonable reading is that the figures apply to different purposes: general education, acquiring a particular skill, a reset. The core sequence (research, experiment, extract, personalize, share) is stable.

#### Why self-experimentation is "the only way"

The strongest claim Koe makes for the method is exclusive: "**Self-experimentation is the only way to solve your problems for good**." He states it in several videos between 2023 and 2025, and each statement adds a reason.

The first reason, from February 2023, is that prescriptions are not tailored. "During these seasons of feeling lost, or really at any time, self-experimentation is the only way to solve your problems for good. People can diagnose and prescribe a solution to your problems, but that's usually a guessing game of back and forth, of trying to align goals and figure out what the best solution for you is. But even a prescribed solution can be given to anyone; it's not tailor-fit to your situation, meaning that it isn't going to be sustainable and that you're going to have to find a new one anyway, so it's better to just self-experiment from the start" (**Source:** `Happiness Is A Skill (How To Get Out Of A Rut).md`, 2023-02-26). A 2024 restatement names what the prescriber cannot know: their prescription "lacks regard for the difference in perspective, goals and experience" between them and the person with the problem (**Source:** `If Your Life Is Spiraling Out Of Control, Here's The Solution To Feeling Lost.md`, 2024-03-10).

The second reason, from the 2024 summary of *The Art of Focus*, is that self-experimentation is the opposite of dogma and the only way to find solutions fitted to "your infinitely unique needs." "Self-experimentation is the opposite of blind trust in a theory, guru, belief system, ideology, how-to advice or dogma." For any problem there are dozens or hundreds of options; limiting yourself to the one or two you know may not solve it. The steps: research a plethora of solutions; test them all without latching onto one; note principles, patterns and truths between them; note what gets you results but may not get others results; begin to create your own solution, which is "where **true value** is cultivated," usable for profit or simply a better life. Don't be discouraged if important problems aren't solved instantly. His examples: for relationships, a retreat, a therapist, an advice book, or working directly with your partner; for money, a budget, a side business, or improving your skill set for a higher-paying job; for health, fad diets such as carnivore or keto, studying nutrition principles, immersing yourself in all sources "until you understand the full puzzle" (**Source:** `The Art Of Focus – Official Book Summary By The Author Dan Koe.md`, 2024-01-18).

The third reason, from May 2024, is economic: self-experimentation is also "the only way to create a unique solution that others can benefit from"; "in other words, it's the only way to create **unique value** that other people want to pay you for that nobody can replicate" (**Source:** `How Smart Creatives Work Less & Earn More LEVERAGE.md`, 2024-05-26). A solution derived from one's own experiments embodies one's particular combination of circumstances, which is why it cannot be copied; this is the bridge to Part VII's thesis that "you are the niche."

The fourth statement, from a 2025 list of twelve rules, adds the language of power. Rule 11: "Self-experimentation is the only way to solve your problems for good. People can diagnose and prescribe solutions to your problems, but they often lack regard for the difference in perspective, goals and experience from the person with the problem." If your relationship struggles, hire a therapist, binge YouTube advice, go on a retreat, experiment until you find the right solution: "the first one you try probably isn't the best way." If your business isn't growing, buy a course, hire a coach, test new software, zoom out, or create a new strategy. "There's always a way to solve your problems, and **you strip yourself of that power when you latch on to one solution** that probably won't solve the problem for good" (**Source:** `12 Rules To Change Your Life In 12 Months.md`, 2025-09-14).

The claim "the only way" is strong, and it should be read with its own qualifications. Koe's lists of experiments include hiring a therapist, buying a course and following a coach. Self-experimentation does not exclude expert help; it changes its status. The therapist's method becomes one hypothesis among several, tried and evaluated, not a prescription accepted on authority. The exclusivity applies to the stance (owning the experiment), not to the sources.

#### Person A and Person B

Koe dramatizes the stance with a pair of hypothetical people, which he uses in 2023 and again in 2025. The 2023 version: "Self-experimentation is the only way to solve your problems for good," and self-experimentation and **self-reliance** go hand in hand; it avoids "the dangerous nature of prescriptions and how-to advice." The problem: not enough money to do what you enjoy. Person A follows a money guru exactly: invests a few dollars, plays it safe with stocks, downgrades the car. Person B pulls advice from multiple sources to decide for themselves, uses how-to advice only to discover principles integrated into their goals, studies religiously but doesn't attach to business, health or social ideologies that keep them stagnant; eventually "it clicks" (**Source:** `Asking For Advice Is Keeping You Unsuccessful (Here's Why).md`, 2023-08-23).

The 2025 version repeats the money example ("they use how-to advice, but only to discover principles that can be integrated into the pursuit of their goals"; with education and effort "it clicks and they know how to make it work in their own unique way") and adds a nutrition example that shows the danger of Person A's stance. Person A finds a guru preaching veganism, cleans up their diet, follows it as law, sees results, attaches to the ideology "and becomes a prophet for it." That is "dangerous and the definition of **low consciousness**": they lost weight and gained energy, but from a lack of understanding decided that only veganism can do that. Koe adds that he uses veganism only as a "punching bag"; he doesn't care which diet one follows (**Source:** `12 Rules To Change Your Life In 12 Months.md`, 2025-09-14).

The vegan prophet illustrates a specific error: attributing a result to the whole package rather than to the principle inside it (here, presumably, eating less processed food or fewer calories). The error is "low consciousness" in Koe's sense because it reflects a narrow understanding of why something worked, which then hardens into an identity defended against evidence (Chapter 3). Person B is protected not by being more skeptical but by having tried enough variants to see the principle.

#### Rotating methodologies: pattern recognition equals dopamine

The diet example becomes a concrete method in 2023, stated twice in nearly the same words. If you weren't attached and tried "veganism for a month, carnivore for another month, flexible dieting for another month, keto for another month, you would make connections between the diets to reveal the fundamentals of health. **Pattern recognition equals dopamine**; it would feel good doing this. You'd pick and choose certain methodologies that you enjoy, meaning they will bring sustainable results. Next you'd refine a system that fits your individual nature to perfection." "You're adopting these different perspectives and seeing them for what they are, which are **impermanent and good guidelines**, and then you would test them out and pull the things that work best for you" (**Source:** `Happiness Is A Skill (How To Get Out Of A Rut).md`, 2023-02-26). In December 2023 he adds the next step: once healthy living is effortless, do the same for finances, social life, romantic relationships, spiritual endeavors and any other domain (**Source:** `You Won't Be The Same Person In 6 Months (Master Anything, Fast).md`, 2023-12-17).

The method has a clear structure: rotation (one approach per period, long enough to observe), comparison (connections reveal the fundamentals), selection by enjoyment (because enjoyment predicts sustainability), refinement (fitting the system to one's nature), and transfer (repeating the process in other domains). "Impermanent and good guidelines" is the epistemic status Koe assigns to any method: useful, provisional, not identity. Whether a month per diet is enough to observe meaningful effects is not discussed; the figure is illustrative.

In a 2024 video on his daily routine, Koe answers the obvious objection that this is just jumping from program to program. What you need to learn comes from education, for example YouTube; he learned the gym by watching people on YouTube and studying their techniques. "You study someone's program and then you try it out: do I like this, do I not like this, am I seeing results? You have to stick to it for a decent amount of time to see progress and feedback," and then you try someone else's program. "**This is not shiny object syndrome.** This goes for business too: you don't just fall into the right business model; you test a bunch of different ones, you fail at them, and eventually you learn the patterns and principles that make it work." Through multiple training programs he learned that you need progressive overload, a certain weekly volume, training close to failure, and enough frequency (once, twice, maybe three times a week). Try different nutrition models too: "experiment with everything in your life and eventually you're able to create your own path" (**Source:** `A Day In The Life Of Dan Koe (My Routine As A Writer & Founder).md`, 2024-04-02).

The distinction between experimentation and shiny object syndrome lies in the phrase "stick to it for a decent amount of time to see progress and feedback." Shiny object syndrome abandons a method before it has produced data; experimentation abandons it after. The list of principles he extracted (overload, volume, proximity to failure, frequency) is the "middle" in which the truths of the programs blurred. In May 2024 he compresses the logic into a sequence: as you pursue a goal and stack ideas to achieve it ("new tactics that you're learning for business or new diet models that you're learning for health"), "you're starting to test and experiment with these things; that's step number two, testing and experimenting" (**Source:** `My Honest Advice For Those Who Feel Lost & Confused.md`, 2024-05-30).

#### Your life's projects as science projects

The December 2023 Mastery Method ends with self-experimentation as its seventh step, and here Koe connects the method to the project of Chapter 9 and to business. "Your life is a project, and the projects that compose your life should be treated as science projects to solve the problems that achieve your goal." The steps: hypothesize an outcome from your goals; experiment with techniques for skill acquisition; document the process as a project; double down on results as a solution. Then you have experience, skills and projects you can turn into a business, a solution to a problem you can charge for in the creator economy: "**solve your own problems and sell the solution**." By improving yourself and helping others achieve the same goals, "you help humanity evolve," earning an income doing what you enjoy (he refers to his previous video on the "anti-niche," his name for the idea that the person, with their own problems, interests and solutions, is the niche, rather than a market segment chosen from outside; Chapter 19 develops it) (**Source:** `You Won't Be The Same Person In 6 Months (Master Anything, Fast).md`, 2023-12-17).

"Solve your own problems and sell the solution" is one of Koe's most repeated formulas, and this passage shows where it comes from: a self-experiment, documented, produces both a solved problem and a record of how it was solved; the record is a product. The entrepreneurial method below makes the business side explicit.

#### Progressive overload for inner skills

Self-experimentation also applies to inner skills, such as calm or the capacity for meditation, which section 15.1 included under "everything is a skill." In the 2023 video on happiness as a skill, Koe joins two of this chapter's principles. "As with all skills, you improve with progressive overload, like you would weights in a gym, and that is by gradually increasing the level of challenge as your skill increases, so that you don't get anxious or bored. If the challenge is too high, then you get anxious and you're not going to do it; if the challenge is too low, then you get bored and you're not going to do it." His example is meditation: "you don't start with an hour-long meditation, right? You start with five minutes, you go to 10 minutes, you go to 20 minutes, because if you sit there for an hour it may be beneficial, but you're not going to want to do it the next day; you're not working the system into your day; you're not making it habitual" (**Source:** `Happiness Is A Skill (How To Get Out Of A Rut).md`, 2023-02-26).

The passage connects the progressive overload of section 15.2 to the challenge–skill balance of Chapter 10: anxiety above, boredom below, the edge between them. The added criterion is habit formation. The right increment is the one that keeps the practice repeatable; an intense session that discourages tomorrow's session is a net loss. This is the same reasoning as the 2.5-pound plate.

#### Weekly reflection: the experiment's analysis step

An experiment without analysis is just activity. In the 2022 video on self-reliance, Koe recommends weekly self-reflection as the second of several activities to do alone, in a journal or on a walk: question what went wrong, what went right, what you learned, what you'll do better, and whether you did anything according to your goals (he suggests looking up self-reflection questions). The rationale is philosophical. Nobody knows what they want in the future; it is impossible to know what hasn't happened; a clear vision is just imagination, a potential. "**You will never know what you want in the future until you achieve it**," and then self-reflect: did I actually want that, did I make progress, do I have what I want now, do I need a new goal? It is an infinite game that never ends, which is why you need to **fall in love with the process**, since you can't fall in love with an imaginary ideal (though vision is good). You must continuously set new goals and make progress, because the alternative in our modern world is getting distracted and regressing (**Source:** `Why You Can't Be Yourself (The Power Of Being Alone).md`, 2022-11-13).

Reflection is the "analyze" step of the scientific sequence applied at the scale of a week, and it is also how the hypothesis itself (the goal) is revised. Koe's claim that one cannot know what one wants until one achieves what one thought one wanted makes goals themselves experimental: they are tested by being reached. Section 15.5 develops the same idea in the vocabulary of mistakes.

#### The entrepreneurial method

In October 2022, in a video on starting a one-person business, Koe named a business version of the scientific method: "the **entrepreneurial method**," a "spin-off of the scientific method," which he calls a universal principle that can be used daily to increase your quality of life, solve your own problems, and profit from your own self-development and skill acquisition. It has five steps: "you find a problem, you learn how to solve it, you document how you solved it online, you systemize your process, and you share your discoveries." Iteration, he adds, is a big part of the process (**Source:** `If You Are High Value, Start A One-Person Business.md`, 2022-10-02; reissued with a summary of each step in `The One-Person Business Model (How To Productize Yourself Full Guide).md`, 2024-02-06).

He develops each step in turn.

**Step 1: find a problem.** Find a problem in your life. "All stories, marketing, literally everything that drives human behavior are problems." A story that begins "there was a cold spot on the side of the bed" opens a **curiosity loop**, and people want to learn more. Once you become aware of your own problems, and aware that they are actually problems, you will self-educate to solve them, which leads to step two (**Source:** `If You Are High Value, Start A One-Person Business.md`, 2022-10-02). The example of the story opener shows why the problem comes first in business as well as in life: problems are what capture attention, so the same problem that drives your learning will drive your audience's interest. The curiosity loop belongs to Koe's writing vocabulary (Chapter 23).

**Step 2: learn how to solve it.** Self-education, directed by the problem.

**Step 3: document how you solved it online.** Koe illustrates steps one to three with a money problem: a broke college student understands that college will give them cash flow but also a cap on their income, and doesn't like that, so they start a freelancing business by learning a skill. The problem leads to self-education; they get results; then they talk about those results, which is documenting how they solved it online. Documenting is also how you learn more about yourself and the skill (**Source:** same file). The example is close to Koe's own path, which his 2022 framework summarizes as: broke college student, learn skills, freelance results, post online, digital product.

**Step 4: systemize your process.** Distill it into a replicable process. People want step-by-step advice to reach a specific end result; that is what every product does, unless you create a tool or a product that is simply useful. If you want to make money from the start, focus on distilling a process or creating a system. This ties to self-education and self-reliance: if you hire someone to do it all for you (paying for fitness coaching and following it to a T), you learn nothing for yourself. You must experiment, try different things and see what works for you: "you have to find that **discovery** by figuring it out and struggling and not taking the easy route," so that you can teach it from your own unique point of view (**Source:** same file).

**Step 5: share your discoveries.** Give your discoveries or your process to someone who wants to be helped. Koe wraps this step in a discussion of the meaning of life and ends with a caveat: you can't help people who don't want to be helped (**Source:** same file).

Step 4 contains an apparent paradox that the whole section resolves. People want step-by-step advice, and Koe tells creators to sell it; yet he also says that following step-by-step advice teaches nothing. The resolution is that the process is valuable *because* it was discovered through struggle and is offered as a starting point, not a law. The buyer gets a scaffold, which (in Koe's other statements) they should eventually make their own through their own experiments. This is the tension the corpus records between Koe's rejection of any given path ("there is absolutely no set path that someone can give you... or else that's an assignment") and his practice of teaching step-by-step methods. His partial resolution, stated in several places, is that prescriptions are good for beginners ("I'm kind of against prescriptions, but as a beginner prescriptions are very good") and that courses and advice are maps, not territory: training wheels to be removed. The entrepreneurial method thus describes a cycle in which each person's discovered process becomes the next person's training wheels.

| Method | Origin | Steps | Distinctive emphasis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Life as a science project (2022) | Scientific method | Observe, experiment, hypothesize, test, develop systems, replicate | Life domains as experiments; replicable results can be passed down |
| "My Scientific Projects" notebook (2022) | Same | Categories, observations, plans, findings, steps, test | A written log; "lifestyle design as a whole" |
| Entrepreneurial method (2022) | "Spin-off of the scientific method" | Problem, learn, document, systemize, share | Problems drive behavior and attention; the process becomes a product |
| Intelligent imitation (2023) | Mad scientist | Research, test, experiment, discover, document | Against the NPC; truth blurs in the middle |
| Self-experimentation process (2024) | Own | Research, (daily habit), experiment, patterns, own process, pass it down | "Nobody can teach you"; true education |
| Mastery Method step 7 (2023) | Own | Hypothesize, experiment, document, double down | "Solve your own problems and sell the solution" |

The table shows one method under six names. What changes is the endpoint emphasized: a better life, a product, an original voice, or a contribution to others' education.

### 15.5 Mistakes as a Compass

Self-experimentation, as section 15.4 described it, produces results, and most results of most experiments are failures. A method built on trial and error therefore stands or falls with its attitude toward error. Koe's attitude is summarized in a coined term, **Nature's Compass**: mistakes are the negative feedback that tells a goal-seeking system which way to turn. This section reconstructs the idea, its cybernetic basis, the chain of reasoning that makes mistakes necessary for meaning, the practical attitudes it supports (toward risk, regret and correction), its radicalization in 2025 into the claim that mistakes are "the only source of truth," and its application to Koe's own most expensive failure.

#### Nature's Compass: mistakes as negative feedback

The term appears as step 6 of the December 2023 Mastery Method. "People are so afraid of making mistakes that they make the biggest mistake of them all: not making mistakes." Mistakes "are nature's compass"; "people who don't make mistakes don't give themselves a chance to achieve successes." You must act in alignment with your big goal so as to form new systems through the **negative feedback** of mistakes. Make a habit of adopting the perspective of the highest version of yourself, and let that lens unveil new opportunities when you make a mistake, using it as direction for your next choice. With time, "you won't even realize that you have become an artist" in your chosen skill, achieving what others find difficult, "like you are able to walk while most are still crawling" (**Source:** `You Won't Be The Same Person In 6 Months (Master Anything, Fast).md`, 2023-12-17).

The language is that of Chapter 6. A cybernetic system steers toward a target by detecting deviations from it and correcting them; "negative feedback" is the technical name for a signal that reduces the deviation. A mistake, in this frame, is not a verdict on the person but a measurement of the gap between action and goal. Two conditions follow from the passage. The mistake must be made "in alignment with your big goal," because a deviation can only be measured relative to a target; and the person must interpret it through a lens (here, the highest version of oneself, the future self of Chapter 4) that turns it into direction. The term has its own chronology, and it runs from the narrower sense to the broader one. In this December 2023 video it appears twice: here, as the negative feedback of mistakes, and a few minutes earlier, as the trial and error (the negative feedback of what one consumes and does) through which a person who wants to improve changes their actions over time toward a goal, a process that social media algorithms, Koe adds, make "like 10 times worse" when the goal is mediocrity (Chapter 1). Three months later, in March 2024, Koe widens the term: Nature's Compass becomes the name for experimentation itself, "the path out of meaningless living," which "is already available to you; it is deep in your core" (**Source:** `If Your Life Is Spiraling Out Of Control, Here's The Solution To Feeling Lost.md`, 2024-03-10; Chapter 1 develops this use). In December 2024 and again in September 2025 he returns to the formulation centered on mistakes ("mistakes are nature's compass"), now qualified by the path on which they are made, as "Mistakes on your own path and on the assigned path" below describes. The feedback sense is therefore the first, not a narrowing of an earlier, broader one.

Koe illustrates the idea with machines, in the same video. A self-driving car has received years of negative feedback that refines the system that "shapes the mind of the car"; a Tesla now navigates roads with ease thanks to machine learning, and he argues it is, and will be, safer than most human drivers because it lacks negative thoughts or distractions: "I'm a system to achieve this goal." He had watched a video of Elon Musk presenting Optimus, a robot that will probably fill most homes as a personal assistant (doing laundry and more); it was the third iteration in a year, because "**you have to fix the bugs in the system; you have to fix the bugs in your life**." When you were born you were "the **minimum viable product**," and you have been improving since, though most people have been degrading mentally, in the systems that compose their minds. Machines doing this, he adds, open room for humans to perform creative tasks ("the future of work is play") (**Source:** same file).

The comparison works on two levels. The machine shows how a system improves purely through accumulated negative feedback, without needing to get things right the first time. And the contrast (the car "lacks negative thoughts or distractions") points at what makes humans worse at learning from error: the emotional reaction to the mistake interferes with reading it. "Minimum viable product" is a term from software development for the simplest version of a product that can be released to gather feedback; Koe's application of it to a newborn person reframes the whole of life as iteration on a first release. The claims about Tesla's safety and Optimus's future are his predictions, not established facts.

#### Failure as a data point and the reference point of success

Earlier the same year Koe had stated the idea autobiographically. "My business journey was simple: I tried everything and failed." Failure is a blessing: "a **data point** that reveals what can be improved." Those who don't fail don't succeed, and it makes no sense to expect success without failure "when **success only exists from a reference point of failure**." He proposes a thought experiment: if you had been successful since the day you were born ("which you were, in many ways"), would you see it as success or as normal life? His prescription: "set a new goal as a high, embrace massive failure as a low, and dance through the struggle to marry the **meaningful contrast**" (**Source:** `I Had To Learn These High-Income Skills (If I Wanted To Make Money).md`, 2023-08-16).

The passage contains two distinct arguments. The first is informational: a failure is a data point, so avoiding failure means collecting no data. The second is phenomenological: success is experienced as success only against a background of failure, so a life without failure would not contain the experience of success at all, only "normal life." The second argument links the topic of this chapter to the philosophy of contrast that Chapter 39 develops (meaning comes from highs and lows).

In 2024 Koe adds an asymmetry. "Failure is a very good thing": you don't learn anything from praise and success, which "can actually make you go blind"; you learn everything from negativity, feedback and failure, if you don't drown in it and can pick it apart and notice the **signal**. He immediately qualifies: most negative feedback is just people angry at you because your worldviews don't mesh and your goals don't align (**Source:** `How Smart Creators Will Grow An Audience From Zero In 2025.md`, 2024-10-20). The qualification is important for a creator. Not all negative feedback is information about the work; some is information about the critic. The skill is separating the two, which requires the big-picture understanding of section 15.3: you need to know what the work is for to tell whether a criticism measures a deviation from that purpose or from someone else's.

#### The chain from risk to meaning

Koe also places mistakes inside a causal chain that ends in purpose. In a 2023 video he says that the quality of your life a year from now depends on tiny choices that compound. You don't need perfect choices; it is better to make mistakes. "**The greatest risk is no risk at all**," because without risk you can't fail; without failure improvement is impossible; without improvement you have no aim for your life; and without an aim everything becomes meaningless. "Becoming a better person is how you live with purpose" (**Source:** `If Your Life Sucks, Here's How To Reprogram Your Mind.md`, 2023-10-22).

The chain can be laid out step by step:

| Link | Because |
|---|---|
| No risk → no failure | Failure requires attempting something whose outcome is uncertain |
| No failure → no improvement | Improvement requires the feedback that failure provides (Nature's Compass) |
| No improvement → no aim | An aim is a direction of improvement; without movement it is empty |
| No aim → meaninglessness | Meaning, in Koe's account (Chapters 8–9), is the experience of moving toward a goal |

The argument converts risk avoidance, which feels like safety, into a path toward meaninglessness. Its last step depends on the account of meaning given earlier in the book: meaning as the experience of pursuing a goal, which makes improvement itself, "becoming a better person," the content of a purposeful life.

A 2023 heuristic turns the chain into an instruction. "**Invest in your portfolio of failures until you can afford to succeed**." "You have to be a failure": approach the girl and get rejected; look like an idiot in the gym; start the business and watch people criticize your first moves. "Everyone else did it" (**Source:** `Your Future Will Be Determined By 3 Things.md`, 2023-03-30). The financial metaphor treats failures as deposits that accumulate until they "pay out" success. The three examples are chosen from the three domains where fear of embarrassment is strongest (romance, the body, public work), which is where the emotional charge described in section 15.1 blocks the first step.

#### Mistakes on your own path and on the assigned path

In December 2024 Koe delivers the most rhetorically intense version of the idea, addressed to a particular kind of viewer. "**The greatest mistake is not making mistakes**." You are different: aware, observant, maybe quiet and afraid to speak because "they won't listen anyway," but that silence is killing you. You tried to fit in, trusted others with your future, demonized money and success because people said you don't need them. But you need to build: that is how you contribute, connect to something greater, and embark on a unique journey that ends **robotic living**, because money removes your dependency on that robotic living (**Source:** `How To Make The Greatest Comeback Of Your Life.md`, 2024-12-15).

He continues: "You aren't where you want to be because you're afraid of making mistakes." If there were one sentence by which to orient your life, it would be "mistakes are nature's compass." If happiness can't exist without sadness, success can't exist without failure, "a universal law, because something can't exist without nothing" (the transcript is unclear at this point). Then a distinction: on the conventional path (school, jobs), mistakes still serve the narrow goal and don't lead to a new path, only to feeling sorry for yourself. When you reject the goals assigned at birth that made you think small, "**your mistakes are your light in the dark**" (**Source:** same file, 2024-12-15). Nine months later, in a 2025 video on twelve rules, he repeats the passage almost word for word as rule 12, adding that you are still looking for the one true path and "there isn't one" (**Source:** `12 Rules To Change Your Life In 12 Months.md`, 2025-09-14).

The distinction between the two paths is the most precise part of the passage, and it explains why the same mistake can be useful or useless. On an assigned path, the goal is fixed and narrow (the grade, the promotion), so a mistake can only tell you that you fell short of it; it cannot tell you that the goal itself is wrong, and the natural response is self-pity. On a self-chosen path, the goal is open and revisable, so a mistake can also redirect: it reveals not only how to reach the target but which targets are worth reaching. This connects to the theory of assigned goals in Part I: Nature's Compass works only when the person is navigating by their own goals.

The same 2024 video adds a claim about self-knowledge. The problem is that you don't know what you want, and you don't realize that you never will: it is in the future, imaginary; what you want now will differ tomorrow and next decade. But you will never begin "this process of refinement and purification," because you can't allow yourself to fail. "Failure and mistakes are the process of **refinement and purification** of your character." What you want becomes clearer when you realize what you don't want and work the other way. Without mistakes on your own path, of course you don't know what you want (**Source:** `How To Make The Greatest Comeback Of Your Life.md`, 2024-12-15).

This is the weekly reflection of section 15.4 ("you will never know what you want in the future until you achieve it") restated as a theory of character. Wants are not discovered by introspection in advance but by elimination in action: each mistake removes something you thought you wanted. It is also the logic of the anti-vision of Chapter 7, which defines a direction by what one refuses.

#### No right or wrong actions, only correctable ones

The attitude toward mistakes has a practical corollary about decisions. In a 2023 video Koe says: "There are no right or wrong actions here." If you want something surface-level and status-based (start a business, make money, buy a good car), do it, then reflect on whether it was a mistake, because you can always correct it: sell the car, make a better decision, restructure your business or lifestyle. "I just need the control to do that, and if you aren't able to do that, then that's a problem; solve it." If you have a job and no time, that is a problem: start a business (**Source:** `Society Is A Pyramid Scheme (Take Back Control Of Your Life).md`, 2023-01-15).

The principle replaces the binary of right and wrong decisions with a criterion of correctability, and adds a condition: the freedom to correct. Mistakes are cheap when they can be undone, and expensive when one lacks the time, money or autonomy to undo them. This explains Koe's otherwise abrupt conclusion: a job that leaves no time is a problem precisely because it removes the capacity to correct, which is what makes experimentation safe. The principle also connects to Chapter 9's acceptance of superficial goals as portals: pursuing a status goal is fine if one keeps the ability to recognize it as a mistake and change course.

#### Regret as cracks, not stains

What about mistakes that cannot be undone? Koe's answer, in a 2023 video, concerns regret. "Regret is a necessary part of life; you can't avoid it, and those that try to avoid regrets end up regretting their decisions more, because they're like, I wasn't supposed to do that," whereas the person who knows regrets are part of life says "I regret that; I'm gonna change." "Most people dwell on their regrets as if they can change them when they can't; they can only change the choices that they make right now." There are two options: "view them as ugly stains that make life worse, or view them as **cracks that can be sealed with better future decisions**" (**Source:** `A Dangerous (But Effective) Strategy To Get Out Of A Rut.md`, 2023-10-02).

The image shifts regret from the past (a stain, permanent) to the future (a crack, repairable by what comes next). It completes the correctability principle: some mistakes cannot be reversed, but their meaning can be changed by the decisions that follow them. The paradox Koe notes, that people who try to avoid regret regret more, follows from the same logic: treating regret as something that should not happen makes each instance a violation, while treating it as normal makes it a signal.

The same video opens with an observation that frames its argument about tactical stress: reflecting during the week, Koe realized that "the best decisions that I've made in my life are the ones that other people think are stupid" (**Source:** same file, 2023-10-02). The remark, which introduces a chronological list of risky decisions from 2018 to 2023, is an opinion drawn from his experience. Its relevance here is that the decisions others judge as mistakes, in advance, are a different category from mistakes revealed by feedback; the first are judgments from another person's goals, the second measurements against one's own.

#### Lessons that can't be taught

If mistakes are information, can the information be passed on so that others don't have to make the mistake? Koe's answer is: only partly. Opening the 2023 video on happiness as a skill, he recounts a mistake made during a trip to Costa Rica, from which he "learned a very valuable lesson that someone else couldn't teach me. Someone else could tell me, oh, don't do that, all day long, but unless I go and do it myself and learn the actual lesson, that's the only way I'm going to **internalize** it" (**Source:** `Happiness Is A Skill (How To Get Out Of A Rut).md`, 2023-02-26). The corpus does not describe what the mistake was.

A 2023 account of his path to a million-dollar income makes the same point about sequence. Approaching $100,000 a year, "a few things happened at this point, and they could only happen at this point. Why? Because I wouldn't understand them without my prior experiences or failures." The four realizations that follow in the video (the power of social media, the experience needed to grow on X, that everything points to writing, that income grows with readership) are presented as unlockable only through that sequence (**Source:** `How To Make $1 Million A Year As A Digital Writer.md`, 2023-10-08).

The two passages distinguish knowing a lesson from internalizing it. Advice can transmit the proposition ("don't do that"); only the mistake transmits its weight, the felt connection between the action and its consequence that changes future behavior. And some propositions cannot even be understood until enough mistakes have supplied the context: the realizations at $100,000 were not hidden before, they were unintelligible. This is the reason, consistent with section 15.3, that Koe rewatches a principles video every year and understands more each time.

#### "Mistakes are the only source of truth"

In March 2025 Koe radicalizes the idea in a video on strategic thinking, calling it a "crucial and counterintuitive realization": "**Mistakes are the only source of truth**, not the thoughts in your head, not the advice of a billionaire." "Failure is the only teacher that is absolutely 100% tailored to your situation." "Failure has a **signal-to-noise ratio of 100 to 1**." Yet "you hate failure, you let it rule your life, you ignore it and dig your head into more courses, books and podcasts." "Everything you learn that is not derived from mistakes is derived from theory... from a map... a conjecture formed through the interpretation of mistakes made by another person." The realization leads to two questions he then addresses: how to make better mistakes in the right direction and learn from them, and how to fail before you even start, which is the premortem of Chapter 17 (**Source:** `How To Take Back Control Of Your Life With Strategic Thinking.md`, 2025-03-16).

The 2025 formulation is a change of degree with consequences. In 2023, Nature's Compass coexisted with the daily self-education habit, emulation of mentors and reading; mistakes were the compass, and learning from others supplied the map. In 2025, everything not derived from one's own mistakes is reclassified as "theory," a map drawn from someone else's mistakes. Read literally, this demotes the reading, courses and emulation that sections 15.1 to 15.3 recommend. Koe does not address the tension. Two observations from the corpus suggest how the positions fit. First, his own description of the map is generous: theory is "the interpretation of mistakes made by another person," which means books and courses are compressed records of other people's failures, valuable as hypotheses. Second, the self-experimentation process already places others' methods at the research step and one's own results at the discovery step; the 2025 claim can be read as saying that only the discovery step yields knowledge one can trust for one's own situation, because only it is "tailored." On that reading, "only source of truth" means "only source of truth about what works for you," and the 100-to-1 ratio is a vivid way of saying that a personal failure is almost all signal for the person who suffered it. The figure is rhetorical, not measured.

#### A series of necessary mistakes: Kortex

The corpus contains a case in which Koe applies the philosophy to his own largest failure. In November 2025 he published a video titled *Kortex, the $3 Million Mistake*, which he describes as "very attention-grabbing and polarizing." His philosophy, he says, is that "mistakes, you have to make them in order to actually improve." His cofounder Matt describes the venture as "**a series of necessary mistakes** for us to get where we need to go": the idea of building Kortex, a second-brain app (the same software called Cortex in section 15.2 and in section 15.7; the two spellings alternate across the transcripts), wasn't bad, but as first-time founders they made many mistakes. Koe had talked about Kortex nonstop for months or years and then stopped; they decided to pivot and build a new app, Eden, rolled out to Kortex users the Monday before Black Friday, with an early-access public window over Black Friday weekend (web-only, treated as a beta). Where they stopped with Kortex "wasn't our vision for it... we were forced to" (**Source:** `Kortex The $3 Million Dollar Mistake.md`, 2025-11-24). The $3 million figure appears in the title; the transcript gives no breakdown.

Near the end of the conversation one of the cofounders (the transcript does not make clear whether Matt or Ari, the technical cofounder) adds the principle that distinguishes useful from useless mistakes: "We've made mistakes in the past... $3 million of mistakes... We will continue to." "**What sets people apart is whether you can take your mistake and not repeat it**, because as humans we're very prone to remaking the same mistakes over and over again." New mistakes will come, and you must watch for them and learn from them as with Kortex; viewers "will see it in real time" (**Source:** same file, 2025-11-24).

The case brings the section's ideas into a concrete, costly situation. The framing of "necessary mistakes" applies the data-point view; the pivot to Eden is the correction that the correctability principle requires (and that was possible because the company still had the control to make it); the rule about not repeating mistakes adds a criterion the earlier passages lacked. Making mistakes is necessary; making the same one twice means the feedback was not read. The case also shows a shift in Koe's thinking about the business. In 2023 he had planned to fund the software with an education business so that it would not matter whether the software was profitable at first; in 2025 the central problem is acknowledged as one of product, a product that was not compelling enough. The corpus does not connect the two moments or say whether the 2023 strategy was carried out, so the link should not be overstated; Chapter 37 treats the trajectory.

| Formulation | Date | What it adds |
|---|---|---|
| Failure is a data point; success exists only against failure | 2023-08 | Information and contrast |
| Nature's Compass; you were born an MVP | 2023-12 | Cybernetic feedback; iteration on the self |
| The greatest risk is no risk at all | 2023-10 | Chain from risk to meaning |
| Learn from negativity, not praise; separate the signal | 2024-10 | Asymmetry of feedback; critics' worldviews |
| Mistakes are your light in the dark on your own path | 2024-12, 2025-09 | Assigned vs. self-chosen goals |
| Mistakes are the only source of truth; 100-to-1 signal | 2025-03 | Radicalization; theory as someone else's map |
| Not repeating a mistake sets people apart | 2025-11 | Criterion for learning from error |

### 15.6 The Path of Mastery

The preceding sections described the mechanics of skill (techniques, overload, patterns, principles, experiments, mistakes) as if progress were steady. Koe insists that it isn't. Progress on what he calls the **path of mastery** is non-linear: long stretches with no visible change, followed by sudden jumps. Most people quit during the flat stretches, because they read the absence of visible progress as evidence of failure. This section reconstructs Koe's account of the path: George Leonard's definition of mastery, the pattern "nothing happens, then everything happens," the stages of mastery and the end of beginner's gains, the commitment thresholds he recommends, his several and partly inconsistent time horizons, and the idea flow that produces the jumps.

#### Leonard's definition: the opposite of instant gratification

Koe takes his definition of mastery from a book. In a January 2023 video he quotes George Leonard's *Mastery*: "Mastery is the mysterious process during which what is at first difficult becomes progressively easier and more pleasurable through practice." His interpretation is that this is the opposite of **instant gratification**, and hard to internalize without action, because everyone wants to understand immediately. Instant gratification, he says, goes beyond material desire: it is the need for immediate understanding, for immediately fixing an emotional problem. "People just want everything right now, and you can't have it; you have an entire life ahead of you; calm down." That is why he won't give exact steps "to baby you along"; he gives the meta-skills to research things yourself and follow your curiosity (for example, "what are the fundamentals of marketing and sales? Go look it up") (**Source:** `The $1 Million Dollar Skill Stack (Learn In This Order).md`, 2023-01-08).

**Complementary context:** George Leonard (1923–2010) was an American writer and aikido teacher. His short book *Mastery: The Keys to Success and Long-Term Fulfillment* (1991) describes the learning curve as a series of brief spurts of progress followed by long plateaus, and argues that mastery requires learning to love the plateau, the practice itself, rather than only the spurts. Koe takes the definition and adapts it, opposing it not only to the desire for things but to the desire for immediate understanding.

The extension is the interesting part. Wanting to understand immediately is a form of instant gratification, and it is the form most relevant to learning: the person who demands that a new domain make sense right away experiences the normal confusion of the early stages as failure. Leonard's definition implies the opposite: difficulty first, ease and pleasure later, through practice. Koe's refusal to give step-by-step instructions in that video is the pedagogical consequence: steps would relieve the discomfort and remove the practice.

#### "Nothing happens, then everything happens"

The same 2023 video names the pattern that Koe calls "the most important pattern." It appears as part of the third element of a skill stack, "stack experience for nuance and navigation." "**Nothing happens, then everything happens**": when you are on the path of mastery for life, "not in one skill but in one domain, aka your life and what you're interested in," you will experience this lesson multiple times. Your job is to hold it in mind along the journey: by sticking things out you will experience short bursts of intense progress; lean into those and enjoy them (**Source:** `The $1 Million Dollar Skill Stack (Learn In This Order).md`, 2023-01-08).

He then describes the cycle in time. "One percent of 50 years is six months, and six months is just the start of the beginning." See your work as your life's work, with that fifty-year horizon (Chapter 9). Mastery is "a cyclical process of slow or no progress followed by intense bursts of progress." In business, the first exponential leap to the next stair step usually comes after about six months, a pattern he says he has noticed in many people: if you stay consistent for six months, around that mark you have the leap and know "this is possible," which is usually when most people commit for life (some still fall off). A few months later comes "**massive resistance**": you feel you aren't progressing as you should. "This is normal." Zoom out: months of potential despair are part of the journey; "nobody said that you're supposed to feel good or bad; nobody said it's going to be easy or hard; those are expectations that you hold in your mind; see beyond them" (**Source:** same file).

The account has the shape of a staircase, not a ramp, and Koe adds a phase most descriptions omit: the resistance that follows the first leap. The leap creates an expectation that progress will now be continuous; when it isn't, the disappointment is sharper than during the first flat stretch. Naming the phase ("this is normal") is a way of defusing it in advance. The "six months" figure is his observation of people he has seen, not a measured regularity, and he presents it as usual, not universal.

Once on the path, Koe says in the same video, you can't leave it, because the only reason you start is that "you got that **missing piece** in your mind that finally made it click," made you realize it was possible and let you see through all your excuses. Once you see that, it will pop into your head when you are doing nothing: "**I know my potential; why am I wasting it right now?**" (**Source:** same file, 2023-01-08). The "missing piece" here is the same term as in section 15.1, but its function is reversed: there, the missing piece of skill explained the absence of results; here, the missing piece of understanding (the realization that it is possible) explains why one cannot go back. The click of section 15.1, "it is actually skill and not luck," is an instance of it.

#### Slowly, then all at once: trusting the supercomputer

In February 2024 Koe describes the same pattern from inside a single learning episode. When he learns something new, none of it makes sense, and he too suffers from thinking it should make sense when it shouldn't in the first place. In reality, when things don't make sense, "my subconscious mind is just in this state of pattern recognition," which is difficult for it. If he sticks with it despite not knowing what's going on, "**slowly then all at once** the click happens." Some call it the aha moment or insight: "the **avalanche of insight** goes into your head." The condition is that it only happens if you lean into the discomfort and allow your mind to make sense of it. "You need to have more trust in **the supercomputer that is your mind**. Nothing happens, then everything happens" (**Source:** `The Fastest Way To Acquire High-Value Skills (And Finally Change Your Life).md`, 2024-02-11). He presents this as part of his philosophy for "working less, earning more and enjoying life," the subtitle of *The Art of Focus*.

The passage supplies a mechanism for the pattern. The flat stretch is not empty: the subconscious is doing pattern recognition (section 15.2) on material that has not yet organized itself. The jump is the moment the patterns complete, the puzzle reaching the threshold at which the image can be inferred. The instruction that follows is to tolerate the confusion rather than escape it, which section 15.7 will connect to overwhelm. "Supercomputer" is a metaphor for the capacity of non-conscious processing; Koe does not offer it as a technical claim. **Complementary context:** the phrase "slowly, then all at once" echoes a line in Ernest Hemingway's *The Sun Also Rises* (1926), in which a character says he went bankrupt "gradually and then suddenly"; Koe does not cite it, and the phrase circulates widely in its modern form.

Six months later he gives the pattern an image. Describing non-linear progress: "one moment you're lost in the darkness, the tension builds until the star explodes and creates atomic nuclei that spread across the galaxy; **all of the little candles you lit along the way start to light up the room as a whole**, allowing you to see that new domain of life with clarity and focus" (**Source:** `This Simple Reading Habit Will Change Your Life (I Promise).md`, 2024-08-04). The image contains two metaphors that do different work. The exploding star describes the suddenness and the accumulated tension behind it. The candles describe what the flat stretch was producing: each small piece of learning (a book, a technique, an idea) is a candle that gives almost no light alone; at some point there are enough of them that the room becomes visible. The star is the event; the candles are the explanation.

The pattern's names change across the corpus ("nothing happens, then everything happens" in 2023; "slowly then all at once," keeping the earlier phrase, in 2024; the exploding star in mid-2024), but the position does not.

#### Mastery over misery: stages that become unconscious

What happens during the stretches? A 2024 reissue of a 2022 video describes the practice of fundamentals as "**mastery over misery**." Sushi chefs take years to perfect the preparation of rice. Mastery comes in stages: a tennis player first learns how to hold the racket ("a very specific way to do that well"), then how to angle the racket, then how to hit the ball, practicing each over and over "like how you were learning to walk, until it becomes effortless or unconscious." Once a stage is unconscious, it "opens up more mental energy to move on to the next thing." This, he says, is what puts you ahead of people trying to get "a result that would usually take 10 years to get in 2 weeks," which "is just not going to happen" (**Source:** `Get Ahead Of 99% Of People With Deep Work & Monk Mode.md`, 2024-03-21).

The phrase is a play on words with a serious meaning: the repetitive, apparently miserable practice of one stage is what produces mastery of it, and mastery of it is what frees the mind for the next stage. This is the mechanism behind "one project, one skill at a time" in section 15.2 and behind the observation, in section 15.1, that mastering the mechanics of social media frees attention for creativity. Chapter 12 used the same images (the sushi chef, the tennis player) for the boring fundamentals; here they illustrate why fundamentals must become unconscious before the next stage can be learned.

The passage also contains a sentence that contradicts, on its surface, the "learn anything in two weeks" of section 15.2: a result "that would usually take 10 years" cannot be had in two weeks. Both statements come from Koe and both use "two weeks"; the 2025 distinction between substantial progress and mastery is what reconciles them. The 2024 sentence is about mastery-level results; the 2025 promise is about the first stage.

#### The honeymoon phase and the end of newbie gains

Why do so many people quit after a promising start? Koe's answer combines the dopamine model of Chapter 11 with the gym. In a 2024 video he says the **honeymoon phase** applies to "almost any area of life." At the gym you get into a honeymoon phase: you are focused, making a lot of progress quickly ("**newbie gains**"); once that fades, many people quit because slower progress demotivates them. The same happens with relationships, new hobbies or habits. This is "the shift from superficial pursuits to a **philosophical sense of mastery**": eventually "you have to appreciate it, you have to master your craft, you need to focus on the boring fundamentals and show up to them every single day," and "move from dopamine to those down chemicals that allow you to savor and appreciate what you have" (**Source:** `The Cheap Dopamine Epidemic Stop Ruining Your Life.md`, 2024-11-24).

The "down chemicals" refer to the distinction, drawn in Chapter 11 from Daniel Lieberman and Michael Long's *The Molecule of More*, between dopamine (the chemistry of anticipation and wanting) and the "here-and-now" neurotransmitters associated with satisfaction in what one has. The honeymoon phase runs on novelty; when the novelty ends, continued practice requires a different source of motivation, which Koe calls a philosophical sense of mastery: valuing the practice itself.

In 2023 he had explained the same phenomenon with a game analogy that adds a reason why most advice doesn't fit the reader. Most advice isn't applicable to your current level of goals and understanding. In a game, going from level 10 to 11 might require 300 experience points; going from 99 to 100 requires a hundred times that. "**The difference in experience is exponential**." As a beginner you don't need to change much: change a few habits, set aside an hour a day, and "you can replace your income within a year-ish." After that, "the real self-development journey begins," and progress slows, like newbie gains in the gym, where you gain strength and muscle rapidly for about a year and then face a slow, painful grind. If this isn't backed by "a philosophical sense of mastery and meaning," you won't stick it out. If your identity isn't patient, long-term focused, risk tolerant and "a lover of failure," you will lose (**Source:** `Asking For Advice Is Keeping You Unsuccessful (Here's Why).md`, 2023-08-23).

The passage contains two claims. The first, about experience curves, explains why advice from a level-100 person rarely helps a level-10 person (the heuristic of section 15.2 to learn from those slightly above you), and why beginners progress fast: the early levels are cheap. The second, about identity, ties the path of mastery to Part II: the traits needed for the slow phase (patience, long horizons, tolerance of risk, love of failure) are traits of an identity, which means sticking it out is less a matter of willpower than of who one has become. "Lover of failure" connects to section 15.5.

#### Sticking power: the first weeks

The most common point of abandonment, in Koe's account, comes much earlier than the end of newbie gains: in the first weeks. In a 2023 video on micro-education businesses, he describes the goal as starting a business today and letting momentum "compound and snowball over one, two, three years of iteration and persistence" into a following that pays for your services and expertise. "As the path of mastery goes, it starts as difficult and becomes more pleasurable with time" (Leonard's definition again). Things won't make sense at the start: you'll start a newsletter and think "what do I write? I can't do this," and waste a week overwhelming your mind. "Stick it out." People quit after two weeks because they lack "**sticking power**." Those who persist "without needing a dedicated answer" or "absolute clarity" are the ones who succeed. Those who call it a scam because they didn't see immediate results are, he says, "idiots; kindly, I say that kindly" (**Source:** `The Micro Education Business Model (How To Monetize Your Knowledge).md`, 2023-04-23).

The key condition is "without needing absolute clarity." The demand for clarity before commitment is the instant gratification of understanding that Leonard's definition opposes. Sticking power is the capacity to act while confused, which is the only way to reach the point at which things become clear.

A 2024 compilation gives the practical threshold with a game image. Try it out and stick out the initial period of not knowing what you're doing: when you start playing a game without an instruction manual, it isn't fun until you pick it up. "Give it two weeks, give it a month, and then see if you become obsessed with it"; you'll see the first spark of growth ("this is possible") and double down repeatedly. Eventually, three years later, Koe had "close to 500k to a million followers across platforms" (**Source:** `The One-Person Business Model (How To Productize Yourself Full Guide).md`, 2024-02-06). The manual-less game is the same image Chapter 10 used for beginnings. In January 2023 he had given a longer minimum for trying something: "committing to it for even just three months and acquiring some form of skill in that domain" (**Source:** `How To Do Whatever The Fck You Want.md`, 2023-01-12).

The difference between the two thresholds (two weeks to a month, versus three months) reflects different purposes. The shorter one is a test of attraction: does the activity start to grip you once the initial confusion clears? The longer one is a test of skill: have you acquired enough to know what is possible in the domain? Koe does not distinguish them explicitly; the corpus shows the commitment figures varying across videos (two weeks to a month in 2022, three months in 2023 and 2024, sixty days for a business in 2024).

In January 2026 he applies the same pattern to building software with AI. This is like any skill: you don't ride a bike immediately; you fall off, try again, get frustrated. People want quick results and quit if they don't get them the first time: "that's not how skill acquisition works." You'll feel weird, overwhelmed, as if you're not progressing. "You're going to have to build three to four apps before you feel like you can actually put a price tag on one." And start now, because change is fast: information products lasted ten to fifteen years before dying; this may die in two to three years; after that nobody knows, and you will have to adapt on the fly (**Source:** `How I'd build a one-person business (if I started over in 2026).md`, 2026-01-03). The passage is a useful check on whether the path-of-mastery account applies to new technologies: Koe says it does. AI may compress the time per iteration, but the structure (falling off the bike, several projects before one is sellable) remains.

#### Long horizons: twenty years, ten years, capacity for luck

Against the impatience of beginners, Koe sets long horizons. The 2023 video on the skill stack ends with a synthesis: **commit to the path**; stack evergreen skills for profitability (the medium, the message and results-oriented skills); stack personal interests for individuality; stack experience for nuance and navigation of the domain. "**Give yourself 20 years, not two weeks**" (**Source:** `The $1 Million Dollar Skill Stack (Learn In This Order).md`, 2023-01-08).

In 2024 he describes the reasoning that led him onto the path ten years earlier. His mindset then was: "If I can monetize any of these passion projects, I'll be set. All I need to do is learn and build until one works. **I need to increase my capacity for luck with skill acquisition and experience**. It may take 10 years, but some people go to school for 12, and even if I fail I'd be in a similar position" (**Source:** `This High-Income Skill Will Make You Irreplaceable (Full Guide).md`, 2024-01-28).

The reasoning has the structure of a bet with limited downside. Its cost is measured against a familiar benchmark (twelve years of school, which most people accept without hesitation), and its worst case is no worse than the alternative. "Capacity for luck" is a coined phrase that reconciles the skill frame with the existence of luck: luck is not denied, but skill and experience increase the number of situations in which a lucky break can be recognized and used. It is a softer version of the 2024 definition of luck as "a lack of understanding of a system" (section 15.1), and the two coexist in the corpus.

A third long-horizon formula comes from Naval Ravikant, whom Koe quotes in 2022 and again in 2024: "**It's not 10,000 hours, it's 10,000 iterations**."
