His application: "build, build, build, build, build"; iterate on products instead of waiting for them to be perfect (**Source:** `You Have A $100,000 Product In Your Head (One Person Business Series).md`, 2022-12-04; repeated in `The One-Person Business Model (How To Productize Yourself Full Guide).md`, 2024-02-06). **Complementary context:** the "10,000 hours" figure was popularized by Malcolm Gladwell's *Outliers* (2008), drawing on Anders Ericsson's research on deliberate practice; Naval's reformulation shifts the measure of progress from time spent to cycles of trying, receiving feedback and adjusting. Koe adopts it because it fits his account: the path of mastery is counted in experiments and mistakes (sections 15.4–15.5), not in hours.

#### The time horizons do not agree

The time frames Koe gives for learning, mastery and change vary widely, and the variation should be stated plainly rather than smoothed over.

| Claim | Date | Scale |
|---|---|---|
| "Give yourself 20 years, not two weeks"; first leap around month six | 2023-01 | Mastery of a domain; a business |
| Commit at least three months | 2023-01 | Trying a domain |
| Replace your income "within a year-ish" with an hour a day | 2023-08 | Beginner's results |
| Build your "natural physique" for about 10 years before "business steroids" | 2023-09 | Business foundations (section 15.7) |
| 1–5 years of daily education and building | 2023-11 | Skill acquisition |
| Top 10% (then top 5%) in 6–12 months | 2024-01, 2024-03 | Competence relative to others |
| "Six years of results in six months" | 2024 | Thought experiment about focus |
| "You can learn anything in two weeks"; most take six months | 2025-03, 2025-08 | Substantial progress toward a goal |
| Bench 315 lb ≈ a million dollars, about three years | 2025-08 | A major milestone |
| "Six months is all you need to change your life" (20–40% of the skill) | 2025-08 | Life-changing income |
| Three to four apps before you can price one | 2026-01 | A new technical skill |
| "2 to 5 years" to master brand, content, marketing and sales, even with AI | 2026-03 | Mastery of the business skills |

The emphasis moves from patience (2023) toward speed (2024–2025) and back to years (2026), and Koe does not reconcile the figures. His one explicit reconciliation is the 2025 distinction between substantial progress toward a goal (weeks to months) and mastery of a skill ("obviously that takes like 10 years"). Read through that distinction, most of the figures describe different scales: a technique, a beginner's results, competence relative to others, a business, mastery of a domain. What the corpus does not support is reading any single figure as Koe's answer to "how long does it take?" His answer to that question, when asked directly, is that it does not matter if one intends to do it for life (section 15.4).

#### Idea flow: why the jumps come

What causes the jumps? In a December 2024 video Koe gives an answer in terms of ideas rather than skills. "What is the answer to all of this? It's something called **idea flow**." "Robert Greene reads 100 books before he writes one. Founders have a thousand ideas before one changes everything. Creators post a thousand times before one makes them an overnight success. **More ideas lead to more exponential events. Nothing happens, then everything happens**." You don't find these ideas by asking ChatGPT for 100 ideas, "because you're still missing the overarching vision and story; you're missing experience, meaning, purpose." Two people who don't know what is in Koe's head would type similar prompts and get similar responses. He distinguishes problems that can be solved outright (a physics problem, an explanation) from something "so personal and evolving, like an idea that strikes you at the right point in your human experience," which is hard to find because you are navigating "this vast unknown landscape," and which "10 minutes from now could be useless" (**Source:** `A Daily Routine To Work Less, Earn More & Enjoy Life.md`, 2024-12-29).

**Complementary context:** Robert Greene is the author of *The 48 Laws of Power* (1998) and *Mastery* (2012), among other books, and is known for long periods of reading and note-taking before writing; Koe gives the "100 books" figure without citing a source for it. Koe's later views on AI and ideas are more permissive: by 2026 he uses AI to generate variations of good posts and to choose a topic, keeping the opinions and the final selection for himself (Chapter 16). The 2024 claim should be read as being about the source of the life-changing idea, which he locates in experience and vision.

In August 2024 he describes the mechanism that produces idea flow. You can't get six years of work done in six months because you aren't aware of a way; you aren't aware of it because you don't have great ideas flowing. "Your mind has three functions: **consume, connect, create**," which is idea flow. If you don't connect or create with ideas, they sit in your head and weigh you down. You must actualize an idea to discover the one that can only be discovered once it is actualized. "**The tractor couldn't be conceived without the plow**." You can't generate a life-changing idea without acting on the boring or shallow ideas that lead to it (**Source:** `Minimalist Productivity Work Less, Do More.md`, 2024-08-11).

The tractor and the plow complete the account of non-linear progress. The jump ("everything happens") is the arrival of an idea that could not have been conceived earlier, because it depends on the actualization of earlier, unremarkable ideas. The flat stretch ("nothing happens") is the period of building plows: acting on ideas that are not themselves transformative but make the next one thinkable. Consuming without connecting or creating clogs the flow, which section 15.7 calls information fat. This is also why the jumps cannot be scheduled or shortcut by asking for a list of ideas: the idea that matters is downstream of one's own actions.

### 15.7 The Mind as a Body

The bodybuilding analogies that run through this chapter (progressive overload, ego lifting, the bench press, newbie gains) are not incidental. In a series of videos between 2022 and 2026, Koe develops them into an explicit model: the mind is a body, information is its food, building is its training, rest is its recovery, and it can be underfed, overfed, bloated or overwhelmed. The model draws on Chapter 3's idea of identity as a **mental body** and turns it from a description into a training program. This section reconstructs the model in its successive vocabularies: mental bodybuilding and mental aesthetics, mind building, bulking and cutting, information fat and intellectual obesity, mental metabolism, and the reinterpretation of overwhelm as a sign of learning.

#### The mental body and mental bodybuilding

The starting point is a September 2023 video structured as a letter around four ideas, in order: (1) the **mental body** and how it rules your life; (2) **mental bodybuilding** as your path to intelligence; (3) why **mental real estate** is the most valuable resource; (4) how to **monetize your mind** to create your own source of income. Koe frames the whole as "**mental aesthetics**," which "is your master key to the doors of The Good Life." The sequence is cumulative: understand the self-image (the mental body), train it deliberately (mental bodybuilding), use the built mind to occupy others' attention (mental real estate), then give the people you attract something worth paying for (mental monetization). He recaps at the end: "understand your mental body, train that body like you would in the gym, know that modern power comes from attention or mental real estate, use writing or business as a vessel for self-understanding and monetization" (**Source:** `How To Reprogram Your Mind & Build Your Intelligence.md`, 2023-09-24).

| Idea | What it is | Where the book develops it |
|---|---|---|
| Mental body | The self-image, the concept of self, identity as a "body" | Chapter 3 |
| Mental bodybuilding | Deliberately training that self through information and practice | This section |
| Mental real estate | The space one occupies in others' attention; "the most valuable resource" | Chapter 25 |
| Mental monetization | Turning the built mind into products others pay for | Parts X–XI |

The term "mental bodybuilding" is one Koe loves, though he says "I don't think I'm the one that came up with it." He explains it by quoting the opening of a chapter of *The Art of Focus*: "When most people have a sense of self that is the product of the external world, you have the chance to peel back the layers; you can build a self that is a **conscious personal creation** that works less, earns more and enjoys life." Mental bodybuilding is the path to intelligence: sculpting and crafting the ideal self deliberately (**Source:** same file, 2023-09-24).

The contrast between a self that is "the product of the external world" and one that is "a conscious personal creation" is the thesis of the book's title (create or be created) applied to identity. The 2024 summary of *The Art of Focus* explains how the first kind of self forms. "You are being attracted to your highest version, and the depth of your core can sense it." The external call to evolve requires you to "chisel inward beneath the mental constructs that have been layered through your conditioning"; your internal state must become one with the ever-changing external state. Humans are **pattern recognition and learning machines**; from birth we absorb ideas like a sponge and adopt ideologies as law, narrowing our minds and limiting what we perceive as important. Society gets to us early, because the friends, parents and teachers who condition us were conditioned by theirs. "Few people have a self that is a conscious personal creation through critical thinking, self-generated goals and forging their own path" (**Source:** `The Art Of Focus – Official Book Summary By The Author Dan Koe.md`, 2024-01-18).

The passage connects the mechanics of this chapter to the diagnosis of Part I. The same faculty that makes skill acquisition possible (pattern recognition, section 15.2) is what makes conditioning possible: a learning machine learns whatever its environment supplies. The difference between conditioning and mental bodybuilding is not the mechanism but its direction: absorbed by default, or chosen through "critical thinking, self-generated goals and forging their own path," which are the elements of self-experimentation in section 15.4.

In November 2023 Koe ties the model to business. "When you deconstruct the mind and body you can map patterns that deepen your understanding across most domains of life," and he connects these patterns to the financial domain via business. Think of yourself as "a mental body that you build like you would in bodybuilding": you digest information like you digest food, and acquire skill like you build muscle. Building a business today is "displaying your character, or yourself, or the mental body that you've built and constructed to be valuable over time," to create content and a product that sell. "A business is just that, a **vessel for value exchange**. **Personal growth is self-development; business growth is other development**" (**Source:** `Turn Your Knowledge Into A Business (How To Productize Your Mind).md`, 2023-11-26).

The final formula states the bridge between this chapter and Parts X–XI. If the business is a display of the mental body, then building the mind (self-development) is the precondition for building the business, and the business's growth consists in developing others with what one has built in oneself. It is the economic consequence of "solve your own problems and sell the solution."

#### The self as a house occupied by tenants

The 2023 letter adds a second image for the mental body, one that emphasizes what enters it. "Let's consider yourself as an intellectual construct, a house not a home, a psychic body," a house that can be occupied by tenants. Tenants can nurture and build the house, or destroy it "by partying inside of it and tearing it down and leaving it a mess." With the internet and social media we face more information than ever as a species; we are letting all these ideas, these **tenants**, into our minds without paying attention to which destroy the house and which improve it; we are not kicking out the destructive ones nor inviting those who build (**Source:** `How To Reprogram Your Mind & Build Your Intelligence.md`, 2023-09-24).

The phrase "a house, not a home" makes a specific point: a home is where one belongs and which one does not question; a house is a structure that can be renovated and whose occupants can be chosen. The self, in this image, is something one manages rather than something one is. The tenant image also prepares the nutrition metaphor that follows: in both, the danger is indiscriminate intake.

#### Mind building: tension, food and rest

In February 2024 Koe compresses the model into a three-part analogy, which he calls **mind building**, and asks the viewer to bridge it with business building "because they're all the same thing." In bodybuilding you train to the point where your muscles can't lift more; you eat enough food, but not too much, to fuel growth (a caloric surplus; too much and you gain unwanted fat); and you get ample rest. In mind and business building, you increase the resistance of your mind, take on more emotional labor and "**emotional weight**," and train your mind by showing up to "**the learning gym**, AKA just self-education every day." Tension comes from building something: "you can study all day and learn nothing"; you need a project to apply what you learn. While building and facing resistance, you increase your "**mental food intake**," which is learning or information; then you must rest and recover to solidify it (**Source:** `The Fastest Way To Acquire High-Value Skills (And Finally Change Your Life).md`, 2024-02-11).

| Bodybuilding | Mind and business building |
|---|---|
| Training to the limit (tension) | Building a project; taking on emotional weight |
| Food (a modest surplus) | Learning, information ("mental food intake") |
| Rest | Recovery that solidifies what was learned |
| Too much food → fat | Too much information → overwhelm, "information fat" |

The analogy assigns each element of the learning process a role and makes their interdependence explicit. Food without training produces fat, not muscle: information without a project is not converted into skill. Training without food produces exhaustion: building without learning stalls. Both without rest produce no adaptation: Chapter 13's case for rest as half of the work is the third component. The analogy also explains why Koe insists that the project comes first (section 15.2): only the project supplies the tension that makes the food useful.

The 2023 letter had already stated the conclusion in the same terms. To build muscle you need an environment conducive to it, both lifting weights ("practicing skills or building something like a project or a business") and eating food ("learn information... so that you can actually do that"). "You need to use your skills and you need to learn new skills, so you need the habit of both"; "**you need to build and learn in unison**, because they work together to build your mental body" (**Source:** `How To Reprogram Your Mind & Build Your Intelligence.md`, 2023-09-24).

In January 2024 Koe turns the analogy into the two habits of section 15.1, now named **the cornerstone habits of the good life**: (1) learning, for novel information to fuel skill acquisition and knowledge; and (2) building, to "**metabolize the information and build mental muscle**." Start with thirty minutes of self-education in the morning and thirty minutes of building a project that contributes to your vision. He adds a threshold: if you can't set aside one hour each morning, when distractions are minimal, to build your future, go back to the previous step of the protocol and get your priorities straight (**Source:** `How To Reset Your Life In 7 Days.md`, 2024-01-07; he mentions his course *2 Hour Writer* as one option for learning digital writing). The hour is presented as a test of priorities rather than a recommended maximum: someone who cannot find it has not yet made the future a priority.

#### Bulking and cutting

The 2023 letter extends the analogy to the cycles of bodybuilding. When bulking, you eventually gain some fat: you get overwhelmed, you do too much, you push too far in business, or you learn too much information that you don't know what to do with. Then you need to cut: "stop consuming so much information... rest more and... produce more... build with the information that you already have so you can metabolize it" (**Source:** `How To Reprogram Your Mind & Build Your Intelligence.md`, 2023-09-24).

The idea had appeared six months earlier in a conversation with Dickie Bush, where it was co-constructed. Bush introduced the image of obesity: an overweight person displays a "physical culmination of their choices and doing things incorrectly for a long period," visible to all. He asked himself: "where am I that, but I'm not able to see it? Where am I compounding these small decisions day after day that are leading me to being **metaphorically obese**, but I just can't see it?" Koe extended it with bodybuilding, as if applying survival and reproduction to the mind: "bulking and cutting." You bulk, push too far, "gained too much mental fat and it's overwhelming," and eventually you "cut back down to reveal the muscle that you built underneath," which becomes the **new baseline**. He gave a business example: monthly revenue. A promotion spikes you up, and while you can drop back down, you won't drop all the way; the baseline increases (**Source:** `Dan Koe & Dickie Bush On One-Person Businesses, Creative Workflows, and Lifestyle Design.md`, 2023-03-16).

The attribution matters: the obesity image is Bush's, the bulking-and-cutting extension is Koe's. And the extension adds something the obesity image lacks: a positive account of excess. Bulking is not a mistake; it is a phase. Overreaching (in learning, in work, in business) adds both muscle and fat; cutting removes the fat and reveals the muscle; the net result is a higher baseline. The model thus legitimizes periods of intense intake and activity, provided they are followed by periods of consolidation.

The same letter adds a warning about the speed of the bulk. "This is where people go wrong: they try to learn information so quick, like, oh, how do I build a seven-figure business in six months? That's not going to happen, because you're not giving yourself enough time to build the muscle." There are "**steroids for business**, like paid ads and other things, or networking, but those come in later." "You have to build your **natural physique** for like 10 years, and then if you want to take steroids, you can" (**Source:** `How To Reprogram Your Mind & Build Your Intelligence.md`, 2023-09-24). The analogy classifies paid ads and networking as accelerants that work on an existing base and do damage without one. The ten-year figure belongs to the list of horizons in section 15.6 and should be read as an illustration of order (base first, accelerants later) rather than a schedule; elsewhere Koe recommends networking from the start, so the claim concerns networking as a growth accelerant, not as relationship-building.

#### Information fat, intellectual obesity

The earliest version of the overfeeding image is from 2022. Learning blindly makes you gain "a bunch of **information fat**." In bodybuilding, a **dirty bulk** gains much more fat than muscle; a **lean bulk** optimizes for lean muscle while accepting some extra fat. If you dirty bulk too hard, "learn so much that your thoughts are just scattered," you feel slow, sluggish and tired, until you feel so bad that you must go into a **cutting phase**, ruthlessly eliminating much of what you learned because it has no practical application in your life (**Source:** `Learn New Skills FAST (How I Remember Everything I Learn).md`, 2022-11-27). The implication is to optimize for lean learning: intake tied to application, accepting a little surplus.

In 2026 the same idea returns as a diagnosis of an epidemic. Koe announces a future video on "**intellectual obesity**," which he calls "a crisis or an epidemic." "Information is food for your mind. If you're eating too much food and you're not exercising... you're not using the food or shuttling it to muscle growth... The same thing applies to the mind." "Just consuming, consuming, consuming, even if it's self-improvement... that's no better than just consuming brain rot if you're not doing anything with it, because it's making you mentally obese." People think scrolling self-improvement content makes them better than people scrolling brain rot, "when you're doing the exact same thing; you're still getting the cheap dopamine hit. And honestly, it could be worse, because you're just getting a **false sense of progress**." He admits: "I was the same way" (**Source:** `How To Learn Anything 10x Faster Than Anyone.md`, 2026-08-09).

The 2026 passage is more severe than the 2022 one. In 2022 information fat was an inefficiency to be managed by cycling; in 2026 unused self-improvement consumption is placed on a level with the cheap dopamine of Chapter 11, and possibly below it, because it disguises itself as progress. The added argument is about self-deception: brain rot is at least recognized as idle; self-improvement content without application feels like work and therefore postpones the realization that nothing is changing. This is the "tutorial hell" of Chapter 14 described in the language of the body.

In March 2026 Koe gives the same diagnosis a quantitative frame. "Think about fitness or health... your metabolism can only go so fast." Niche groups try to speed it up, "but there's a limit. You aren't just going to burn 10,000 calories a day without running or doing cardio for that amount of time... If you eat over that... you get fat," over an extended period. "Most people don't realize that this applies to the mind as well. **You have a set amount of information that you can digest and metabolize and actually use**." People feel they must listen to ten podcasts a week to keep up. His nuance: "there's a time for consuming... a curated set of information that helps spark more ideas. But if it isn't kept under tight control, then you overeat. You overconsume." He later calls the result being "mentally overweight, or mentally bloated, or overstimulated" (**Source:** `If you've lost your creative genius, watch this.md`, 2026-03-28). The passage names the condition **infinite input, zero processing**.

The nuance keeps the model from becoming an argument against reading. Consumption has a legitimate role: a curated set of information "sparks more ideas," which is the idea flow of section 15.6. The problem is the ratio of input to processing, not input as such. The metaphor's vocabulary changes across the corpus without a change in position: information fat (2022), metaphorically obese and mental fat (2023), mentally overweight (2025), mentally bloated (2026), intellectual obesity (2026). What changes is intensity: from a recommendation of lean bulking to the diagnosis of an epidemic.

#### Mental metabolism and the edge

The metabolic version of the model explains not only overconsumption but the right dose of novelty. In a September 2023 video Koe says that body and mind are metaphorically similar: you are overloaded with information "because you don't have a fast enough **mental metabolism** to digest that information in the situation that you're in." So the chaos and novelty you expose yourself to "has to progressively overload with time," so that you can handle more difficult and stressful situations. Push too far beyond your edge into the unknown and there is too much stimulus: you can't metabolize the experience, information builds up and creates anxiety and overwhelm. Shy too far into the known and there is little of the novelty that makes life worth living: the mind isn't stimulated, information is easy to digest, and we become bored. He later calls the training "mental bodybuilding": being exposed to all of infinitely complex consciousness at once would be "like trying to physically eat the universe" (**Source:** `Life Is A Video Game (You Can't Escape The Matrix).md`, 2023-09-05).

The passage joins the metabolic model to the challenge–skill graph of Chapter 10. Anxiety above the edge, boredom below, growth at the edge: the same three regions, now described as rates of digestion. And it joins both to progressive overload (section 15.2): the edge moves outward as the metabolism adapts, so the dose of novelty must increase over time.

A month later Koe applies the limit to tactical stress, the deliberate leap into a demanding situation. "The purpose of tactical stress is to launch yourself into the unknown, or the land of infinite potential." But "if you launch too far, you become overwhelmed with information; it becomes difficult to metabolize that information" (he refers to his previous video on "mental aesthetics, or mental bodybuilding"). Push too far out of your comfort zone and "you're exposed to all this chaotic information that you don't yet know how to order in your mind or actually make use of... you can't filter it," like your body when you eat so much that you feel bad. The magic happens "when you do this consciously and you know that you can acquire the skill and education necessary to make this goal work" (**Source:** `A Dangerous (But Effective) Strategy To Get Out Of A Rut.md`, 2023-10-02). The condition, knowing that one can acquire the necessary skill, is the same that Chapter 10 gave for tactical stress: the leap is calculated, not blind.

#### The mind as the digestive system of reality

In December 2023, as step 5 of the Mastery Method, Koe gives the metaphor its widest formulation. "Think of your mind as **the digestive system of reality**." If you're overwhelmed, feel you're not learning, or can't retain a book, "it's because you're not stopping and digesting the information with practice and building": pull back from consuming, build with what you have, and refer back to material you've used. When writing notes in Cortex, he says, he reads books extremely slowly, digesting a page at a time to dissect and understand it, which has greatly helped his articulation in newsletters, YouTube and other content. Extending the metaphor: eat just enough and you create an environment conducive to muscle growth, "a **season of pure progress**"; eat too much (hard bulks) and you feel terrible; eat too little and your body or business lacks the resources to build. So you go through cycles: bulk, cut, maintain. "Adopt the perspective of the universe": zoom out and "go meta" instead of hunting for little tactics to fix feeling bad instantly, since it is part of life. "Life is the mental model" (**Source:** `You Won't Be The Same Person In 6 Months (Master Anything, Fast).md`, 2023-12-17).

Two details deserve comment. The first is the reading method: one page at a time, digested before the next. In a 2025 video on reading books "fast" with AI, Koe still advises "you're not in a race to finish the book; in fact, the slower the better," which keeps the 2023 method despite the title; Chapter 16 discusses the tension between speed and depth in reading. The second is an internal tension in the Mastery Method. Step 5 is titled "reinvent yourself" and summarized at the end of the video as "reinvent yourself with information overload," changing physical and digital environments to force an open mind (section 15.1). But the content of the same step advises pulling back from consumption and digesting. The two can be reconciled through the bulk-and-cut cycle (a deliberate overload to break an old pattern, followed by digestion), but the video does not make the reconciliation; it presents both under the same step.

In January 2024 Koe adds the concept that names what digestion produces. In bodybuilding, the optimal muscle-building environment is training hard at your edge and then eating enough to fuel growth: not too much (groggy, bloated, disliking how you look), a little above maintenance; and not too little unless you are in a planned cutting phase (or you'll lack energy and won't want to push). The same holds for information: if you aren't learning, you lack the energy to move and build; if you learn too much without building a business, practicing or using it, you are not training your mind and not giving the information, the "**mental nutrition**," somewhere to go: you can't "**partition** it into the muscle," the skill you are trying to build (**Source:** `How To Reset Your Life In 7 Days.md`, 2024-01-07). "Partitioning" is a nutrition term for how the body allocates nutrients between muscle and fat; Koe's use makes the point that whether learning becomes skill or fat depends on whether there is training (building) to direct it.

#### Overwhelm means you are learning

The last component of the model reinterprets a feeling that most people take as a reason to stop. In February 2024 Koe opens a video on acquiring high-value skills with a reassurance: "**You're supposed to feel overwhelmed; it means you're learning**, it means you're expanding, it means you finally left your **bubble of comfort**. The worst thing you can do is go back and hide from situations that make life meaningful. Give your mind time to adjust." People learning something new or changing their lives have "the wrong mindset": they enter the situation, feel overwhelmed, and ask why; the answer is that they haven't put themselves in such situations with enough repetitions. When you first feel discomfort and haven't trained yourself to be okay with it, you "lash back" to something pleasurable and comfortable (phone, food, memes, videos), anything except what you should be doing, closing yourself off to expansion and to understanding of that domain simply because you didn't give your mind time to adjust. "That's what we call learning": bringing your mind from here to an **expanded circle**, which requires discomfort (**Source:** `The Fastest Way To Acquire High-Value Skills (And Finally Change Your Life).md`, 2024-02-11).

He explains the feeling with the same muscle analogy. It is like training a muscle that gets sore the first time; you go again and again, it stops getting sore, the weight becomes easy, and eventually you lift heavier and expose yourself to a harder stimulus. "That's how you build **mental muscle** to learn or change your life, and continue changing your life until you reach the ideal future that you want" (**Source:** same file). And he defines it: "You feel overwhelmed because **you can't digest reality fast enough**." You can't deal with it because it consumes your attention: all you can focus on are negative thoughts about how it won't work, how you'll fail, and how you could be doing something better with your time (**Source:** same file).

The definition explains why overwhelm is self-reinforcing. The feeling itself occupies attention with negative thoughts, which leaves less attention for digesting the new material, which prolongs the feeling. The "lash back" to the phone or food is an escape from that loop, and it is the specific behavior that prevents adaptation. The soreness analogy supplies the way out: repeated exposure, not avoidance, is what makes the stimulus manageable.

Later in the same video, Koe makes overwhelm a step in his learning method. By this point you have started a project, learn by solving problems while building, and teach, "and now you probably feel overwhelmed, and that's a good thing; it means that your mind is primed for pattern recognition." So: (1) launch yourself into the unknown, get more uncomfortable, immerse yourself in the culture, environment and information related to what you are learning; (2) condition your mind through repetition and exposure, slowly understanding the lingo, vocabulary and skill set of those who have succeeded in that topic; (3) let your mind expand through the discomfort: "the worst thing you can do is quit when you are feeling **growing pains**" (**Source:** same file, 2024-02-11). The step's title is "expand to a new level of mind," linking overwhelm to the developmental vocabulary of Chapter 4. A month earlier, in a guide to writing, he had said the same about a specific body of material, the structure of long-form content and storytelling: "If this doesn't make sense yet, because it won't, because **overwhelm is a good thing**, and you're going to feel overwhelmed, you have to actually practice until it's solidified or digested into your mind" (**Source:** `This High-Income Skill Will Make You Irreplaceable (Full Guide).md`, 2024-01-28).

#### Good overwhelm and bad overwhelm

The corpus therefore contains two judgments about overwhelm. In the 2024 passages it is good: a sign of learning, of a mind primed for pattern recognition, to be pushed through. In the 2023 and 2026 passages on mental metabolism and overconsumption it is bad: a sign that one has launched too far beyond the edge, or eaten more information than one can metabolize, to be corrected by pulling back. Elsewhere in the corpus (Chapter 5) overwhelm appears as a symptom of psychic entropy, the disorder of a mind with too many open loops.

The tension is not chronological; both judgments coexist. It is resolved by context, and the corpus supplies the criterion even though Koe never states it as one:

| | Overwhelm as a sign of learning | Overwhelm as indigestion |
|---|---|---|
| Source of the overwhelm | Practice and exposure in a domain one is building in | Consumption without processing; leaping too far beyond the edge |
| What is happening | The mind is doing pattern recognition on new material | Information accumulates without being used or ordered |
| What it feels like over time | Decreases with repetitions, like soreness | Persists or grows; scattered thoughts, sluggishness |
| Right response | Stay, repeat, immerse; don't "lash back" | Stop consuming; build with what you have; rest; cut |
| Koe's terms | Growing pains, mental muscle, expanded circle | Information fat, mentally bloated, mental metabolism exceeded |

The criterion that separates the two columns is the one the whole section has been building: whether the intake is being converted by building. Overwhelm while building is the soreness of training; overwhelm while only consuming is the discomfort of overeating. The first is pushed through; the second is corrected by producing.

#### The model as a whole

Gathered together, the mind-as-body model describes the same process the rest of the chapter described in other terms. Learning (food) supplies techniques and ideas; building (training) converts them into skill (muscle) by forcing their use against resistance; rest consolidates the adaptation; progressive overload raises the load as capacity grows; overwhelm marks either productive soreness or indigestion; excess intake without use accumulates as information fat, which must be cut; and over cycles of bulking and cutting the baseline rises. The self that results is, in Koe's phrase, a conscious personal creation rather than the product of whatever information the environment supplied.

The model also defines the task of the next chapter. If information is food, then what one reads, how one captures it and how one uses AI to process it are questions of diet. Chapter 16 turns to those inputs: moving from consumer to researcher, reading to change one's mind, building a second brain oriented toward creation rather than accumulation, and using AI as a tutor.

### Exercises

1. **Find the missing piece.** Choose one area of your life in which you have put in sustained effort without the results you expected (an audience, an income, a relationship, a physical goal). Following section 15.1, assume for the sake of the exercise that "it's still a skill problem." List at least five candidate missing pieces, from large to very small (Koe's example was a space before a question mark). Which of them could you not have noticed without more skill? How would you find out which one actually matters? Then identify where your self-image (as "skilled," "credentialed," or "unlucky") might be preventing you from looking.

2. **Decompose a skill into techniques.** Pick a skill you want, stated the way people usually state it ("get good at video," "learn business," "be better in conversations"). Explain why, in Koe's terms, this is a "disordered task." Then define a concrete project that would require the skill, and list the first five problems you expect the project to throw at you, each paired with the technique that would solve it. Estimate at what point you would be "not blocked" (the Spanish example) and what you would still be unable to do.

3. **Design a progressive overload protocol.** For one capacity you want to build (focus, writing volume, a meditation practice, the difficulty of the problems you work on), design a twelve-week progression with the smallest increments you can justify. Specify how you will know the current load has become easy, what the next increment is, and how you will avoid "ego lifting." Then compare your protocol with Koe's opposite register (being extreme, changing everything at once): for this capacity, which tempo is more appropriate, and why?

4. **Run a rotation experiment.** Choose a domain in which you hold a strong opinion about the "right way" (a diet, a training method, a productivity system, a way of getting clients). Design a self-experiment in the manner of section 15.4: at least three competing approaches, each tried long enough to produce feedback, with what you will record and how you will decide what to keep. Before starting, write down what you expect the shared "fundamentals" to be. What would you need to observe to conclude that you had been a Person A rather than a Person B?

5. **Read a mistake.** Take a recent mistake that still bothers you. Analyze it with the tools of section 15.5: Was it made on an assigned path or on your own? Relative to which goal is it a deviation? Is the feedback you received about the work or about a clash of worldviews? Can the action be corrected, and do you have the control to correct it? What would it mean to treat it as a crack to be sealed rather than a stain? Finally, state the specific behavior that would show you did not repeat it.

6. **Question a strong claim.** Koe says in 2025 that "mistakes are the only source of truth" and that everything else is theory, while sections 15.1–15.3 recommend daily self-education, emulation of mentors and reverse engineering. Write a short argument for each side: one defending the 2025 claim as stated, one defending the value of others' knowledge. Then propose the formulation you think is most defensible, and identify a situation in which relying only on one's own mistakes would be dangerous or wasteful.

7. **Map your own time horizons.** Section 15.6 lists time frames that range from two weeks to twenty years. For one goal you are pursuing, separate it into the scales Koe's distinction suggests: the first "not blocked" stage, competence relative to others, sustainable results, and mastery of the domain. Assign your own honest estimate to each. Where are you now on the path ("nothing happens," first leap, "massive resistance")? What evidence supports your answer, and what would you need to believe in order not to quit during the next flat stretch?

8. **Audit your mental diet.** For one week, log what you consume (books, podcasts, videos, feeds) and what you build or produce with it. Using section 15.7, classify the week as a lean bulk, a dirty bulk, a cut or maintenance. Identify one episode of overwhelm and decide which column of the "good overwhelm / bad overwhelm" table it belongs to, and why. Design the change to your inputs or outputs that the model would prescribe, and say what the model might be missing about your situation.

## Chapter 16 — Reading, Note-Taking and Learning with AI

Chapters 14 and 15 dealt with learning as an activity: the meta-skill of learning how to learn, curiosity as a guide, the warning against information that outruns execution, the prescription to build in order to learn, and the mechanics by which skills accumulate through techniques, progressive overload and pattern recognition. Both chapters kept returning to the same diagnosis. Most people consume a great deal and change very little, because what they take in is not filtered by a goal, not applied to a project and not tested against reality. This chapter turns to the inputs themselves. What should a person who wants to create do with the books, posts, podcasts and videos that fill their days? How should they read? Where should the ideas that strike them go, and how should those ideas come back when they are needed? And what changes now that an AI model can summarize a book, answer a question at the moment of struggle or interview a person until it understands their project?

Koe's answers form a sequence that mirrors the structure of the chapter. Section 16.1 describes the change of stance that comes before any technique: the move from **consumer** to **researcher**, the intermediate step between consuming and creating. Section 16.2 gathers everything Koe says about reading: why to read, what not to read for, what to read, and how to read, including his 2025 method of reading in two layers with AI. Section 16.3 follows his long and changing relationship with note-taking systems, from the 2022 "dissect and distill" template and the database of intellectual property to the 2026 verdict that the second brain is "a false god" and his preferred alternative, the **second subconscious**. Section 16.4 presents AI as a tutor, from the return of apprenticeship to the detailed method he calls using AI "better than 99% of people." The chapter prepares Chapter 17 (how to think) and Chapter 18 (creativity and originality), which take the ideas collected here and ask how they are combined into something new, and Part VIII, where those ideas become writing.

Three earlier threads should be kept in view. From Chapter 6 comes the goal as a lens: the mind notices what serves the goal it is pursuing. From Chapter 11 comes cheap dopamine: consumption that feels like progress but produces disorder. From Chapter 14 comes the principle that information without application is false progress. Much of this chapter is an application of those three ideas to the specific acts of reading, saving and prompting.

### 16.1 From Consumer to Researcher

#### The consumer: used by the internet rather than using it

The figure against which this section is written is the **consumer**. Koe gives the word a specific sense that goes beyond "someone who buys things." In a 2023 video titled "If Your Life Sucks, Here's How To Reprogram Your Mind," he asks why people keep doing things they hate. He does not claim to be immune: he describes himself as someone who has escaped and sees the situation from higher up the mountain, "until he inevitably falls back down after crossing the peak." The consumer's life, as he paints it, is praying for the weekend, dreading Monday, hiding who you are to talk to people you don't like working with, and using the internet as an escape: scrolling, clicking, shutting the mind off "because when it's on you don't like what it's doing." "This is the life of the consumer, the person who is used by the internet rather than the one who uses it" (**Source:** `If Your Life Sucks, Here's How To Reprogram Your Mind.md`, 2023-10-22).

The definition places the difference not in how much a person uses the internet but in the direction of the relationship. The same feed, the same platforms and the same hours can either use you or be used by you. That is why Koe adds that there is no escaping the new world: you can fight it or flow with it, and the internet is "a big problem and also the solution." The consumer is the person for whom it is only the problem.

In the same video Koe traces the consumer's condition backward through a causal chain, which is worth reconstructing step by step because each link names a deficit that later sections of this book address:

1. Your life feels bad because you don't contribute to humanity.
2. You don't contribute because "you don't have something so valuable that you can't help but share it."
3. You don't have it because you ignore the problems in your life that beg for a solution.
4. You ignore them because you lack clarity on how to achieve the goal that would solve them.
5. You lack that clarity because you have nothing to build: nothing to frame and guide your learning.

(**Source:** `If Your Life Sucks, Here's How To Reprogram Your Mind.md`, 2023-10-22.)

The last link is the one that matters for this chapter. Learning without something to build has no frame, and without a frame, information has nothing to attach to. The consumer is not someone who consumes too much; it is someone whose consumption is not directed by a project. Read backward, the chain also explains why the cure Koe proposes is not "consume less" but "consume differently."

A few months earlier, closing a video about getting angry at where you are in life, Koe had already summarized the way out as a six-step sequence: (1) feel into the situation you are in; (2) transmute that energy toward a goal; (3) acquire the skills necessary to reach that goal; (4) "pursue your curiosity to avoid the mechanical nature of prescriptions"; (5) exchange your knowledge, projects and solutions for attention and income; (6) use your **self-reflective consciousness** to identify gaps in your ability and fix them. You have the resources, he says; it will take years; you may not start now, because "awareness takes time to blossom." Push forward in reality at your experience level, seek big-picture understanding, and don't get trapped in technical details (**Source:** `Get Mad At Where You Are In Life (A Deep Explanation).md`, 2023-06-11).

Two steps in that sequence belong directly to this chapter. Step four warns that learning by prescription, following someone else's steps, becomes mechanical; curiosity keeps it alive. Step five names the economic end of the process: what a person learns is eventually exchanged for attention and income. Between the consumer who uses the internet to escape and the person who exchanges knowledge for income there is a missing role, and Koe names it.

#### The intermediate step: researcher before creator

The usual self-improvement advice says: stop consuming, start creating. Koe thinks the jump is too large. "It's not about transitioning from consumer to creator, it's about transitioning from consumer to researcher first." The reason is that you must research and gather your own knowledge before you can create with it: you dissect other things through reading in order to reconstruct them into your own creation, whether that is writing, a video or a newsletter. A **researcher**, in this sense, "implies that you are intentionally consuming information": you have a goal for how you will use and apply what you take in (**Source:** `The Rise Of The Value Creator (A Career Path For Polymaths & Self-Improvers).md`, 2022-10-31; the passage reappears almost word for word in the 2024 compilation `The One-Person Business Model (How To Productize Yourself Full Guide).md`, 2024-02-06).

The researcher is therefore defined by two features. The first is intention: consumption is directed by a goal. The second is the operation performed on what is consumed: dissection followed by reconstruction. Neither feature requires consuming less. A researcher may read more than a consumer; the difference lies in what happens to what is read.

Koe adds an example that shows where a researcher's originality comes from. Suppose you are working toward a big goal, such as financial freedom, while being very interested in spirituality. Ask how spirituality is helping you get there. The connection between the two is "a very unique perspective... a very unique connection." No one else holds that particular combination of a goal and an interest, so the researcher who consumes through the lens of their own goal produces connections that a generic consumer cannot. This is the seed of the argument, developed in Part VII, that the person is the niche: the uniqueness of a perspective comes from the intersection of what someone is pursuing and what they are curious about, and research is the activity that makes those intersections visible.

#### Research instead of consume: the hermetic law of use

Koe states the principle in its shortest form in a 2023 video: "Rather than consuming information, research information" (**Source:** `The Most Important High-Income Skill To Learn (In The Next 10 Years).md`, 2023-11-05). The fullest explanation of why comes earlier, in a 2022 video titled "Stop Trying To Be Unique... Do This Instead," where "stop consuming and start researching" is step two of a creative process.

"Consuming," he explains, implies that you aren't doing anything with information. You are not enacting what he calls "**the hermetic law of use**," so you will lose what you take in. Koe borrows the phrase from Hermetic philosophy without specifying a text; in his usage it amounts to "what is not used is lost." When you adopt the perspective of a researcher, by contrast, "everything starts to gain utility," because you are actively trying to connect and apply it; there is intention and purpose behind the consumption. You are no longer on social media to be entertained and "mentally masturbate," but to research: to take something, dissect it, expand on it, summarize it, connect the dots to other things you have learned, and form a new perspective that you can create and make make sense to others. His example is modest: while re-reading the first chapter of your favorite book, something lights up your brain, so you take a note (**Source:** `Stop Trying To Be Unique... Do This Instead.md`, 2022-05-28). That note is the first step of the system described in section 16.3, which in 2022 he packaged as a free guide called **7 Days to Genius Ideas**.

The list of operations deserves attention, because it is the researcher's toolkit: **dissect, expand, summarize, connect, form a perspective**. The consumer receives; the researcher performs these five operations on what is received. Each of them is a small act of creation, which is why research is the bridge to creating: it is creation practiced on someone else's material.

The negative image recurs in 2025 in stronger language. "Most people don't know how to learn because they fry their brain with podcasts and YouTube videos and books and textbooks and social media, and six months later, after learning so much, they have nothing to show for it." "Why are you even learning in the first place if not to do something with it?" "Learning for most people has become a form of **mental masturbation**. It's the same cheap dopamine you get from scrolling on your phone, but even worse, because it makes you feel as if you're learning something, but the reality is you'll forget about it by tomorrow" (**Source:** `How To Learn Anything 10x Faster Than Anyone With AI.md`, 2025-03-09). The phrase "mental masturbation" is Koe's recurrent name for learning without doing: an activity that produces the pleasure of progress without its result. The connection to Chapter 11 is direct. Learning-as-consumption is a form of cheap dopamine that disguises itself as its opposite, which makes it more dangerous than ordinary scrolling, because the person does not feel the need to stop.

The 2023 formulation adds a practice that makes research concrete in the place where most people consume most: the feed. While scrolling, ask yourself what caught your attention, why you are still reading, and how the writer is holding your attention. Look for the principles of attention (the "10 commandments" of the video in question) on the timeline. "Pattern recognition helps with learning": when you spot one of them in the wild, you feel a dopamine increase ("oh, that's what Dan was talking about") and you remember it so you can use it in your own content, writing or speaking (**Source:** `The Most Important High-Income Skill To Learn (In The Next 10 Years).md`, 2023-11-05). Here the dopamine that the consumer spends on novelty is redirected to recognition. The same scrolling session that drains one person trains another, depending on the question each brings to it. This links to the pattern-recognition mechanics of Chapter 15: recognizing a pattern you have learned is both the evidence that learning happened and a reward that reinforces it.

#### Reading like a researcher: how Koe started on Twitter

Koe tells the origin of his own writing career as a story of researching rather than consuming. He never cared for Twitter. One day he saw a self-improvement post, followed one person, liked content, followed more, and his feed filled with that kind of content. Then he saw a man selling web design services and products through Twitter at a full-time income, and asked himself "why can't I do the same thing?" He "started emulating their content structure and posting the ideas in my head." His background in marketing, sales and copywriting let him notice patterns: "I wasn't reading it like a consumer, I was reading it like a researcher." He describes what that looked like from the inside: "that's a hook... this is leading people down the page... this is where it delivers value... this is the conclusion or call to action that actually leads to engagement. I'm going to take these pieces and put my own thoughts related to my own interests in them." He adds a caveat: content alone is not everything; it also needs eyes on it, which is the subject of a separate video on growth (**Source:** `How To Make $1 Million A Year As A Digital Writer.md`, 2023-10-08).

The story illustrates the reconstruction half of the researcher's work. Reading the post as a researcher meant separating its structure (hook, body that leads down the page, value delivery, conclusion or call to action) from its content, and then filling the structure with his own ideas. Koe calls this **emulation**, and it returns in Part VIII as the use of proven structures as "training wheels" for articulation. It is an experience, not a law: Koe's marketing background gave him the vocabulary to see structure where others saw only posts. Part of what the researcher stance asks is that the reader acquire that vocabulary.

#### Consumer mindset versus creator mindset

The same contrast appears in 2022 under a slightly different pair of names. Don't just scroll and consume the content, Koe says: "that's the **consumer mindset**." The creator takes a post, looks at it and deconstructs it: why did this do so well? Why is this type of post performing well? How do I take "the essence of this post" and make it my own so I can grow and "play the game"? (**Source:** `The Rise Of The Value Creator (A Career Path For Polymaths & Self-Improvers).md`, 2022-10-31; repeated in `The One-Person Business Model (How To Productize Yourself Full Guide).md`, 2024-02-06.)

The phrase "the essence of this post" carries the method. What is taken is not the post's wording, which would be copying, but its essence: the underlying idea or the mechanism that made it work. "Play the game" connects the practice to the game metaphor of Chapter 10: social media has rules that can be learned, and dissecting successful posts is how a player learns them.

Two examples from Koe's videos show what dissecting the essence looks like in practice. In 2026 he walks through a post that reads: "Major cheat code for life: increase your recovery speed. You will get rejected. You will lose money. You will embarrass yourself. The goal isn't to avoid the fall, it's to shorten the time between the fall and the reset. Fast recovery compounds." The essence, "increase your recovery speed," is in his words "kind of Sahil Bloom coded," an idea associated with another writer. But the opening, "major cheat code for life," "you could definitely use that as a hook. Why not?" And reading into the body ("you will get rejected, you will lose money"), "you start to think, hmm, do other ideas spin off of that? And most of the time, they do" (**Source:** `How To Grow An Audience If You Have 0 Followers (It's Only 2 Habits).md`, 2026-05-14). A single post, dissected, yields at least two kinds of material: a reusable hook and a set of spin-off ideas suggested by its body. Neither is a copy of the post.

The second example shows how fast the process can be when it has become habitual. While preparing a 2023 video, Koe had to create a post within an hour, so he found an idea quickly in a Medium headline: "10 habits that changed my life." The post he wrote for X was: "How to clear your mind: walk more, read more, write more, listen more, lift more, strategize more, build more; scroll less, indulge less, criticize less, ruminate less, sit less, procrastinate less. Clarity is reserved for those who don't resist reality but engage with it." He explains a formatting choice: he could have used bullets, but X cut off long posts at the end at the time, so he did not space it out; with a shorter list he would have used bullet points (**Source:** `How Intelligent Creators Will Make Money In 2024 (The Build Teach Earn Method).md`, 2023-12-03). The headline supplied a format (a list of habits); Koe supplied the content and the closing line. The example is minor, and Koe presents it as such, but it shows the researcher's operation at its smallest scale: a source becomes a structure, and the structure is filled with one's own view.

#### The edge of understanding and anomaly research

In a 2025 video on personal branding, Koe gives the researcher stance its most systematic form. He starts with a diagnosis of why people struggle to find ideas worth writing about. There are two reasons, which he presents as mirroring the reasons for poor performance and low excitement: "their mind isn't trained to be articulate, and they don't consume information at the **edge of their understanding**." The single most beneficial fix for writing, he says, is to "use high-performing post structures as training wheels for your articulation," so that an idea can become something others like, share and follow you for (**Source:** `How To Build A Better Personal Brand Than 99% Of People.md`, 2025-06-08).

The second reason is the one that bears on reading. Consuming at the edge of one's understanding means choosing inputs that are slightly beyond what one already grasps: neither so familiar that they add nothing nor so foreign that nothing attaches. It is the reading equivalent of the challenge–skill balance of Chapter 10, and it explains why the consumer, who consumes what is comfortable, runs out of ideas.

The fix comes as an exercise that Koe calls finding **anomalies**, which can be reconstructed step by step:

1. In a notebook or notes app, list five to ten writers, thinkers or creators you admire for their articulation.
2. Spend one hour a day for the next week scrolling their accounts.
3. Find their anomalies: "posts that have at least 2x the engagement as their other posts." Screenshot them or write them down. The key shift, he says, is to "stop reading ideas on the internet as a consumer... start doing so as a researcher": you are reading for your own writing, not for entertainment.
4. Once you have saved at least 20 to 30 posts that represent the articulation you want, break down why they work. Under each, write three to five bullets: why it did well, what psychological patterns it uses, how it captured attention, what the value is, why people care.
5. Optionally, paste a prompt he provides into an AI along with a post to get a breakdown of why it worked, its structure, and a step-by-step way to replicate it with your own ideas. (The prompt was shown on screen; its contents are not in the transcript.)

The point, he concludes, is that "you are dissecting why already validated ideas have done well." Writing that stops the scroll and "nearly demands readers to absorb the idea" makes "growth a byproduct" (**Source:** `How To Build A Better Personal Brand Than 99% Of People.md`, 2025-06-08).

Three design choices in the exercise are worth making explicit. The sample is restricted to people admired for their articulation, so the researcher studies what they want to become, not what is merely popular. The anomaly criterion (twice the writer's own average) controls for the writer's audience size: a post that outperforms its author's usual results reveals something about the post, not about the author's reach. And the written breakdown forces articulation: the researcher must say why the post works, which is the skill the exercise is meant to train. The exercise therefore addresses both of the reasons Koe gives for lacking ideas at once.

In 2026 he extends the logic to topics. "**Foundational content topics** are just those that are evergreen. They're the ones that you know work, the ones that you see everywhere, and you should probably implement under your own brand in your own voice because they just work." "**High-performing topics** are the outliers that tend to do very well": when you see a YouTube video "doing so much better than everyone else's videos or even that person's own videos, that's an outlier. That's a signal that you should probably take note of that and put it in your **swipe file**." Then "you take your own ideas and you start to reformulate them so that they work better" (**Source:** `How To Build A $1M One-Person Business Faster With AI.md`, 2026-03-15). The swipe file, a marketer's term for a collection of proven material to study, becomes in section 16.3 one of the forms of the idea museum.

The same 2026 period contains Koe's assessment of how most people actually do this research. Some bookmark posts "and hope that they come back to it and remember it when it's time to actually create," then stare at a blank page, write something that isn't good and "wonder why it didn't do well since they're actually doing the steps." Others search YouTube for similar titles before writing ("a solid way of doing it") or go to a creator's account, filter by most popular and study those titles. Others jot ideas as they come "and hope that those ideas are good enough... and sometimes they are." "All of those are fine, but they're not really strategized. They're not really a system... you can rely on. And frankly, they're just time consuming and they're slow" (**Source:** `How To Grow An Audience If You Have 0 Followers (It's Only 2 Habits).md`, 2026-05-14). The verdict is measured: the habits are not wrong, only unreliable. What they lack is what the anomaly exercise supplies: a criterion for selection and a step of analysis. The complaint about bookmarks that are never revisited anticipates the critique of second brains in section 16.3.

#### Researcher and a vessel

In 2026 Koe raises the researcher stance from a technique to a vocation. Addressed to people with multiple interests, the claim is unusually absolute: "Your sole job is to become a researcher and a vessel. And I'm serious about this. You must consider it your full-time job to research": reading books, watching YouTube, listening to podcasts, using the discovery features of his software, "because that's what writers, creatives, and visionaries do. That's what Jordan Peterson does. That's what Andrew Huberman does. That's what Marcus Aurelius and all your beloved figureheads of the past did. They probably don't care about being a 'personal brand', but they do care about their interests." Creating content, "which was once just considered writing before it took the specific form of media on the internet, is their chosen vessel for earning an income" (**Source:** `If You Have Multiple Interests, Start A One-Person Business.md`, 2026-06-13).

The term **vessel** recurs across Koe's work for the container through which accumulated knowledge reaches others and returns as income (the "creative firepower, vessel, currency" sequence developed in later chapters). Here the order matters: research first, vessel second. The figures he names are offered as examples of people whose public output follows from private research into their interests, not as evidence that research alone produces an audience. The claim also completes the arc of this section. The consumer uses the internet to escape; the researcher uses it to learn with intent; the researcher who treats research as a full-time job and content as the vessel for it has turned consumption into the raw material of a career.

The rest of this chapter describes the researcher's instruments: how to read (16.2), where to keep what is found (16.3) and how to use AI to learn faster without outsourcing the learning (16.4).

### 16.2 Reading

Reading is the researcher's main instrument, and Koe has said more about it than about any other input. His statements span 2022 to 2026 and do not always agree: he recommends summaries and later condemns summary culture; he presents a tactic for reading only the first chapters next to a tactic for finishing books; he titles a video "How To Read Books Fast" and advises within it that "the slower the better." This section reconstructs his position in four movements: why to read, what reading is not for, what to read, and how to read. It ends with his most developed method, reading in two layers with AI. Where his positions conflict, both versions are presented.

#### What reading does

Koe's most compact case for reading comes from a 2024 video called "This Simple Reading Habit Will Change Your Life." If you want a more fulfilling career, better relationships, more intelligence, to rediscover the depth of life and to slow down in a busy, distracted world, read. "Reading is how you acquire new knowledge. Reading is how you expand your worldview. Reading is how you spot new opportunities. Reading is how you train your focus. Reading is how you absorb 10 years of experience in 8 hours." And then a rule that requires no justification: "When you're bored, pick up a book, not your phone. You don't need a reason to read" (**Source:** `This Simple Reading Habit Will Change Your Life (I Promise).md`, 2024-08-04).

The list names five functions, and they are of different kinds. Acquiring knowledge and expanding a worldview concern content. Spotting opportunities concerns perception, in line with the goal-as-lens idea of Chapter 6. Training focus concerns the act of reading itself: sustained attention on long-form text is practice for the attention that deep work requires (Chapter 12). Absorbing years of experience in hours is a compression claim. The figure is rhetorical rather than measured, and Koe does not hold it constant: a few weeks earlier, in a 2024 video on life as a video game, he said that "books give you 10 years of effort from 6 hours of reading" (**Source:** `Life Is A Video Game (Here's How You Win).md`, 2024-07-21). The two numbers are not reconciled anywhere in the corpus; what stays constant is the idea that a book compresses someone else's years into a reader's hours.

The same video then reframes the question. Once the case for reading is made, the remaining questions are what to read so that you want the habit, how to read to get the most from it, and which tactics make the change enjoyable. "It's not if you read, it's what you read and how you read it" (**Source:** `This Simple Reading Habit Will Change Your Life (I Promise).md`, 2024-08-04). The rest of this section follows that division.

In 2025 Koe reduces the habit to its minimal form as part of a set of daily commitments (one project, one book, and so on). The **one book** habit is to read a single book 30 minutes a day; at that rate you are bound to finish it within six to twelve months, and you can read more, but "one book" matched the structure he was proposing. The reasoning is that to change your life you need knowledge, school probably won't give it to you, so you must self-educate by immersing your mind "in the thoughts of those who have lived the life you want to live." Learning out of curiosity, he says, is "a prime representation of the true," and exploration brings the novel ideas that lead to progress (**Source:** `You Need To Be Extreme If You Want Your Life To Change.md`, 2025-06-29). The time figure (30 minutes) appears elsewhere in his work as part of a 30–60 minute daily self-education habit; the numbers vary across videos, but the principle of a small daily dose sustained for months does not.

#### Why most people read badly

If reading does so much, why does it seem to do so little for most readers? Koe's 2025 video "How To Read Books Fast With AI (And Remember What You Read)" opens with a provocation. He quotes a tweet: "Reading books is now a waste of time. AI reasoning models can distill key insights and tell you exactly how to implement them based on everything they know about you." He was upset at first, he says, and now "kind of just feel[s] bad for this guy." But he concedes a point: "There's some truth to what this guy is saying, but that's because most people in general don't know how to read and they don't know how to remember what they read." Not because they are illiterate, but because they learned to read in a "Prussian style education system designed to create obedient soldiers, compliant citizens, civil servants, and well-behaved workers" (**Source:** `How To Read Books Fast With AI (And Remember What You Read).md`, 2025-04-20).

**Complementary context:** The "Prussian model" refers to the system of compulsory, state-run, age-graded schooling developed in Prussia in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries and promoted in the United States by reformers such as Horace Mann. Koe uses it, here and in Part I, as shorthand for an education designed to produce compliant workers; in his reading it explains why people read to pass tests rather than to change.

The diagnosis continues with a description of how most people read. "Reading to most people is a **performative act**. They read to find specific information for a test, be it a school test or a life test. They read to show others that they've accomplished something. Like how people flex that they've somehow both read and retained information from 52 books in a year. They avoid reading difficult books because if they don't understand it, what's the point?" (**Source:** `How To Read Books Fast With AI (And Remember What You Read).md`, 2025-04-20). Reading as performance has three forms: reading for a test, reading for display and avoiding difficulty. All three are oriented toward an outcome outside the reader's mind: a grade, an impression, a feeling of competence.

A year earlier Koe had put the motive of display in sharper terms. "Why are you reading?" For some it is status: to be able to say you have read a lot and seem like you are doing something with your life, to impress others. "That's fine, but if you haven't created anything that benefits humanity, the pursuit of status will leave you hollow" (**Source:** `This Simple Reading Habit Will Change Your Life (I Promise).md`, 2024-08-04). The phrase "that's fine" matters: Koe does not condemn the motive, he predicts its outcome. Reading for status without creation is the consumer's condition from section 16.1 in a more respectable form.

In the 2025 video Koe then lays out the consequences as a chain of four problems:

1. Very few people read.
2. When they read, they don't remember any of it.
3. People don't like discomfort, so they don't read difficult books.
4. Since they don't increase the complexity of knowledge they can make sense of, they can't take on more challenging situations, "the ones that lead to more than superficial and short-lived success."

"They turn 50 years old with the intellectual maturity of a 15-year-old" (**Source:** `How To Read Books Fast With AI (And Remember What You Read).md`, 2025-04-20).

The chain runs from avoidance of difficulty to the absence of growth in the complexity one can handle, and from there to the inability to face real challenges and, finally, to shallow success. The logic connects reading to the developmental themes of the book. The capacity to make sense of complex material is not an academic luxury; in Koe's account it limits the complexity of the situations a person can navigate, and therefore the kind of success available to them. The final line is hyperbole, but it states the mechanism: intellectual maturity is a function of the difficulty one has been willing to face.

#### You don't read to find answers

The most counterintuitive part of Koe's position is his claim about what reading is not for. "You don't read to find a specific answer. That's just stupid. Why would you waste 8 hours reading a book just to find a few steps to accomplish something when you can type a question into Google, Reddit, or now AI?" "If you need to figure out how to be more productive or start a business, a book is probably the last place you should look," if you are actually trying to learn "rather than to feel as if you're making progress." He qualifies this immediately: for the big picture of productivity or business, a book is a good place; "but I'd still argue that intelligent and calculated research is still a better option for that specific use case" (**Source:** `How To Read Books Fast With AI (And Remember What You Read).md`, 2025-04-20).

The positive claim follows. "You don't read to find information that can already be found. You read to explore the unknown and pursue your curiosity. You read to discover things you didn't know before and didn't even think about searching with Google or ChatGPT. You read to expand your mind to places you didn't know were there. You read to slowly **reprogram** who you are by exposing yourself to new ideas that can't be intentionally searched by an identity that didn't even think to search for them" (**Source:** `How To Read Books Fast With AI (And Remember What You Read).md`, 2025-04-20).

This is the core of Koe's answer to the tweet. The claim that AI makes reading irrelevant, he argues, "assumes that everyone reads because they want to find information that is already known," information everyone else can also find, "and that means you're replaceable if you're going after that information." A search, whether in Google or in an AI chat, can only return what the searcher thinks to ask for, and what a person thinks to ask for is determined by their current identity. A book written by someone else, with a different identity, contains answers to questions the reader would never have asked. Reading is therefore one of the few ways to get outside the closed loop of one's own questions, which is why it serves the identity change described in Part II. The argument also distinguishes two uses of text: reading for how-to (where search and AI are better) and reading to change one's view of the world (where they cannot substitute for the book). This distinction resolves several apparent contradictions in the corpus, as the following subsections show.

#### Reading is about changing your mind

The next step of the 2025 argument goes further. "It's not about what information you have. It's not even about what you do with that information. It's about changing your mind. Because your mind is how you interact with reality. It's how you make decisions that lead to a good or bad life. Your mind doesn't change with a few key points from a book summary or an AI generated summary. It changes when new ideas, actionable or not, fill in missing pieces, challenge old beliefs, or give you a new angle to view a situation from." And because each reader brings different beliefs, goals, problems, story and interests, "no single person reads a book and gets the exact same lessons out of it" (**Source:** `How To Read Books Fast With AI (And Remember What You Read).md`, 2025-04-20).

The passage names three mechanisms by which a mind changes: new ideas fill in missing pieces, challenge old beliefs, or provide a new angle. None of them requires the idea to be actionable ("actionable or not"). This is a notable nuance in Koe's work. Elsewhere he insists that "the purpose of knowledge is action," and Chapter 14 is built on that insistence. Here he places mind change first and lets action follow from it. The two positions are compatible if action is understood as the downstream effect of a changed mind rather than a requirement each piece of knowledge must meet on its own; but the shift in emphasis is real and he does not comment on it.

The same video gives the change a precise image. "Most people read to memorize as much as possible because that's how they were trained to read in school." But "you don't read to remember every single sentence in a book. You read to change how you view the world by adding a few nodes to the **web of ideas** that compose your mind, helping you see situations in a new, more complex and meaningful light." He recalls, while admitting he is unsure of the exact quote, Richard Feynman saying that physics deepened his appreciation of nature, because he understood a deeper layer of how it works. Likewise, understanding the inner workings of a plant deepens your appreciation of it, and this applies to "literally any topic or domain of knowledge" (**Source:** `How To Read Books Fast With AI (And Remember What You Read).md`, 2025-04-20).

The web of ideas is the model that holds this whole section together. A mind is a network of connected ideas; a worldview is that network seen as a whole. Reading adds nodes. A single new node can reconfigure the network because it connects to many existing ones, which is why a book can change a reader without the reader remembering most of it. The Feynman example adds that the change is not only cognitive: a more complex network makes the world appear richer, so that the same plant or the same night sky is experienced differently. Reading, on this model, changes perception, not just knowledge.

This position marks a change from Koe's earlier work. A 2022 video was titled "Learn New Skills FAST (How I Remember Everything I Learn)" and aimed at retention, through intention, curiosity and closing the gap between learning and execution. By 2025–2026 remembering everything "is not the point of reading at all," and the purpose is mind change and identity change. The two can be reconciled if the 2022 retention is read as a consequence of practice rather than a goal in itself, but the emphasis has moved, and Koe does not explain the move.

#### Against summaries, and against the obsession with remembering

The model of the web of ideas explains Koe's hostility to summaries. In the 2025 reading video he observes that "book summaries have been around for forever." Many of the most helpful books, "the books that will make you millions of dollars," are available as summaries.
