"At a 2.5% conversion rate on a landing page, meaning 2.5% of the people that go to the landing page actually buy the thing that you're selling, you need about 720 people to visit that page a day to make 18 sales on a 150 dollar product." Alternatively, one could have "a post go viral once or twice a month, which I wouldn't bet on, but is becoming more and more of a thing as the social media platforms are becoming more interest-algorithm related." "Even if you're just starting off, if you can create good content, you can post your first reel [and] it'll go mega viral," but "most people don't know how to create content, so that's usually not going to happen unless it's based on luck."

**Source:** How To Build A $1M One-Person Business Faster With AI.md

A February 2025 version of the same math adds an estimate of what traffic is achievable. Getting 720 people to a page converting at 2.5% "is pretty doable." It takes a while, but beginners writing on Twitter wisely can get 100,000 impressions in their first month, and one TikTok or Reel can go viral for a million views. Get 720 people to a page once a day at 2.5% conversion, "split up as much as you want." "Not easy by any means, but it's feasible when you understand the moving parts of business."

**Source:** A Full Guide To Making Your First Profitable Product (Beginners, Take Notes).md

The value of the exercise is not the final number but the chain. Revenue becomes daily sales; daily sales become daily visitors; daily visitors become a content and distribution problem. Each link names a lever (price, conversion, traffic), and the levers correspond to the four variables of Section 30.5. The 2.5% conversion rate is an assumption Koe uses for illustration; actual rates vary widely with the offer and the audience. The impression figures are his estimates of what is achievable, not guarantees.

#### Your standard is how much you make

Koe adds a psychological mechanism that explains why a large number can help rather than overwhelm, which might seem to contradict the Gap of Section 30.2. In July 2024: "If you have the goal of making a million dollars a month and you aren't there yet, that shines a light on the potential problems in your business that you can then see and fix and move forward and get closer to that goal; and as you move forward, new problems emerge that you start to think, 'oh, that's why I'm not hitting that number,' and then you eventually achieve it." "The reason you don't make as much money as you want to make is because... your standard is how much you make. If you raise your standards higher and actually mean it, then that is what identifies problems, and then once you solve those problems, then you reach the standard."

**Source:** Learn This Skill If You Want To Be Relevant In 10 Years.md

*Your standard* is Koe's term, and it applies Chapter 6's thesis that problems exist only relative to a goal (and Chapter 3's claim that standards define what is perceived as a problem). A higher standard makes problems visible that a lower standard leaves invisible. The difference from the Gap is the qualifier "and actually mean it" combined with a path: a goal held as a standard, with its problems being solved one by one, organizes attention; a goal admired from a distance, without a path, disorders it.

#### The $1 Million Creator in eight steps

In May 2024 Koe embeds the money question in a broader sequence he calls "the $1 million Creator." The steps are: (1) choose a vision, not a skill; (2) stack the future-proof skills (marketing and sales, writing and thinking, entrepreneurship); (3) solve problems with experimentation; (4) become a value creator; (5) monetize your mind, not your time; (6) turn it into $1 million, through the levers of writing, promotion and iteration; (7) rest, because work contracts the mind and rest expands it; (8) "[expletive] being busy," that is, stop work that does not move the needle toward your vision. He notes that only "two, three points" are directly about making money; the rest concern "the skills, mindset, beliefs, habits associated with that."

**Source:** How Smart Creatives Work Less & Earn More LEVERAGE.md

The sequence is a compressed map of this book. Vision (Chapter 7), skill stacks (Chapter 35), experimentation (Chapter 15), the value creator (Chapters 18 and 35), monetizing the mind (Chapter 34), rest (Chapter 13) and the refusal of busyness (Chapter 12) surround the two money steps. That proportion is Koe's point: income is the output of a person built in a certain way, not a separate project.

#### Follower-to-income benchmarks, and why they do not agree

The second family of numbers relates audience size to income. In December 2022, describing stage two of the roadmap, Koe says it begins around 10,000 followers, when "you should feel you have the growth game down." He advises not waiting until then to monetize, but says this is "where real money comes in." Then he shares his own numbers: "at 500 followers I had a 3K month, at 10,000 followers I had a 10K month, at 50,000 followers I had a 50K month," and at 200,000 a $200,000 month (he corrects himself mid-sentence), "because of Black Friday." He shares them "as a baseline," hoping "it breaks some people out of their limiting money beliefs." About two years earlier, he says, he thought $100,000 in a month was insane, until he saw a trustworthy person he talked to frequently, doing the same thing he did, making $100,000 a month; that "blew his mind." He wanted $10,000 a month and was happy with it, "but it's fun to push more in business." The passage is repeated, almost word for word, in the 2024 compilation.

**Source:** The One Person Business Roadmap (99% Make This Mistake).md; The One-Person Business Model (How To Productize Yourself Full Guide).md

The story about the peer is the mechanism of the previous subsections in miniature: a belief changed by seeing someone similar achieve something, and with it the set of outcomes Koe considered possible.

In October 2023 he discusses a ratio he read in someone else's post: one can make 50 cents to $1 per follower per month. He qualifies it: this is "only possible with your own product or service... not possible with banking on the algorithm or using something like AdSense." "You need to create an independent source of income... not rely on the algorithm or AdSense as your boss like you would a job... you don't want another boss," a corporation deciding your income by your views and how much you cater to it. The ratio held for him "to a point": in his first three years he made about $1 per follower per month (10,000, then 50,000, then 100,000 dollars a month), with $800,000 in his third year, and about $3.1 million in revenue so far in the year of the video. But with 2.8 million followers, he does not see himself making $2.8 million a month: "maybe I've just gotten lazy with how I promote... then again that could very well be a limiting belief." His conclusion: "If you slowly build a decent readership, launch a new product and get 80% of the things right, I find it hard to believe that you couldn't make a million dollars."

**Source:** How To Make $1 Million A Year As A Digital Writer.md

The ratio is adapted from an unnamed post, and Koe's own figures show where it breaks: it holds in the early years and fails at scale. His two explanations for the break (laziness in promotion, or a limiting belief) are offered as possibilities, not as a diagnosis. The insistence on "your own product" connects the ratio to Section 30.3's argument against income based on algorithms or platform payouts.

In December 2023 he gives a different illustration. If you have 10,000 followers and make $3,000 a month, you know you can reach 100,000 and make $30,000 a month; at a million or more, or by optimizing your offer stack and value ladder, you could make $100,000 a month at 100,000 followers; and "if you know what you're doing, you can have 5,000 followers and make $100,000 a month; I see people do it all the time."

**Source:** The Future Of Work Is Play (How To Create A Digital Career).md

The three sets of numbers are not consistent. The 2022 numbers imply about $1 per follower per month; the December 2023 illustration implies about $0.30, and then detaches income from audience size altogether. The difference has an explanation in the sources themselves. The 2022 figures are Koe's personal history; the 2023 ratio is a rule he tested and saw break; the December 2023 figures are an illustration of leverage whose outcome depends on the offer. Read together, they support one conclusion that none of them states alone: the audience sets an upper range, but the offer (its price, structure and promotion) determines where in that range the income falls.

#### How much is enough

Koe also gives thresholds for what is sufficient. In May 2025 he says most people can live fine on $5,000 a month; with a family, $10,000–$15,000, "that's three clients a month" at $5,000, which he admits is a cliché in online business, "but it's true." A $10 subscription with 500 buyers yields $5,000 a month in recurring revenue, though it takes longer because many more sales are needed (and he does not recommend subscriptions for beginners, pointing to a separate Q&A video). "500 people on an internet that has four to five billion people, there isn't that much to ask for." Over a year one can build an offer stack, a high-ticket product, a low-ticket subscription and something in between, and then one needs about one high-ticket buyer a month, ten subscription buyers and ten product buyers. Given how attention flows (people constantly follow new people; fluctuations invisible to outsiders occur naturally), "there's really more than enough attention to go around."

**Source:** The Future Of Work (How To Become AI-First).md

The passage reframes the $1M math at a human scale. The point of the "500 people" line is proportion: the required number of buyers is tiny relative to the internet's population. Chapter 34's "enough" develops the idea that the goal is sufficiency and autonomy, not maximization.

#### How little competition there is

In July 2025 Koe adds a claim about competition. "If you actually commit to it, which 99% of people don't, then you will probably make 10 to 100K a month," provided you can improve, iterate and not quit after two weeks. "Those who are not in the game just don't understand how little competition there actually is": the successful online businesses you see on social media are "like 10 to 50 people... maybe a 100, maybe 200," out of seven to eight billion; your echo chamber is "so incredibly small, it's actually mind-boggling." The only successful online business people are those who do not care about competition and know they can grab their piece of the pie.

**Source:** I'm 28. Here's How To Get Ahead Of Most 20 Year Olds.md

The figures are impressions from inside Koe's network, not counts, and the "10 to 100K a month" is conditional on a commitment he says 99% of people do not make. The claim's function is to counter the saturation fear of Section 30.2: what looks like a crowded field is a small, visible group of creators that the algorithm shows repeatedly to people interested in it.

#### The labor theory of value and asymmetric income

Why are such numbers hard to believe for people coming from employment? Koe's answer, from October 2024, names an economic idea. People who have only worked jobs (nothing wrong with that, he adds; he is "not one of the guys" saying quit your 9-to-5) understand only "the labor theory of value": I do this much work, I get this much every week or two. "It's not asymmetric," and it is not how the world works: "you're not getting paid in accordance with the value that you provide." Once you are paid by value, it takes time for the mind to shift to "I can send one email out" and make large amounts depending on time, skill and product. He first says $500,000 to $1 million and then corrects himself: "I can make $10,000 in an email."

**Source:** How Smart Creators Will Grow An Audience From Zero In 2025.md

**Complementary context:** the labor theory of value is a doctrine of classical political economy (associated with Adam Smith, David Ricardo and, in a different form, Karl Marx) according to which the value of a good derives from the labor required to produce it. Koe uses the term loosely, for the employee's expectation that pay is proportional to hours worked, and contrasts it with income tied to perceived value (Chapter 31). His use is a reinterpretation for his own purposes, not an engagement with the economic theory.

The concept explains the resistance the earlier numbers meet. A mind calibrated to hourly pay reads "$10,000 from an email" as implausible, because it measures income by the hours behind it. The mind shift Koe describes is the business version of the identity change of Chapter 4: the new numbers become believable only after the person has experienced, at least once, being paid for value rather than time.

#### Timelines

The third family of numbers concerns time, and here too the figures differ by video. In May 2023 Koe says being a creator "has been a three-to-five-year thing" for him, including a two-year gap of "not really taking it seriously," during which he made his first $10,000; then income rose slowly: about $100,000, $150,000, and $800,000 "when I finally figured this out," and higher since. His advice is to "just stick it out... take action and be consistent for what would be getting a four-year degree, but it's not like you're not getting paid along the way if you offer a product or service."

**Source:** I Made $800,000 In One Year Writing 2 Hours A Day.md

In March 2023 he says he had some prior freelancing experience but started his "creator journey" personal brand about three years earlier, which led to his current results. If you do it optimally and approach it from experience, give yourself three years to hit big numbers, which does not mean you cannot make a good amount in the first year. "$1,000,000 is a lot of money; you don't need that much. Give yourself five years to make $1,000,000 in this space; I bet you can if you commit to it."

**Source:** The Best Online Business To Make $1 Million In 3-5 Years.md

In April 2023, promoting Digital Economics, he relays that someone told him they would have to go through the course repeatedly while executing for a year. "Business takes time": "a year of going through and executing on a course I believe is invaluable; of course it can take less time, but expect a year to see some decent results and to make some decent money."

**Source:** Self Improvers Are Creating Their Own Careers (The New Economy).md

Section 30.1 already recorded the August 2023 figure, "a hefty income in two to four years with persistence and iteration," and Section 30.5 the cadence of launching every quarter for two to three years.

| Milestone | Timeline Koe gives | Source (date) |
|---|---|---|
| Decent results and decent money from executing a course | About one year | 2023-04 |
| "Big numbers" | About three years | 2023-03 |
| $1,000,000 | About five years | 2023-03 |
| "Hefty income" | Two to four years | 2023-08 |
| His own trajectory as a creator | Three to five years, including a two-year gap | 2023-05 |
| Quarterly launches | Two to three years | 2023-12 |

The figures look inconsistent but measure different milestones (first decent income, large income, $1M, a launch cadence), and Koe does not present them as contradicting each other. The "four-year degree" comparison is the most useful frame: a multi-year commitment comparable to the one most people accept without question for a degree, with the difference that a product or service pays along the way.

#### What not to worry about yet

The last threshold is administrative. In December 2024 Koe notes that many people ask "how do I actually start" because other things come to mind with the word *business*. For a long time, he says, do not worry about building a website, forming an LLC or handling taxes if you have not made at least $10,000 to $50,000. He adds a caveat: he does not know tax or business rules outside the United States, so do your own research. In the US you do not need an LLC; you can be taxed as self-employed indefinitely; $10,000–$50,000 is a lot to you but minuscule to the IRS, which, in his view, "won't audit you over it." "Remove those from your mind and let's focus on actually making money first."

**Source:** Build A One-Person Business As A Normal Person (From $0 To $10K).md

The threshold is Koe's rule of thumb from his own situation, not legal or tax advice, and the claim about audits is his opinion. Its purpose is prioritization: administrative setup feels like progress and protects the founder from the exposure of selling, which is the avoidance Chapter 28 describes.

### 30.7 The Writing Business and the Process with AI

#### Writers should not try to monetize their writing

The roadmap so far has been general. Koe's most frequent application of it is to the writer, because writing is the base skill of his system (Part VIII). His first claim about the writing business is counterintuitive. In October 2023: "Most writers try to sell their services on social media; most writers try to just sell their writing" (a paid blog, a paid newsletter, a paid community), "but that's so limiting." "Writing is both the traffic mechanism and the means to create an information product, or to create the education and the marketing around whatever product you want to sell, even if it's like a physical product." Writers "think that they have to monetize their writing rather than create a solution to the problems that they're talking about in their writing." Since "writing starts with a problem and creates steps and value to get to a solution," the writer should sell "a product that the people that are interested in those interests are already buying." "When you know how to write, market and sell, you can earn an income writing about whatever you want"; creatives generally "don't know how to market and sell."

**Source:** How To Make $1 Million A Year As A Digital Writer.md

*Traffic mechanism* is Koe's term for whatever brings people to see a business, and here he gives writing two roles at once: it attracts the audience and it constitutes the product (the course, the guide, the sales page). Selling the writing itself, as subscription content, uses only the first role and caps income at what readers will pay to read. Selling the solution to the problems the writing discusses uses both. The argument is Section 30.1's distinction between service and product applied to the writer: writing sold as writing is a commodity; writing that leads to a solution is a business.

A related heuristic, from January 2024, explains why writing in particular. If you are a creator, focus on writing rather than posting shirtless pictures (he has in mind fitness creators), "because you need to monetize your intelligence, not your looks; that way you can pivot with the times and you can build a sustainable income." What he teaches, he specifies, is "high impact digital writing," not academic or technical writing, "not how to write a research paper."

**Source:** This High-Income Skill Will Make You Irreplaceable (Full Guide).md

*Monetize your intelligence* (in other videos, "monetize your mind, not your time") is the positive form of Section 30.3's and 30.4's warnings about looks and algorithms: an income based on thinking can follow the thinker into new topics, which is what "pivot with the times" means.

#### The minimal model: newsletter, account, solution

In June 2022 Koe describes a writing-based business that requires very little: (1) a newsletter, (2) a Twitter account and (3) "a creative solution or potential solution to iterate on," which he glosses as "something to talk about." He explains why the newsletter comes first. Traffic platforms such as Twitter, Instagram and short-form video are "very shallow," algorithm-based; you can game the algorithm and grow fast, but "there's no depth, there's no authority, there's nothing there that will inherently make people buy from you." You can sell from social media, and many do, but he wants to set the reader up to develop themselves and write long-form to make sense of their ideas. The newsletter is where services and products are plugged in; it can be weekly or monthly. He adds that his own long YouTube videos serve the same purpose, packaging what he learns, and that "the newsletter is the foundation of these videos."

**Source:** How To Make Money As A Creative On The Internet.md

The three points correspond to the three parts of Chapter 28's minimal business: traffic (the account), trust and depth (the newsletter, which Chapter 24 calls the hub) and an offer (the solution). The word "potential" in the third point matters. The solution does not have to be finished; it has to be something the writer can iterate on in public, which is the content ladder of Section 30.3.

#### Nine steps (2022), six steps (2024)

Koe gives a step-by-step version of the writing business in August 2022 and repeats it in the February 2024 compilation. The steps are: (1) choose a topic you cannot shut up about; (2) brainstorm a unique perspective; (3) write 1,000+ words on the topic in a structured way; (4) set up a blog or newsletter platform and post it; (5) repurpose the actionable, step-by-step section into a Twitter thread (and from there an Instagram carousel); (6) learn how to grow on a platform, through branding and through getting eyes on your profile by networking; (7) turn the impactful ideas from the long-form piece into individual tweets (with his PPP framework), so that "you have a perpetual cycle of content"; (8) develop your own writing system; (9) branch out to other platforms when you are ready and have validated ideas. He frames this as what one can do with one to two hours of writing a day, assuming one has a product or service, or an idea for one that can be built and fueled with the audience. With belief, an abundance mindset and the understanding that the internet is infinite, he says, such a writer can earn a higher monthly income than "one of the world's highest paid doctors," because the doctor has a cap. (In the spoken recap of both versions he misnumbers the steps, saying "five" twice; the body lists nine.)

**Source:** Learn This Skill If You Want To Thrive In The Next 10 Years.md; The One-Person Business Model (How To Productize Yourself Full Guide).md

*Perpetual cycle of content* is Koe's name for the loop that steps 3, 5 and 7 create: long form generates short posts; short posts that perform are expanded into new long form (Chapter 24's ecosystem). The comparison with the doctor restates Section 30.1's distinction between time-capped and leveraged income; it is a rhetorical contrast, not a claim about actual earnings.

In January 2024 he gives a simpler version in six steps: (1) choose the topic you cannot shut up about, without overthinking it ("pick a topic and practice writing"), and, if you are already a creator, use your *topic tree* (Chapter 22); (2) brainstorm your unique perspective; (3) write 500–1,000 words on the topic per week; (4) deconstruct and simplify the ideas into daily posts; (5) learn how to get your writing shared; (6) monetize your experience: with writing, a growing audience and traffic, create a product or service (he points to his video on seven digital career paths for options).

**Source:** This High-Income Skill Will Make You Irreplaceable (Full Guide).md

The change between the versions is a simplification. The weekly volume drops from 1,000+ structured words to 500–1,000; the topic tree enters; and in the 2024 version threads on X can stand in for a newsletter at the start. Koe gives no reason for the revision, but the later version is the current one and the two are compatible.

#### Two even simpler starts

Two other passages give entry points for people who have not yet started writing at all. In August 2023 Koe says that to become a good writer one needs psychology, to structure a message that "captures, holds and spreads attention," and that psychology is best learned by studying marketing and sales, which he calls applied psychology. His path: (1) choose a topic you would be interested in making your full-time work; (2) block 30 minutes to learn about marketing, sales or your interests; (3) do not skip a day of learning, whether from videos, podcasts, books or internet content; (4) take notes on the ideas that stick out; (5) start posting your ideas on Twitter/X or Threads; (6) study social media as a skill, so that you can grow. Over three to six months of actually trying, you should gain enough followers to be confident it can become full-time. "If you can gain one follower, you can gain a million": learn to replicate the process and make it efficient (if you gained 500 followers in three months, repeat and improve). With enough readers, create a product or service to monetize; by then the marketing and sales knowledge has compounded.

**Source:** You Aren't Successful Because You Care Too Much (How To Stop).md

In March 2025 the entry is framed as learning in public. (1) "Write a newsletter once a week to summarize what you've learned and... teach what you're learning." Many people start newsletters or social accounts this way; Sahil Bloom, who has millions of followers on Twitter, had for a long time a bio along the lines of "exploring my curiosity and sharing what I learn along the way," but "your bio doesn't matter here; what matters is the content: is it interesting, are you teaching it?" (2) Replicate formats you see, for example: "I learned about this insane concept this week, it's called the Zeigarnik effect, and it's the best way to overcome procrastination; here's what you do." Give credit when needed; weaving concepts with personal experience helps you learn more. (3) Write posts on X, Threads or LinkedIn about your opinions, beliefs, personal experiences and what you are learning and building, then "tack on social media as a skill you need to learn the same way." (4) Add a 30–60 minute writing block every morning. If the blocks add up to too much, split them across days: learn on Monday, build on Tuesday, write on Wednesday, walk every day. And use AI while writing, for example by asking: "You are an expert at crafting engaging social posts; what's the best way to start a post on this topic that I'm learning?"

**Source:** How To Learn Anything 10x Faster Than Anyone With AI.md

**Complementary context:** the Zeigarnik effect, used here only as an example of a post topic, is the finding associated with the psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik that unfinished tasks tend to be remembered better than finished ones; Chapter 6 discusses Koe's use of open loops.

The writing time recommended varies across the corpus (30 minutes, 30–60 minutes, one to two hours a day, two hours, two or three days a week), but the principle does not change: a block of morning writing as the base of the business. The figures for beginners are lower than Koe's own routine, and he attributes the drop in time needed partly to growing efficiency as skill increases.

The sequence of these versions (nine steps in 2022, six in 2023 and 2024, a weekly newsletter and a short daily block in 2025) shows the roadmap becoming simpler as it is repeated, not changing direction. Every version keeps the same order: topic, perspective, writing, distribution, growth as a learned skill, and a product once the audience exists.

#### The Writer's Bootcamp: the roadmap as a program

Koe also packages the writing route as a program. In October 2024, promoting the Writer's Bootcamp (run under Cortex, beginning October 28), he says it promises to help participants master digital writing in five weeks, with everything needed to build an audience, which he calls important "as a creative worker going into the future of work," or to develop a skill that opens new career options (freelancing, marketing, writing a book). There is also a curriculum-only version for people who dislike cohorts. Within the bootcamp, "we actually use your anti-vision and your vision as your brand vision, so that's how you turn yourself into the niche."

**Source:** It's actually pretty easy to focus 12 hours a day (if you do this).md

The source gives only the program's premises, not its method. The one detail it does give links two parts of the book: the anti-vision and vision of Chapter 7 become the brand vision of Chapter 27, which is how "you are the niche" (Chapter 19) is made operational.

#### The same process, enhanced by AI

The last question the chapter must answer is whether AI changes the roadmap. Koe's answer in March 2026 is that it does not change the process, only its speed. He asks whether anything has changed since his earlier popular videos on the one-person business, given that "AI's taking over everything," with agents and new features launching daily. "You do the same thing that you would have done before, but now you use AI to enhance that process." "The core difference between starting a one-person business a few years ago and now is just AI." He lists what remains: "You will still generate traffic, you still write content, you still write emails or newsletters, you still create a product or service, you still create a customer avatar, you still formulate a compelling offer, you still build a landing page, you still write persuasive copy for that page, you still put the offer in front of people and see if they buy, and then you iterate from there."

**Source:** How To Build A $1M One-Person Business Faster With AI.md

The list is the whole roadmap compressed into one sentence, and its last clause ("then you iterate from there") is Section 30.5. What AI changes is described in the same video: "To build a business with AI, you just implement AI in the correct places so that you can do things faster, with higher quality, and with less guesswork. AI in this sense is a catalyst to avoid a lot of trial and error." "You can still build a business the old way, that's fine; it'll just take a bit longer, especially if you're not a person who is high agency or knows how to iterate or refine, or not just accept the output of AI as law."

**Source:** How To Build A $1M One-Person Business Faster With AI.md

*Catalyst* is a common word Koe uses here in a specific sense: AI shortens the trial-and-error loop without replacing it. The condition he attaches is important. The benefit goes to people with *agency* (in his redefinition, the ability to act and iterate without permission, Chapter 35) who treat the AI's output as a draft rather than a verdict.

He then addresses whether courses and coaching still make sense when AI can answer questions. "You don't really need a course or a coach anymore, although those things are still valuable, because there's specific knowledge that you probably wouldn't think to look up with AI or even do with AI, and the AI probably isn't going to give you that out of the box." "Coaching is still going to be a thing just because the default response of the AI usually isn't that good. Getting specific knowledge from the source of someone who's done something is still superior, and if it costs 25 to 100 to 200 bucks, big whoop."

**Source:** How To Build A $1M One-Person Business Faster With AI.md

The argument preserves the education product of Section 30.3 under new conditions. AI supplies generic answers; what it lacks is *specific knowledge* (Naval's term, Chapter 20), the knowledge acquired by doing something, which is what a good course or coach transmits.

#### Code democratized, and the products that follow

In June 2026 Koe describes how AI alters the media-versus-code balance of Section 30.3. "Now AI has become a thing, and the ability to code or program, another form of leverage, has become democratized." You probably will not build the next Notion, Salesforce or social platform without a development team, "but most average people can absolutely build a small-scale digital product that they can sell, accompanied by a full marketing funnel that they can have the AI build out." Not everything should be written by AI: "you have to impress your personal taste on it so that it sounds like you, and so that it actually works." Building a prototype is faster than ever: "you can do the thing that used to take a team of 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 people as one person." This was always possible with social media and information products, he notes, recalling his older formula (build an audience, write content two hours a day, create a digital product, sell it in your content), "but information products are abundant." He does not think they will die.

**Source:** If You Have Multiple Interests, Start A One-Person Business.md

*Taste* (Chapter 18) is the variable that keeps the person necessary: AI can build the funnel, but only the founder's judgment makes it sound like them and work for their audience.

In January 2026 he answers an objection to building on AI. His shared prompts, he says, could easily become micro software: create an interface and set the prompts as system instructions. Rather than a general ChatGPT, one could build a hyper-specific chat or tool that helps people learn, practice and do the thing taught in the information product. The objection: isn't building a "ChatGPT wrapper" cheating? "By that logic building anything on the internet is cheating." Typeform, a billion-dollar company, is in his description an HTML wrapper; Cursor is a GPT wrapper; any information product is wrapped by the platform it is built on. If AI is the next cloud (which he believes), every piece of software will be a wrapper. For one person, savvy with resources and using third-party tools, a wrapper is a great way to go.

**Source:** How I'd build a one-person business (if I started over in 2026).md

*Wrapper* is a common software term used with Koe's own emphasis: it describes any product built on top of a more basic technology, and the argument removes the stigma by generalizing it. His characterizations of Typeform and Cursor are simplifications for the argument.

In May 2025 he had already described the endpoint of this line of thought. He imagines (as an "endgame" for Cortex) sharing a workspace containing all of one's knowledge plus custom prompts and AI workflows, so that people not only learn what is in one's mind but can do things with it. He could create "a clone of myself" with the knowledge base and the AI workflows for how he makes YouTube videos, writes books or stays focused. No digital products do this yet, he says; the digital product world is static: a course in which you learn passively and do not actually do the thing, whereas with AI you can. "A prompt that you refine and reuse is a reflection of your understanding of the task. It is an externalized clone of a creative process that no longer needs to sit in your head or in a static SOP document."

**Source:** Harsh Truth You Don't Need To Grind 247 To Be Successful.md

*Externalized clone of a creative process* is Koe's coinage, and it extends the meaning of "productize yourself" from Section 30.1. The first productization packaged a service into a course; this one packages a process into a tool that performs part of it. Chapter 33 treats the broader idea that "systems are the new product."

#### How far one person can go

AI also raises Koe's estimate of the ceiling of a one-person business. In December 2024 he cites Sam Altman, the founder of OpenAI, saying in an interview that he has a group chat with friends "betting on who's going to be the first $1 billion one-person business," because there are already one-person businesses making $1 million and $10 million, and surely others making much more. Koe adds that this was not possible in the past; it is possible now because of technology, social media, the internet, the ability to connect with anyone and attract an audience to who you are, and digital products that take no extra effort, labor or capital to build and distribute.

**Source:** Build A One-Person Business As A Normal Person (From $0 To $10K).md

The Altman anecdote is reported secondhand and is a bet, not a prediction. It belongs to a sequence in which Koe's estimate of the ceiling rises with each technological stage: in 2023 "nobody's really pushed the boundary past five, ten million as one person"; in mid-2024 one-person businesses making "$10 million a year"; in late 2024 the billion-dollar bet; and in 2026 a reinterpretation of the pre-AI model as "a comfortable lifestyle business" after which "you would eventually have to hire a team." The reason Koe gives is that AI lets one person do more. Chapter 37 examines the limits of the one-person model from the other side, through his experience of building a team.

#### A beginner's progression into a future of AI

Koe's February 2025 progression for a beginner's first product brings the chapter's threads together under the conditions of AI. "The best progression to follow going into a future of AI" has five steps: (1) build an audience as a free, high-leverage traffic source; (2) become an authority in your interests or expertise; (3) start a *personal system digital product* that you can test fast, "that's the secret... that's what separates you"; (4) persist and iterate until you reach $100,000 or more; (5) since you then have so much data and so many results, turn that system into something like software or a physical product. Build the audience where attention is right now: social media today, "tomorrow it could be intergalactic space"; it is free, accessible, you can write and grow for free, and it is a skill. Authority comes before the product: "you aren't Marcus Aurelius. From the start, these philosophical quotes that you're posting aren't going to do anything until people care about you." Then a digital product generates cash flow, and with cash flow and an audience, building a startup or a dream business is not far off; or one can simply live as one wants and focus on one's craft.

**Source:** A Full Guide To Making Your First Profitable Product (Beginners, Take Notes).md

The progression restates the whole chapter in order. The audience and authority are stages one and two of Section 30.2; the personal system digital product is "productize yourself" (Section 30.1) in its system form; persisting and iterating to $100,000 is Section 30.5; and turning the validated system into software or a physical product is "media first, software later" (Section 30.3). The ending keeps the openness of the August 2023 path: the product is not the destination but what pays for the next vision, or for the freedom to stop expanding. The Marcus Aurelius line gives the reason authority precedes the product: borrowed wisdom has no pull until the person posting it has earned attention in their own right.

There is a tension between this progression and other passages in which Koe recommends launching immediately, before having an audience, or monetizing from zero followers (Chapter 29). The corpus supports holding both: authority is built while selling something small, a service to start and a product to scale, a first product launched quickly to learn and a later, data-driven product that is iterated. What the progression adds is the endpoint, which in the age of AI is a system that can become software.

### Exercises

1. Koe calls an unproductized client business "a new 9-to-5." Using the elements of the diagnosis in Section 30.1 (the income cap, the number of bosses, "invoice to invoice," "skill for someone else compared to art for you"), analyze a service business you know, whether yours or someone else's. Which of these features does it show, and which does it not? What would its first evolutionary move be, in the sense of the table of three moves?

2. In 2023 Koe presented freelancing for corporations as superior to a job; from 2024 to 2025 he described client work as a new 9-to-5; in 2026 he called it "a necessary step." Construct the strongest argument for each position, then explain whether you think the three can be reconciled by stage, as the chapter suggests, or whether one of them should be preferred. What evidence would change your mind?

3. Place yourself (or a creator you follow) on the three-stage roadmap of Section 30.2. Identify the lever-moving actions appropriate to that stage, the trap of that stage, and one piece of advice you have recently taken that was taught "from an advanced level" and was therefore inappropriate for your stage.

4. Koe argues that "media first, software later" is a ranking of tests by cost, not a ranking of value. Design a content ladder (in the sense of Section 30.3) for an idea you would like to turn into a software tool, a physical product or a service. What would count as "doing well" at each rung, and at which rung would you stop if the signal were weak?

5. The chapter records several tensions: digital products as "the highest form of leverage" and as a stepping stone that can enslave; persistence as the one trait of the successful and "we should have called it quits earlier"; refusing to give a business model and recommending "the best option." Choose one tension and explain under what conditions each side is true. Then identify a situation in which the distinction would fail to guide a decision.

6. Redo the $1M math of Section 30.6 for an income goal of your own (monthly, then daily). Choose two routes (for example, a product and a service), estimate the volume and the traffic each requires, and state which assumption in your calculation you are least sure of. Then explain, using Koe's idea of "your standard," which problem in your current situation the goal makes visible.

7. Koe says the quickest fix is the longest path, and also that it is "impossible to fail if you persist and iterate" with an audience and a digital product. Identify the conditions each claim depends on and describe a case in which persisting would be a mistake. How does the distinction between persisting in a direction and iterating on an implementation apply to that case?

8. Suppose AI makes it trivial to build the small software tool that an information product would once have taught. Using Section 30.7 (catalyst, taste, specific knowledge, the externalized clone of a creative process), argue either that the roadmap from service to product still holds or that it must change. Which step of the roadmap do you think AI affects most, and which least?

# Part XI — Value, Persuasion and Product

## Chapter 31 — What Value Is

Part X ended with a business that has an audience, a service and a roadmap toward products. All of it rests on a word the book has used dozens of times without examining it: *value*. Creators are told to "provide value," to "become high value," to "deliver value up front." Dan Koe noticed, in 2022, that nobody using the word could say what it meant. This chapter reconstructs the answer he built over the following years. Most of it was assembled between 2023 and 2024, and it was refined until 2026.

The answer comes in layers, and the chapter follows them. Section 31.1 gives the deepest layer: value is the reversal of entropy. Koe applies this one idea to biological and technological evolution, to the price of a product, to the slow disappearance of labor work and to spirituality. Section 31.2 adds the second layer: value only exists when someone perceives it, and perception depends on the era, on the identity of the person looking and on how aware that person is of their problem. Section 31.3 turns the first two layers into method. It covers the "value creation" framework of 2023, the "Legos" of persuasive writing and the 2024 "Value Equation," with its macronutrients and micronutrients of value. Section 31.4 gives the practical test of value: behavior change. A brand, a piece of writing and a product are valuable to the degree that they move people. Section 31.5 applies everything to the product Koe considers the natural starting point: the education product. It sets out his defense of it against the objections he heard over five years, and includes his own story as a buyer of courses.

The chapter depends on earlier ones. From Chapter 5 it needs entropy and psychic entropy, because the central definition of value is built on them. From Chapter 4 it needs the *level of mind*, because the perception of value depends on where a person's mind is. From Chapters 6 and 8 it needs the goal as a lens and the triad of goal, path and problem, which reappears here as the structure of every valuable message. From Part X it needs the one-person business and "solve your own problems and sell the solution," because this chapter explains why that formula produces something people pay for. Chapter 32 then takes the second layer (perception) and develops it as persuasion, and Chapter 33 takes the third (the frameworks) and turns it into a product.

### 31.1 Reversing Entropy: One Law Behind Evolution, Value, Work and Spirit

#### The question nobody answered: "you need to become high value"

The chapter's starting point is a confession. In October 2022 Koe opens a video with the kind of post that circulates on self-improvement social media, "hey bro you need to become high value," and admits he has written tweets like it himself. Then he asks what "high value" or "valuable" actually means, and he lists candidate answers without settling on any. Is it acquiring a certain number of marketable skills? Is it how you combine those skills? Is it the result the other person receives, and how that result shapes what you do for them? Is it how you look, so that others perceive you as high value? Is it your personality?

He then extends the question beyond skills. He asks about objects: is a Ferrari more valuable than a Kia Soul to someone who loves their Kia Soul? He asks about people: is an NFL cheerleader more valuable than the person you passed on the road without looking twice? His conclusion is blunt: "I don't think anybody knows the real answer to the question of what is value." The word makes intuitive sense. But the culture demands that people become high-value individuals with high-value skill sets and deliver value to others in order to "make it," and in that culture, Koe argues, one should understand value "to the point of being able to create it." He adds: "I haven't seen many if any people bring value to the word value."

**Source:** Why Cheap Dopamine Prevents You From Becoming High Value.md (2022-10-09)

The examples already contain, in unformed state, the answer he would give later. The Kia Soul owner shows that value depends on who is looking. The cheerleader and the stranger show that it depends on what is noticed. The list of candidates (skills, combination, result, appearance, personality) mixes what a thing *is* with how it is *perceived*. Koe's later framework separates those two dimensions and then reconnects them. In 2022, however, the question is presented as open, and the chapter records it as such. It also records the change of position: the open question of 2022 becomes, by March 2024, a closed and layered definition (developed below). Koe gives no explicit reason for the change. The most plausible reading is that the entropy framework he was building in those years supplied the answer, since the definition he eventually gives is stated in terms of entropy.

#### Value requires development over time: the pearl in the oyster

The same 2022 video contains the first firm statement Koe makes about value, and he calls it "a universal principle": "value requires development over time." His image is a pearl. A pearl forms inside an oyster that is closed off to the world, and only after some time does the oyster open and reveal it. People believe value is "so readily available," Koe says, because of the attention game. Social media shows the tips, the conclusions and the polished results, but not the time spent developing the depth that produced them.

**Source:** Why Cheap Dopamine Prevents You From Becoming High Value.md (2022-10-09)

The principle matters for the rest of the chapter in two ways. First, it explains why the attention economy distorts the perception of value. What is visible is the pearl, so viewers underestimate the closed oyster. The same distortion returns in Section 31.5, where free online content is criticized for showing the high-performing topics and hiding the boring fundamentals. Second, it sets a condition on the person who wants to create value: depth comes first. This links the chapter to the "build to learn" process of Chapter 14 and to the realistic timelines of Chapter 30. When Koe warns buyers of education products that results take "three to five years" (Section 31.5), he is applying the pearl principle to his own customers.

#### Entropy as the driving force of evolution

The answer Koe eventually gives to "what is value" starts from a law that Chapter 5 introduced: entropy. In July 2023 he states it in its simplest form. "Entropy is that everything tends towards disorder": one day you will die, the sun will die out, the universe will die. Anything tangible eventually decomposes, unless humans attempt to reverse entropy. "That's all we're really doing here," he says, "is trying to solve the problems that lead to things falling apart." We try to extend our life on Earth. Even something as small as organizing a bookshelf after it gets dirty is done, in his reading, with the larger survival goal in the back of the mind: "we need to live as long as possible, we need to become immortal, and that's what really everyone is [trying] to do."

**Source:** A Full Guide To Reinvent Your Life (In 6-12 Months).md (2023-07-25)

**Complementary context:** In physics, the second law of thermodynamics states that the total entropy of an isolated system does not decrease over time. Living beings and human artifacts maintain local order only by consuming energy and exporting disorder to their surroundings. Koe uses the law as a general metaphor and organizing principle, as Chapter 5 explained. He does not present it as a technical claim about thermodynamics, and the bookshelf example should be read in that spirit: as an interpretation of human motivation, not as a measured fact.

In February 2024 Koe draws the strongest conclusion from the law. "Entropy is the driving force of evolution": since everything tends toward death, and we are aware of that, "out of fear we are pushing towards something related to immortality or youth extension, and problem solving is the way we do that." He goes further. Disorder is not just an obstacle to purpose; it is the condition of purpose. "If things didn't tend toward disorder we would not be in the situation we are today. We wouldn't have any motivation to do anything, we wouldn't have a reason to be here, we wouldn't have a purpose."

**Source:** Disappear For 2-4 Hours A Day (The Millionaire Productivity Routine).md (2024-02-18)

This inversion is the key move of the section. Entropy usually appears in Koe's work as the enemy: the chaos of an unfocused mind, the decay of a neglected routine (Chapters 5 and 13). Here it becomes the source of meaning. A world without decay would offer no problems, and a world without problems would offer no purpose. Chapter 8 defined purpose as the most urgent problem, and this passage gives that definition its cosmic foundation. Problems exist because things fall apart, and solving them is what living beings do.

#### "Even to remain still we must advance": the unattributed quote and the tractor

Koe supports the idea with a quotation he reads aloud twice: in "The 4-Hour Workday" (January 2023) and again in a March 2024 compilation that reproduces the same passage. The transcript does not attribute it to anyone. "Evolution is forced on us by the fact that systems fall apart with time unless they become more efficient. We can't stop and remain in the same place; even to remain still we must advance." He uses the quote as "another reason why this productivity system is important." Standing still is not a neutral option. A system either becomes more efficient or decays, and that holds for a person, a routine and a business alike. It is the same corollary Chapter 5 drew from the entropy law: there is no such thing as staying the same.

He then adds an argument of his own. Humans have "a natural desire to know more, the curse of knowledge," which he describes as "an endless thirst to learn things that will aid in our survival." With unique minds and knowledge, "we build systems to solve problems that lead to better outcomes in all domains of life": society, culture and personal life. His example is agriculture. Carrying water and plowing fields took enormous physical energy, so humans "used our creativity to create a solution like a tractor and a system to use that energy more efficiently."

**Source:** The 4-Hour Workday (Focused Work Changed My Life).md (2023-01-01); Get Ahead Of 99% Of People With Deep Work & Monk Mode.md (2024-03-21)

Two clarifications are needed. The first concerns attribution. The quotation is a third party's words, and the corpus never names its author. The argument about the thirst for knowledge and the tractor is Koe's own. The second concerns terminology. Koe uses "the curse of knowledge" in an idiosyncratic sense, and the corpus does not use it consistently. In these passages it names the desire to know more, a neutral or even positive drive. Elsewhere in the same 2024 compilation it names something negative: learning without questioning what one learns, and so absorbing the conventional game. The corpus never resolves whether "curse" is meant pejoratively. A reasonable reading is that the same drive serves both ends. The thirst to learn can condition a person, and it can also equip them to build their own systems.

**Complementary context:** In cognitive psychology and economics, "the curse of knowledge" usually names a bias: once people know something, they find it hard to imagine not knowing it, which makes experts poor at explaining to beginners. Koe's usage is unrelated to that standard meaning.

#### Speculation: the next phase of evolution

In July 2023 Koe pushes the idea toward the future, and he marks it explicitly as speculation. He says he has been "down rabbit holes," and recommends a short story, "The Gentle Seduction," as something that opens the mind to the potential of the future. He is "not sure what the next phase of evolution is," but he is "pretty sure" it will be chemical enhancement, as discussed in the biohacking community, which would bridge humans toward becoming cyborgs and living forever. For now, he says, the goal seems to be prolonging health with longevity practices, to the point of reversing aging. The sentence that ties this to the chapter is: "That's all we're doing with evolution: we're trying to reverse entropy and the problems that come with entropy." He then sets the topic aside "for another time."

**Source:** Focus Is A Superpower (Take Back Control Of Your Life).md (2023-07-11)

**Complementary context:** "The Gentle Seduction" is a science-fiction short story by Marc Stiegler (1989). It follows a woman who gradually adopts transformative technologies over a lifetime. The transcript does not name the author.

The passage is an opinion about the future, adapted from fiction and from a subculture. It is not a thesis Koe develops or defends. It belongs in the chapter because it shows how far he extends the entropy principle. Longevity, biohacking and the tractor are, for him, instances of the same activity: solving the problems that decay creates.

#### The 2024 answer: value is not labor

The pieces come together in a March 2024 video titled "The Value Equation." Koe begins with what value is *not*. The labor theory of value ("I worked one year on this, you owe me $100,000") is "not how value works." Instead, "value works by me giving you something useful, but if you don't see it as useful through persuasion then it's not valuable."

**Source:** The Value Equation How To Become A High-Status Individual.md (2024-03-17)

**Complementary context:** The labor theory of value belongs to classical political economy (Adam Smith, David Ricardo) and to Karl Marx. In its classical forms it holds that the value of a commodity is determined by the labor required to produce it. Koe does not engage with that technical tradition. He uses the name for an everyday attitude: the belief that effort entitles one to payment. Chapter 34 shows the same target in his critique of the employee mindset (payment by the hour). This book reports his use of the term and does not correct his reading of the economic theory.

The definition has two parts, and they become the two layers of the rest of the chapter. Something must be *useful*, which is a matter of substance. And it must be *seen as useful*, which is a matter of perception, achieved "through persuasion." Koe names them immediately. The *macronutrients of value* are the perspective, meaning how the value is framed and constructed. The *micronutrients of value* shape how the value is perceived. Section 31.3 reconstructs both. The dietary metaphor fits the definition: macronutrients are the bulk of a meal, and micronutrients are small additions without which the meal does not nourish.

#### Value as structured communication, sense-making and a signal of meaning

Koe then states what the framework lets a person do. It lets you change your life, help others for money, write, speak and think clearly, and create content, landing pages or marketing that sells. It lets you navigate relationships in a mutual way, and understand and move past emotions. The breadth of the list follows from the definition he gives next: "Value in this case is structured communication or sense making to the mind." Value is how a mind makes sense of the world, packaged and given to someone else. It is also a framework for creating solutions to problems, and he connects it to his picture of the good life: solve one problem, then the next, contributing to evolution as you go. He calls it the foundation of human behavior, business and communication.

The passage ends with a string of equivalences: "Value is truth, value is story, value is progress, value is transformation, value is reversing entropy, value is a signal of meaning in your psyche." He presents these terms as "synonymous or heavily related."

**Source:** The Value Equation How To Become A High-Status Individual.md (2024-03-17)

The list is better read as a set of angles on one object than as a set of strict synonyms. Koe does not argue that truth and story are identical. Each term ties the definition to a part of the book. *Truth* and *sense-making* tie it to the thinking of Chapter 17. *Story* ties it to the mind as a story machine (Chapter 23). *Progress* and *transformation* tie it to behavior change (Section 31.4). *Reversing entropy* ties it to Chapter 5. *A signal of meaning in your psyche* ties it to the subjective experience Koe calls "the click," treated in Section 31.4. A reader can test a claim of value against any of these angles. Does it make sense of something? Does it move someone from one state to a better one? Does it reduce disorder in someone's mind or life?

These 2024 equivalences are not Koe's only definitions of the word. *Value* is a common word to which he gives a meaning of his own, and he defines it several times, each time from the angle of the problem at hand. In March 2023, explaining why a writer is not bound to a topic, he says that content is "limited to value," and that "value is ideas written from the lens of a specific goal or problem," whatever the topic; Chapter 22 builds the method of choosing what to write on that definition. In December 2023 he says that "value equals positive behavior change," the test this chapter develops in Section 31.4. And in March 2024, a week before the video quoted above, he gives a relational definition: "Everyone tells you to become valuable but nobody tells you what value is. Value is the relationship between what you do, why you do it, how you do it and who benefits from that equation." Chapter 34 takes up that definition and its four parts, because it describes the exchange that ends in money. The definitions do not compete. The 2023 one tells a writer what to do with an idea, the behavior-change one tells a seller how to judge a product, the relational one places value between a person and the people who benefit, and the 2024 equivalences name what all of them share: something that makes sense of the world for another mind.

**Source:** The Best Online Business To Make $1 Million In 3-5 Years.md (2023-03-19); How Intelligent Creators Will Make Money In 2024 (The Build Teach Earn Method).md (2023-12-03); If Your Life Is Spiraling Out Of Control, Here's The Solution To Feeling Lost.md (2024-03-10)

#### The value equation: reversing entropy by creating systems

The video closes with the formula that gives it its title: "Value is reversing entropy. Entropy is the decline into chaos. Entropy is reversed by creating systems to achieve goals by solving problems. That's the value equation."

**Source:** The Value Equation How To Become A High-Status Individual.md (2024-03-17)

The formula is a chain with four links: chaos is reversed through *systems*, which serve *goals*, which are reached by solving *problems*. Each link connects to earlier chapters. Systems connect to Chapter 12 (systematizing) and to the tractor example above. Goals connect to Chapters 6 and 8, where the goal is a lens that turns information into relevance. Problems connect to Chapter 8's definition of purpose. The formula therefore unifies the personal system of the book (anti-vision, vision, goals, projects, focused work) with the economic system (offers, products, marketing). Reversing entropy in one's own life and creating value for others are the same operation, applied to different targets.

Koe attaches a lifestyle to the formula, which he calls the *lifestyle of the 1%*. All high-level individuals, he says, reverse entropy daily. They pursue goals, solve problems, hypothesize, test, and create solutions to distribute. This demands constant learning, building and distributing value, and he calls it "literally the one thing that will set you apart." The "1%" here is a rhetorical marker of rarity, not a measured statistic.

**Complementary context:** Alex Hormozi, an entrepreneur and author whom Koe mentions as a reference on education products (Section 31.5), popularized a different "value equation" in *$100M Offers* (2021): perceived value rises with the dream outcome and the perceived likelihood of achievement, and falls with time delay and effort. The corpus does not connect Koe's formula to Hormozi's. The two share a name and an interest in perceived value, but Koe's equation is a definition in terms of entropy, systems, goals and problems, not a ratio. Some of Hormozi's factors resemble Koe's micronutrients (proof raises perceived likelihood; risk reversal lowers perceived effort), but the corpus does not draw that parallel.

#### Evolution phases out labor work

The entropy definition has a consequence that Koe develops at length, and it explains part of his view of work and AI. If evolution means solving the problems that cause decay, and repetitive labor is one of the problems people hate most, then evolution will keep eliminating labor. The idea appears first in June 2022, in a plainer form: "Humans are lazy; they tend to phase out what they don't like doing." This is why, Koe argues, the people who make the most money or see the most success are creative people, not people in manual low-skill labor. He says the pattern shows across human evolution. When people got tired of plowing fields by hand, a creative person innovated and made a tractor, "expanding their mind until the imaginary idea of a tractor became an actual tractor," pulling together all available resources. Over time, things keep getting phased out.

**Source:** How To Make Money As A Creative On The Internet.md (2022-06-25)

The tractor appears in both lines of argument, the 2023 productivity argument and the 2022 labor argument, and it does the same work in each. It is the model of a system that reverses entropy by spending less energy for the same result, and the model of a creative act that makes a whole class of labor unnecessary.

In the same video Koe gives a present-day example. He saw a tweet complaining about automated touch-screen ordering at McDonald's and other fast-food chains, which phase out cashiers because they save the company money. Many people see this as bad. But people who believe in themselves, or know they have higher potential and can learn new skills through self-education ("the endless ocean of resources online"), spending a few hours a day, are not worried, or are worried only a little at first. The lesson he draws: "consistently improve yourself and acquire high value skills and become a student of life." Doing so opens room for creativity in yourself, and your creative solutions open more opportunity and creativity for others. The creator economy is his example.

He then cites a source and adopts it. He has been studying Naval Ravikant and finds his philosophy "very aligned with mine." Naval's tweet reads: "If the work doesn't require creativity, delegate it, automate it, or leave it." Koe's interpretation: take personal responsibility for your future and increase your skill set, so that you are not phased out by "human nature's continuous creation of a better future."

**Source:** How To Make Money As A Creative On The Internet.md (2022-06-25)

**Complementary context:** Naval Ravikant is an entrepreneur and investor (co-founder of AngelList) whose aphorisms on wealth, leverage and specific knowledge, collected in a 2018 tweetstorm titled "How to Get Rich (without getting lucky)," are among the most adapted sources in Koe's corpus (see Chapters 20, 25 and 34).

#### "A gradual erosion of human labor"

In April 2023 Koe gives the idea a name borrowed from a third party. He reads a tweet from Zero HP Lovecraft, an account he finds interesting but does not follow. The tweet says that the real AI singularity, if it happens, will not look like a science-fiction doomsday. The real, and probably inevitable, form is "a gradual erosion of human labor."

**Source:** Self Improvers Are Creating Their Own Careers (The New Economy).md (2023-04-16)

**Complementary context:** Zero HP Lovecraft is the pseudonym of an online writer of speculative fiction and commentary, known mainly on Twitter/X. The phrase is his. The use Koe makes of it, as a description of the evolutionary process he has been describing, is Koe's.

In the same video Koe states his own position, and in 2023 it is enthusiastic: he "only see[s] good" in automation and AI. "A decline in labor work means an incline in creative and knowledge work for people that choose to continue working." He considers universal basic income (UBI) and is skeptical of the assumption behind it, that people with free time will naturally self-actualize: "either they'll have more time to self-actualize or they'll have more time to destroy their lives." People who want control can use the moment. Between the two futures he prefers "the AI route" to UBI, "because it forces people to get creative if they want to survive; it forces people to be human."

**Source:** Self Improvers Are Creating Their Own Careers (The New Economy).md (2023-04-16)

The phrase "it forces people to be human" assumes a definition of the human that the passages that follow make explicit: to be human is to create. The preference for pressure over provision mirrors Koe's ideas about tactical stress (Chapter 10) and about money or pain on the line (Section 31.4). In each case, a constraint is what produces action.

#### Bet on the mind: evolution as problem-solving

In February 2024 Koe restates the argument directly in terms of entropy. "Evolution is the process of solving problems that reverse entropy. Labor work and long work days are a massive problem; people hate it, so social media, the internet and artificial intelligence were born." AI, he says, "will solve the problem of overwork potentially in this lifetime, especially if we solve the problem of aging." His practical conclusion: "You are better off banking on the creative ability of your mind than you are going into a labor work job." He makes an explicit exception: "If you want quick cash then yes, that is actually a very good option right now." For the future, though, and "to earn unlimited because your intelligence is scalable infinitely," he advises choosing work that allows a four-hour workday (Chapter 12) and contributing "your time, energy and focus into the aspects of reality that you want to see flourish."

**Source:** Disappear For 2-4 Hours A Day (The Millionaire Productivity Routine).md (2024-02-18)

A week later he answers an objection he expects. Society needs construction workers, plumbers and labor workers. Koe agrees, but suggests that "maybe in our lifetime those jobs won't exist." He then asks two questions and answers them separately. Should everyone bank on creative work for meaning and income? No. Should smart people? Yes. With robotics, and factories like Tesla's being over 75% automated (his figure, given without a source), he does not see why robots cannot solve labor. Personal robots doing laundry and cleaning seem to him not far off, which would leave people free to focus on creative work and self-actualization. Will everyone pursue that? No: "some people are going to end up like Wall-E," mainlining Coca-Cola in a floating lounge chair with dopamine channels. His advice is to stop worrying about it. Wise people who flow with nature cannot succumb to that life, because "once you've had that taste of self-actualization and flow and meaningful living, there's no going back." He calls that the awakened point.

He states the principle behind the whole argument in one line: "Success is reserved for the creative; your psyche craves creativity." Creating feels good. By all measures, creating something of your own "lights your brain on fire," and "that is enough of a sign that humans are meant to do this."

**Source:** Zero To $1 Million As A One-Person Business (Working 2-4 Hours A Day).md (2024-02-25)

**Complementary context:** *WALL-E* (Pixar, 2008) depicts a future in which humans live on a spaceship in hover-chairs, consuming screens and drinks while robots do all the work. Koe uses the image as shorthand for automation without self-actualization.

Several distinctions keep this argument from being read as a universal prescription. First, Koe separates the advice by person and horizon: quick cash favors labor now, and the long run favors creative work for those able to pursue it. Second, the claim that "humans are meant to do this" rests on felt experience ("lights your brain on fire"), which is an interpretation rather than evidence. Third, the "Wall-E" outcome is admitted as real for some people. The argument does not promise that automation liberates everyone. It claims that automation rewards those who choose creative work.

#### If a machine can replace your job

By May 2025 the same argument has a sharper edge. Koe addresses the comfortable majority who complain about AI taking jobs: "what's the issue? Why are you complaining?" Average 9-to-5 jobs, he says, suck. He does not mean the 0.1% with nap pods at Google. "We've collectively hated jobs for decades." "Evolution solves problems": one of life's most painful problems, working a job, is being solved, and people are angry about it. In his reading, they are presented with one of the greatest opportunities of a lifetime and fall into "the most cliché trap of comfort and playing victim." They hold on to an old way of life "when all good things aren't permanent." Then he states the diagnostic: "If you work a job that a machine can replace, your life probably lacks novelty and meaning and fulfillment and challenge and complexity and continuous growth and learning." That, he says, is a massive signal to do something new.

**Source:** The Future Of Work (How To Become AI-First).md (2025-05-25)

Koe asserts that this is not opinion but "documented psychological patterns." The transcript cites no study, and the claim should be treated as his interpretation. It is consistent with the flow research he draws on elsewhere (Chapter 10), where novelty, challenge and growth are conditions of optimal experience, but it is not demonstrated in the passage.

In February 2026 the tone changes, and the change should be recorded. Koe distinguishes two types of work. *Mundane busy work* is repetitive and mechanical, like an industrial assembly line, and he does not mind it going away. He says so "in the kindest way possible," which acknowledges that livelihoods are at stake. *Creative work* is "the ability to see reality from your own lens, pull it into your mind, synthesize things together, create something, share it with another person, and then get feedback for your contribution in the form of money" or another form of value. "That's where humans find meaning."

**Source:** The Future Of Work (& The New High-Income Skill Stack).md (2026-02-12)

The 2026 definition of creative work is a compact version of the value chain this chapter builds. It moves from perception (seeing reality through one's own lens), through synthesis (making sense), creation (packaging) and sharing (distribution), to feedback in money (value exchange). It also shows the evolution of Koe's position on automation and employment, which the corpus records across several videos:

| Period | Position on labor and AI | Tone |
|---|---|---|
| 2022–2023 | Humans phase out what they dislike; "I only see good"; labor is "on the horizon of complete removal" | Enthusiastic |
| Early 2024 | "Maybe in our lifetime those jobs won't exist"; smart people should bank on creative work; quick cash still favors labor | Confident, with exceptions |
| 2024 | "Computers will only replace those who deserve to be replaced" (a line recorded elsewhere in the corpus) | Harsh |
| 2025 | A job a machine can replace signals a life lacking meaning; complaint is "playing victim" | Provocative |
| 2025–2026 | AI's impact "probably not going to be as drastic as many people made it out to seem, myself included"; busy work goes away "in the kindest way possible"; livelihoods acknowledged | Moderated, self-correcting |

Two changes are visible. Koe corrects his own estimate of how drastic the change will be. And he moves from blaming the person who gets replaced toward a broader framing, in which AI threatens meaning as well as jobs, with more care for people whose circumstances give them less control. He gives no explicit reason for either change.

A third change runs underneath the table and should not be smoothed over: what happens to employment itself. In April 2023 labor is "on the horizon of complete removal," and in February 2024 "maybe in our lifetime those jobs won't exist." But in June 2024, answering an objection about megacorporations, Koe says: "I don't see employment going away." Work, he now argues, is decentralizing: corporations turn executives and employees into creators, large creators hire other creators as contractors, and work becomes "more remote, more contract based." In February 2025 the picture changes again: "the jobs of the future will be reserved for the elite, the top 1%, the NBA of jobs. The entry level is going extinct because replaceable work is replaceable." For ambitious people with multiple interests, he concludes, the only path left is to become an entrepreneur. Read in sequence, these passages amount to an implicit correction. The early prediction was that employment would disappear; the later one is that it will be transformed and reserved for an elite, with the entry level vanishing first. The reason he gives for the later view is that AI and automation turn entry-level work into senior work; for the June 2024 shift he gives no reason beyond answering the objection. The two views partly describe different horizons, a long-term one for labor as such and a short-term one for corporate jobs. Chapter 36 follows this evolution in detail.

**Source:** Ideas Are The New Oil (How More People Get Rich In The Digital Age).md (2024-06-09); How To Thrive With Multiple Interests.md (2025-02-23)

What holds across all these versions is narrower than "employment disappears": evolution keeps solving the problem of repetitive labor, and creative work is where meaning and value remain.

#### "If you are not a builder, you are going to be built over"

Koe's shortest formulation of the consequence comes from October 2022, in the video that introduced his idea of the *value creator*. Humans think and build. We build tools and solutions that make life easier, and "this is never going to stop." So "if you are not a builder then you are going to be built over, or you are going to build for someone else." He says this introduction "lays the framework" for everything that follows.

**Source:** The Rise Of The Value Creator (A Career Path For Polymaths & Self-Improvers).md (2022-10-31)

The sentence turns the entropy argument into a personal choice with three options. You can build, which means reversing entropy through your own systems. You can be built over, which means having your work absorbed by someone else's system, the way the tractor absorbed manual plowing. Or you can build for someone else, contributing your energy to systems you do not own, which is Koe's description of employment (Chapter 2). *Builder* is a common word that Koe uses in a specific sense: a person who always has a project aligned with what they are learning (Chapter 14), and who therefore produces systems rather than only consuming them. Chapter 35 develops the value creator as a role.

#### Spirituality as your part in the whole

The last application of the entropy law is the most surprising one, and Koe develops it in several videos between 2023 and 2024: spirituality. The context is his argument against people who reject money and business on spiritual grounds.

In November 2023 he starts from their own premise. "If the entire goal of spirituality is connection to something larger than yourself, and money in the material world is a way to connect with society as a whole and distribute goods and information that benefits them," then rejecting money contradicts spirituality. Many spiritual people, he says, think that buying a product or service cannot help a specific person. When you peel the belief back, "you know that that's wrong, but the unconscious assumption is just that everything related to money is evil, when everything near you, you watching this right now, is only possible because of money."

From there he goes further. "You are unconsciously allowing the entire universe to tilt in the hands of evil by not becoming a conscious business owner that impacts his customers, employees, readers, economy and the rest to infinity." And then he gives his definition: "Spirituality is understanding your part in the whole of the universe. Spirituality is not disconnecting from that whole to live in the woods and letting the universe decline into chaos thanks to entropy. Spirituality then can be considered and felt when you attempt to reverse entropy by putting effort and energy into the progress and evolution of humanity."
