"Code is the vessel for content": code is structure (a landing page, an email, a video), while content is what people actually see, what catches attention, persuades and changes behavior. You cannot post and expect it to do well; you need mechanics and psychology. "Marketing and sales are applied mechanics and psychology."
- **Personal interests** (which he calls "the fourth piece"). They set you apart and determine what you sell; they can come from mind, body, spirit or business. "Your job is to use your skills to monetize the interests that make you unique." If you cannot monetize an interest, you have not learned or practiced the skills well enough.

The downside, he admits, is that you have to learn everything that goes into a profitable business. He refers to the million-dollar skill stack video for details.

**Source:** The Future Of Work Is Play (How To Create A Digital Career).md (2023-12-31)

The "fourth piece" wording suggests that Koe counts four components (the meta skills themselves, results-oriented skills, evergreen skills and personal interests), but the graphic he refers to is not recoverable from the transcript, so the exact structure is uncertain. The essential relation is clear: **code is the vessel for content**. Technology provides the container; psychology-based communication provides what fills it; personal interests decide what it is about. The claim that failure to monetize an interest indicates insufficient skill places the burden on the stack, not on the interest, which is the "you are the niche" thesis in its strongest form.

**Complementary context:** elsewhere in the corpus, from the same period, Koe credits the investor and writer Balaji Srinivasan with the argument that learning both code and content "is not optional." Naval Ravikant's description of code and media as forms of leverage that require no one's permission (Chapter 25.3) is the broader background of the code-and-content pair.

In January 2024, in the official summary of his book *The Art of Focus*, Koe reads a passage that states the relation between the evergreen and the changing layers most precisely: "Results-oriented skills are how you apply your message and medium of choice; they are the vessel for distributing your value. The message and the medium are evergreen, while results-oriented skills change with the landscape; you must keep your finger on the pulse of advancements and your interest so that you don't fade out." Today they are digital, he adds: we do not live at the moment when the printing press was just invented and profitable skills revolved around it. His examples are email marketing, graphic design, videography, photography, editing, animation, artificial intelligence and social media. They are useful for your own business and for others', since all brands, creators and students have problems to solve, and stacking them with evergreen skills lets you practice on your own business or create a product or service to grow someone else's.

**Source:** The Art Of Focus – Official Book Summary By The Author Dan Koe.md (2024-01-18)

The printing-press analogy is the key to the distinction. Every era has its results-oriented skills (typesetting once, video editing now), and they are valuable only while the technology lasts. The message and the medium (communicating with humans through writing and speech) persisted across all those eras. A person who invests only in the changing layer must reinvest each time the landscape shifts; a person who invests in the persistent layer carries it into each new technology.

#### Persistent principles applied to a changing landscape (2024)

In July 2024 Koe formulates the same distinction as a general principle: "I'm a fan of basing your success on persistent principles applied to the modern landscape, which will continue to change. Writing, speaking, persuasion, entrepreneurship, creativity: these are things that have been around since the first two humans came into contact with each other, and that means you should bank on them for your success, but apply them to the technology that continues to change. That's how you stay on top: you apply the deep generalized principles of reality and move forward with things like graphic design or email; you learn the skills that come up, and then eventually AI, or just technology in general, helps you do those things faster."

**Source:** Learn This Skill If You Want To Be Relevant In 10 Years.md (2024-07-13)

The coined phrase **persistent principles** generalizes the evergreen skills. The list now includes entrepreneurship and creativity alongside the communicative skills, and the criterion of selection is explicit: what has existed "since the first two humans came into contact" will continue to exist, whatever the technology. The sentence also contains the first explicit placement of AI in the stack: it is a technology that helps you do the changing tasks faster, not a replacement for the persistent principles. The same video, as Section 35.1 showed, defines agency as the difference between employee and entrepreneur; the persistent principles are what the agentic person banks on.

#### The future-proof skill stack (March–May 2024)

The 2024 version of the stack was prompted by a post by Devon Eriksen, nine months before the conversation that Section 35.1 reconstructed. In March 2024, in "The Future-Proof Skill Stack (How Average People Become Millionaires)," Koe says that Eriksen's post stood out because he had already learned these skills "in a unique way," within his own worldview of starting a creator-based business, "because you are naturally a creator," meaning a creator of value distributed as a content creator, viable as a one-person business with technology. He maps the stack as three pairs:

| Pair | What it covers | Koe's justification |
|---|---|---|
| Marketing and sales | Rhetoric, psychology | "If you don't know how to attract and persuade, you will never get what you want, and your only option will be for an employer or the government to give it to you." |
| Writing and thinking | Logic, research | The ability to communicate the value in your unique mind; the foundation of getting in front of others |
| Entrepreneurship | Statistics, agency, investment | Taking your future into your own hands, "hunting for my survival," building products you want to see that others care about |

**Source:** The Future-Proof Skill Stack (How Average People Become Millionaires).md (2024-03-24)

The stack is adapted, not invented: its skeleton comes from Eriksen's post, and Koe reinterprets it through his creator model. The justification of marketing and sales is an agency argument: without the ability to attract and persuade, you depend on an employer or the state, which is the dependence that Section 35.2 identified as the enemy of sovereignty. Agency appears inside the stack, under entrepreneurship, as one of the competences it covers; two years later, it will move to the top of the hierarchy.

Koe then explains how the three pairs interlock. With entrepreneurship as your vessel, "you set the scene for true education and sovereignty." With writing and thinking, you continuously create, test and iterate on your value: "social media, as an example, is a testing ground for ideas." Both require practical psychology (marketing and sales) to understand readers' and customers' minds, so that your creations are actually valuable. "You then persuade, not force or deceive, to inspire people to care about the value you have to offer." These skills, he adds, are the foundation of Cortex University, "my school for becoming a synthesizer in 60 days."

**Source:** The Future-Proof Skill Stack (How Average People Become Millionaires).md (2024-03-24)

The interlock gives each pair a role in a single process: entrepreneurship sets the stage (the context in which one can educate oneself and be sovereign), writing produces and tests the value (with social media as a laboratory, as in Chapter 24.5's "a tweet is the new MVP"), psychology calibrates it to real minds, and persuasion delivers it. The parenthesis "not force or deceive" fixes the ethical boundary that the mutual-fund metaphor left implicit.

In the same video Koe adds the changing layer, which he now calls **technical know-how**: social media, building a name as "your storefront for the value you create, the command center for your business"; content, writing or video to educate, entertain and inspire people to see your value; email marketing, newsletters or sequences to nurture the audience; visual design, to illustrate the vibe of your brand and spark emotion; and funnel building, landing pages and websites fueled by content and email. Technical know-how is "how you apply the future-proof skill stack," and "these can change and will change with time." He cites Sam Altman: coding will still be around but may take a completely different shape, perhaps not the same language, perhaps written freely, but "the ability to think through problems is still going to persist." The conclusion is to balance creative work and specific work: specific domain knowledge to understand the inner workings, plus creativity to adapt and change course.

**Source:** The Future-Proof Skill Stack (How Average People Become Millionaires).md (2024-03-24)

A week later, in "Working Hard Won't Make You Rich (Do This Instead)," the video that also presented the seven traits of the Irreplaceable individual (Section 35.2), Koe connects the two. He lists the future-proof stack as five items ("writing, thinking, marketing, sales and entrepreneurship") and says that this video focuses instead on "the internal traits that you need to cultivate rather than the external skills that you need to acquire." The skills are "the result and balance of those traits"; the two "go hand in hand." If you do not have the traits, "you're not going to be able to deploy those skills or even learn them in the first place or stick with the process."

**Source:** Working Hard Won't Make You Rich (Do This Instead).md (2024-03-31)

This sentence is the hinge of the whole section. It states, in March 2024, the principle that the 2026 hierarchy will make structural: traits come before skills. Agency, self-reliance and self-education are not additional skills in the stack but the conditions for acquiring and using any skill.

In the same video Koe diagnoses the anxiety about skills: "There is a path to get what you want; you just lack the knowledge, skill and awareness to forge that path; you just lack creativity." You worry about which skills will be relevant twenty years from now "because you are dependent on everyone else but yourself for your success." Successful people "aren't worried, because they understand what makes a person successful."

**Source:** Working Hard Won't Make You Rich (Do This Instead).md (2024-03-31)

Here "creativity" is used in a specific sense, equivalent to the knowledge, skill and awareness to forge one's own path. The diagnosis anticipates, by almost two years, the "opportunity paralysis" of Section 35.3: the anxiety about choosing the right skill is a symptom of dependence. A person who expects someone else to employ their skill must guess which skill others will want; a person who will use their skills toward their own vision chooses by the vision.

Two months later, in May 2024, Koe restated both points in "How Smart Creatives Work Less & Earn More LEVERAGE": "You're worried about what career skills to learn that will be relevant in 20 years because you are focused on the viability of the skill, not the vision." To secure your future you need "a foundational skill stack," and he repeats the three pairs with their justifications (marketing and sales as attraction and persuasion; writing and thinking as "the ability to communicate the value in your unique mind" and "the foundation of getting in front of other people"; entrepreneurship as "the process of taking your future into your own hands, hunting for your survival, and building products that you want to see in the world that others care about"). And he adds the pairing that completes it: "When you pair this foundational skill stack with the interests and skills that you have to learn as you are creating your vision, you become unstoppable."

**Source:** How Smart Creatives Work Less & Earn More LEVERAGE.md (2024-05-26)

The phrase **the viability of the skill, not the vision** compresses the argument. Choosing skills by their market viability makes you dependent on the market's forecast; choosing them by your vision makes the forecast less important, because the vision determines which skills are needed and can be revised as you learn. The stack is foundational (it serves any vision); the interests and specific skills are added as the vision demands.

The five-item list and the three-pair grouping are the same content arranged differently, a small inconsistency of presentation rather than of substance.

#### The five steps to take control of your future

The body of the March 31, 2024 video turns the stack into a sequence of five steps, each building on the previous one. Koe repeats the accumulating chain as he goes ("after learning to sell and learning to write and becoming an entrepreneur and building distribution is number five"):

1. **Become an entrepreneur**: the only path to full control of time and income.
2. **Build distribution**: become a one-person media company.
3. **Learn to write**: the greatest skill of the irreplaceable individual and the foundation of media.
4. **Learn to sell**: sales equals survival.
5. **Learn to build**: the technical know-how to create what you want.

**Source:** Working Hard Won't Make You Rich (Do This Instead).md (2024-03-31)

The sequence adds an element absent from the three pairs: **learn to build**, the technical capacity to create one's own products, which is introduced with the "learn to sell, learn to build" quotation discussed in Section 35.2. It also orders the stack. Entrepreneurship comes first, as a decision about one's position, before any skill is learned; distribution comes before writing, which is surprising until one notices that "build distribution" names the goal (a media company of one) that writing then serves.

#### The micro skill stack and the medium and message (2024–2025)

For beginners, Koe compresses the stack further. In a September 2024 guide, "The Fastest Way To Build A One-Person Business (Beginner Guide)," he says that to start making income you need two things: a traffic source and a product or service to sell. "The two skills that simplify that process are writing and sales, and if you combine the two together you get persuasion," building on his earlier video "Master persuasion with four frameworks," where "everything's persuasion." Writing is accessible: you need no design or video experience; "you don't even need to write well, you just need to write with impact." "All social media content starts with writing, yes, even video scripts": if you write persuasively, you will speak and make videos persuasively, and you can put writing into designs for Instagram. "Ask anyone that you respect in the social media space and they will say that they write every single day. I don't care if you're not a writer, you are now if you're building a business."

**Source:** The Fastest Way To Build A One-Person Business (Beginner Guide).md (2024-09-15)

The **micro skill stack** maps two skills onto the two components of the minimal business of Chapter 28.5 (audience plus product): writing generates traffic, sales converts it, and their combination is persuasion. It is the smallest version of the stack that still produces income, and it explains why Part VIII treats writing as the base skill.

In February 2025, in "How To Thrive With Multiple Interests," Koe reorganizes the communicative skills around the old pair of "medium" and "message." To attract people to your interests and creative work, "you need a medium and a message." "Writing and speaking are the medium": you write posts, threads, newsletters, products, ads, emails and articles, or speak to a camera. "Psychology, marketing, sales and persuasion help form your message": you need "to write or speak in a way that captures attention, articulates value and builds trust." He refers to his "futureproof skill stack" and "$1 million skill stack" videos, and to the Writer's Bootcamp, a quarterly cohort he ran for Cortex on turning one idea into seven days of content.

**Source:** How To Thrive With Multiple Interests.md (2025-02-23)

The 2025 framework is a clarification of the 2023 one. In January 2023 "message" and "medium" were two of three evergreen skills; in February 2025 the four communicative skills are sorted into them, with writing and speaking as the medium and the psychology-based skills as the message. The three verbs of the message ("captures attention, articulates value and builds trust") summarize Chapters 23, 31 and 27 respectively.

#### The post-AI skill hierarchy (2026)

By 2025 the premise of the earlier stacks had begun to change. In the February 2025 video Koe states: "Intelligence is no longer a differentiating resource. AI models continue to get better and better while the price of those models gets closer and closer to zero. Everyone has all the answers they could ever need, and yet 99% of people don't realize or utilize it, because intelligence has proven to be a poor resource in isolation. There's more to the story of success."

**Source:** How To Thrive With Multiple Interests.md (2025-02-23)

The argument reproduces, at the level of the economy, Eriksen's argument at the level of the individual. Eriksen said that among people, intelligence is necessary but not sufficient; Koe says that now that machines supply intelligence at almost no cost, intelligence has become abundant and therefore cannot differentiate anyone. The phrase **a poor resource in isolation** is the key: intelligence still matters, but only combined with what AI does not supply. The "99%" figure is rhetorical, not measured. The statement belongs to a sequence in Koe's thinking about what is scarce: information in 2022, ideas and attention in 2023–2024, then taste and finally meaning in 2025–2026, each becoming the new "currency" as the previous one is cheapened (Chapter 36.6 develops the meaning economy).

In August 2025 Koe named the next layer. Against the objection that AI will generate "slop" and turn the internet into a wasteland ("the dead internet is accelerating," he says, referring to his own video on the topic), he answers: "The internet's been dead for a while now, AI or not, and there's still very much a living internet." To be on the living side, "taste is the new intelligence."

**Source:** You Have About 36 Months To Make It.md (2025-08-17)

**Complementary context:** the "dead internet theory" is an online idea, circulating since around 2021, that much of the internet's content and activity is produced by bots and automated systems rather than by people. Koe accepts the observation but rejects the pessimistic conclusion.

**Taste is the new intelligence** means that when anyone can generate content, the scarce capacity is judging which content deserves to exist: choosing, curating and refining. Chapter 18.5 develops taste in full; here it matters as the second level of the hierarchy below.

The same August 2025 video contains an intermediate stack that marks the first step away from market skills. Whether or not one uses the three layers of power transfer that Section 36.1 describes, Koe says, everyone now has three **superpowers** with which to take control of the future. **Learning** is "the ability to adapt and figure out what actions to take to get specific results." **Persuasion** is the ability to build trust and attract people to a mutually beneficial vision or narrative: "We're talking about persuasion and mutual benefit, not manipulation." **Execution** is the ability to turn ideas into reality through automation, creation and delegation.

**Source:** You Have About 36 Months To Make It.md (2025-08-17)

The three superpowers sit halfway between the earlier stacks and the 2026 hierarchy. Persuasion survives from the micro skill stack and the medium-and-message framework, now defined by its effect (trust, a shared vision) rather than by its channels. Learning restates the self-education that runs through the book (Chapter 14). Execution absorbs what earlier stacks called results-oriented skills and technical know-how, but defines it by function (automation, creation, delegation) rather than by any particular tool, which is the move that allows AI to enter the stack as one means among others. None of the three is a career skill, and none is tied to a specific technology: the criterion that the 2026 hierarchy will make explicit is already at work.

A third element of the 2026 synthesis comes again from Eriksen. In the December 2024 conversation he coined a term: "our research into artificial intelligence has actually discovered **natural stupidity**," because it revealed that "a lot of people are only functioning on the level of ChatGPT," "either because they're dumb or because that's how we've educated them." "We have created an education system that makes human beings into single-purpose tools, and then we feel threatened when we can build computer single-purpose tools." But humans "did not evolve to be single-purpose tools; we evolved to be navigators of an ever-changing environment." The remedy, he says, is to recapture that ability: "stop looking to our society and to our so-called leaders for what we're going to do next," take responsibility for our own lives, and ask what I need to learn, what I need to do, what my goals are and what is important to me. Then AI will not feel so threatening, because AI cannot do any of that.

**Source:** The Most Important Skill To Learn In The Next 10 Years With Devon Eriksen.md (2024-12-08)

"Natural stupidity" inverts "artificial intelligence" to make a point about education rather than about machines. The threat that people feel from AI, on Eriksen's account, measures how far schooling has reduced them to the kind of task a machine can perform. The questions he lists (what to learn, what to do, what my goals are, what matters to me) are the questions of agency, and they are precisely what a single-purpose tool cannot ask. **Navigators of an ever-changing environment** is the positive term: the human is defined not by a function but by the capacity to steer in changing conditions, the cybernetic definition of intelligence in Chapter 6.4.

In August 2026, in a video on strategic thinking, Koe opens a principle with a quotation attributed in the transcript to "Devin Erickson," almost certainly the same Eriksen: "Worry less about which career skills AI will take over and more about whether you are training to be, and training your kids to be, high-agency, perceptive, self-motivated people who can navigate an unknowable future with an adaptable mind."

**Source:** The Art of Strategic Thinking (How to Become Wildly Successful at Anything You Do).md (2026-08-19)

The quotation turns the question of the uncertainty clip in Section 35.3 ("nobody has any idea what to teach young people") into an answer. If the future is unknowable, train the traits that navigate unknowable futures. The list (high agency, perception, self-motivation, adaptability) is a list of traits, not of skills.

#### Agency at the top: the five levels of the post-AI hierarchy

With these premises in place, Koe presented in February 2026 a new stack that he explicitly describes as a different kind of object. In "The Future Of Work (& The New High-Income Skill Stack)," he says that he previously listed marketing, sales, writing and speaking, and now abstracts higher: "this is more of a skill hierarchy than it is just a list of skills." These are not career-specific skills, because "you aren't going into a specific career"; they are human skills, "uncovering what your nature is and how to lean more into it." The order is deliberate: the skills are "umbrelled under one another, and one comes before the other."

**Source:** The Future Of Work (& The New High-Income Skill Stack).md (2026-02-12)

| Level | Skill | Role in the hierarchy | Where developed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Agency | The meta-skill: "the ability to act without permission or prompting"; allows all the others to develop | Section 35.1 |
| 2 | Taste | The skill of discernment: "curation matters more than creation"; developed by building and putting things out | Chapter 18.5 |
| 3 | Perspective | "Expanding your human capacity": perspective development, synonymous with ego development; one becomes less conformist, less ideological, less dogmatic | Chapters 3.3, 18.3, 27.5 |
| 4 | Persuasion | "The ability to make people care about what you do"; learned through marketing, sales, copywriting and building on social media | Chapter 32 |
| 5 | Technical know-how | "The vessel for how you're doing what you're doing"; currently mostly AI tools | Chapter 36.5 |

The video details each level in successive passages, and the table quotes Koe's own definitions. Two of them need comment. **Taste** is justified with two thought experiments that Koe uses without attribution: a library containing every possible permutation of words would be worthless, with "no opinion worth looking at," and infinite monkeys typing for a billion years would eventually produce Shakespeare without knowing what they wrote. The lesson is that selecting what matters and sharing it with another person is worth more than generating text. **Perspective** is the level most easily misread. Koe does not mean a point of view in the ordinary sense. He means "expanding your human capacity," and he explicitly equates it with the levels of ego development discussed earlier in the same video ("synonymous with perspective development"), without naming the source of those levels. As perspective develops, a person becomes less conformist, less ideological, less dogmatic and less stuck in a bubble, able to hold complexity and contradiction, see systems and understand nuance. That, he says, is what allows "genuine agency and sophisticated curation": a narrow mind contains only narrow opportunities and ideas, and "you can't create something unique if you're extremely dogmatic."

**Source:** The Future Of Work (& The New High-Income Skill Stack).md (2026-02-12)

The definition of perspective closes a circle that this chapter opened. Section 35.1 began with conformity, "a stage of development where your mind operates entirely through cultural programming," as the opposite of agency. The 2026 hierarchy places, two levels below agency, a capacity defined as development beyond that conformist stage, and it presents that development as a condition of "genuine agency." Agency at the top and perspective in the middle are therefore not independent items: the first is the disposition to act without permission, the second the widening of mind that keeps the action from being a copy of someone else's. Chapter 38 develops the stages of ego development to which the term refers.

On the fifth level, Koe says that technical know-how means using the tools available: "the vessel for how you're doing what you're doing," the practical thing to start from the ground up. Right now that means mostly AI tools; he suggests trying Claude, ChatGPT, Claude Code, Manus and others. The passage then becomes a promotion for Eden, his own product: a drive that handles busy work so that you can focus on creative work, where you store files, footage and videos, paste social links to be transcribed, and ask an agent, for example, to pull all of his YouTube videos into a research document, with "projects" for writing a newsletter with sources (comparable, he says, to NotebookLM, but all in one place). His claimed differentiator is that other tools lack the drive foundation needed for team sharing, compared with dragging, copying and pasting files or connecting local files or Google Drive to Claude.

**Source:** The Future Of Work (& The New High-Income Skill Stack).md (2026-02-12)

The promotional content is part of the source and is reported as such: it illustrates what Koe means by technical know-how in 2026, and it also shows that the author's recommendations at this level coincide with a product he sells. The structural point is independent of the promotion: technical know-how is placed last because it is the most changeable and the most dependent on the levels above. Tools change every few years; the human levels persist.

Placing the hierarchy beside the earlier stacks shows what it absorbs. The evergreen communicative skills (writing, speaking, marketing, sales) are contained in "persuasion." The results-oriented skills and technical know-how of 2023–2024 are contained in level 5. Entrepreneurship and agency, which in 2024 were one pair among three, with agency listed only as one of its competences, become level 1. And two levels appear that the earlier stacks lacked as named skills: taste and perspective, the capacity to judge what to make and the widening of mind beyond conformity that makes original judgment possible. The hierarchy completes the movement that the March 2024 hinge sentence announced ("the skills are the result and balance of those traits"): the traits now sit inside the stack, at its top.

Two qualifications from later in 2026 should be read alongside it. In June 2026, as Section 35.1 showed, Koe called "high agency" a buzzword and said that agency is "not the only one thing," listing five ingredients (agency, taste, persuasion, persistence and iteration) that cannot be learned from a video but only by doing one's own thing. The five ingredients overlap with the hierarchy (agency, taste and persuasion appear in both) but replace perspective and technical know-how with persistence and iteration, and they are presented as a list rather than an ordered hierarchy. The corpus does not say whether the five ingredients replace the hierarchy or complement it; read together, the hierarchy says what to develop and in which order, and the ingredients say what sustains the development over time. And in July 2026, Koe began to call "human nature" the meta-skill that never goes out of fashion, a further abstraction whose development belongs to Chapter 32.

#### Two pillars of becoming futureproof

In a January 2026 video, "How I'd build a one-person business (if I started over in 2026)," Koe states the aim of his whole brand in a form that organizes this chapter and the book. His goal is to help you become **futureproof**, and that rests on two pillars. Pillar one: how do you figure out what you want in life? That is psychology, philosophy and personal development. Pillar two: how do you succeed with that in today's world? That is skill acquisition, business, technology and now AI. Previously, he says, pillar two, especially for one person, was largely handled by a personal brand plus an information product or coaching ("kind of the same thing, just one is one-on-one, the other is mass scale"), and the information product could evolve by levels: a simple ebook, then a course, then a cohort, then a community.

**Source:** How I'd build a one-person business (if I started over in 2026).md (2026-01-03)

The two pillars correspond to the two halves of this book: Parts I–IV and XIV address the first (what one wants, who one is), Parts V–XII the second (how to achieve it in the present world). Agency sits at the junction. It is the capacity that turns the answer to the first question into action in the world of the second. The remark that pillar two was "previously" handled by personal brand plus information product signals that, in 2026, Koe sees the second pillar changing under AI, which is the subject of Chapter 36.

#### How the stack changed, and what stayed constant

The following table summarizes the successive versions reconstructed in this section.

| Date | Name | Components | What it adds |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jan 2023 | $1M skill stack | Evergreen skills (message, medium, result-oriented skill) + personal interests + direct experience + internet → "you," irreplaceable | Stacking as layers: profitability, individuality, nuance |
| Feb 2023 | Digital Renaissance graphic | Modern skills + evergreen skills (marketing, sales, writing, speaking) + life experience + personal interests → profitable problem → irreplaceable solution | A target (the profitable problem); evergreen redefined as psychology-based communication |
| Aug–Dec 2023 | Meta skills | Code and content; under them results-oriented skills, evergreen skills, personal interests | "Code is the vessel for content"; meta skills as umbrella for skills that change every ten years |
| Mar–May 2024 | Future-proof skill stack | Marketing and sales; writing and thinking; entrepreneurship (with agency as one competence); plus technical know-how; or five steps (entrepreneur, distribution, write, sell, build) | Adapted from Eriksen; skills as "the result and balance" of internal traits |
| Jul 2024 | Persistent principles | Writing, speaking, persuasion, entrepreneurship, creativity, applied to changing technology | The criterion of persistence ("since the first two humans") |
| Sep 2024 | Micro skill stack | Writing + sales = persuasion | Minimum viable stack for traffic and product |
| Feb 2025 | Medium and message | Writing and speaking (medium); psychology, marketing, sales, persuasion (message) | Sorting communicative skills by function |
| Aug 2025 | Three superpowers | Learning, persuasion, execution | Capacities defined by function, not by career or tool |
| Feb 2026 | Post-AI skill hierarchy | Agency → taste → perspective → persuasion → technical know-how | Ordered hierarchy of human skills; agency at the top |
| Jun 2026 | Five ingredients | Agency, taste, persuasion, persistence, iteration | Learned only by doing one's own thing |

Koe gives reasons for the changes at different moments. In 2024 he explained that skills are "the result and balance" of traits; in the same year he argued that persistent principles outlast changing technologies, and that AI takes over the technical layer, which changes every few years; in 2026 he argued that one is no longer preparing for a specific career. The change is best described as a refinement: the emphasis moves from external, market-oriented skills to traits and judgment not tied to any career. The two kinds of list can coexist. The earlier stacks say what to learn; the later hierarchy says which capacities make it possible to learn and deploy it, and it explicitly contains the earlier evergreen skills (in persuasion) and the results-oriented skills (in technical know-how).

Several things remain constant across all versions. First, the stack is always combined with personal interests or perspective, the element that makes each person's version different and connects the stack to Chapter 19. Second, communication with humans through writing, speech and persuasion appears in every version, and it is always ranked above the technical layer. Third, the technical layer is always described as changeable, the "vessel" that must be relearned as the landscape shifts. Fourth, from 2024 onward, the stack is always subordinated to the person who deploys it: traits before skills, vision before viability. The 2026 hierarchy is the formal expression of that fourth constant. Agency, which this chapter began by defining as the refusal to let society set one's direction, ends at the top of the list of what to learn, because without it the rest of the list would be learned for someone else's purposes.

### Exercises

1. **Mapping your own conformity.** Koe argues that whatever your survival depends on, material or conceptual, becomes a domain of low agency. List the three domains of your life in which you depend most on someone else's approval or income (a job, a group, a belief system, a platform). For each, distinguish what you do as *mechanical conformity* from what you do as *conformity used as a tool* for a goal you chose. What evidence would tell you which category a given behavior belongs to?

2. **Easy, impossible, hard.** Write down five goals you have abandoned or never started. Classify each using Eriksen's definition of "impossible" (you do not know how to close the distance), then using Koe's October 2025 definition ("outside the laws of physics"), and finally using his December 2025 version ("only impossible right now," until a series of difficult goals makes it possible). How many move from impossible to hard when you switch definitions? For the goals that remain impossible under the December version, what series of difficult goals would bring them within reach? For one of them, design a sequence of steps in the manner of Eriksen's weight plates, each only slightly beyond your present capacity, and identify the first step you could take this week.

3. **Acting versus iterating.** Koe redefines agency from "the ability to act without permission" to "the ability to iterate without permission." Choose a project you started and quit. Reconstruct the moment you stopped: what failed, how you interpreted the failure, and what "comforting conformity" you returned to. Then explain what a single iteration (reflect, adjust, retry) would have looked like at that moment. Does the redefinition capture something the original definition missed, or does it only add a demand?

4. **Weighing the intelligence debate.** Eriksen holds that IQ-type intelligence is biological and fixed while agency can be taught; Koe defines intelligence more broadly and, in December 2025, restores it as one of three ingredients of success alongside agency and opportunity. Construct the strongest version of each position, identify which disagreement is about facts and which is about definitions, and explain what practical difference it would make, for how you raise a child or train yourself, to adopt one view rather than the other.

5. **Questioning "nobody is coming to save you."** The principle that you must take responsibility for "digging yourself out of the hole," and the catastrophe-cycle argument about people who are broke, both locate the decisive variable in the individual. Identify a situation in which this framing is useful and one in which it would mislead a person or overlook something important. Which features of the situation make the difference? Does Koe's own three-ingredient formula (agency, opportunity, intelligence) help you draw the line?

6. **Opening the aperture.** Apply Sahil Bloom's method to one ordinary day. On a blank sheet, list every point of friction you notice in your own life and in the lives of people around you, without proposing any solution, until you have at least fifteen. Then choose the one that seems most solvable and describe its "kink in the hose," the single limiting factor. Finally, consider whether your solution could be passed on to others, and in what form.

7. **Auditing your skill stack.** Take the 2026 hierarchy (agency → taste → perspective → persuasion → technical know-how) and the 2024 future-proof stack (marketing and sales; writing and thinking; entrepreneurship). For each level or pair, assess where you stand and what evidence supports your assessment. Then identify where your current learning effort actually goes. Are you, in Koe's phrase, choosing skills by "the viability of the skill, not the vision"? Defend or revise the allocation.

8. **Is the creator path a dogma?** Koe asks himself whether "become a creator" has become a dogma, and answers that "anyone ambitious can." Write the objection in its strongest form, using Koe's own criticism of business ideologies and copied models, and then the best reply available from this chapter (the sovereignty triad, the value-creator path, the argument from *Purpose and Profit*). Under what conditions, for what kind of person or at what moment, would the creator path stop being the best application of agency?

## Chapter 36 — The Economy of the Individual in the Age of AI

Chapter 34 treated money as a unit of value and argued that wealth comes from leverage, not from hours. Chapter 35 argued that agency, not intelligence, is the bottleneck, and that the individual who iterates without permission becomes hard to replace. Both chapters assumed a particular world: one in which a single person, with an internet connection and a few skills, can reach an audience, sell a product and live from the value they create. This chapter examines that world directly. It is the place where Koe's system meets its historical moment. His claim is that the economy is reorganizing around the individual, that artificial intelligence accelerates the reorganization, and that the one-person business, the personal brand and the education product are responses to a structural shift rather than fashions.

The chapter has six steps. Section 36.1 presents the thesis of a transfer of power from institutions to individuals, together with the signals, figures and predictions Koe uses to frame its urgency, and the framework of three layers (internet, social media, AI) and three "superpowers" that he built in 2025. Section 36.2 explains what he means by the "creator economy," why he regards creators as a decentralized education system that replaces a school system unable to keep up, and why he says that every business is now a media business. Section 36.3 shows what kind of work AI replaces first: replicable, formulaic, entry-level work, the work of "technicians" rather than "creators." Section 36.4 turns to what AI cannot do on its own: it lacks direction, executive function and vision, so the decisive distinction becomes the one between "doers" and "directors." Section 36.5 gathers Koe's practical teaching on using AI well: why its output depends on your skill, why most people use it like a slot machine, how to become "AI-first," how to automate yourself out of work, and what he thinks of agents and "vibe coding." Section 36.6 closes with what he calls the "meaning economy": the thesis that machines will take over utility, that humans will be paid for meaning, and that AI threatens meaning as much as it threatens jobs.

Three features of the corpus shape how this subject is presented here. First, most of Koe's statements on it come from videos published between 2023 and 2026, a period in which Koe's mood about AI changed visibly: from "I only see good" in automation (2023), to being "pretty worried" (March 2024), to declaring himself "indifferent" to the forecasts (August 2025) and admitting that the change would "probably not" be "as drastic as many people made it out to seem, myself included" (September 2025). These shifts are marked where they matter. Second, Koe supports his urgency with many figures that he does not source, and some of them do not agree with each other; the chapter reports them as he gives them and says so. Third, a considerable part of the relevant ideas comes from third parties (Sam Altman, David Patterson, the CEOs of Fiverr and Shopify, Balaji Srinivasan, Naval Ravikant, Dickie Bush, Devon Eriksen, an anonymous writer called Signal, David Shapiro), and the chapter keeps their contributions separate from Koe's own adaptations.

### 36.1 The Transfer of Power to the Individual

#### The context of disruption: signals, figures and predictions

Koe usually opens his videos on the future of work with a burst of signals. They are not the argument itself; they are the atmosphere in which he wants the argument to be heard. Reading them together shows both the kind of evidence he relies on and the conclusion he draws from it, which is almost always the same.

In "The Future Of Work (Avoid Learning These Skills)" (July 2024), he begins with layoffs. In 2022 Elon Musk acquired Twitter for $44 billion and soon fired 80% of its staff, "upward of 6,000 people," and headlines are "flooded" with layoffs that leave people worried they are "next on The Chopping Block." He adds that freelance work "has increased from 36% of the workforce to 46.6% since 2020," that the creator economy "is projected to double from 250 billion to 480 billion by 2028," and that, according to his own research, some prominent figures predict artificial general intelligence "by the end of this year," while others say it may take "up to 2 years because costs are increasing and development is slowing down." He names no sources for these statistics. What worries people, he says, is concrete: their skills are becoming outdated, and their means of survival, their family's lifestyle and their ability to find new work are on the line. His conclusion does not depend on which forecast is right: whether we live to 500 or have robots doing chores in four months or ten years, "the only solution is to take matters into your own hands that's what you should have been doing in the first place." **Source:** The Future Of Work (Avoid Learning These Skills).md.

In "The Future Of Work (How To Become AI-First)" (May 2025), the signals come from third parties. A post on X by David Patterson claimed that the top AI model is already smarter than 85% of humans and will be smarter than 99.9% by the end of 2026, "and you think you will still have a job?"; Elon Musk replied "roughly correct." The CEO of Fiverr (transcribed as "Micah Kaufman") sent his team an email with three points: the "unpleasant truth" that AI is coming for your job, his job and every job; the prediction that "easy tasks will no longer exist. Hard tasks will become the new easy and impossible tasks will become hard"; and the instruction to scream into a pillow, pick yourself up and become future-proof. The CEO of Shopify emailed his staff that everyone should become AI-first, and an article reported that Duolingo was going AI-first and replacing contractors with AI. Koe acknowledges that such signals frighten people who do not know which skills, careers or jobs will remain. He nevertheless says that "this is one of the most incredible times to be alive": the task is to find the opportunity and take advantage of it. **Source:** The Future Of Work (How To Become AI-First).md.

A year earlier his tone was different. In "The Future-Proof Skill Stack" (March 2024) he admits to being "pretty worried," deep in "the AI and AGI rabbit hole," and lists the questions on his mind: what can humans do that machines can't; what will the future of work look like; which jobs, if any, will persist over the next twenty years; and what can we do to secure an above-average future. He singles out one worry that he thinks most people share: "we don't know what to teach children because we don't know what will be relevant in 20 years." **Source:** The Future-Proof Skill Stack (How Average People Become Millionaires).md.

The same worry appears in an interview clip that Koe inserted into his July 2024 video. An interviewer recalls that "we told our kids to learn Russian in the '80s Japanese in the '90s Chinese probably in the 2000s and then engineering," and asks someone described as being "on the board of OpenAI" (Mustafa Suleyman, who "runs AI for Microsoft," is also mentioned) what he would tell a grandchild to study. The answer: "I would be telling my grandchild not to go study coding... it was only 15 years ago that everybody was supposed to learn how to code." The speaker compares coding with skills the world stopped requiring of individuals: his father told him he had to learn to fix a car when he got his driver's license, but he never told his own children that, because "the world kind of figured out how to do it"; just as nobody needs a slide rule or to calculate a square root on paper, "coding is going to be like that." The transcript does not clearly identify the speakers, so the attribution is uncertain. Koe uses the clip as evidence that specific skills become obsolete; it matters later in the chapter (Section 36.2) because his own position on learning to code oscillates. **Source:** The Future Of Work (Avoid Learning These Skills).md.

Alongside the warnings, Koe offers predictions in favor of the creator. In December 2023 he cites the projection that the creator economy will grow from $250 billion to $480 billion "over the next 5 years," admits that he is "somewhat biased" because the creator economy is part of his identity, and says he "only see[s] that increasing exponentially." He imagines a world in which everyone is a creator, employers hire creators, creators work under other creators to gain experience, and creators are self-sufficient through products that solve real problems they have experienced. **Source:** How Intelligent Creators Will Make Money In 2024 (The Build Teach Earn Method).md. In 2022 he offered, as a "fun fact," that 60% of future jobs have not yet been created, citing "marijuana therapists" and "twitter ghost writers" as examples of jobs that did not exist before and noting that creators are creating their own; the creator economy as the future, he said, is "a big theory and philosophy" of his. **Source:** Stop Trying To Be Unique... Do This Instead.md. In 2023 he went further: being a creator, doing your life's work, "is going to be for I believe 80 percent of the population over the coming 50 years." **Source:** The 4 Hour Workday (How Creatives Work Less & Earn More).md.

The most revealing of these predictions concerns freelancing, because Koe gives a mechanism for it. In April 2023 he said that 36% of the workforce are freelancers and that, given AI and automation, he "genuinely" believes the figure will "skyrocket to 90 percent plus." He labels it himself: "I like making delusional predictions." The mechanism is economic: companies will realize that they can pay one freelancer $1,500 as one client for the same work for which they pay a full-time in-house salary, and freelancers can earn more by taking on several clients. "Everyone will be a freelancer because the state of work will demand it," until they decide to evolve into a creator: "everyone will be a freelancer until they decide they want to evolve into a Creator." **Source:** The Micro Education Business Model (How To Monetize Your Knowledge).md.

Two further data points complete the picture. In a 2026 video Koe states that intangible digital assets, which do not appear on a company's balance sheet, represent 90% of the value of the S&P 500; he again gives no source. He uses the claim to argue for building digital assets, and immediately qualifies it: Kim Kardashian, Taylor Swift, Ryan Reynolds, MrBeast and Elon Musk have massive audiences and brands, but you probably do not want that kind of fame, "and that's perfectly fine because you don't need millions of followers to make this work." **Source:** The Writing System That Saved My Brain (Learn Faster & Think Clearly).md. And in a 2025 video he plays a short clip of someone whose name is garbled in the transcript, saying: "I would focus on the content creator side of things because I believe that's where the puck is going. That's a much more important shift in how we all consume information and content and are entertained." The speaker cannot be identified from the transcript. **Source:** How To Thrive With Multiple Interests.md.

The figures are easier to evaluate when placed side by side.

| Claim | Date stated | Source given | Koe's own framing |
|---|---|---|---|
| 36% of the workforce are freelancers; will rise to 90%+ | April 2023 | None | "I like making delusional predictions" |
| Freelance work rose from 36% to 46.6% "since 2020" | July 2024 | None | Context of layoffs |
| Creator economy: $250 billion to $480 billion (in five years / by 2028) | December 2023; July 2024 | None | "I'm somewhat biased" |
| 60% of future jobs not yet created | May 2022 | None | "Fun fact" |
| 80% of the population doing creative life's work within 50 years | June 2023 | None | "I believe" |
| AI smarter than 85% of humans, 99.9% by end of 2026 | May 2025 | David Patterson's post, Musk's reply | Third-party signal |
| Intangible assets are 90% of S&P 500 value | July 2026 | None | Argument for digital assets |

The table makes one inconsistency visible. The same 36% figure appears in 2023 as the current share of freelancers and in 2024 as the 2020 baseline from which the share grew to 46.6%. Koe does not reconcile the two. Elsewhere in the corpus he also cites "a projected 62% of jobs being threatened by Automation," again without a source. None of these numbers should be read as established fact; they are rhetorical supports for a conclusion he reaches on other grounds. That conclusion, repeated across years, is that the individual must take responsibility for their own future, because nobody else will secure it for them.

#### "About 36 months": from worry to indifference

The video that gives this chapter its frame is "You Have About 36 Months To Make It" (August 2025). Its title repeats a claim that was circulating online, and Koe is careful to say that he neither endorses nor rejects it. The circulating claims were that AI will keep replacing jobs; that money as we know it will change or cease to exist, because millions of artificial superintelligences will execute tasks beyond human comprehension; and that crypto is seeing its last great gains because it is being regulated and adopted and will become more like stocks. Koe says these are not his opinions, that he is "indifferent" to them and expects most of them to be wrong. He reframes the claim instead: "you have about 36 months until the definition of making it changes drastically." Whether the horizon is 24 months or ten years, the change is "still probably happening." His stated intention is to provide a perspective from which to notice opportunities in a future that is arriving fast. **Source:** You Have About 36 Months To Make It.md.

"Making it" is an ordinary phrase used here with a specific sense: not success in the abstract, but the standard by which success is measured at a given time. Koe's point is that the standard itself is moving. What counted as making it under the old arrangement (a stable job, a degree, a career ladder) may not count under the new one.

The reframing also marks a change in Koe's attitude. In 2023 he said he saw only good in automation; in March 2024 he was "pretty worried"; in August 2025 he was "indifferent" to the forecasts; a month later he said that the future of AI was "probably not going to be as drastic as many people made it out to seem, myself included." This is an explicit self-correction of his own dramatism, though he does not explain what changed his mind beyond the general uncertainty. What does not change is the practical conclusion. The urgency to prepare survives the downward revision of the expected magnitude, because the preparation he recommends (taking responsibility for your own learning, audience and income) is the one he was recommending before AI entered the picture.

#### Sam Altman's premise and the three layers of power transfer

In the same 2025 video Koe sets the scene with a quote he calls famous, from Sam Altman: "The amount of power that an individual has is vastly more now than it has been at any time in the past." The quote is Altman's; the explanation of how that power was transferred is Koe's own. **Source:** You Have About 36 Months To Make It.md.

He describes three successive layers, each of which moved power away from a particular kind of institution.

| Layer | What it gave the individual | From whom power was transferred |
|---|---|---|
| The internet | Access to any and all knowledge | Schools and institutions |
| Social media | Leverage to attract your own audience | Employers, publishers, centralized media, record labels |
| AI | The ability to create, automate and outsource almost anything | Traditional gatekeepers and intermediaries |

The first layer removed the institutions' monopoly on knowledge. The second removed their monopoly on distribution: people can now "learn, build and earn without dependence on someone else's authority." The third removes much of their monopoly on execution: "people will soon be able to operate at the level of large teams with a fraction of the manpower." Koe qualifies the claim himself: it is "not true for all situations, but... largely true." He adds a generational observation. Gen Z, and the "zillennials" born roughly between 1995 and 2000 (his own cohort), are digital-first; Gen Z's lives are both substantially better and substantially worse than those of earlier generations, because they have the tools but have not learned to negate the worst of them. **Source:** You Have About 36 Months To Make It.md.

The three-layer framework is the formalization of an argument Koe had been making for years without the third layer. In 2022, in "Learn This Skill If You Want To Thrive In The Next 10 Years," he was amazed that people did not see the power of modern tools: building a membership platform for a course or community used to take a team of web developers, and now there is a website where you can build one in "less than maybe 10 to 60 minutes." He deliberately refused to name the tool ("go research, you have Google") and asked: "how does this not fuel you with like the most insane energy," since modern internet tools let you do whatever you want. **Source:** Learn This Skill If You Want To Thrive In The Next 10 Years.md. In March 2024 he condensed the idea into a formula: "To build you need technical know-how: you must either learn to code or use the technology available to you." "What used to take 10 people now takes one; what used to take 10 hours now takes one; what used to take $10 now takes one." You live in "a beautiful time where humans can leverage technology to build what they want": website builders, email marketing software, AI, social media, course builders. "It is your job to create and distribute value by learning and building on the internet." **Source:** Working Hard Won't Make You Rich (Do This Instead).md.

The same month, he stated the political side of the argument as a list of gatekeepers that are no longer necessary: "You no longer need startup Capital to start a business you no longer need a job board to find a career you no longer need a publisher to launch a book you no longer need a record label to make music you no longer need a formal education to become an expert you no longer need religious institutions to feed you meaning." His conclusion: "The centralized authority over learning meaning and earning is only a thing for those who are still asleep." All you need is "an internet connection social media account and the courage to teach fail improve and pursue." **Source:** If Your Life Is Spiraling Out Of Control, Here's The Solution To Feeling Lost.md.

The word "asleep" ties this passage to the diagnosis of Part I: the person who still depends on centralized authority for learning, meaning and earning is the person who has not yet become aware of the default path (Chapters 1 and 2). The list also anticipates the whole structure of this chapter. Learning without a formal education is the subject of Section 36.2; earning without a job or capital is the subject of Sections 36.3 to 36.5; and finding meaning without religious institutions is the subject of Section 36.6. Between 2022 and 2024 the argument rested on the internet plus no-code tools; in 2025 AI was added as a third layer that extends the same movement.

#### The three superpowers

Having described how power moved, Koe asks what an individual needs in order to use it. Whether or not you have taken advantage of the three layers, he says, you have three "superpowers" with which to take control of your future:

1. **Learning**: the ability to adapt and to figure out which actions to take in order to get specific results.
2. **Persuasion**: the ability to build trust and attract people to a mutually beneficial vision or narrative. He insists on the qualification: "We're talking about persuasion and mutual benefit, not manipulation."
3. **Execution**: the ability to turn ideas into reality through automation, creation and delegation.

**Source:** You Have About 36 Months To Make It.md.

Each superpower corresponds to one of the layers. The internet made learning possible without institutions; social media made persuasion possible without intermediaries; AI made execution possible without a team. The list is also a compressed version of the skill stacks that Koe had proposed since 2023 (writing, marketing and sales, entrepreneurship, technical know-how), and of the post-AI hierarchy he would propose in 2026 (agency, taste, perspective, persuasion, technical know-how). Section 35.5 treats those stacks in detail. The direction of the change is from market skills toward human traits and judgment: the superpowers describe capacities, not job descriptions.

#### The condition: self-education and self-reliance

The transfer of power does not benefit everyone equally, and Koe names its condition. In "Become A Digital Renaissance Man (And Join The New Rich)" (February 2023), the first aspect of what he calls "the new rich" is technology: "the internet has democratized wealth generation for the self-educated and self-reliant." The internet lets you learn skills that schools will not teach, often precisely the skills that make you irreplaceable. The logic is comparative. If schools mass-educate people, those people are replaceable, because the next generation passes through the same curriculum and competes for the same positions. The alternative is to learn "in a non-linear way via curiosity and through the internet in alignment with your personal goals," not goals assigned by school. That is how you forge your own path: by acquiring skills in alignment with your own hierarchy of goals (the structure developed in Chapter 8). Koe's practical advice follows: invest time, and money if you have it, in education that will not lead to a static salary; use that education to get results; and then use the results as leverage to make more money and free up time. **Source:** Become A Digital Renaissance Man (And Join The New Rich).md.

This condition is what turns the thesis of power transfer into a demand. The power is available, but only to those who take responsibility for their own education. The same technology that frees the self-educated individual also exposes the person who waits to be taught, which is why Koe's conclusion to every list of disruptive signals is the same: take matters into your own hands. The next section examines where, in his view, that education now comes from.

### 36.2 The Creator Economy and the New School

#### What Koe means by "creator economy"

"Creator economy" is a common term in the technology press, where it usually refers to the market of platforms, sponsorships and tools that serve people who publish content. Koe uses it in a broader and more normative sense. He gives several definitions, each from a different angle.

The first is social. In "Solve Your Own Problems And Sell The Solution (Your Niche Is You)" (April 2023) he opens with: "the Creator economy is a decentralized society where people can learn teach and create a better life for themselves," a realization he says he made over the past decade. Later in the same video he adds the community angle: "The Creator economy is where you find people with shared goals, cur[ate] your own Community, provide value to that community and get paid for your contributions." **Source:** Solve Your Own Problems And Sell The Solution (Your Niche Is You).md. The second is economic. In June 2023 he describes it as composed of individuals distributing value in the form of content and products: they educate their audience on the skills and interests that help them actualize their goals, and their products or services are meant to generate results and move people faster toward those goals. **Source:** The One Person Business Model 2.0 (Turn Yourself Into A Business).md.

Read together, the definitions describe a cycle. Content educates people toward goals they already have; products accelerate the results; the community forms around shared goals; and payment is the return for a contribution. This is the value-for-value exchange of Chapter 34 organized as a society rather than as a single transaction.

The word "creator" in the phrase also has a specific meaning. In 2025 Koe calls creators "decentralized teachers," "the new school system on the internet," and then clarifies: "Creators, not content creators. Just people who create their life are those who forge new paths and pass down the esoteric information that allow you to take advantage of new opportunities." **Source:** A Full Guide To Making Your First Profitable Product (Beginners, Take Notes).md. A creator, in his usage, is defined by the life they make, not by the format they publish in. Publishing is how a created life is passed on.

He also distinguishes the creator economy from what he calls the "influencer economy." In his 2023 conversation with Dickie Bush, he explains that he labels it the creator economy "because being a Creator implies growth." An influencer "could be static," and "the influencer economy can definitely get saturated"; the creator economy "assumes that you're consistently trying to make progress in life" individually, and the community you bring up with you evolves too. **Source:** Dan Koe & Dickie Bush On One-Person Businesses, Creative Workflows, and Lifestyle Design.md. The distinction connects to Koe's claim, discussed in Section 27.6, that the creator economy cannot be saturated because each creator is an extension of a unique self, whereas an economy of static personalities competing for attention can be.

In a 2023 video built around the metaphor of life as a video game (Chapter 10), Koe maps the creator economy onto the game:

| Element of the game | Element of the creator economy |
|---|---|
| Virtual reality | The creator economy |
| Your character | Your personal brand |
| The game and its progression | Online business |
| A powerful tribe | Networking |
| How you make a living | Purposeful products |
| Marketing firepower that attracts those like you | The intrinsic philosophy you cultivate throughout your journey |

**Source:** Life Is A Video Game (You Can't Escape The Matrix).md. The mapping ends with a question rather than a description. You are already part of the creator economy, he says; the only question is which side you are on: whether you engage in a mutual exchange of value (product for money), or whether you drain attention, overload your mind and waste your creative ability by producing nothing in return for the value you take. Consumption without contribution is still participation, but on the losing side.

Koe's most idealized image is that of a "self-sufficient Utopia." In the April 2023 video he says that education is "only one aspect of the Creator economy but it is a very important one" and that he believes everyone should start with an education business, but that he sees the creator economy as something wider. He buys from individual creators: shoes, kitchenware, blue light glasses, apparel, coffee and supplements, fresh herbs, milk and meat. "All of these hold philosophies behind them." The kitchenware seller does it out of passion and because he does not want you buying plastics that damage your health; the blue light glasses are stylish but also prevent eye strain and help you sleep. **Source:** Solve Your Own Problems And Sell The Solution (Your Niche Is You).md. The image is of an economy in which almost every purchase is a vote for someone's philosophy. At the end of the same video he generalizes it into a principle: "The future belongs to people that pass down their valuable experiences to improve others lives. That's what all the best businesses do." He proposes a test anyone can run: "take a look at the next social media post you see from the lens of a Creator not a consumer and you can verify this for yourself." **Source:** Solve Your Own Problems And Sell The Solution (Your Niche Is You).md.

Why do creators sell knowledge rather than objects? In 2024 Koe offered an explanation based on commoditization. You follow creators for education and entertainment because what they say is new to you, and "ideas shape society." Creators earn an independent income by pursuing their interests: they solve problems in their own lives and sell the solution. Most of them sell knowledge because commoditized products are increasingly the norm: "we can order anything on Amazon." So "the only thing left to share is Unique Systems and processes that come from the life we experience," passed down "by documenting our mind on the internet." Productivity systems, psychology practices, meditations and business advice are examples. On business advice in particular, he notes that college professors probably do not own a business (unless they teach out of passion after getting rich), so creators are among the few people qualified to teach it. **Source:** The Age Of The Generalist (How To Earn A Living Doing What You Enjoy).md. This is the same logic that Section 33.5 develops as "systems are the new product."

Koe also answers the suspicion that everyone selling to creators is jumping on a bandwagon. "Creators are small businesses. It's a B2B business to business or C to C, creator to creator." Everyone sells to creators "because there's so frickin many," and the business-to-business and creator-to-creator markets are both huge: "You think everyone's just hopping on the bandwagon. No, it's because that's a massive market." His practical conclusion in that 2025 video is to build an education product first; otherwise you will waste a great deal of time "unless you have a lot of money and experience already." **Source:** A Full Guide To Making Your First Profitable Product (Beginners, Take Notes).md.

The strength of his conviction is clearest in a March 2024 statement: "I can tell you with confidence through my own experience that the Creator economy is the most true model that you can follow while doing this especially considering human nature post- labor economics and the future of work." "This" refers to building, teaching, selling and evolving a project around your obsession. **Source:** If Your Life Is Spiraling Out Of Control, Here's The Solution To Feeling Lost.md. Two later developments complicate this confidence. In January 2026 Koe asked himself, "am I just like promoting this dogma?", and answered that "the more I break it down, the more it seems like the one true way"; he kept the thesis but acknowledged the objection that not everyone can do this, reformulating it as "anyone ambitious can." In the same period he moved from saying that the creator economy grows "exponentially" and cannot be saturated to admitting that models and tactics within it can "become saturated quite quickly" and that a "lower class" of the creator economy exists (Section 36.3). The two positions can coexist if the distinction is kept: the market of identities and interests may be unsaturable, while specific formats and business models within it saturate fast.

#### The Golden Age: where Koe's conviction comes from

Koe's belief in creators as teachers has a biographical origin, which he told in "The Death Of The Personal Brand (& The Future Of Creative Work)" (October 2024). As a teenager he was deeply into fitness and watched small creators on YouTube when the platform was first gaining popularity. He calls that period "the Golden Age of the creator economy," "a peak in authenticity where people were just picking up cameras to share their passions" and teach what they were learning. He names Matt Ogus and Chris Levado (spelled as transcribed) and others in the fitness world as people who strongly influenced his life.

The contrast he draws with his own situation at the time is specific. He was a kid who came home from school, played video games all day, cooked frozen burritos, drank five Dr Peppers and woke up early to maintain his Halo 3 rank so that a friend would not pass him. He had "massive ambitions" but no knowledge or awareness of how to make them real. The only plan he had was to become an anesthesiologist "because it paid a lot," since he had been told his whole life to go to college; that plan framed his perception and everything he absorbed. For a week his search history was universities, majors and top-paying degrees, because he did not want to spend eight to twelve years becoming an anesthesiologist. He says he "can't thank those creators enough" and hopes to be that person for others, which he names as a driving force behind his videos. **Source:** The Death Of The Personal Brand (& The Future Of Creative Work).md.

The story is a small-scale version of the whole thesis of this section. The school offered him one assigned goal (a high-paying degree); a handful of independent creators, teaching what they were passionate about, offered him a different model of how to live. It is an instance of the decentralized education system before he had a name for it.

#### Two modalities of education

Koe's central claim about education is that two systems now coexist. He stated it in December 2022 and repeated it, in nearly the same words, in a February 2024 compilation. The formal education system trains you into the employment system it is directly tied to. The creator economy consists of people who put out free information after forging a new path and teach you how to do it yourself. If you want a career of independence, you may not find it in formal education, nor, he adds, entirely for free online. But if you think critically and find a person worth investing in, someone whose course teaches what they do, what they discovered as a better way, or a new career path created by the internet, that is a good route. "Those are the modes of education that are going to teach you how to do your own thing rather than how to do someone else's thing." He concedes that some courses get a bad reputation, while many course buyers know incredible ones that changed their lives. **Source:** You Have A $100,000 Product In Your Head (One Person Business Series).md; The One-Person Business Model (How To Productize Yourself Full Guide).md.

In March 2023 he presented the contrast as a diagram (his "visual of the week"). The visual itself was on screen; the transcript allows the two paths to be reconstructed as lists, but not their exact layout.

| The school system path | The creator economy path |
|---|---|
| Prefers conformity | The student pursues their curiosities |
| Memorization | Finds a community |
| Standardized tests | Learns relevant skills you can actually make money with |
| Convergent thinking | Starts a real-world project without needing credentials: "there's no Gatekeepers on the internet" |
| Becoming a cog in the machine | Acquires the specific knowledge necessary along the way |
| Trained into the societal system, the social fabric, as an employee | Becomes an entrepreneur |

**Source:** The Future Of One-Person Businesses (Take Advantage Now).md.

A few months later he described what the creator path allows the individual to do. In the "creator society," passionate creators research topics they love and distribute lessons through their own lens to people who resonate with it. This lets individuals pursue their curiosity; find the teachers or creators they learn best from; treat learning as part of life rather than an obligation; learn modern skills to adapt quickly to a changing environment; find specific knowledge that contributes to self-generated rather than assigned goals; and prioritize entrepreneurship as "the only logical end goal for those that want more out of life." "The new school system is internet content and courses"; none of it is labeled as school, it is simply part of virtual life. **Source:** The One Person Business Model 2.0 (Turn Yourself Into A Business).md. The distinction between self-generated and assigned goals is the one Chapter 2 and Chapter 8 develop: the school assigns goals, and the creator economy is where a person learns to choose their own.

In 2022 Koe had already framed this as a job description for anyone who publishes. He believes that the one-person business, personal branding and the creator economy are new "for a reason": society has advanced to the point where "everyone and their mother" can have their own business, and as people "we are creators." He promotes being a "value Creator," whose "job is to educate and entertain better than the schools can," because schools cannot keep up and cannot cover every aspect of reality the way everyone researching their own unique interests can. Synthesizing what you learn into articulate educational content "is just the best way to learn," a claim he says he can make only because he has done it. **Source:** Learn New Skills FAST (How I Remember Everything I Learn).md.

#### Why school cannot teach this

Koe's critique of school is treated at length in Chapter 2. What matters here is the specific argument for why formal institutions cannot teach the skills of the individual economy. He makes it in several layers.

The first layer is structural. In "The One-Person Business Model (How To Productize Yourself)" (October 2022, re-edited in the February 2024 compilation), he argues that the internet makes a new business path possible. Because social media and the internet are accessible and cheap to start with, you do not have to pay to post something online and ask for money in exchange for a valuable service (freelancing, consulting or a beginner-level coaching call) that you then build up as you gain experience. It is "a new path," a new business model created by technological advancement. People consider it taboo because they "aren't in the game" and because it has not been around long, but "it's here to stay." He then generalizes: "every single person on YouTube that is a value Creator rather than an entertainment Creator is an educator," whether or not they label themselves that way; and he counts himself as one. This is a new method of education that college and formal institutions cannot keep up with, because their curriculum cannot be updated to match something that does not lead to a job. The school system, corporations and government are tied together, "training into one another." The internet threatens that arrangement by giving the individual the power to make a creative income on their own, and the education around that income, delivered by individuals on social media and course platforms, is something the school system cannot follow. He mentions "some statistic about the education industry increasing by XYZ" without giving a figure. His conclusion: it is completely in your hands. **Source:** The One-Person Business Model (How To Productize Yourself).md; The One-Person Business Model (How To Productize Yourself Full Guide).md.

The second layer is temporal. In April 2023 he observed that freelancing and online business offer endless options (niches, skills to stack, outreach strategies, content tactics), and that every step that feels like progress is met by another roadblock, producing "overwhelming uncertainty" just as you leave the previous phase, "because it's all so new." The online business world has been prevalent "for maybe a decade," which he calls "insane on the grand Scale of the Universe." That is why "College isn't going to teach you any of this right they can't catch up with a decade's worth of curriculum like that fast." **Source:** The Micro Education Business Model (How To Monetize Your Knowledge).md.
